Locke's Life: Principal Dates for this Volume
This table is planned to provide dates that should be serviceable to readers of the correspondence. It is not a chronological framework for Locke's life.
The principal difficulty in its compilation is that for many incidents in his life precise dates do not exist. Thus, if the mention is accurate, Locke was acquainted with Robert Boyle on 20 May 1660; there is nothing to show how much earlier the acquaintance was made. Unsatisfactory as many of them are, the dates are the best available.
In the dates a. (for ante) is to be taken to imply shortly before. In the dates for books when a precise date accompanies the word 'published' it is to be taken as the date of the earliest notice that the book had been, was, or was about to be, published, and not necessarily as the day of publication.
          
1700 	14 May. Locke attends almost all Board of Trade meetings until his resignation on 28 June. 
Late May? Coste's translation of the Essay published. 
21 October/1 November. Charles II of Spain dies. 
1701 	18 January. Peter King returned M.P. for Bere Alston (he continued to sit until 1714). 
Late May. Burridge's translation of the Essay published. 
5/16 September. James II dies. 
1702 	8 March. Queen Anne succeeds William III. 
4 May. Queen Anne declares war on France and Spain. 
5-6 May. Locke's last recorded visit to London. 
1703 	4 May. Locke's first extant letter to Anthony Collins.

Letters Nos. 2665-3286
1700
January
2665. George Anderson to Locke, 27 January 1700 (2926)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 22-3. I have failed to trace the writer outside the present correspondence.
Sir
That Paper concerning Comparative Theologie which you had long ago at Mrs Lockharts,†1 if it have not fall'n below your notice, I would be glad to know if (as I did then suspect) it be agreeable to that Sincere impartiality wherwith Religious concerns especially should be treated. I thought it so rationall an advance towards the regaining of our freedom and unhampering us from our formalities which have so long been our bussiness, and the directing us to the true substance of Religion; so just a detection of the more or less concern and Esteem that we ought to have for the different parts therof, as I was perswaded it would meet with your approbation, since I think I heard you sometimes express a like just distinction betwixt the Religion of the End and that of the means. My Inclinations would have moved me to ask your opinion of it, when I had the advantage of comming sometimes into your Company. but was asham'd to interrupt better converse by my litle Impertinencies.
I should not now force myselfe to this Rudeness if the Author were not like to stand in need of your advice and assistance. he hath had a Reputation fair enough in that University where he was Professor of Divinity, tho' he hath been now of a long time out of all Employment for no other reason than a steady adherence to that freedom of mind, and a scorning to be limited and confined to any compacted, and much less to what he judged erroneous Confessions of Faith.†2 A Crime that recommends!
He now designing to come into England to provide for that family which God hath given him, I think my selfe oblig'd for his sake to presume to ask of you who are so well able to give advice and direction to him how he may, with most freedom and least
― 2 ―
restraint, serve both himselfe and others in this Kingdom with that Learning and sincerity which he is master of and which will give sufficient evidence of themelves to all who shall know him.
May I beg it of you that you would be pleased to Let My Lady Marsham†1 know the esteem that I shall still preserve for her ingenious and obliging Qualities, and how sensibly I resent†2 that notice which her Ladyship in the Excess of her civility was pleas'd to take of me in some of her letters to Mrs Lockhart. All the return that I can make to her Ladyships and your own no less condescensions to me, is, to entreat you would believe I mean sincerely when I say that I am
Your much oblidged and most humble servant
GEORGE ANDERSONE
London January 27 1700
Address: For Mr Lock att Oats
Endorsed by Locke: G: Andersone 27 Jan. 99/00 Answered Feb. 19
2666. Dr. (later Sir) Thomas Molyneux to Locke, 29 January 1700 (2589)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 90-1. Probably forwarded by Burridge: p. 14.
Sir
last week I received Your oblidging Present of the fourth Edition of Your Essay concerning Humane Understanding:†3 for which Favour should I truly express my Thanks in proportion to the high Value I have for it, I am afraid I may run the hazard of being thought unsincere or extravagant: this I can say, that few of Your Readers gave a more full and early Approbation in their thoughts of that Work than I did; for in the Year 1689, as I remember, I chance first to light on't in a Booksellers shop in Chester,†4 and looking into it for an Houre or two, I was so surprised and delighted with the strength of its Reasoning, the Truth and Correctness of it's Observations, the Clearness of it's stile, and the Ingenuous Candor that runs thr'o it all; that scerce any Book I ever
― 3 ―
mett with gave me that real satisfaction and complacency of mind I found in this, and that long before I understood You were the Author of it; upon finding a Treasure so instructive, I soon communicated my Thoughts to my Brother, Who (as we agreed in our sentiments in most things) told me, he ne're was so much delighted with any Treatise of this Kind, and I must needs own, I never mett with any Discourse on so abstracted a subject, that did not growe tiersome in the reading besides it self, that ingages, informs and diverts in every Chapter. but I doupt not You have heard these Truths, and a great deale more said of your Excellent Essay by far abler Judges, so that I have no Reason to trouble You with them, only I shall beg leave to add, that the Remembrance of Your oblidging Conversation in Holland,†1 the Knowledge and Pleasure I have had from Your Writings, the Friendship You had for my Dear Brother, and the singular Favours and Civilitys You have been pleased to shew me, must ever engage me to subscribe myself
Worthy Sir
Your most truly Faithfull and Humble servant
T. MOLYNEUX
Dublin. Jan: 29th 1699/-700
Address: For John Locke Esqr at Mr Robert Pauletts opposite to the Plow in Little Lincolns Inn Fields London
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Molyneux 29 Jan 99/00

2668. Locke to Edward Clarke, 9 February 1700 (2667, 2680)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 137. Printed in Rand, pp. 552-3.
Oates 9 Feb 99/00
Dear Sir
Haveing soe lately writ to you I should not soe soon wast any of your pretious time with an other letter but that by the last post I received a letter from Dr Guenellon of Amsterdam. where to what he said formerly concerning your son John he now farther addes that at his arival he will receive him in his house, and will him self take care of placeing of him and what else concernes him.†1 I have here inclosed returned him your and my thanks, and desire you it may be sent away by the post to morrow.
Pray in your next send me word whether the business of the old East India Company be dead in your house or whether there is like to be any attacks upon the new one this session.†2 I am desired to enquire by some that would I think buy in the new company
A word too if you please what you are doeing and how the world goes, for we are here out of the world. My service to the Batchelor. I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
― 5 ―
I see Sir John Stanley named in a late Gazette Warden of the Mint, pray what then is Mr Newton?†1
Endorsed by Clarke: Mr. Lock That Dr. Guenellon will take Jack into his House, if I will send Him over etc: And to Know how the World Goes etc: Received the 12th. February 1699. Answered fully the 24th and sent Betty's Letter inclosed etc:

2670. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 12 February 1700 (2669, 2674)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 61-2.
Oates 12 Feb 99/00
Dear Cosin
Had I known I should have received a letter from you today I should not have troubled you with one on Friday.†2 But your long silence, (which when it would end I could not tell) put me in some pain. But you being well all is well. What the businesse of Next
― 6 ―
Tuesday is I doe not know.†1 You will doe me a kindnes to write it me that night for I know noething here and in the same letter pray let me know, for how much the Exchequer notes were sold. Mr Churchil writ me word that the money they were sold for was paid to you, but in his brothers absence not knowing how much was received for use due upon them he could not tell me the precise summ, which for the keeping my accounts right it is necessary for me to know. My Lady and all here give you their service I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
Address: For Peter King Esqr at Mr Potmans in the Middle Temple London
Postmark: FE 14
Endorsed by King: Mr Lock february 12. 1699.
2671. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 13 [February 1700] (2541, 2682)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 78-81. Month and year from Locke's endorsement.
I had troubled you before now but that I have been beyond the common pretence more then ordinary buisy in the affairs of my familly my Lord Forfar's concerne has not been the least care has lain upon me who has been drawn in to concerne himself in this Nationall adress so unluckilly set on foot in that poor countrey which as I have long been telling You is now in such a Flame that it is not easy to cast one thought that way.†2 my Brother†3 whom when You left the town was as I aprehended under a very dangerous mellancholly did soon discover the reason to be being more in love then he thought reasonable to own and tho that is an ill character for a lover, yet if he had not found a kind Mistress I don't kno where it might have ended. I was allways as I have told you timerous in his taking any speedy resolutions of settling as his circumstances stood and am still of opinion it might have been his advantage to have Endeavor'd the pushing his fortune some other way first. but
― 7 ―
he put it out of my power to be more then passive in the matter for finding me not leaning to the side of his inclination he made a short work and the first account I had of his positive resolution's was that he had Concluded the bussiness with the Yong Lady and I had nothing but Excuses from him and complements from her.
this being the case I have thought it my duty to make the best on't and am resolv'd to doe them all the service I can. the sister's has disagreed Extreamly the reasons are not fit to be in a letter. I reserve them for a conversation tete a tete. however she as lady's when they are angry are apt to doe vent's it in spight and is in the menagement of such as make it their bussiness to give them all the trouble imaginable. and this has cost me some pains and time to give 'em the best assistance I could. I hope now a little time it will be over and as to the advantage on my Brothers side it dos not apear Yet to be Enufe to have tempted any man without the assistance of an inclination since if there estate were sold when some debt is paid and an abatement for some land that is not worth above 16 years purchass, they will not make much more then 4000ll to Each of them. some say if twere taken good care of the rent might be rais'd: for it is certain it has been very ill menage'd. when things are settled so as my Brother medles with his bussiness in the country give me your opinion if he may trouble Sir Francis for his advice. It will be high time for me now to talk to you of things you're more concern'd in then this long story but you kno Women are allways full of what's upermost in their thoughts. besides you are accustome'd to allow my complaints and sometimes to pitty me which I find a reall plesure in. and now tho I have not inform'd you or my Dear Lady Mashame so often as you might have Expected Yet I have not ommitted any thing I thought might advance what you desire'd.†1 when Mr Johnston†2 came first to town upon talking with him I found him very shy. however I try'd a second and third time and am now fully convince'd that it proceeded from the ill aprehensions he had both of his own and the Bishop's†3 affairs. I suppose they have had their heads and heart's full, and the allarme they had at the begining of the winter is not yet off. I can't tell you at
― 8 ―
this distance the circumstances they both are under at present this winter has so unhing'd ev'ry body that there is but small hopes of doing any thing at present in our bussiness in which I may without flattery say the most concern'd has not more hearty wishes then my self. all things are now so much in the dark that one do's not kno where to aply. there has hapn'd some things come to my Ears that gives me to beleive tho you are at great distance from the broils we live in, Yet you are no more out of the War civill then Eclesiastick.†1 I can't doubt you'le be inform'd of what is proper for you to kno on your own subject from better hands then mine and shall leave to a meeting what perhaps you'le not think worth hearing.
Thus far of my letter was writ before I had to thank you for your last kindness to me in your's to my self and Brother, for which accept in few words many and hearty thanks. and tho no new favour Can more ingage me to my Dear son†2 yet Ev'ry new Expression of your kindness is a reall plesure to me. I thoughtt to have added more to this letter but Waiting for the news of the day has made it too late and I have that so imperfectly I can only send the inclos'd Vote.†3 Excuse my hast for the post Calls and to my Lady Masham to the next
Adieu
13th
Address: For Mr Lock [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Fr†a Cutts†a
Endorsed by Locke: M: Lockhart 13. Feb 99/00 Answered 19
2672. James Lockhart of Lee to Locke, 13 February 1700
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 1-2. For the writer see p. 6, n. 3.
London february 13th 1 699/700
Sir
I humbly thank yow for your most kind and obligeing Letter, which I am as unworthy of, as Unfitt to Answer. I must Own to yow
― 9 ―
freely, I am under the same Constraint in Writting, that I us'd to be in Speaking When I had the Honour, as well as the benefite to be in Your company. I humbly beg therefore Yow will accept of this, as a fitt Answer from Me, in return to yours, And that Yow will believe me to be in the greatest Sincerity, and with the most profound respect immaginable.
Sir
Your much obliged and most humble servant
JA: LOCKHART
I beg my humble Service to my Lady Marsham†1 and on her Ladyships†a account to all the family tho Unknown
my Wife returns Yow Her humble service
Address: For Mr Locke To be Left at Mr Jocelin's <a shop>keeper†b <in Bishops Starford>†b Hartford Shire
Endorsed by Locke: J: Lockhart. 13 Feb 99/00
2673. J.-B. Du Bos to Locke, 14/24 February [1700] (2612, 2748), with postscript by Nicolas Toinard (2644, 2693)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 234-5. Du Bos's letter is printed by G. Bonno in Revue de littérature comparée, xxiv (1950), 503-4. Year from Locke's endorsement and contents. Toinard answers no. 2644.
Le livre que je vous envoié monsieur est louvrage dun neveu de monsieur L'abbé Gendron qui a eté de vos amis.†2 il fait a present honneur a son oncle et a son maitre a qui monsieur Toinard dit quil en pouroit bien servir maintenant.
les flibustiers ont fait imprimer une relation de la prise de Carthagene ou il racontent les choses dune maniere tres differente de monsieur de Pointis. le livre est encore rare et cest ce qui m'empeche de vous en envoier un exemplaire.†3
L'abbé Boileau frere de Despreaux vient de publier un livre quil apelle Historia flagellantium in†c 12.†c il i fait voir que lusage de la
― 10 ―
discipline monastique est tres recent dans leglise et dangereux pour la santé quand lon l'aplique sur le dos: plus dangereux encore si lon se la donne sur le derriere pour les violentes tentations qui en provienent.†1 le livre de Meibomius†2 i est fort cité, aussi les moines ont ils fait leur possible, pour le faire defendre, mais leurs tentatives ont eté inutiles.
un anonime a donné sur Mezeray des reflexions critiques, mais elles ne valent point grand chose et il ne si agit presque que de stile.†3
un maitre a danser a concu que lon pouvoit noter les pas et les figures des danses come lon fait les tons et le mouvement dun air de Musique. il vient de publier son systeme quil apelle, choregraphie.†4 je suis sur les inventeurs dans les sentiments de monsieur Pascal et je les tiens estimables quelque peu de consequence que puissent estre les choses sur les quelles ils inventent.†5
un de mes amis qui travaille a la Marche du royaume ou a lhistoire de nostre frontiere souhaiteroit d'avoir comunication des titres que les Anglois enleverent autrefois de france lesquels se conservent a la tour. il ma prié de minformer si lon ne permetroit pas a un homme quil envoieroit expres en Angleterre de voir ces titres et d'en copier ce quil i trouveroit dhistorique utile a son dessein. jay cru monsieur que je ne pouvois pas mieux m'adresser qu'a vous qui estes des ami de Mylord Chancellier pour estre informe de la possibilité de la chose que lon souhaite.†6
trois ou quatres jeunes auteurs on travaillé dans le gout de La Bruiere et nous ont donné des livres d'apres le sien sur les caracteres, mais il sont touts fort inferieurs a l'original.†7
monsieur Toinard vous salue et vous souhaite autant de santé quil en a. il promet que cet esté ne se passera point sans que son livre se publie.
― 11 ―
un monsieur Andry medecin de Paris vient de publier une dissertation sur les vers des petits enfans.†1 je ne lai point encore lue.
un Jesuite nous a doné depuis un mois une relation des isles Marianes, ce sont les isles des Larrons aux quelles il done ce non parce que la feu reyne mere dEspagne Mariamne dAutriche i avoit fondé des missions. il i a peu de choses curieuses dans ce livre, excepté la decouverte de Nombre disles qui sont au sud de celles de Larrons. le reste nest que devotion et miracles.†2 a entendre l'autheur ces isles ne produisent rien qui soit propre pour le comerce et le seul zele de la maison de dieu i mene leurs peres, cependant lon voit par son livre quils envoient de temps en temps des vaisseaux chargé a Agua pulco.†3
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
DU BOS
A Paris le Mercredy 24 de febvrier.
[Toinard:]
Je fais travailler, monsieur, à quelque chose qui ne vous deplaira pas c'est à des etofes de laine de beuf cibola†4 aux deux tiers, et l'aine d'Angleterre au tiers. Si cela reüssit je vous en enverrai. Je vous remercie de la copie des letres dont vous m'avez parlé.†5 Je les avois avant q'iceles†a deça la mer passent en Angleterre, et j'ay eu dans le tems les reponses. Je collationerai neanmoins le tout, et vous en enverrai une note afin que si j'en ay que vous n'aiez pas je vous en fasse tenir une copie, et contra.
Je suis—
Endorsed by Locke: (i): f. 235v: Du Bos 27 Feb 99/00 Answered Mar. 15;
(ii): f. 234v: Du Bos.

2674. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 16 February 1700 (2670, 2676)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 63-4.
Oates 16 Feb 99/00
Dear Cosin
I thank you for your last good news. Is not £90 per annum considering taxes and all very scanty security for £1200 espetialy at 5 per Cent. But the reputation and honesty of the man is with me of great weight. But I must leave it all to you to doe as for yourself.
In your next pray let me know what was received for the Exchequer notes. And what Tally it is you have, on what fund and when like to be paid and what per Cent interest is allowed upon it. And whether it be a Tally that the Bank will discount at any time.
All here remember you. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
Address: For Peter King Esqr To be left at Mr Potmans in the Middle Temple London
Postmark: FE 19.
Endorsed by King: Mr Locke february 16. 1699
2675. Mrs. Frances St. John to Locke, 16 February [1700] (2551, 3140)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 56-7. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Febewary the 16
That part which friends bear in the Afflictions of others, as it's a great instance of their sinceer kindness for the person under the affliction, and upon that account extreemly oblidging, so allso a great allay to the trouble as my self has expeirenced in this laite tryall I have mett with, the loss of a Dear Friend having in it, many reflections, some of which allow of pleasure tho' intermixed grief, Freindship, being that most Valuable and desirable felicity in this life, and therfore will admitt of a pleasing thought in the very Idea of that person who was once so indearing, of whome I am now deprived;
And from the sence of such a loss do I desire to improve my time, by advantaging my self from the remaining friends I am yet
― 13 ―
so happy to injoy, and make a right use of their kindness, which has bin greatly testified to me upon this occation, and amongst many, your self, and not the least; for when I consider the relation others bore to my Dear Sister,†1 could not but occation them to share in the concern;
But that which Good Mr Lock has expresed for me upon this loss, must proceed from the goodness of his nature, which can be the on'ly motive to incline your taking so kinde a part with me; which kindness I would own with the greatest sence of thankfulness could I express it, and perticuler for that part of your letter which you seemingly designed to avoide, Reason and Religion being arguments allways usefull and nesesary upon such occations, be they never so offten repeatted there being so great a duty in considering how to make a right use of the Affliction sent, and which our nature requirs many helps and assistances for the performance of, therfore must with great thanks acknowlidg the kinde hand, from which I reseive, such cautions as will ingaig to thought, which must first be in order to practice, and for this; to your self I am greatly owing in thanks for your oblidging letter wherin was so much goodness and kindness as must allways ingaige me to be what I allredy am with great sincerity
Sir
Your humble servant and oblidged friend
FRANCES ST JOHN
Mr St John desires his humble servis to you, and I beg my own to you and the rest of our friends with you
Address: To Mr Lock [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: FE 17.
Endorsed by Locke: F: St John 16 Feb 99/00
2676. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 19 February 1700 (2674, 2678)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, f. 65.
Oates 19 Feb 99/00
Dear Cosin
I thank you for yours of the 17th particularly for the news in it.
― 14 ―
For some hereabouts (as I heard this morning) report with great joy that the Tuesdays debate was again resumed and caried quite contrary to Tuesday and there upon I know not what.†1 From what coloured coat it comes you may guesse. I now repete here the desires in my last (because you are soe soon goeing out of town) to know by your next what money you received of Mr Churchil for the Exchequer notes, what number and date the tally has you have for me, on what fund, what interest allowed on it and whether the Bank will discount it if there shall be occasion for the money. You will also I suppose leave that tally in some safe hands by whom you may turn it into money if you should have occasion for it in the country for a good mortgage there. I am sorry you goe soe soon for I intended to have troubled you with some memorandums about my tenants there before you went, and hoped to have finished Mr Lydes accounts by that time; but haveing mislaid a paper relateing to those matters which I found not till the later end of the last weeke I fear I shall not be able to ballance his accounts with respect to all my tenants and their arears time enough to send you what I shall have to say before you goe. Pray therefor in your next send me word whether you intend to goe to Sutton and when you think you shall be there, and how I should direct a letter that may come to you before you get thither I am
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
Endorsed by King: Mr Locke february 19. 1699
2677. Ezekiel Burridge to Locke, 21 February 1700 (2501)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, ff. 211-12.
Lond. Febr.21. 1699
Sir
Last night I receiv'd a letter from Dr Molyneux with the inclos'd for you,†2 and Mr Masham.
He has given me instructions about geting a monument made here for his brother, your good friend. I have herein inclos'd the
― 15 ―
Latin Inscription he sent me, he desireing me to submit it to your censure. There is one passage in it which I will have no hand in procureing the having it cut in marble. To me it seems much too long, and the Elogies more fulsom than usual. Having been before employ'd, since I came to town, to have such a remembrance made for Another friend, I had occasion to view†a the moniments in Westminster Abbey and other places, but no where found so turgid an Inscription. I shew'd it to Mr Freake, I need not tell you his opinion of it.†1
You have seen, but, I believe, hardly read through a scandalous book not long since publish'd here, which gives account of mr L.'s Religion, the Author without doubt is your old mighty Adversary Ed-s. I don't find that any body heeds it, I never heard any one speak in the least favourably of it.†2
Dr. Sherlock some time since preach'd three sermons about the Resurrection of the same (sometimes he call'd it Specifical) body, and several times quoted a late Author, but did not name you. two of the sermons I heard, and attended several sundays for the third, but miss'd it. The reasoning was very odd and weak as ever I heard; and the very text was not at all to the purpose.†3 This way of falling on men in sermons I never thought fair, because they have not an opportunity of justifying themselves. I have heard that the Bishop of Worcester bequeath'd his controversy with you to Dr Sh. and desir'd him to prosecute it. I don't know whether carrying it on in the pulpit will fulfill the will of the dead, 'Tis certainly the securest way, and the Doctor had manag'd his Christian warfare with more prudence if he had fought all his battles there.
I hope Mr. Churchil and I in about six weeks time shall finish the translation,†4 that which I desire is that I may do you as little injury as may be, I take the more time, that I may be the more just. I receive a greate deale of kindness from your good friends
― 16 ―

2684. Samuel Locke to Locke, 8 March 1700 (2642, 2704)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 206-7. Written by an amanuensis, apart from the subscription. Transmitted by Bonville: p. 25.
Sir
I long since resolved to have answered your Last most acceptable letter per Mr Bonvile (wherein was your orders for some Wine) but God hath prevented me by visiting me with a severe fitt of a feavor the danger of which I hope am now free'd from but still Languish under the Weakness thereof. I hope God will restore me to health againe.
I cannot in the meanetime forbear to acquainte you Sir that I have lately received from France some excellent Wines which I sent for for Some Persons of Honour but I have made a reserve for my friends and selfe of which I presume to send you a taste of
― 24 ―
12 pinte bottles viz. 4 of a sort†a of any of them you Shall please to make Choice you may command what quantity you please more or less. I shall only tell you they are the most Highly esteemed of any grouths in France. Pray accept a handfull of French Poires and grapes newly arryved but will not keep long. I have a little Chocolate lately come from Spaine of which also send you a taste and beg your acceptance.
Sir I take the boldness to entertaine you with a view of the inclosed which I lately received from my Dear Son John whom I hope is safely arryved (after the dangers he mentions therein) at Surratt,†1 after your Peruseal please to commit to any Conveyance to me as you Shall think fitt, the ships for Surratt intending to saile in 10†b- or 15 days time-†b when shall not faile to Performe your Commands to him. I conclude with my Prayers for your good health. I am
Sir
Your most humble servant and Cossin
SAM LOCKE
London the 8th March 1699/1700

2686. John Freke and Edward Clarke(?) to Locke, 9 March 1700 (2683, 2695)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 232. Written by Freke. Answered by no. 2695. This is the latest extant letter written by Freke and Clarke in conjunction. There is later a separate letter from Freke, no. 3620.
March the 9th 1699/1700
Sir
In answer to your French friends Question I can onely tell you that I believe noe foreigner will be admitted to inspect our Records either in the Tower or else where unless it be for some particular matter named to the officer in whose Custody they are, nay I am Confident noe Englishman can have that liberty without a Speciall Warrant from the King. But however your friends friend that is writing the History need not want the materialls that our Records
― 26 ―
afford if he apply himself to mr Rymer the Kings Historiographer (who has free recourse to all the Records). He may write to him either in French or Latin and Address it to his Lodgings in Norfolk Street and he may assure himself he will in the same language receive an answer from him and a full satisfaction in any Enquiry he can make mr Rymers humanity being equall to his great learning†1
I presume you read the votes and therein see the order on your Board to lay before the House an Account of the advancement of the Trade of the Kingdom since the Establishment of your Comission.†2 But I doe not yet hear there is any order for the Privy Councill to lay before the House the benefits the Kingdom has received by the Counsell and advice given by that board though Dom Com†3 is looking very narrowly into all offices. They say tis to Cure and prevent all abuses and if soe I know a Certain Chappell†4 that wants much to be inspected
Give our service to all at Oates and believe the College to be your faithfull friends and humble servants
Endorsed by Locke: 9 Mar 99/00 Answered 22
2687. Samuel Bold to Locke, 15 March 1700 (2628, 2771)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, ff. 37-8.
Steeple 15 March 99/00
Honoured Sir
Yours of the 13th of the last month found me under some Indisposition, which had confined me to my chamber for some days, but the reading of It was so extreamly pleasing to me, It almost perfectly freed me from the Disorder which had so long discomposed me, It did greatly revive me, and ever since I have sensibly recovered, so that now I bless God, I am as easie, and well, as I use to be when I think my self best. I returne you now my heartiest thanks for your Essay of the last Edition, The most valued present,
― 27 ―
I ever received.†1 I wil not say you cannot imagine how sensible I am of the mighty obligation you have laid on me in vouchsafing to think on me, when you designed to present any of your Friends with your Book, but I must assure you I have not words that can express the grateful sentiments which reign in my breast, otherwise I would testify my acknowledgments after another rate.
If you had not honoured with your letter, I could not have entertained any hard thought of you, but tho I had continued without the great satisfaction every line from you affords me, I must have concluded that you had very just reasons to deny me one of the most pleasing entertainments in the whole world. I am extreamly satisfied with what you write concerning Rom: 1.17. And am perswaded I should always have continued Ignorant of the meaning of, From Faith to Faith, if you had not instructed me in It; whereas now the thing is exceeding plain and clear to me.†2 I agree with you as to the sense of Rom: 5.12. And tho I was puzled when I wrote to you, yet in a little time, I had thoughts concerning it, something like those you have imparted to me; And some passages in the Reasonableness of Christianity contributed very much to my forming (as I thought) such apprehensions of that place as gave me satisfaction, but this is not the only portion of Scripture that Book hath yeilded me much light about. It hath given me great assistance in almost all parts of the New testament, where I met with difficulties, which neither my own thoughts before I was acquainted with that treatise, could conquer, nor any of the Commentators I had to consult, could help me over. I thank you for your kind acceptance of that long and tedious letter I writ you concerning the Doctors Book you formerly sent me.†3 Should I have writ all I took notice of when I read over that book, I should have filled 2 or 3 sheets of paper, and yet the most had bin only observations on passages which I apprehended had no determinate sense, and on such passages, as I thought could not wel consist with what was to be found in other parts of his book. The last part of your letter makes me often wish I could frequently wait on you, that I might receive from you those Informations which I am perswaded would mightily assist me in reading those parts of the new Testament you are reading. But were I near you,
― 28 ―
I am so very Indulgent to my self, my continued pressing on you, would give you too frequent occasion to wish me (in order to your own quiet) at as great a distance as now I am.
And Sir you have reason to reckon It an advantage (now you have honoured me with the Title of your friend) that writing at length is very troublesom to me, and what I can but seldom reconcile my self to, for otherwise I should before this time have so loaded you with Discourses on several subjects, you might have bin under some temptation to have repented your admitting such an Intemperate Scribler to your acquaintance. But tho my aversion to writing in words at length, hath contributed something to your ease, yet when I hear you are got to London, I hope to get an opportunity to wait on you there, and I purpose to bring two of my Discourses with me; The first is on Titus. chap.I.V.I. part last. the other is on John chap: I.V.47.†1 The former I am sensible is a loose discourse, therefore I would only trouble you with one part of It, where I endeavour to shew that no Rational objection can ly against the Gospel. The latter discourse being but short, I would desire you if you can have so much leisure, to read over. It is concerning the Temper and disposition of mind necessary to peoples entertaining aright Divine Truths, when duly propounded to them. A little after I received your last letter, A pamphlet, called the History of the works of the Learned for the month of Jan: came to my hands. Where I found an account of a Book writ against you. I readily guessed at the Author. What sort of language the Book is made up of, I know not, for I never saw It. But I am sure It is scandalous in It self. Were it worthy to have any Reflections made on It, I would bestow a little time to read It; But by the account given of what is contained in It, It appears to me, a very pittiful thing, and fit onely to convince the world that the Author is nothing but a lump of Ill nature. I am of opinion that the writers of the History etc have set off the book to the best advantage they were able, for they seem to be of the same kidney with the author.†2
― 29 ―
I have lately bin reading Mr Le Clerc's Parrhasiana,†1 and the Bishop of Sarum on the 39 Articles.†2 The former is filled with very fine and Useful Observations. I am perswaded the Bishop's book would have bin much better than It is, if he had thoroughly studied your Essay, and had bin wel acquainted with the Reasonableness of Christianity. I was sometimes ready to think in reading the Bishops Book, that some passages were inserted rather to comply with the custom of the past and present Age<s>†a than to express his Lordships real sentiments. But I say n<o>†a more, having detained you too long already, only I am with t<he>†a greatest sincerity Sir
your most obliged humble ser<vant>†a
SA: BOLDE
Address: To the Honoured Mr Locke
Endorsed by Locke: S: Bold 15 Mar 99/00

2689. Arent Furly to Locke, 16/27 March 1700 (3030)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 1-2. Sent with no. 2690.
(English) Amplissime Clarissimeque Domine
Optarem equidem me loco fratrum meorum†1 adfuisse, ut tam clarissimi viri colloquendi occasionem habuissem, simulatque gratiam egissem quam maximam oretenus pro dono a me haud merito fratribusque meis mei causa oblato, id quod nunc hisce perficio, præterea quoque mei studii rationem reddidissem, et ita tua benevola instructione gaudere potuissem; Ast nulla mihi nunc hac in re spes. Attamen hisce paucis lineis indicaturus me ex Schola Erasmiana†2 ad Academiam promotum esse: meus vere dilectissimus Parens haud inconsultum ratus est, me altero adhuc semestri spatio mansurum, quo majorem Græcæ Latinæque linguæ cognitionem adipiscerer; hisce orans Deum Optimum Maximum,
― 31 ―
ut te in suam sanctissimam protectionem recipiat. Vale atque accipe hæc ab illo, qui ob insignia in me collata beneficia est eritque perpetim
Amplissime Clarissimeque Domine
Tuus tibi obligatissimus servus,
ARENT FURLIJ
Dabam Rotterodami Sexto Die Calendas Aprilis MDCC.
(Latin) Excellent and Distinguished Sir,
Would that I had been present instead of my brothers,†1 so as to have had an opportunity of conversing with so distinguished a man, and at the same time of giving him my best thanks by word of mouth, as I now do by this letter, for a gift which I did not deserve and which you delivered to my brothers for me; further I might also have given you an account of my studies and so could have enjoyed your kind instruction; but now I have no hope of this. Nevertheless I shall tell you in these few lines that I have been promoted from the Schola Erasmiana†2 to the Academy; but my beloved father has thought it advisable for me to stay at the school for another semester so as to acquire a greater knowledge of Greek and Latin. I herewith [p. 30] pray God Almighty to take you into His most holy protection. Good-bye and accept this from one who, on account of the signal kindnesses that you have conferred on me, is and will ever be,
Excellent and distinguished Sir,
Your most obliged Servant,
ARENT FURLY
Rotterdam 27 March 1700

2690. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 16/27 March 1700 (2639, 2700)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 157-8. Furly failed to realize that after the end of February of this year the new-style dates were eleven days ahead of the old.
Rotterdam 17/27 March 1699/1700
Dear Sir
Having nothing worthy your notice to write this will be onely to give cover to the inclosed from my son Arent to return you his humble thanks for the presents sent him by his brothers and to let you know that after half a yeares being in the 6 and last schoole, he is gone up with honour even before severall that had been there a year and half: however I resolve to keep him there 6/m longer, the better to root himself in what he has learned. He is extraordinarily dilligent, and covetous, not of mony, but learning, and would part with all for books that may advance him in his studies.
I hope I shall have the happyness this summer to see you, with him, and then to consult what to doe with him. Its pitty but he should go to the outside of his inclinations in his studies, but that
― 32 ―
my circumstances will not admit. Could I get what Swinton owes me,†1 which if I could go to Scotland, I possibly might, at lest in great part, I should more Incline to continue him in his studies, but I must do, not what I would, but what I can—
We have now the fire of war broke forth at Riga, but the Jealousy of the Polish nobility, together with the feare of the Turks attacking the Muscoviter, may possibly be retrieved without any further harm.
And by the interposition of this state, who are fitting out 36 men of war, and our king whom we fancy cannot see the 2 northern crownes make any great earnings†2 upon each other—We are in hopes that a Rupture may be prevented, And our languishing trade retrieved, which by our folly, and neglect in this last war, we have almost lost past recovery.
So with humble service from my wife and self to your self, and the Honourable family, where you reside, with humble thanks for the most kind reception of our sons, I remain
Dear Sir
Your most humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY

2692. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 19 March [1700] (1591, 2712)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 164-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Deare Brother
I am but just out of a scurvey fever that made my Oxford friends fear that it would quickly end my life; And no sooner is my danger over than the cares of this world return, not that I am over solicitous for the old Woman, but having receiv'd a leter from my son which tenderly gives me a new concerne for him, I cannot but impart it to you who are most likely to make it significant to him; he informes me that to mend his smal fellowship†1 he is tempted to accept of a Country living of 25£ a yeare, I have answer'd him, that considering the expence of Orders etc besides the fatigue of cold and hot journeys, as well as the labour of his Brains and Lungs, that the good managment of his present College life will agree better with him. This advice I conclude he will take; Now if I have don ill pray Sir reprove me; and yet punish me no other ways for this fault than by remembering the young man when it comes within your reach to set him more at his Ease; hitherto he has found me as liberall to him as I could, and being sensible that he cannot without inconveniencing a Mother who loves him intirely, expect the usuall suplys during my life; he seemes dispirited with the straitness of his fortune; Elce he would not be so very willing to be thus humbly prefer'd. I conffess I am vaine enough to think he deserves better, And considering that from an Enfant he has bin in your favour, I will not dispare of succeeding by your recomendation of him to those who have it in their power to oblige you. There are variety of Donitives and little Dignitys in my Lord Chancelors guift which Ambitious men disdaine, and ar below his Lordships favorits which are often granted at the request of persons Esteem'd by great men, And why may I not hope this way to prevail? there being few whose intrest exceeds yours; I aime at nothing that looks above my Sons Education and deserts. Tho divers by a lucky word mount high who mirit very litle; I say not this to reproach your friendship for as inconsiderable as I am, I have prevail'd for greater things for others than I now would be glad of for my own good son, and yet I cannot accuse myself for want of kindness for him, and I assure you I am far from fancying
― 35 ―
that you will decline proper ways of setting honest W G more at his Ease, who to endeare him to you is so very like his excellent father in Temper and Mind, tho he falls short of his preferments (when he was many yeares younger than this son) who I hope will live longer; And waite with modesty and patience for what we wish him. Pardon deare Brother this solicitude of mine, and think how naturall it is for a parent to desire a setlement for an only Child, where I may give my helping hand to the fixing him happyly, fancy your old friend setting a Parsonage house in a good Aire in Order, stitching for the poor and making them wellcome to her without giving offence to her richer neighbours, and the Country Parson zealous in doing his duty, then think it possible that Mr Grigg and his mother may be such, and how plesant it will be to you to come and find us happyer than the generality of those who make a greater flutter. I have suffred my pen to run faster than I intended, but I have not slept so well this night, as I use to doe, so that my Wits are not so well compos'd as they ought to be when I write to Mr Locke, but you have accoustom'd yourself to guese at my meaning and excuse faults that are not maliticous, I shall be glad to have it secur'd to me under your own hand, that you are as ready to forgive me now as you were formerly, for with as much respect as ever I am Sir
Your affectionate sister and humble servant
ANNE GRIGG
Oxford from Mr Stacys house March the 19

2693. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 19/30 March 1700 (2644, 2673, 2699)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 207-8. The date in the endorsement is a slip on Locke's part. Answers no. 2644; answered by no. 2707.

A Paris ce 30. mars 700.
Comme vous vous interessez, monsieur, à tout cequi me regarde, je vous diray confidemment que j'aprehende de finir le siecle
― 36 ―
encor plus mal que je n'y ay vecu, c'est à dire avec moins de tranquillité que je n'en ay eu jusques à present.
Il y a pres de trente ans que je fus obligé d'essuyer la sollicitation d'un procez qui dura pour mes pechez plus de huit ans. J'en sortis enfin glorieusement et avantageusement; cela me deroba le tems le plus precieux de ma vie, et je croiois n'en entendre jamais parler. Il renaît cependant comme un hydre, et cequi me cause une extrême inquietude, c'est que je suis sur le point d'etre obligé d'aler poursuivre cete afaire dans un autre Parlement, parceque mes parties ont un grand nombre de parens dans celui de Paris. Jugez quel regal ce sera pour moi, et à mon âge, d'etre excentré d'une si facheuse maniere sans cet embaras qui commença dez l'année passée environ la feste de Pâque, je m'etois fait un plaisir de vous aler surprendre à Oates, et je ne sais plus quand je pouray jouïr d'un aussi grand bonheur que me seroit celui de vous embrasser. J'ay pensé en riant à un Deus è machinâ pour ma consolation, et vous ne devineriez jamais ceque ce peut être. c'est qu'aiant lu le projet de vos deux Loteries que l'on fait en faveur de l'Hopital de Grenwich,†1 il m'a pris envie d'avoir le gros lot de cele dont les billets sont de vint schelings, et par concomitance celui aussi de la petite. si cela m'arivoit, je laisserois la toute la chicane, et irois sans retardement recevoir moi même les presens de la fortune en quoi je ressentirois moins de plaisir quà celui de vous embrasser. La conclusion est que je vous prie, raillerie à part, de metre pour moi à chacune de ces loteries trois billets. On m'a dit que les 20. schelings font seize l̷l̷. monnoie de France, ainsi les 60. seront seize ecus.†2 Les trois autres billets de la petite Loterie font quatre ecus, de maniere que le tout sera de vint ecus, que j'espere que vous voudrez bien avancer pour moi. Vous garderez les billets, et me donnerez avis des numeros que vous aurez pris, et en même tems par quel banquier de Londres vous dezirez que je vous remete cete somme, ceque je feray à votre premier ordre. Les trois noms à chacune seront Abel Antoniaster. François Calloric. Nicolas Kerblanin.†a si les boules tombent favorablement par les tuyaux, ce sera justement pour moi le Deus è machinâ.
― 37 ―
J'ay vu avec une tres grande satisfaction le Traité chronologique de m. de Worcester sur le tems de Pythagore, et cela me fait dezirer extremement son grand ouvrage.†1 Aprenez moy, je vous prie, à quoi il en est. La continuation de celui du P. Pagi s'imprime à Geneve.†2 ses letres à m. de Worcester, alors de st Asaph, et celes du P. Noris, aujourdhui cardinal, ont toutes passé par mes mains, aussi bien que les reponses. J'ay des copies de toutes, et je vous enverrai le commencement et la fin de chacune, afin que vous connoissiez si vous en avez moins que moi, auquel cas je vous ferois copier cequi vous manque. Vous n'avez peutêtre pas les reponses de m. de Worcester, qu'il vous importeroit d'avoir. Le Card. de Noris a reglé son année Syromacedoniene sur le sentiment de ce grand Prelat. c'est moi à qui le public a obligation du commerce que j'ay lié entre ces trois savans hommes. Je dis le public, parceque leur letres pouront parêtre un jour, et cela auroit deja eté fait si le card. de Noris ne m'avoit instamment prié de ne les pas publier, par la raison qu'il n'est pas permis en Italie d'avoir commerce avec des gens d'une autre religion que la catholique, et c'est pour cela que dans son bel ouvrage intitulé: Annus et Epochæ Syromacedonum, il cite les letres de m. de St. Asaph, †a avoient eté ecrites, quoique je les receusse seulement sans cachet pour les faire tenir apres les avoir luës, et en avoir mandé mon sentiment.†3 La même chose se pratiquoit à l'egard de celes du feu P. Pagi, mais ce savant Cordelier ne se faisoit pas une afaire que l'on sceust qu'il ecrivoit à des Protestans, comm'il faisoit à M. Cupper†4 et autres.
Je vous dirai presentement un seul mot sur <ce>†b que vous m'avez demandé sur le nombre des sacrificateurs qui tenoient dans le Temple lors de l'immolation de la Pâque.†5 Dans le plus grand nombre il n'y a qu'un exemple qui va jusques à 100000.†c (cent mille) et autant de victimes, et non 250000. Je ne dezirerois rien tant que d'être à Oates pour vous faire demeurer d'acord de cela,
― 38 ―
et c'est bien assez pour lespace que l'on peut donner à l'aire du Temple selon les mesures que Josephe en donne avec beaucoup d'obscurité.
Je vous ay parlé de la laine des beufs qui sont dans l'Amerique Septentrionale le long de la Riviere de missisipi.†1 J'en ay receu quelques peaux, mais j'en atens en plus grand nombre et de mieux conditionnées, cependant j'en fais faire un essai d'etofes, melant la laine de beuf avec un tiers de mouton. Vous avez cy-joint de Cete laine comme l'on la coupe sur la peau de la bête morte, et comme l'on en a filé sans aucun melange. Ele n'est pas filée fin, parcequ'aiant eté filée sans huile, ele ne sest pas etandüe. Vous seriez bien etonné si j'alois vous voir avec un habit de cete laine sur le cors. Dieu le veuïle de quelque maniere que ce soit, et cependant je me consolerai en m'aprenant des nouveles de votre bonne santé.
Vous pouvez metre dans le paquet de m. Fraiser pour m. clement les livres que vous jugerez me convenir, et vous m'en manderez le prix.†2 Je suis parfaitement Votre—
J'oubliois de vous dire que le Triumvir capiténe de Marine est alé à Rome avec son patron m. le Card. de coislin. On deziroit que je fusse de la partie, et m. le card. Detrées†3 vouloit que ce fust au moins à cause de m. le card. de Noris. J'ay repondu que s'ils en faisoient un Pape, j'irois lui baiser la pantoufle. ce card. papable est Bibliothecaire du Vatican à la place du card. casanata.†4
Les trois noms et surnoms des Loteries sont Abel An<t>oniaster.†a François Calloric. Nicolas Kerblanin. Si vous avez des raisons pour ne vouloir pas y metre pour moy, vous prendre la peine de m'en donner avis.
D'autres de mes amis metent à ces Loteries. mandez moi si vous voudriez bien garder leurs billets, quand ils les auront ete†b paiéz par des banquiers qui en ont l'ordre.

2695. Locke to Edward Clarke, 22 March [1700] (2686, 2697)

Oates 22 Mar
Dear Sir
I love my country and I love you and by that you may guess how much I am pleased with the news you sent me in your last. As to the silent Gent.†1 I am perfectly of your mind unless there be some thing in it that you and I know noe thing of. But of this whole matter when I see you. This favourable winter made me hope it would be now in a little time. But these late Easterly winds have pinchd me shrewdly, and to them I impute the spiting of bloud which happend lately to me and which I am sure came from my lungs
Pray give my hearty service and thanks to the Batchelor for the information he sent me about the Records, and for the peice of News he joynd with it. I joyn heartily with them that are for Cureing†a- or preventing-†a abuses, may they prosper that mean it in earnest. But timorous men are apt to think that Reformation will not goe far unlesse it begin at the house of god.
I shall be glad in your next to hear from Chipley and from beyond sea,†2 For I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
Oates Salutes the Colledg with great respect

2697. Locke to Edward Clarke, 25 March 1700 (2695, 2703)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 146. Printed in Rand, pp. 555-6.
Oates 25 Mar 1700
Dear Sir
Sir Francis being told yesterday that the house would rise this week He and my Lady desired me in their names to envite you hither the next being an holy day week and of leisure which they would be very glad you would doe them the kindness to spend here.†1 And truly if you will have my opinion I know noe thing you can doe better when the Session is over than to take a little country air to wipe of the fatigue of soe long a service and give your self a little freshness before you return to business and fatigue. I could give you an hundred reasons for this but they are many of them soe obvious that I think I need not wast your time about them. But if this little excursion will be of use to your health you ought to come even for your business sake, since that keeps pace with ones health and cannot be donne without it. Come then and mix some fresh air with soe much smoak, some mirth with your Chagrin. My service to the Batchelor. I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate and most faithfull servant
J LOCKE
I beg your pardon for this repeated trouble of my letters to the post

2698. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 26 March/6 April 1700 (2624, 2785)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 133-4. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 116-17.
A Amsterdam le 6 d'Avril 1700.
Il y a longtemps, Monsieur, que j'aurois dû vous écrire pour vous
― 43 ―
remercier de la quatriéme édition de vôtre Ouvrage;†1 mais en attendant de vous mander en même temps des nouvelles de la dédicace, je m'apperçois que j'ai differé trop longtemps.
Mr. l'Avocat Vanden Ende n'a pas trouvé plûtôt l'occasion de parler à nôtre homme, qui l'a refusée, sous prétexte que l'on disoit que l'Auteur avoit quelques sentimens qui ne sont pas du goût des Druïdes. C'est un homme qui dans le fonds n'est rien moins que superstitieux, et qui est très-ennemi de toute persecution; mais c'est un homme, d'un autre côté, si timide, ou si amoureux du repos, et du calme, qu'il ne veut pas donner à ses gens là la moindre occasion, pas même éloignée, de parler de lui comme d'un homme qui favorise quelque nouveauté. Il est monté au plus haut degré, auquel il puisse aspirer, et il en jouït plus que qui que ce soit, de sorte qu'il ne pense qu'à jouïr tranquillement, et à éloigner de lui tout ce qui peut troubler cette indolence. Mon ami est bien vû de lui, et le voit même souvent. Il ne manquera pas de lui faire sentir, à la premiere rencontre, que c'étoit un honneur qu'on lui faisoit, que de le joindre au Président du Conseil Privé du Roi d'Angleterre, et de le mettre à la tête d'un livre aussi estimé que celui-là. Il lui fera valoir l'honêteté de l'Auteur, qui par là prétendoit, avec raison, lui marquer son estime. Je ne manquerai pas de vous mander ce qu'il aura répondu.†2 J'ai lû, avec beaucoup de plaisir et de profit, les additions de vôtre 4 édition, et sur tout le Chapitre de l'Enthousiasme. Bien des gens en ont besoin. Je vous prie, Monsieur, de faire demander à Mr. Huguetan la nouvelle édition de ma Critique, en lui offrant le billet ci-joint.†3 Ces trois tomes ne vallent pas le vôtre, si bien que vous avez fait comme le Glaucus d'Homere, χρύσεα χαλκείων.†4 Mais si je ne
― 44 ―
puis égaler la bonté, il faudra que je tâche de surpasser le poids. Jespere de vous envoier, dans peu de semaines, mes Quæstiones Hieronymianæ, qui est une Critique du S. Jerôme des Bénedictins de Paris. Le P.Martianay, qui est le principal directeur de cette édition aiant parlé mal de moi, dans divers endroits de ses notes sur S. Jerôme, j'ai entrepris de le censurer à mon tour, non tant à cause de ce qu'il dit, que parce que S. Jerôme étant un livre de Bibliotheque, on gardera ses impertinences, en le gardant. J'attaque en même temps l'érudition de S. Jerôme, que vous verrez avoir été trèspetite.†1 On criera, chez vous, que je maltraite les SS. Peres, mais je ne m'en mets guere en peine, et je ne crois pas desormais que je doive garder plus de mesures avec ceux qui feignent de les admirer, qu'il n'en gardent avec moi. Après cela, je ne me querelle plus. Le troisiéme Tome de ma Critique et ces Questions feront taire les Censeurs, ou me mettront au moins en droit de mépriser leurs censures. Je reprendrai incessamment ma Bible. Je vous prie d'assurer Madame Masham de mes très-humbles respets. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC
Mr. Coste trouvera ici mes civilitez.

2700. Locke to Benjamin Furly, 30 March 1700 (2690, 2754)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 47-8. Rough draft, written on the covers of two letters addressed to Locke at Oates. Answers no. 2639.
Oates 30 Mar 1700
Sir
Befor I answer to the three questions inclosed in your letter of 10 Dec.99†1 relateing to the controversie between your wife and her brother It is necessary to premise†a you that I am neither Lawyer nor Merchant that it may be an excuse for the mistakes which my ignorance in both may make me commit in a place where I am remote from any helps that might set me right.
1 As to the first then my opinion is that the Compartnership is to be accounted to begin when it is first set down to be soe in the Fathers journal and not till then. My reason is because amongst merchands their journals are as I take it lookd upon to be as their private records to which they appeale in controversies between them where no other deciseve writeings are produced to determine the Cause without the testimony of their account books. This seems to be the same case here as if it were a controversie between merchants. For the daughters claiming by right of their father and under his name must be determind by their fathers and brothers books, the only records that can give a determination in this case unlesse the Brother can produce some authentique writeing to shew the contrary
2 To the second what may be judgd to have been the share that his father allowed him in the profits of the Compartnership. I answer I cannot at all guesse nor doe I thinke it possible for any one to determin it being perfectly arbitrary in the father upon considerations that can <be>†b only Known to him self. But I thinke there is an other question more proper to be askd which will determine this, and that is what share in the stock his father may be judg to have admitted into. And to this methinks there is a very plain and direct answer, and that is such a share as the law of the Country would have alotted to his son if he had died intestate. For if by noe will or writeing the father has divided his estate
― 47 ―
amongst his children, it is plain he intended not any other alotment but that of law, and this takeing his son into company with <him>†a can†b- be interpreted to be noe more than his legal share in the estate.-†b If the father intended otherwise tis fit some positive writeing or contract should be produced to make it out and if you state the matter of fact right it is probable there was some such which since the son does not produce it may be presumd it did not setle on him a greater portion of his fathers estate nor of the accrueing profits than would have come to his share by the law without it
To the third Question I answer. That if his father gave him noe part of his stock when he admitted him into partnership it cannot be guessed what part of the profits he allowed him, though it cannot but be supposd he told his son whose testimony in the case cannot be admitted. But if he gave him a certain part of his stock let us suppose 1/3 It can not be thought that he should allow him ½ of the profits of the whole unlesse his son paid him interest for 1/6 of the stock in trade.†c For where the profits are equall equity <requires>†d that the stocks must be soe too. Now supposeing the son had £1000 in the common stock and the father £2000 the sons £1000 is equal to £1000 of the fathers and the fathers other £1000 in respect of the partnership is as if it were borrowed whereof the father must pay interest for one half and the son for the other half i e for £500.
But takeing the case to be in respect of the sons share just the same as it would have been if the father had died intestate the next day after the admitting his son into Company with him. I think there is noe consideration of interest to be had in the case but the father or those claiming under the father are to have their shares in the profits in proportion to their shares in the stock. which is such as the law would have allowed them the father dyeing†e- without any positive setlement-†e the next day after the Copartnership began. For what the sons part was the day immediately after the Copartnership began the same it was ever after unlesse some
― 48 ―
new grant or setlement could be produced. But†a- here noe thing appearing but of a Copartnership without any positive grant or declaration of what share the son was admitted to which lay wholy in the breast and will of the father <whether>†b it should be 1/10 or 1/4, one ½ or 3/4 or any other portion. the father for ought appears being silent, the allotment of the law is to be followed†c which assignes to children their portions where the father is silent and says noething-†a

2702. Mrs. Elizabeth Berkeley, later Burnet, to Locke, 4 April 1700 (2627, 2705)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 226-7.
Sir
That a letter from you should be a very valuable and extraordnary pleasure is not strang, but I own my self grown hardy enough to
― 49 ―
find a delight in asking as well receiving Instructions; I have had such experience of your condisention and gentleness to the ignorent (owning them selves such) that the uneasyness apt to arise from the shame of being mistaken or the fear of sencure is quit overborn by the satisfaction as well as advantage of being better informed; I find allmost as litle reluctancy in exposing the weekness's of my mind as the deffects in my health because the same Charity I find disposed without severity to amend both.
But perhaps this will look oddly to be folowed by acknowledging that the letter I now return my thanks for is of three mounths date: my Value for your time and defference to your better imployments would have taught me a reasonable distence, but since their was in your last something requierd (which is to me a Command) it makes it like a fault to obey so slowly. I own were it not from you, I should suspect it a complement you thought I expected, when you bid me send the papers I mentioned;†1 but I am perswaded you never misleade those who depend on you, or bid them do what you disaprove if they obey; therefore without more niceness I now send them, and had don it some time since had I not ben without one days health some time before I had your letter and ever since, I think I begen to mend a litle tho slowly; I fond by reading then lately (when my first thoughts were out of memorie) the sense very obscure (if 'tis not too much to suppose any part disarves to be called even dark or confused sense) I can but just find my own meening and doute much if a stranger to my thoughts can often find any meening at all, besides the trouble they will give in reading for want of setting down the Texts in words at lenth, this made me purpose to writt them over mending at least the last fault and leveing out some less probable Texts; but tho I began I was so ill and so listless I could not go on; I send them because you bid me, but do not ask their reading. they are not worth your time; I thank you for your very obliging letter, and good advise; I am too sensible both of my want of Judgment and information to beleeve those who differ from me must be in eror; the contrary is a fault I more incline to; concluding I am wrong when I can not easyly think as others do, and were I not some times incourged by finding persones whos goodness and knowledg I esteem in the same sentiments, I should be very defident; the severe and sensorious side is so contrary to my temper, that it is
― 50 ―
rather a prejudice then an alurment to that side; as I had only the Bible when I writ the inclosed papers, so I have not since consulted farther, but 'tis most probable the sense I have given is only what I have heard or read and has insenseable stuck to my memorie; Thank God I am not uneasyly curious about what is obscurely revelled either with respect to what is future or in other matters above our clear and full comprehension; I look on the scripture more as a rule of life in order to a future and better state, then a designed information of the Nature of that happeness; and if I can but rightly understand and Honestly perform my part, I shall I hope quietly comit my future being to God as unto a Faithfull Creator, who first gave and will preserve it in such a state as is sutable to his wisdom and Goodness; these Generalls will I trust secure my duty and render such inquier's that are made in Charity and in a disposission ready to submit to truth and the Holy scripture inosent and pardonable tho I may mistake— I hoped to have made amends for my long papers by a short letter, but these faults are like others one disposes for another, an excuse will be an agrevation, therefore I will only intreat a pardon for
Sir
Your greatly Obliged and most Humble se<rvant>†a
E BERKELEY
April: 4: 1700

2704. Samuel Locke to Locke, 5 April 1700 (2684, 2784)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 208-9.
Sir
I have the favour of yours of 13th past: which brought me Infinitely more thanks for a small presant than it could deserve. your acceptance was sufficient. that which I highly esteeme is the affectionate Care and Kindnesse you Take for mee and mine express'd in your Letter of 25 ditto to mr Bonville, wherin is such kinde and Cordiall caution for mee to take in order to Recover my health, that I am obliedg'd in thanks to you Sir beyond what I can expresse. my feavor brought me verry low but I am I prayse God recover'd to that degree, that I am able to Ride into the Country once a weeke and Returne to buysinesse in the Citty. where I goe about pritty strong, and hope by the Intimation in your Letter I shall soone have the honnour to see you in London which I shall be proude off. to ad personall thanks for your favours. and to Impart (if agreeable) somwhat of the state of our Company†1 who next Tuesday seventh night the 16th: instant have apointed to Choose Directors.
for my owne part I seeke it no further than as I may be Capable to serve the Company; to have the satisfaction of looking into the Improovement of my owne and friends Estates. and the advancement of my son John: who hath volluntarily adventerd in to theyr service.
― 52 ―
Envy etca insteed of unanimity in the presant Court of Directors is too apparent, for that one or 2 men to promote theyr private intrests hath much incroacht upon the whole: to say no more: Only doe presume to send you one of our printed lists for your speculation. begging your pardon for deviateing on this subject.
we are under strange apprehentions what the Ill Consequence will attend, that the Parliament setting up one Company one session (who by the way paid 2 millions for it) and theyr setting up another (for nothing) this session to trade to the same parts in opposition to us, or rather to destroy the Trade, and setting us to pull one anothers throates out here at home. but Especially in India: is such an unpresidented hardship (to say no worse), that never was practis'd in this Kingdom: espeially where a publicq fund is Concern'd: and the said Act mention's Expressly that the old Company was to determine the 29 Sept: 1701:†1 and the King sent an Ambassador to acquaint the Mogull the same:†2 I pray God blesse the King. I am affraid hee will be made as uneasy as wee are.
Sir I pray for your good health giveing you my hearty and humble Respects: also to that worthy Gentleman Sir Fran: Massam and my Lady Massam whose judgment in Chooseing the Margaux wine. is infalliably Right, for a more dellicat grouth of wines is not in the Kingdom of France and allways Esteemed so. I shall reserve what you have directed. and keepe it safe in my vault till further order next weeke or the weeke affter if the hogshead†a be fyne shall bottle it off and acquaint mr Bonville: I am Sir
Your most obliedged servant and Cossin
SAM: LOCKE

2708. William Popple to Locke, 13 April 1700 (2651, 2714)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 238-9.
London. April, the 13th: 1700.
Sir,
After I had sent away my letter last night to your Carryer, I received one from the Secretary of the Admiralty†2 acquainting me that there were several Packets from the Earle of Bellomont sent thither by the Secretarys of State, amongst which was one for the Lords Commissioners for Trade etc, and that the Secretarys having opened and read their own packets at the Admiralty Board, and†a- left there all that related any way to Kid,-†a it was expected the Lords Commissioners for Trade would do the like. Upon this
― 56 ―
I sent to your Bretheren that are in town, that they might meet this morning.
Three of them came (Sir P, mr B, mr P,.)†1 And I thereupon stept to the Admiralty†2 to know more particularly what had been done by others, and what was expected from them. I found, and returning told them, that the Secretarys had left all their letters as was said; And that I found there Sir John Stanley†3 and some others waiting to do the same thing. So they ordered me to return and open the packets, and take away or leave as the Lords of the Admiralty should think fit. When I came there again I found Sir Edmond Harrison,†4 then Mr Lownds,†5 then Sir Tho: Littleton,†6 one after another passing before me upon the like occasion. And there was also one from the Custome house to follow. Mr Yard†7 and my Lord Chancellor's Secretary came a little before I was call'd in. When†a- I was admitted the Lords-†a told me (as before) what the Secretarys of state had done. I told them I had order to open, and leave what they thought convenient. So I opened; And one packet with a great many papers referd to in it by numbers (according to my Lord Bellomont's method) relating wholly to Kid and other Pirates, I left it with them; Without reading any more of it than the Endorsments of every paper which shewd Pirates to be the general subject of all. The next packet was principally upon other matters; But in reading the titles of the papers belonging to it, some of them seeming to have some relation to the busyness of Pirates they kept those, and let me take the rest and†b- that letter-†b away with me.†8 There was also a packet directed to my self, which was a letter from the Secretary of the Massachusetts†c Colony with some Minutes of Council etc.†9 The letter I read openly: And they let me take it
― 57 ―
away with the inclosed Minutes etc. There was yet another packet to my self, which was from the E: of Bellomont: So I read my letter openly to them, and there being nothing in it for their purpose, they let me take it:†1 But in that letter of mine were inclosed one for Mr Blathwayt, and one for you: Concerning which I told them I had no Directions. So they desired me to leave them, and to give him and you notice of it. I intend to tell him on Munday. And upon this account that I now give you, I know you will let me know what you desire to have done about your said letter.†2
I should have said that all these Packets came by his Majesty's Ship the Advice†3 who has brought over Kid, with the rest of the Pirates; in all Two and thirty.†4 The Lords of the Admiralty it seems are to have the examination of them: But how the matter has been thus concerted, and put into that Channel, I do not understand, though I have just now told this same story to Mr Clarke: For he also is a little in the dark about it. They keep all these letters, in order to prepare themselves for the Examination of Kid (and I suppose of the other Pirates) And when that is over they will restore to every one their own. I am
Sir,
Your most faithfull humble Servant
WILLIAM POP<PLE>†a
Address: For John Locke Esquire [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmarks: AP 13; GC.
Endorsed by Locke: W: Popple 13 Apr 00 Answered 15

I send yow againe ane other Packett from Hanover which came
― 58 ―
not long agoe, Containing ane letter to my self,†1 And ane Continuatione of Remarques by Mr Leibnitz upon your Controversie with the late bishop of Woster.†2 As he heth red with lazure all yow have writt upon that subject save one peice which is not come to his hands, so I find he wold be pleased to have your Judgement of What he writes.†3 His dissent from yow in some things is in such ane Amicable way, as preserves the respect which he hath alwayes professed for yow. These subtile distinctiones As they are best found out by such metaphisicall heads as Monsieur Leibnitz, So they can be best Judged of by such as yow, who knows most what use they can be put to. 2712. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 15 April [1700] (2692, 3068)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, f. 166. Year from Locke's endorsement.
April the 15th
Deare Brother
I thank you for your Ladyday answer to my last and for your continued favours to my son which are the more nessesary because his mothers cares grow useless to him, and the fair prospect she had of prefering him by her services for his sake are vanish'd: If in what I writ to you I exprest myself weakly, let it be pardon'd because I am still dispirited by my late ilness besides you know Sir that I am very unskillfull in those affairs which make wiser women speak more pertenently. I will not admire that my sons fortun is no better, nor that men of less value and intrest meet with greater advantages (by unexpected hits) than I figure out for him; there are unacountable ways of dispossing of most worldly maters, and even the plainest ways are I find too hard for me which makes
― 62 ―
me humbly return to my deare husbands reflexions, who with great satisfaction and thankfullness own'd all his preferments to be from God alone, his being chosen Chaplin to the Bishop of London†1 was not by the usual way of recomendation, nor what his age or his humility permited him to expect; This I crave leave to ad that you may see that tis not mens being out of the ordenary road of preferment can hinder vertious men from being provided for, and much better than we can contrive, let me then please myself with a surer care of my son than I can forecast for him, and no more venture to write upon others sugestions tho they are much wiser than
Your most humble servant
A GRIGG
Tho I cannot be upon the watch for my son and spy out things before they fall I will never decline any way of setting him at his Ease that is within my reach, he knows I have bin more liberall to him than to myself, and tis for his sake that I chuse the cheapest way of living and make the best of what is left. he may live to be old, and dispis'd to, if he has not something to bribe those who are most likly to be usefull to him. I bless God I am not burthensome to any, but I find better people than I am friendless because they are poor, May my son ever be as happy as his Father and mother and much more carefull to be good than rich he has many good qualitys, he gratfully considers his obligations to you and would perhaps blush if he knew that I troubled you upon his account,

2714. William Popple to Locke, 19 April 1700 (2708, 2740)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 240-1.
Whitehall. April, the 19th: 1700.
Sir,
I have your letters of the 12th and 15th. After the Receipt of the last of them I went to the Admiralty Board, and there opened and read to them your letter from the Earle of Bellomont: But there being nothing in it relating to Kid, they consented that I should take it away: And so I send it to you here inclosed.†1
The three inclosed Copies of our Minutes shew you what this Board are now doing.†2 The ground of this Conspiracy of the Indians which you will finde there mentioned arises wholly from an Artifice of the French. It seems the Commissioners who came over to treat here in winter 169 8/9 agreed with our Commissioners that letters should be writ by the French King to the Governor of Canada, and by his Majesty to the E: of Bellomont, about disarming the Indians on both sides, upon pretence of keeping them in peace, and with certain conditions to be agreed on between those Governors: Which letters were writ accordingly. But instead of concerting any thing with the E of Bellomont thereupon, who
― 64 ―
also on his side not thinking fit to do any thing in it did not propose any thing about it to the Governor of Canada, the French have industriously spread Reports through the five Nations and all the rest of those Indians that the Earle of Bellomont was designing to take away their Arms in order to the utter extirpation of them. This Belief instill'd into them by the French Missionaries (whom they call the Governor of Canada's cunning men)†1 has put them into such a rage that they are all of them, from the Eastermost parts of New England to the Westermost of our New-York Indians, enter'd actually into a combination against the English on that Continent: And God knows what Mischief they may have already done. However the preventing or remedying of any such Mischief has been the subject of this dayes Deliberation, upon which I am now to draw up a Representation: But what it will be I can give very little guess till the Board shall have agreed upon the Draught of it. Presents for our Indians; One hundred Recruits, and Clothes for the four Companies; A Sod fort in the Onondage Country; And a Credit for the E: of Bellomont to draw a limited sum upon the Treasury here; are some of the Heads.†2 I am
Sir,
Your most obedient humble Servant
WILLIAM POPPLE.
The Letter about the New-Establishment is chiefly in favour of my son:†3 But I have little expectation of success in it.
Endorsed by Locke: W: Popple 19o Apr 00 Answered 26
