2716. John Lock (later Sir John) to Locke, 20 April 1700 (2502, 3046)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 171a-173. Forwarded by Samuel Locke in London on 11 January 1701: p. 221. Documents relating to the rival East India Companies' activities in Surat, 1700-7, are published in Selections from the Letters ... preserved in the Bombay Secretariat, ed. G. W. Forrest, 1885-99, Home series, i. 226-68 (Sir John Gayer was in charge for the Old Company; Sir Nicholas Waite, for the New). The principal secondary works bearing on Lock's service in the east from 1700 to 1704 are, besides Bruce (no. 2437 n.), Hill (no. 2614 n.), and Morse (no. 2224 n.), Philip Anderson, The English in Western India: Early History of Surat, etc., 1854, and Harihar Das, The Norris Embassy to Aurangzib (1699-1702), 1959.
Honourable Sir
The Rooke Gally†1 arrived here the 27th. past, brought mee under my Fathers cover the Honour of yours dated the 17th of June,†2 a Favour noe Less then from a Person whose Goodness Obliges all men to bee wanting in suteable returns; therefore from mee Sir I know you expect nothing elce then acknowledgments which I hope you'l accept for that, as well as your kinde and admirable Advice for the preservation of my Health, which would still bee more pretious to mee, if could in any respect bee serviceable to one whose name is honorable to bear.
My imployment being in the Service of the honourable the English Company tradeing to the East Indies, I desire your Pardon if I presume to trouble you, with a Shorte relation of their beginning a Settlement in this parte of India, under the care and management of the honourable Sir Nicholas Waite†3 his Majesties Publick Minister and Consull, and President for the Company, with whome I came in the Mountague,†4 that Lost her masts neer the Cape Verde Ilands, and this retarded his arrivall till the 19th January last, which after his Majesties Consull had signifyed to the English in these parts and to the Governor of the Place,†5 he proposed several Articles to him, to secure the Estates of our honourable Imployers from the debts and engagements of the Old Company who are deeply intangled with this Goverment, that thirty months
― 67 ―
Since forced them and the other European Companies here by Irons and confinement to signe an Obligation for securing their Shipping from Pyrates, which had often ryfled them of their treasure and comitted Severall Villanies in these Seas, and after all the Obstructions and oppositions the Old Company in conjunction with the Dutch and French could invent to impeed obtaining a freedom from their Chains,†1 a Perwana†2 was granted by the Governor in a months time and, sent downe to the Consull at Swally Hole,†3 where till then he continued aboard his Ship, the articles are at Large in the Paper that goes herewith. The 19th february Last the Consull was received a mile from the Citty by the Governor his Son, and the rest of the Great Officers who conducted him to the Governors House, and was presented by him with a horse and severall Pieces†a of Atlass†4 and treated with a great deal of respect.
The Last Letters from his Excellency Sir William Norris†5 his Majesties Embassador to the Mogull were dated the 19th January Last from Metchelapatam†6 on the Coast of Choromandell and are inform'd by the Governor here that the Mogull has orderd a Strong Garde of Soldiers to conduct his Lordship up to Courte where hope will now shortly bee, and by next Shipping shall take the freedom you are pleas'd to grant of comunicateing what passeth and the Success of his Embassy
All Comodities here are rissen 30. to 40. per Cent by reason of soe many Ships from Europe, and our home manufactures fall as much, which many Sellars must needs occasion, and the Natives know how to make an Advantage†b of the differences and disputes that arrises between the two Companies, as well as any People whatever, by raiseing the Price of their Goods and debaseing ours.
― 68 ―
which if not timely prevented will bee a considerable Loss to the Nation in Generall, besides Large Presents given by both parties to carry on their owne Ends must amount to Great Sums that never returns to the Nations Capitall any more, the consideration and redress of these mischiefs humbly comitt to you honourable Sir, whome his Majesty hath wisely apointed for the Advantage of trade, to bee the properest Judge. not to trespass any Longer on your Patience, I desire your permission to bee amongst the rest of your Servants.
Honourable Sir
your most Obedient and Devoted humble Servant
JOHN LOCK.
Surat. 20th Aprill 1700
Sir I have recomended to my Father a few Triffles of this Place, to bee deliverd you, for which crave your acceptance.

2724. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 30 April/ 11 May 1700 (2653, 2742)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 135-6. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, f. 188. Printed from the copy and omitting a passage in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 458-60. Answers no. 2653; answered by no. 2866.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Quod hactenus ad amicissimas tuas siluerim, ullâ tui oblivione factum credas nolim. Multa responsum distulere: præcipue quidem tristis ille filii mei casus, tibi satis notus, et mœror inde contractus, in primâ ex subito ac prorsus inexspectato infortunio consternatione vehementior, qui animum meum ita afflixit, ut vix me recolligere potuerim. Tu, si singulatim omnia quibus tum obruebar tibi enumerarem, justum meum esse dolorem agnosceres. Illud vero hactenus aliquatenus animum solatur meum, quod paucissimis, et vix aliis nisi quorum interest, innotuerit: nam et nos, quantum possumus, etiam alias intimæ admissionis amicis, celatum volumus. Ita spero fideli hoc amicorum silentio filio meo nullam hoc quicquid damni passus est resarciendi præcidendam occasionem. Credidit sibi cum homine candido et sincero rem esse, ideoque nullam fraudem metuit; atque ita credulitate nimiâ fraudi opportunus fuit. Deus spero honestis ejus laboribus benedicet, et
― 76 ―
imposterum ab ejusmodi fraudulentorum hominum imposturis præservabit. Ego ad studia, hoc infœlici casu multum languentia, reversus sum, recuperatâ jam sanitate quæ valde afflicta fuit. Relegi epistolam tuam; video nihil eam continere quod promtum responsum flagitet; attamen benevolus tuus, quo propositum meum promovere contendis, affectus citius merebatur responsum: tu autem tarditatem facile condonabis mœrori meo.
(English) De Bilibrâ†1 hic apud nos altum est silentium. Verum vidi Reverendissimum Episcopum Bathoniensem ac Wellensem in præfatione tertiæ partis contra Judæos, eam breviter et generatim oppugnasse.†2 Ego velim genuinum controversiæ statum ingenue ac terminis minime ambiguis proponi, et argumenta candide ac solide in utramque partem expendi; quod prolixiorem tractatum, et animum non studio partium abreptum, sed veritatis sincerè studiosum requirit. Prodiit hac hyeme liber Gallice scriptus, cui autor titulum præfixit, le Platonisme devoilé.†3 Autorem jam obiisse præfatio docet. Dicitur in Angliâ scriptus, indeque huc missus ut in lucem edatur. Quamvis eruditus sit tractatus, multis displiciturum credo: et licet ego discrepantes de religione sententias sine ullâ
― 77 ―
erga autores indignatione investigare soleo; non possum tamen dissimulare, aculeatos ipsius sarcasmos in materiâ sacrâ mihi quam maxime displicere. Licet enim credere posset, adversarios quos oppugnat illos meruisse; materiæ tamen quam tractat majestas cohibere eum debuisset, ne hic quicquam gravitati Christianæ adversum immisceret. Tum et prudentiæ fuit, mordacibus ejusmodi sarcasmis adversariorum contra se ac suos indignationem, alias satis acrem, non magis exacerbare. Audio plura illius exemplaria in Angliam esse missa: quare a te visum esse nullus dubito.
(English) Burmanni filios, dehortantibus nequicquam amicis, contra me tractatum scripsisse ajunt, eumque jam sub prælo esse, et brevi proditurum.†1 Waijenum habuere continuum instigatorem, qui cum Burmannum purgare non potuit, illius filios in me concitavit, ut ipsi sub specioso defendendi patris prætextu, inanem in se ac inglorium laborem susciperent: Non enim verba parentis sui, nec Spinozæ, è libris editis eradere possunt; neque inficiari, eadem esse quæ in Spinoza, et parentis sui Synopsi Theologiæ leguntur verba. Quæstio facti est, quæ prolatis ex utroque autore testimoniis, in dubium vocari nequit. Ego talia scripta maximâ animi serenitate
― 78 ―
contemnere possum. Vale Vir Amplissime. Salveat Domina Masham cum totâ familia. Omnes mei te salutant.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS À LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 11 Maji
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I should not wish you to think that it is through any forgetfulness of you that I have hitherto been silent about your very friendly letter. Many things have delayed my reply: chiefly indeed that sad mischance of my son's, which is sufficiently known to you, and the grief caused by it; grief the more violent in the first dismay at the sudden and altogether unforeseen misfortune, which so distressed my spirit that I could scarcely collect myself. If I should tell you one by one all the things by which I was then overwhelmed you would acknowledge that my sorrow was reasonable. But so far one thing somewhat comforts me, that it has become known to very few persons, and scarcely to any except those concerned, for we want to keep it secret, so far as we can, even from those who are otherwise intimate friends. I accordingly hope that, thanks to this sure silence of friends, my son will be deprived of no opportunity of repairing whatever loss he has suffered. He believed that he was dealing with a candid and upright man, and so did not fear any deceit; and thus by too great trustfulness made himself liable to be deceived. I hope that God will bless his honest labours and preserve him in future [p. 75] from the frauds of such deceitful men. Having now recovered my health, which was exceedingly troubled, I have returned to studies that were languishing owing to this unhappy mischance. I have read your letter again. I see that it contains nothing that demands a quick answer; nevertheless your kindness in striving to advance my design deserved a speedier answer; you will readily forgive my slowness in view of my grief.
(Latin) Here with us there is a profound silence about the Bilibra.†1 But I have seen that the Right Reverend the Bishop of Bath and Wells has assailed it briefly and in general in the preface to his third part against the Jews.†2 I could wish that the genuine state of the controversy were set out frankly and in unambiguous terms, and that the arguments on either side were candidly and solidly weighed; which requires a lengthier treatise and a spirit not carried away by zeal for party but sincerely desirous of truth. This winter there has appeared a book written in French to which the author has prefixed a title, Le Platonisme dévoilé.†3 The preface says that the author is now dead. It is said to have been written in England and thence sent here to be published. Although the treatise is erudite I believe that it will displease many; and although I am wont to investigate differing opinions about religion without [p. 76] any anger towards their authors, yet I cannot conceal that his stinging sarcasms in dealing with a sacred subject displease me very greatly. For although he could believe that the adversaries whom he assails had deserved them, yet the majesty of the subject that he is treating ought to have restrained him from intermixing here anything adverse to Christian gravity. Then, too, it would have been prudent not to provoke further by such biting sarcasms the anger of adversaries against himself and his fellows, which was sharp enough for other reasons. I hear that many copies of the book have been sent to England, so do not doubt that you have seen it.
(Latin) They say that Burman's sons, their friends dissuading them in vain, have written a treatise against me, and that it is now in the press and will shortly appear.†1 They had van der Waeyen as a persistent instigator: since he could not exculpate Burman he stirred up his sons against me, to undertake a task, empty in itself and inglorious, under the specious pretext of defending their father. For they cannot erase their father's words, or Spinoza's, from published books; or deny that the same words are to be read in Spinoza and in their father's Synopsis Theologiæ. It is a question of fact: when the evidence from both authors is produced it cannot be called in question. I can disregard such writings with the greatest calmness of mind. Good-bye, [p. 77] excellent Sir. Please give my regards to Lady Masham and her whole family. All mine send you their greetings.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH

B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 210-11. Date: Toinard apparently visited Orleans after he had received no. 2717 of 23 April/4 May; he wrote after his return to Paris; allowing four days for transmission of the letter and a week for the visit, this gives 4/15 May as a terminus post quem. Locke's Journal suggests that he travelled to London on 13/24 May; he received the letter five days later: no. 2726; this gives a terminus ante quem of 14/25 May. The date can perhaps be narrowed further: Toinard expects Du Bos 'dans huit ou dix jours'; Du Bos wrote from Beauvais on 3/14 May that he could not be in Paris 'avant quinze jours' (Lombard, no. 104); the two statements taken together indicate roughly a date about 8/19-10/21 May. The letter answers nos. 2707 and 2717, and is answered by nos. 2726 and 2728.
+
Depuis les deux letres que vous m'avez fait l'honneur de m'ecrire, j'ay eté obligé de partir precipitamment à cause de la nouvele de
― 79 ―
l'extremité de maladie où etoit une de mes sœurs qui me mandoit, et qui est la seule que j'aye dans le monde.†1 Je l'ay trouvèe en meilleure santé que ne portoient les diferentes letres efraïantes que l'on m'avoit ecrites sur son sujet, et l'aiant vuë en parfaite convalescence je m'en suis revenu ici. Il y avoit dix années que l'on ne m'avoit vu en mon païs, et personne ne m'y a meconnu. Tout au contraire tout le monde dit que je me porte mieux que je ne faisois lorsque j'en partis, et je souhaite que vous me diriez la même choze par raport à notre derniere entrevuë si jamais je suis assez heureux pour vous pouvoir embrasser. Je ne vous flate point quand je vous dis que je le souhaite passionêment, et je partirois dez demain pour jouïr de cete satisfaction, si un cruel procez dont l'evenement est fort douteux, ne me retenoit ici. Personne ne fait la moindre dificulté touchant mon bon droit; trois de mes parties l'ont reconnu en s'acommodant avec moi, mais les trois autres se croiant plus puissantes, ne me rendent point de justice ni à eles mêmes. Eles ont extremement de credit, et je n'ay de mon côté qu'un Avocat qui est honête homme, et qui me defend de son mieux par ses ecritures. Jugez si pareille conjoncture ne deconcerte pas fort une harmonie. Toute ma consolation seroit de me plaindre une fois en votre presence de la malheureuse etoille qui me commet avec de pareilles parties qui auroient pu, et même du, me procurer sans peine plus de bien que je n'en peux atendre du gain de mon procez.
Vous voiez bien apres cela que je ne dois pas negliger de vous prier d'avoir soin de la grande loterie. Le Deus è machinâ y sera plustost un Jupiter (id est. Juvans pater)†2 que dans la petite. Au reste je peux vous assurer que l'on donne ici de frequens ordres pour les billets de la grande. Je le vois tous les jours chez un Banquier de ma connoissance, c'est pourquoi ne la laissez pas remplir que je n'en sois.
Vous dites parfaitement bien par le peu de disposition que vous avez trouvée à reformer votre calendrier que les Erreurs se confirment par l'âge. Je nescai cequi arivera d'une Parænesis†3 que je destine pour la celebration de la Pâque. Il me semble que ceque je propose termine toutes les dificultez et n'interesse ni les Grecs ni les Latins, ni les catholiques ni les Protestans.
― 80 ―
J'ay deja regalé m. Gendron†1 du present que vous lui devez envoier, et il vous en remercie par avance.
Quand vous serez à Londres, il sera bon de demander à m. De Worcester la premiere letre du P. Pagi, et sil a repondu aux deux de ce Pere du 10. Decembre 1686. et du 19. Octobre 1687.
Quand vous m'aurez marquè les letres qui vous manquent dans le receuïl en question, je vous en enverrai les copies si vous les dezirez. A l'egard des trois petites que vous avez, je crois les avoir negligées parcequ'eles ne contienent point d'erudition.
Il y a au bas de votre derniere du 23. Avril un langage non chretien que je doneray à expliquer a m. Du Bos quand il sera ici.†2 Je l'atens dans huit ou dix jours. Il est à Beauvais où il receuïlle la succession de m. sa mere, qu'il a perduë depuis peu.
On travaille à diferens essais de la laine des beufs, dits cibola. J'espere vous envoier dans peu des echantillons d'une etofe que je fais faire, et je vous ensegnerai de quelle maniere ele aura eté faite.
L'homme dont je vous demandois des nouveles est Auteur d'une vie du Roi Louïs XIII. qu'il avoit voulu dedier à Mylord Portland, mais il n'a pas voulu acepter cet honeur, et l'on en a suprimè l'Epître dedicatoire. Il y a dans ce livre, que l'on voit ici, des choses choquantes pour le successeur de Louis XIII.†3
J'aurois tort de ne vous pas dire que le capitene de marine me mande de Rome que le jour du vendredi saint le Pape donnant à diner à tout le sacré colege, mons. le card. de coislin et mons. le card. de Noris etant placez l'un aupres de l'autre, l'Eminence Italiene porta ma santé à l'Eminence Françoise qui lui en fit raison. Jugez apres cela si je ne dois pas avoir un grand fond de santé, car revoqueriez en doute l'infaillibité de teles santez?

(Latin) I wish you such e machinâ as you want, and that not only for your sake but also for mine, for you can scarcely conceive how much I detest the suit from which so much evil hangs over you, and from the evil to you over myself. Ill health, growing daily more burdensome, together with age, 'forbids me to entertain far-reaching hopes',†1 and I should bear it ill to be disappointed of a hope so near as was that of seeing and embracing you again when you were lately considering a journey to this country. I anxiously wish that you may be released from your troublesome business in the courts, and myself from this distress. If it is granted to me to enjoy your presence and company again you will fill with joy what remains to me of life. Meanwhile I am very glad that you enjoy such steady health, as your letters testify after a [p. 81] ten years' lack of them.

Je m'aquite, monsieur, de ma parole en vous envoiant cet echantillon, que je vous avois promis, de l'etofe que j'ay fait faire par curiosité du duvet ou laine des beufs Americains, dits cibola. J'atens la piece entiere, qui n'est pas encore bien degressée, comme vous le reconnêtrez par ce morceau que je vien de recevoir. cete couleur est naturele et sans aucune tinture, mais le melange n'en est pas bien fait, et l'ouvrier dit qu'apresent qu'il connoist la nature de cete matiere, il feroit mieux une autre fois. Je le pretens bien ainsi, car je lui feray laver ce duvet dans de l'urine d'homme avant de l'emploier: et j'en feray filer fin sans melange de laine de mouton, dont on fera la treme, et à legard de la chaîne, qui est la seule qui travaille, ele sera composée de deux tiers au moins de cete nouvele matiere, et de prez d'un tiers seulement de laine ordinere, de maniere qu'il y aura dans l'etofe plus de cing sixiêmes de ce duvet de cibola. Quand j'en auray en abondance, et de bien conditioné, comme j'en atends immediatement de mississipi, je porterai la chose plus loin, et je vous en rendrai bon conte si cela vous agreè.
Depuis mon retour de Province, j'ay toujours eté ocupé dans une chicane injuste et desolante, et rien ne poura m'en remetre que le plaisir de vous embrasser, comme je le dezire passionnement. Veillez à ceque je sois de la Loterie, dont j'espere le Deus è machinâ. J'atendray pour cela de vos nouveles.

A Paris ce mardi 8. Juin 700.
Je fus hier, monsieur, tres heureux en recevant en meme tems de lieux tres elognéz des nouveles de deux personnes pour qui j'ay une extreme consideration. vous entendrez bien que c'est de Londres et de Rome où le capitene de marine se porte fort bien, et se plaist plus qu'il ne faisoit au commencement. J'en ay aussi de M. le Card. Noris qui continuë ses bontéz envers moi.
Votre petite Loterie aura commencé à être tirée avant que cete letre arive à Londres puisqu'on nous a dit que cela devoit se faire le 2. de Juin selon votre style, qui est le 13. du nôtre. A legard de la grande cela n'ira pas jusques au 5. de notre mois de Juillet, puisqu'ele doit etre tirée avant le 24. de votre mois de Juin. Ainsi dans peu le Deus è machinâ doit faire aparition en plus d'une maniere.
Je vous suis bien obligé de l'aquisition que vous m'avez faite de Series chronologica et c. du fils de m. l Evêque de Wigorn. On y reconnêtra le Pere.
M. Du Bos est à Beauvais. Je lui ecris et m'aquite de ceque vous m'ordonnez pour lui, et Lundi prochain je ferai la même chose pour le Capitene de marine.
― 86 ―

Quand je me donnay l'honneur de vous ecrire, monsieur, mercredi dernier,†1 j'etois telement pressé par l'heure du courier qu'il a bien pu ariver que je ne me sois pas bien expliqué sur l'avis que vous me donniez touchant les billets que l'on rend de votre grande Loterie. Comme je vous avois prié d'en prendre trois, qui etant de 20. chelins chacun en font soissante, vous en avez pris trois autres dans la petite, qui etant de 5. chelins chacun en font 15. ainsi un seul de la grande en vaut trois de la petite, c'est pourquoi par la conversion des 60. chelins de la grande, il y en aura 12. dans la petite, que feront les 45. qui restent des 60. dont vous n'avez emploié que 15. pour les trois billets de la petite.
De cete maniere la, monsieur, si je me suis bien fait entendre par ma derniere, j'auray à present quinze billets à la petite loterie: à savoir trois d'ancienneté et douze autres par la conversion des trois de la grande qui font ensemble 75. chelins. A cela, monsieur, je vous prie d'ajoûter encore douze billets de la petite qui font 60.

chelins; ainsi je vous serai redevable de 135. chelins, pour 27. billets, que j'aurai par ce moien dans la loterie.

2736. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 19/30 June 1700 (2734, 2737)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 218-20 (f. 220 is the engraving of the two coins mentioned in the letter). Answers nos. 2732 and 2734; answered by no. 2739.
+
mercredi 30. Juin, 1700.
J'ay receu, monsieur, par un même ordinaire vos deux dernieres, cequi me fait croire que le vent a refusé pendant quelques jours, et me fait souvenir qu'en passant un jour de Douvre à Calais le paquebot portoit les letres de catre ordinaires.
L'afaire de la Loterie sera terminée quand cele-ci vous sera rendüe, ou peu s'en faudra, puisque le terme est le 5. Juïllet S.N. mais on ne m'a pas pu bien expliquer ici si l'acte du Parlement porte qu'ele sera entierement tirée avant le 24 Juin S.V. ou si l'on commencera à la tirer avant ce jour la, auquel dernier cas il y auroit plus de tems pour atendre la reüssite du Deus è machinâ.†1
Puisque vous n'avez pas la derniere edition de l'Education des enfans je manderay à m. Halma de me l'envoier avec un certain nouveau livre d'un Otho Sperlingius intitulé: Dissertatio de nummis non cusis, sive pecunia non signata, in quâ negat Samaritanos et Judæos unquam usos esse moneta signata, omnes utriusque gentis nummos esse supposititios. ce sont les termes dont se sert mr Grævius dans une de ses letres du 10. du courant, qu'il m'a fait l'honneur de m'ecrire,†2 par où l'on voit que ce Sperlingius n'entend pas l'etat de la question, ou bien qu'il est fort ignorant dans la connoissance de l'antique en fait de medailles.
A l'egard de l'etat de la question, l'on n'a jamais demandé si les Samaritains avoient monetam signatam necne,†3 puisque c'etoit un miserable peuple qui n'a jamais eu droit de fraper monnoie, et bien moins d'y metre une legende; mais pour cequi est des Juifs j'ay vu et bien examiné plus de cent de leur medailles tant en
― 94 ―
argent qu'en bronze de diferentes grandeurs, types et legendes qu'il n'y a aucun antiquaire qu'il ne reconnoisse pour antiques, à moins de perdre son nom et de faire voir son ignorance: c'est cequi me fait dire avec assurance ou que cet Auteur n'en a jamais vu aucune, ou qu'il n'a pas le moindre discernement de l'antique.
Mais pour venir au fait, et repondre precisement à ceque vous me faites l'honneur de me demander, quel est mon sentiment touchant les sicles hebraïques, et si on peut s'assurer des anciens caracteres hebraïques, je vous diray que j'estime que tout cequ'il y a de sicles et demisicles d'argent où il y a d'un côté pour type la verge d'Aaron, et pour legende en langue Hebraïque, et en caracteres dits Samaritains, Jerusalem Sancta, et de l'autre côté Siclus Israel, ou bien Dimidius Siclus Israel, et pour type une Urne, ont eté frapéz du tems de Judas macabée, et que les letres qui sont sur l'urne marquent les années à Templo per Judam purgato,†1 qui sont catre en nombre sur ces sicles et demi-sicles, dont la premiere est marquée simplement par un Aleph, qui signifie I. id est, Primo, et repond à la 165. anneé qui precede l'Ere Vulgaire de J.Ch. et que dans la seconde il y a sur l'urne une letre de plus avec un Beth, qui Schin et Beth, et font Anno II. parceque Schin est la letre initiale de Schenath, qui signifie annus. Dans la derniere il y a inline image c'est a dire Schin Daleth. Anno IV. parceque Daleth etant la catriême de l'Alphabet, marque IV. et l'année de cete medaille repond par consequent à la 162. avant l'Ere de J.Ch.†2
A l'egard de toutes les autres medailles Judaïques, tant en grand, moien que petit bronze, aussi bien que celes d'argent qui ont seulement le poids d'une drachme qui est le cart du poids d'un sicle, eles sont toutes de Simon, frere et successeur de Judas macabée, et eles portent pour la pluspart son nom tres distinctement, et les autres ne peuvent être que de lui à cause de la ressemblance des types et de la convenance des epoques, car eles en ont toutes. J'en aussi catre, et ce sont les plus rares, où il y a Simon Princeps Israel.†3
La plus recente de ces medailles a eté frapée 139. ans avant l'Ere de J.Ch. et dans la 5. du Pontificat de Simon. On poura quelque jour trouver de ces medailles qui portent un plus grand nombre, car Simon n'est mort que dans la 135. année avant l'Ere de J.Ch.
― 95 ―
Outre cela j'ay eu depuis peu trois medailles d'Antigonus dernier Roy des Juifs de la race des Hasmoneens, où il y a des caracteres semblables à ceux qui sont dans celes de Judas et de Simon, et leur frape n'a pu être au plutost que dans la 40. année avant notre Ere Vulgaire, auquel tems apres la Pentecôte Antigonus s'empara de la Judée, aiant destitué Hyrcan, son oncle paternel. c'est une chose etonnante qu'il ait emploié cete sorte de caracteres qui causent assez de surprise dans les medailles de Simon, trisaieul de cet Antigonus. Je vous ay autrefois marqué que cela devoit s'etre pratiqué ad servandum archaïsmum,†1 de même que les legendes des monnoies d'Europe sont Latines, quoique la langue Latine ne soit plus en usage chez les peuples qui font fraper des monnoies avec des legendes Latines.
Apres cela vous entendrez de reste que j'estime que les caracteres dits Samaritains, que l'on voit dans les medailles Judaïques, sont les veritables anciens avec lesquels a eté ecrite la Loi de Moyse et qu'Esdras fit changer afin que les Juifs n'ussent rien de commun avec les Samaritains, chez lesquels ces anciens caracteres etoient en usage, aiant eté donéz à ce peuple lorsqu'il fut envoié pour habiter la Palestine, et y servir le Dieu du païs selon le culte qui lui etoit convenable.
Je crois avoir trouvé par un certain passage in loco peregrino†2 quels sont les caracteres qu'introduisit Esdras, et dont sont ecrites les bibles Hebraïques d'aujourdhui.†3
inline image
Vous avez ci-joint deux estampes de medailles qui n'on point encore paru, non plus que plusieurs autres qui sont dans mon receuïl où il y en a 34. outre six Phenicienes. Je vous prie de ne vous
― 96 ―
en point dessaisir de peur que l'on ne me les soufle. c'est à dire, (parceque vous n'etes pas obligé d'entendre ce terme François,) que quelcun de ceux à qui vous pouriez les confier ne me prevint en les publiant. Je vous y ay marquè par deux petites barres l'endroit d'où l'on doit commencer à les lire dans les revers dont la legende est au tour, car pour l'ecriture qui est dans le champ des deux couronnes l'ordre des lignes marque le commencement des legendes. Les letres pointillées sont celes que j'ay supléeez, et qui ne paroissoient plus dans ces deux medailles, et qui sont distinctement dans d'autres.
Dans la medaille qui est à gauche au dessous de la quelle il y a une ligne d'explication en abregé, le champ porte en trois lignes SiMOUN. NaSIA. ISRAeL. ces trois mots signifient Simon Princeps Israel: où vous remarquerez que i dans SiMOUN. a dans NaSIA, et e dans ISRAèL, sont ajoutéz par suplement de prononciation. Dans le revers où es<t le>†a vase il y a: SeNaT. ECHaT. LeGALaT ISRAeL. ANNO. PRIMO.LIBERTATIS. ISRAEL. Le reste à une otre fois.†1
Il†b- faut encore vous dire que le mot ECHaT n'a que trois letres en Hebreu, quoique vous en contiez 4. capitales dans le Latin. c'est que CH repond à une seule Hebraique.-†b

Samedi ce 3.
Par celle que je me donnay l'honneur de vous ecrire par le dernier ordinere, vous aurez eté fort etonné de voir SiMOUN pour marquer le nom de Simon, et NaSIA, pour marquer sa qualité de
― 97 ―
Princeps. Le peu de tems qui me restoit avant le depart du courier ne me permit de vous dire que la letre O qui est dans le nom de Simon, n'est pas proprement une letre, mais une aspiration repondante au caractere ע dit Aïn, qui precede le Π Pe dans l'Alphabet Hebreu, de même que l'O apelé μικρὸν precede le Π dans l'Alphabet Hebreu.†a Or il est hors de doute que les anciens ont rendu cet Aïn par l'O micron, et que c'est par la comme par d'autres raisons que l'on doit reconnoitre que l'Alphabet Ionique vient des Phœniciens, qui sont les Auteurs des letres, dites Samaritaines, que lon voit dans les ancienes medailles Judaïques. si lon vouloit s'areter à la signification du nom que l'on donne à cete letre Aïn, on trouverroit que c'est parcequ'ele ressemble à un œil, car l'O des medailles est ovale ainsi que l'ouverture de l'œil, qui en Hebreu est dit Aïn. La letre U voiele qui suit apres O dans ce nom de Simon repond à Υ ψιλὸν, qui est l'U des Latins, placéz chez les uns et chez les autres apres le T, mais il devroit être apres l'E, parcequ'il repond au ו des Hebreux, et si vous dresséz la figure inline image que vous lui voyez dans les medailles, ce sera inline image . c'est à dire non un Ψ Psi, mais un Υ avec une petite pointe de moins qu'il avoit au dedans, et que ceux qui ont adopté cete letre ont negligé de metre afin que la letre s'ecrivist plus prontement. Or comme Υ des Grecs et l'U des Latins sont une même chose, de la vient que dans plusieurs medailles Greques on voit un V bien formè pour un Υ, parcequ'il aura semblé plus facile de faire deux lignes droites que deux recourbeés par enhaut. Par la même raison la figure inline image qui fait la letre M dans le nom de SiMON, etant dressée, sera inline image d'ou otant la queüe qui est en haut, vous aurez le M des Grecs et des Latins. Mais sans rien suprimer dans le Lamed, les uns et les autres ont pris sa figure inline image comme ele est dans des inscriptions que jay veües qui ont environ deux mille ans, et dans les ancienes monnoies Romaines. ceux qui sont venus depuis ont cru que la figure L etoit plus aiseé à faire, et par la ele s'est introduite au prejudice de cele de inline image Je sortirois de mon sujet si je vous en disois presentement davantage. Il reste le mot de NaSIA, sur lequel je dois observer que la derniere letre A est un Aleph muet apres l'Iod, et que l'on lit simplement NaSI, comme si l'Aleph etoit un H, huitiême letre de l'Alphabet Latin, et qu'il y eust NaSIH, de maniere que pour que vous lisiez ces deux mots de Simon et Nasi, par raport aux caracteres Samaritains', les voici en Hebreu אישׁנ ןועמשׁ.
― 98 ―
Je ferois conscience de vous fatiguer plus longtems par des matieres aussi dezagreables que celes-ci vous le peuvent être, et à quoi je me suis engagé plus que je ne pensois, et seulement pour vous dire quel est mon sentiment sur ces medailles dites Samaritaines.
Je ne saurois vous exprimer la joie que je ressens par la continuité de vos letres qui m'est un temoignage de votre santé, et je vous prie de m'en donner de frequentes marques.
J'ajouterai encore ici que l'on peut letre pour letre rendre en Latin ןועמשׁ par SiMHON, emploiant l'H pour ע Aïn.

Je me fis l'honeur de vous ecrire une letre Monsieur il y a environ huit jours par la quelle je vous marquai les lots qui vous ont êtez un peu favourablez. En fin Monsieur Cunningham (que je vous a nommè pus d'une fois) parte pour Paris. Je lui a mis entre les mains le livre des Series——et le liste de lots fortunès que vous pouvez examiner a loisir pour y trouver des autres à votre avantage que je pourrois avoir passèz. 2742. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 9/20 July 1700 (2724, 2795)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 137-8. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, f. 189. Printed from the copy in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 461-3. Answered by no. 2866.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Ante hebdomadas aliquot tuo nomine mihi datus est præstantissimus tuus de intellectu humano liber in linguam Gallicam versus.†2
― 102 ―
Pro eximio illo dono grates tibi quas possum maximas ago. Nondum eum legere potui: Verum nunc instant feriæ meæ, quibus illius lectionem destinavi. Materiæ enim quæ in illo tractatur gravitas ac varietas, quam ex capitum indice didici, summam animi attentionem, et continuatam minimeque interruptam lectionem requirit. Itaque tempus quo à quotidianis negotiis immunitatem habeo illi impendam, ut tanto majore meo cum fructu eam evolvam.
(English) Legi in novellis nostratibus, quod et D. Clericus literis tuis confirmavit, te ob ætatem ingravescentem et valetudinem minus firmam honoratissimi muneris tibi ante annos aliquot demandati dimissionem obtinuisse.†1 Equidem institutum tuum minimè improbare possum, quin imo laude dignum censeo, quod extremos vitæ tuæ dies, procul a strepitu politico, quieti, studiis ac meditationibus sacris consecrare, quam negotiis, honestis quidem, attamen nihil ultra vitæ hujus tranquillitatem spectantibus, implicatos habere malueris. Hanc tibi quietem ex animo gratulor, Deumque precor, ut senectutem tuam eximiis, quibus vera paratur felicitas, donis magis magisque exornet, ac quicquid corpusculi viribus decedit, vivaciore mentis acie et spiritus robore compenset.
― 103 ―
(English) Tandem prodiit contra me Burmannorum pietas, is libri titulus est;†1 mole ingens, verbosus, contumeliosus, plurimis declamationibus et invectivis refertus. Illi per D. Crucium, fratrem suum uterinum, à civitate Leidensi in Collegium rerum maritimarum†2 deputatum, mihi pietatis suæ exemplar tradi voluerunt. Legi illam, sed cum nauseâ: et nisi in me scriptus esset liber, lectionem absolvere non potuissem. Illi in eo summis viribus probare nituntur, parentem suum à me Spinozismi accusatum, et eum prolixè excusare contendunt. Ægerrimè ferunt, parenti suo à me adscribi imprudentiam, et quod sine judicio Spinozam secutus sit. Ajunt parentem suum hæc cum judicio ex Spinozà exscripsisse, ut merè Cartesiana: Spinozam enim eo in libro doctrinam suam nec apertè inculcasse, nec tectè insinuasse, sed sola Cartesii dogmata tradidisse. Verum ego non credo Cartesianos pro suis agnituros hæc quatuor: 1. Tota natura naturata†3 non est nisi unicum ens. 2.Possibilitas et contingentia non sunt affectiones rerum, sed intellectus nostri defectus. 3.Si homines clarè totum ordinem naturæ intelligerent, omnia aequè necessaria reperirent, ac omnia illa quæ in Mathesi tractantur. 4.De extraordinariâ Dei potentiâ qua miracula facit, non immeritò
― 104 ―
valde dubitari posse: Quæ tamen omnia in illo Spinozæ libro disertis verbis reperiuntur.†1 Sarcasmis plurimis in parallelismum inter Burmani et Spinozæ verba ludunt: Verum nihil in eo reprehendere aut falsi arguere possunt. Ego illi libro nihil reponam, præsertim cum ob molem suam non distrahatur, et a nemine legatur.
Versiculos in me narratur scribere Cinna:
Non scribit, cujus carmina nemo legit.
(English) Idem mihi cum Martiale dicere licet.†2 Addo: quod quicunque meam contra Waijenum Defensionem legerit, novâ defensione non indigebit: Qui eam legere non vult, illi nec decem apologiis satisfecero. Vale Vir Amplissime. Salveat Domina Masham cum totâ familiâ, cui inclusas has filii mei tradi rogo. Uxor ac liberi te quam officiosissimè salutant, imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Some weeks ago I was given in your name the French translation of your most excellent book concerning the human understanding.†2 I give you my very best thanks for that notable gift. I have not been able to read it as yet, [p. 101] but my holidays, during which I intend to read it, are now near. For the importance and variety of the matter treated in it, which I have learnt from the table of chapters, require very great attention of mind and continuous and well-nigh uninterrupted reading. And so I shall spend on it the time when I have freedom from daily affairs, in order to read it with so much the greater profit for myself.
(Latin) I have read in our newspapers, and Mr. Le Clerc has confirmed it from your letter, that, on account both of the increasing burden of age and of uncertain health, you have obtained your discharge from the most honourable office entrusted to you some years ago.†1 For my part, I cannot in any way disapprove of your intention—indeed, I deem it worthy of praise: that you have preferred to consecrate the last days of your life, far from the clash of state affairs, to repose, studies, and sacred meditations, rather than to have them entangled in affairs that are indeed honourable but that have regard to nothing beyond tranquillity in this life. I heartily congratulate you on this repose and pray God to provide your old age more and more with those notable gifts whereby true happiness is obtained, and to make good whatever loss there may be of bodily powers by a livelier acuteness of mind and strength of spirit. [p. 102]
(Latin) There has at last appeared against me Burmannorum Pietas; that is the book's title;†1 bulky, wordy, abusive, stuffed with declamation and invective. They wished a copy of their filial piety to be delivered to me by their uterine brother Mijnheer Crucius, deputy of the city of Leyden in the College of Maritime Affairs.†2 I have read it, but with nausea; and if the book had not been written against me I could not have read it to the end. In it they strive with all their might to prove that their father was accused by me of Spinozism, and they labour at great length to excuse him. They take it very ill that I have charged their father with imprudence and with having followed Spinoza injudiciously. They say that he has copied these things from Spinoza judiciously, as being purely Cartesian; for, they say, Spinoza has neither openly inculcated nor covertly insinuated his own doctrine in that book, but has only transmitted Descartes's dogmas. But I do not believe that the Cartesians will acknowledge these four as their own: 1. All natura naturata†3 is only a single entity. 2. Possibility and contingency are not properties of things, but are defects of our understanding. 3. If men clearly understood the whole order of nature they would find all things just as necessary as those that form the subject of mathematics. 4. There may with good cause be great doubt about God's extraordinary power by which He makes miracles. [p. 103] Yet all these things are to be found in express words in that book of Spinoza's.†1 They ridicule with many sarcasms the parallelism between Burman's and Spinoza's words; but they cannot find fault with anything in it or charge it with falsity. I will make no reply to this book, especially because on account of its bulk it is not selling and is being read by nobody.
Cinna writes trifles aimed at me, 'tis said.
No; he writes nothing who is never read.
(Latin) So I can say with Martial.†2 I add: that whoever has read my Defensio against van der Waeyen will not require a fresh defence; I shall not satisfy with ten apologies anyone who is unwilling to read it. Good-bye, excellent Sir. Please give my regards to Lady Masham and the whole family, and please give her the enclosed letter from my son. My wife and children send you their warmest greetings, as do I,
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 20 July

2743. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 9/20 July 1700 (2659, 2835)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 95-6. Apparently forwarded by Le Clerc in October: p. 156.
Monsieur,
la mort de mon bon pere, que Dieu a retiré il y a 3 septmaines a l'age de 98 ans†1 est cause que jay tardé plus long tems a vous remercier du present de la belle traduction de votre livre. il falloit un Monsieur Coste, et vótre exactitude pour la rendre autant fidelle, et d'un si bon stile. je vous assure que vous avez tous deux rendus un grand service au public. la Langue francoise est si universellement connue, et les expressions en sont si naturelles, que bien des gens, qui ne sont pas anglois, auront moin de peine a suivre vos pensees qu'en lisant l'original, je confesse ingenuement que je suis de ce nombre, et jay desja commencé a le lire une nouvelle fois avec toute l'application possible, j'y trouve tousjours de nouvelles lumieres. Monsieur le Clerc m'a dit que vous travaillez a un nouvel ouvrage, pour decouvrir les maladies de l'esprit,†2 c'est une nouvelle obligation que le public vous aura, quel bien ne sera ce pas, si vous pouvez guerir les hommes de leur fausses idees, et les mettre par methode dans le chemin de la verité!
Vous avez abandonné le poste de conseiller au conseil de commerce, nos gazettes nous l'apprennent, cela nous alarme doublement, le public y pert, et c'est sans doubte vótre état foible qui vous y a determiné. toute la famille vous presente ses treshumbles respects, ma femme se porte parfaittement bien, Monsieur Veen vit contant a la campagne, fort subject a une dureté d'oreille, accompagnée de vertiges, ce qui me fait craindre pour luy une mort subite. que faire? il faut finir une fois, Mon pere avoit constammant un appetit devorant, cela le soutenoit merveilleusement. a la
― 106 ―
fin peu de chose la enlevé. il est mort sans fievre, ses forces l'abandonnant petit a petit. je suis avec un profond respect,
Monsieur,
Votre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON
d'Amst. ce 20 juillet 1700
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke Londres

2746. Pierre Coste to Locke, 12 July 1700 (2609)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 149-50. Printed by G. Bonno in Revue de littérature comparée, xxxiii (1959), 178-9.
Monsieur,
Je vous suis bien obligé de la peine que vous avez pris de m'envoyer la Lettre de Mr. DelaMotte. Comme je pourrai bientôt vous remercier de bouche, ce n'est pas directement pour cela que je vous écris, mais pour vous faire savoir quelques petites choses qu'on me mande de Hollande.
Le Libraire qui a imprimé votre Livre en François,†1 me fait savoir qu'il a présentement, Les Loix Civiles dans leur ordre naturel, 5. Voll. in 4°. Edit. de Paris.†2 Si Mr. King veut avoir ce Livre, ce Libraire les luy enverra.
― 108 ―
Mrs. Limborch, Guenellon et Veen ont reçu chacun un Exemplaire de votre Livre, qui leur a été présenté de vôtre part. Mr. Limborch a dit depuis peu à Mr. DelaMotte qu'il vous écriroit bientôt pour vous remercier.
Il y a cinq ou six jours que les Exemplaires pour Mrs. Toinard et Du Bose sont partis. Mr. DelaMotte en a donné avis à Mr. Toinard. Un Libraire de Paris a demandé un certain nombre de vôtre Livre au Libraire de Hollande.
Mr. LeClerc a donné deux Exemplaires de ses Quæstiones Hieronymianæ†1 à un Libraire de Londres, nommé Buckley. Un de ces Exemplaires est pour vous, et l'autre pour moy. Mr. LeClerc vous écrira au premier jour.
J'avois résolu, Monsieur, de vous faire présent d'un Exemplaire de ma Traduction, mais le Libraire m'a voulu priver de ce plaisir en vous l'envoyant luy-même. Je croy qu'il est déja arrivé à Londres cet Exemplaire.†2 Celui qui le porte, a ordre de le remettre à un certain Mr. Foubert, Marchand de vin qui loge in Leicester-fields near Panton-street at the two white balls. Si vous y envoyez quelqu'un, il n'a qu'à le demander en mon nom, on le luy donnera, si on l'a reçu. On m'a envoyé par une autre occasion un Exemplaire que je destine à Madame. Il est déja arrivé. C'est chez un Marchand Parfumeur nommé Gimbal in the Strand neare Tonne-Tavern. Je luy écris un mot pour le prier de donner cet Exemplaire à celui qui luy donnera ma lettre. Je vous prie de charger James†3 de cette commission, et du soin de porter le Livre avec luy en venant à Oates. Je vous demande bien pardon de la liberté que je prens. Je ne vois guere d'autre voye pour avoir cet Exemplaire si tôt et si surement. Nous vous attendons avec impatience. Je suis avec un profond respect,
Monsieur,
Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
COSTE.

2747. Locke to Edward Clarke, 16 July 1700 (2719, 2759)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 150. Printed in Rand, p. 558.
London 16 Jul 1700
Dear Sir
Your verses and your news were both good and both welcome. My wife had told me before that you and Mr Freke got well to Tunbridg. I am extremly glad to hear that you find benefit by the waters already: This is the welcomest news I could hear from thence. I hope they will soon restore you to your former good temper and that you will bring away from thence a vigorous and well established health.
My Lord privy seals death is I suppose noe news to you there.†1 And some little talke of a new parliament†a that has been revived here since you went I conclude you will not think worth mentioning†2
I hope tomorrow to be deliverd out of this town. I have been very uneasy in it since you went, and breath in pain whilst I write this. Disturb not your waters with writeing or any other thought-fulnesse and beleive me
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant

A Paris le 28 de Juillet
Ce nest point par negligence monsieur que jay esté si lontemps sans vous escrire mais pour avoir esté absent de Paris depuis quatre mois. il i a environ ce temps que je perdis ma mere qui demeuroit en province et les affaires que sa mort ma donnees ne mont point permis de revenir a Paris plutost que la semaine derniere.
Jay publié ma response a ceux qui ont escrit contre lhistoire des quatre Gordiens:†1 cest une petite brochure qui ne vous fatiguera point beaucoup a lire et Jen ai mis un exemplaire a votre adresse dans un pacquet que jay adressé a monsieur Robert Cuninghuam.†2
monsieur Perrault a donné son second volume des illustres Francois le quel en contient cinquante, cest autant quil i en avoit dans le premier. vous auré entendu dire dans le temps que lon l'obligea doster de ce premier volume monsieur Arnaud et monsieur Pascal. je lui donné pour lors un advis dont il a profité, cestoit de mettre des protestants dans son receuil pour faire voir quil ne si agissoit point dorthodoxie. il a doné place dans ce Second volume Blondel Bochard Joseph Scaliger outre plusieurs gens de guerre de la religion protestante et il a remis dans le premier monsieur Pascal et monsieur Arnauld.†3

lon vient de publier une dissertation sur les dents sans non d'autheur qui est fort estimee pour ce quelle contient.
la querelle des Jesuites et des missionaires francois de la Chine sur le culte de confucius et les honneurs rendu aux morts est ici tres echaufee et chaque jours il se publie des livrets de chaque costé ou lon faict son possible pour rendre ses adversaires odieux et pour faire croire aux public que la tolerance des uns pour les ceremonies Chinoises est un effet de leur indifference pour le Christianisme et que le zele des autres est causé purement par leur Jalousie. tantæne animis Cælestibus iræ.†1 la Sorbone doît entrer dans cette querelle et elle va examiner une proposition de la lettre du p. Le Comte, que les chinois ont conservé la veritable religion jusques aux temps de Jesus christ.†2
lon debite ici un livre dont lon conoit l'autheur et auxquel livre monsieur de Saint Evremont na non plus contribué que vous et moy et dont ce pendant voici le titre Saint Evremontiana ou bons mots et pensees de monsieur de Saint Evremont. une pareille audace faict faire bien des reflexions sur ce qui a pu ariver avant que limpremerie fut inventee et lorsque les livres nestoient pas encore aussi comuns. probablement ce livre passera dans un siecle pour estre de mr de st Evremont. il paroistra par sa datte et par les Journaux quil aura esté imprimé du vivant de celui dont il porte le non et pour ainsi dire a sa porte. il est vray que monsieur de St Evremont le desavouera mais ce desaveu sera contenu dans quelques lettres a ses amis les quelles periront et le livre subsistera.†3

Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur

2754. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 9/20 August 1700 (2700, 2761)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 159-60.
Rotterdam 20 August 1700
Dear Sir.
Ever since receit of yours of 30 march by our sons, I have liv'd in hopes, with my wife and son Arent of seing you, and that honourable family with whom you reside, and to have paid my thanks, in person, for the great kindness shewd them, when there, which now I intreat you to doe: seing I cannot yet be so happy. But a Nephew, son of my Nephew Benjamin of Colchester,†1 being at present here returning home, we have resolvd my son Arent shall go with him, and stay in England, till his mother and I, come next summer and fetch him, hoping he will in that time have perfected his English. My son John I have placed at Norwich to learn the manufacture of that place,†2 and serve for a factor, when his time is out, to such of my acquaintance here, and in Amsterdam, as have their goods from thence, which if he behave himself soberly, as I hope he will, wilbe of great advantage to him. I guesse by that Arent gets to Colchester, that he may be there; The Apprentices of Norwich having every harvest time 6 weeks vacation. So I design he shall accompany his brother to London. And in their passage thither, wayt upon you.
Where to place Arent in England I am yet uncertain, Very willingly would I have him under your good Ey and instruction, could a place be found in the village near you, and if it might be
― 118 ―
that he might be your Amanuensis: as being well assured it would be advantageous to him in his studyes: For tho, for reasons I have sub rosa acquainted him with, I cannot promise my self, nor him, that he shall for the future be bred to his studyes alone, yet I would not have him lose, but increase what he has. His whole bent would be, if it might be, that way, but I tell him 'tis so hazardous to rely upon that, alone, for a comfortable, moderate subsistence in the world, merely by literature,†1 that he must think upon some other imploy. His heart is so intent upon books and learning, that he would have me place him with mr. Leers, His choice is not ill. But Leers is furnisht at present, so that what to do with him, I know not, but he is but 15 years and a half old yet, so may spend a year and half yet in his studyes. In this Cuntry to breed him to a Doctor, is to expose him to penury, almost, and not much better for a Lawyer, for many years, except a young man very much excels indeed, and has very good friends to recommend and help him forward. And for the other Learned craft and Craftsmen, you know, I cannot possibly have bred him to have any tolerable reverence for it or them, I mean the art of wrangling about words that most what signify nothing; about which the great High-Waymen of the Church, do ram and damn one another, whose work it is to rob men of their civil and spirituall libertyes, and to pick out their eyes that they may follow them blindfold: From whom and their Artifices Libera nos Domine.
I have not bred my children, to the learning of any their Gibberish Articles, but onely to understand and practice that Religion, which Jesus christ <taught>,†a whom I instruct them to be the Saviour of all men, and not of one party, sect or kirk alone, which is most plain and easy, that is to love and honour God above all, and their neighbour as themselvs, to walk humbly, act righteously towards all, and to shew mercy, and practice charity where it is needed: and to have nothing to do with any of the wrangling Crew, heaps†2 or sects, because they all arrogate themselvs the glorious name of the church of Christ: nor to join with any of them, as such, against all the rest, Till they shall meet with a society of men, that shalbe
― 119 ―
able to prove their title by those signs that Christ said should attend his true church in the world.
I heartily congratulate your resignation, and discharge from secular affairs, of which we have been informd by the Gazets:†1 and hope we shall see the effects of your regained leisure houres. I presume that it wilbe no unpleasant news to you to heare that the affaires in the North are terminated betwixt the Dane and Holsteyner, the former paying the balls†2 for the disturbance he has given, and the later instated in his rights.†3 Now the Swede wilbe at liberty to reckon with the Duke of Saxony alias K. of Poland, who could obtain no assistance from that cautious Republik, who seing the snare, kept their hands at home.†4
'Twil I fancy not be irksome to you, to relate a very remarkable thing happend here last week, about a broad-Phylactery-man, a Deacon of the kirk, forsooth, and father, or Governour of that house of charity of this town, nigh the port,†5 that leads to the dwelling of our friend the Burgermaster—This man was composed of nothing but religious gravity, long and lowd prayers, an exemplary starcht conversation, a painted sepulcher without, but of a most lewd, and vile deportment behind the curtain, who, having sworn to watch over the yong orphans of the house, that no lewdness, nor wantonness be practisd betwixt the lads and lasses; forced two of them, and by threats and treats brought others to satisfy his goatish lust: till at last he so treated a girl (ni fallor)†6 of 14 years old, that the child could not with ease sit, who being askt the reason of her uneasyness, told it to an ancient woman of the house; so inquiry was privatly made whether others were not so handled by him, and he so watcht that he was seen to act his villany. Complaint was made to our Ballju,†7 the thing became a publick talk, He was advisd to pack him away if guilty, But instead of that he scornd it vaunted of his Innocency, said that the godly must go thro' ill, as well as good report, and the righteous be bold as a yong lyon. At length the Ballju (a brave man) cites him up, layes attestations
― 120 ―
before him, produces witnesses, confronts them together. The Parsons espouse his cause, cry shame that eare should be given to such malicious persons, to the stayning the reputation of so holy a man, say that more defference was to be given to his obtestation of the name of god in his own compurgation, than to such persons, who were become his enemys for the severe discipline he practisd among them—So that the Judges let him go 2 or 3 times till the Ballju grew earnest, and got him detaynd. And at last told him it was the utmost impudence to outbrazen such evidence. And that he must bring him to the Torture, giving him time to bethink himself, and ordring him to his chamber, but before he went out, he acknowledged all; begging for pardon; But finding none, (as the custome here is) he was brought into the open street, there to confess his crimes, during which time his heart so faild him, that he was fain to be sustain'd by 2 men from falling. Yet, by the converse of his ghostly fathers, and som of their disciples, he recoverd so much his spirits, and courage, and assurance of his election and salvation, that no man was ever seen, they say, to dy so unconcernd, to the admiration of all that had se<en>†a him 3 days before: his crimes are now so extenuated, and holyness so highly cryed up, that the Judges are by some reflected upon, as having gone to, if not beyond, the rigour of the Law in beheading him, of which they being aware, before they would condemn him they consulted the ablest lawyers in the hague, who unanimously said they must condemn him to dye.
I have troubled you and my self with this relation because of the remarkableness of the thing and so I rest
Sir
Your most humble servant
B F

2755. Locke to Cornelius Lyde, 10 August 1700 (2735, 3034)
The Pierpont Morgan Library, New York. Transcribed from Xerox print. Answers no. 2735.
Oates 10 Aug 1700
Sir
I writ to you before I left London to acknowled the favour of yours of June 19th and to authorize you to pay to my Cosin King what mony you have in your hands according as you desire in that lettre I spoke to my Cosin King about it before he went the circuit and about some other things in your lettre which he will acquaint you with when he sees you. I come now to some other parts of your lettre which I could not soe well answer in town for want of my papers which were here in the country
As to Hannys debt such loose promises as he makes to pay some here after but cannot yet I seldom finde produce any thing. But how he is to be brought to pay me what he owes me and what ways he is to be pressed soe as to get it all at once or by parcels I must leave to you
I know that Jos: Barnes pretended to an abatement of 20s per year for the last year of my Cosin Strattons management. But my Cosin Stratton gave me noe notice of any such abatement, nor did Barnes pretend to it that I know till my Cosin Strattons death. For the year 94 my Cosin Stratton received £25. And for the year ending the 25o Mar. 95. my Cosin Stratton accounts to me received in mony and bills £25. You say in your letter that you find by my Cosin Strattons receits that he received but £24. If he gave any receit for £24 in full for a years rent I think it ought to be allowed him as good and that his bargain was then but £24 by the year. And if that be soe I shall say noe more. But then it will be strange to me that my Cosin Stratton should account to me £25 received and give him a receit in full for £24. But to conclude this matter as I told you in mine of 23 Feb 1699/700 If that receit of my Cosin Strattons be certainly soe, or else that you at any time allowed†a- him that-†a 20s as if it had been his bargain with my Cosin Stratton or upon any consideration forgave it him I shall looke upon my self as satisfied and never mention it more But if by none of these ways he has a right to it, then it is still due to me and I have noe reason to give it
― 122 ―
him. It will be better bestowed on the poor. But in this matter I refer my self wholy to you and my Cosin King
As to William Gullock. I think if you look upon my letter of 23 Feb again you will finde that you have mistaken the £1-12-4 for what it is not. For I doe not charge it on him there as what was due for his 1/6 of the taxes paid for the year ending 25 Mar 97 But I charge it there, as an additional arear which he left un paid by all he had paid you when you sent me your account 6o Jan 97/8. For all that I account due to me from him for the year ending 25o Mar 97 is for rent £2-10-0 for 1/6 of taxes and Lords rent £1-6-4 which is just the same that you make it bateing 4d of which 4d I gave you an account in that letter. Soe that his part of the taxes for that year being allowed to be†a- but £1-6-4-†a he neverthelesse owed me 1o Jul. 99 £9-7-5 or if you think that 4d is to be abated it will still be——£9-7-1. For which debt whether you think it best to take his bond to be paid as he proposes I must leave it to you and my Cosin King to consider togeather. I beg your pardon for this trouble and am Sir
your most humble and obleiged servant
JLOCKE
I desire you would deliver the inclosed to my Cosin King

La letre de change que vous m'envoiâts Monsieur ariva en son temps et Monsieur Philibert à payè le £4-19-0 à mon ordre. Mais permettez moi de dire que vous etez trop pressè de payer cet argent, nous aurions meux adjustè notre compte quand j'aurois l'honeur de vous voir en Angleterre parceque les livres que vous mavez envoiez à ma requête devoient y entrer mais j'ay donnè ordre à Monsieur Cunningham†2 à les payer

Je suis bien aise que Monsieur Du Bos est de retour à Paris. J'ay recue l honeur de sa lettre du 28 de Juilet.†3 à qui j'e reponderais par la premiere occasion en attendant je lui baise les mains tres humblement

2761. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 18/29 August 1700 (2754, 2767)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 161-2.
Rotterdam 29 August 1700
Deare Sir
Till mine of the 20th. Currant was gone, I was not informd, that my whole project of having my Arent, who is bearer hereof, being near you, in the Village, was impracticable, because, as I now understand, by our sons, Sir Francis dwells 3 miles distant from any Village.†1 So that I am at a losse how to dispose of him, or where to settle him this winter. For I dare not propound his stay in the House; tho' I dare undertake for him, he will be as little burthensome, where ever he is, as its possible for any lad of his years, to be.
However I hope Sir Francis and my Lady wilbe pleasd, at your request to let him stay, till by your, or my Lord Shaftesburyes means,†2 I can find some convenient place, where he may stay, to learne English better, and french, if it can be, and not go backward in his latine and Greek—
I have since my last, discourst the Rector here, who intreats me, not for any gain of his, for he saith hele teach him, with pleasure for nothing, to have him but one year to initiate him in the study of the civill Law. Because the method he shall observe with him, will, tho he should not study further in that faculty, be of great Advantage to him, towards the forming his understanding, in what soever stile of life I shall think fit to train him up to. He says its a pleasure to teach him, and he doubts but as he shall have honour of him, I shall have full satisfaction. He gives me Instance of severall that never studyed the Law but <with>†b him, who
― 127 ―
having their promotion at Leyden have had great practice in this Towne, whom I have known, to be the ablest Lawyers in this Town in my time.
So that he has half a promise from me that Arent shal study, at lest one year with him.
This day the Professor Noodt†1 of Leyden honoured me with a visit, and understanding that my son was bound for England, and like to see you, desired his service might be presented to you. he is a hearty man and lover of liberty. And the talk of as well as the wonder of the cuntrey, that he is not dispossessed of his charge, for a free oration of his last yeare, as the Professor De Volder the year before.†2 Both which Arent will give you—
While I am writing this, in comes unexpectedly One of my Cousins from Colchester [Jonathan],†a †3 who desires that Arent may not goe with this ship, but stay and goe with him, who has ingaged to bring him to Oates, so I have thought fit to send this letter forward by post, in hopes that I may receive a letter from you, ere his departure hence, which I humbly pray; I understand my son John is at present at Colchester, at my Nephew Johns;†4 So with my wives and my and our sons humble service to your self, Sir Francis and My Lady Masham with their whole family I rest
Dear Sir
your humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
P.S. my Dearest understanding that possibly Arent cannot be near you, askt me where the child should be, I told her possibly, with Monsieur Le Cene,†5 at which she was troubled and said she had rather he should not go at all, for she would not trust him, with his wife whom she looks upon to be of no good humour, and so was afraid he might be brought out of his owne temper.
So I told her that I did not doubt but betwixt my Lord Shaftesbury and yourself you would dispose of him, where he should
― 128 ―
receive no harm: which pacifyed her: she has a great love, and tender care for him

2763. Locke to Edward Clarke, 23 August 1700 (2759, 2768)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, ff. 91, 90. Letter from Oates, sealed and addressed, and letter enclosing it from Matching Tye. Part of the enclosing letter printed in Forster, p. 63; parts of both letters, in Fox Bourne, ii. 479; the whole, in Rand, pp. 560-1.
― 129 ―
[The original letter:]
Oates 23 Aug 1700
Dear Sir
I cannot but be mightily concerned for the ill state of your health which I received an account of yesterday in yours of the 18th from Tunbridg. My Lady being by when I received it enquired how you did and was sorry to find the waters had had noe better effect upon you. She desired me, hearing that you were in town by this time, to invite you and my wife down hither to trie what this air will doe. She says we will all take a great deale of care of you and trie every one to rectifie your spleen. She very earnestly importunes you to make the triall if it be but for change sake which is good in such cases, and to get out of the town air and smoak which she thinks good in noe distemper. I joyn heartily with her in it, and think you cannot doe a better thing. Mrs Clarkes comeing to town need be noe objection. For though you have sent to her to meet you there, tis likely that will not be presently, you will have notice before of the time, And this place is but at the towns end, you can be presently there upon the least warning. Come then and doe not dispair but we will be merry, and find something to confound your spleen in spight of its perversness: My service to my wife and the Batchelor. All here give their service to you all three I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
If you <heare>†a of the Kings return†1 you will doe me a kindness to let me know

Dear Sir
Carrying the inclosed my self to Mr Jocelin†2 by whom it goes to the post I found there yours of yesterday with the inclosed from

Dear Sir

2768. Locke to Edward Clarke, 2 September 1700 (2763, 2772)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, ff. 92-3. The two leaves are detached; the text is on f. 92; the address and endorsement are on f. 93; the link between the two is the endorsement. Printed in Ollion, pp. 245-6; Rand, pp. 562-3.
Oates 2 Sept 1700
Dear Sir
I have both before and since yours of the 27th of Aug: thought over and over again of the state of your health. And after all the Considerations I have had about it I have these things to propose for the reestablishing of it Either that you take the Jesuits pouder and steele made into pils togeather, Or that you goe away to the Spaw and drink the Spaw waters. If you take the steel pils you must resolve to take them a good while togeather and ride with them every day without which I doe not expect they should have any great effect. And your rideing must not be for an hour or two but soe much and soe long every day as when a man travels a journey. The preparation of steel I should think best in the case, is a preparation of it of Dr Sydenhams made with Extract of Gentia<n>†a which I beleive is to be had at Mr Maltus's,†1 But if any physitian you shall consult there (for that I think is necessary) shall think better of any other preparation of steel to be used with the Jesuits pouder I think it noe great matter if an other be taken in
― 134 ―
stead of that preparation of Dr Sydenhams. But this I think, considering the time of the year, Noe time should be lost, I therefor write this to you not knowing when a swelling lately risen in my back will let me come to town. They who have seen it by its bigness and redness think it a Boyle. I something doubt of it because it has noe head upon it nor is soe extreme <painful>†a as to answer that name though it be tender enough to keep me from airing on horse back these two or three days. What it will come to I know not But to keep my self quiet I find necessary. And an oyntment I use to it I hope will bring it to breake in a little time. I long mightily to see you and since rideing and the air is good for you why should any thing hinder you from rideing down hither though Mrs Clarke be in town, Espetialy since I can at present bear neither horse nor coach, and if you saw me and how I labour for breath in the morning when I rise you would not think the town air very fit for me. Pray give my humble service to Mrs Clarke and those others that remembered me in your last letter. I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant
JOHN LOCKE
My Lady Masham is heartily concerned for your health and gives you and Mrs Clarke Mr Freke and my wife her humble service

2771. Samuel Bold to Locke, 9 September 1700 (2687, 3243)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, ff. 39-40.
Steeple 9th Sept: 1700
Honoured Sir
Having an opportunity to write by a Neighbour to mr Churchill I cannot excuse it to my self, if I should neglect to inclose a letter to you, to return my hearty thanks for your most Noble and Generous Kindness to me when I was last at London,†1 as wel as at other times. When I call to minde (which is not very seldom) what expence you have put your self to on my account, I cannot but bewail your Misfortune in happening to be acquainted with One, who through the Frankness of your own spirit hath bin so very chargable to you. You have honoured me with the Title of your Friend, and you may very justly stile me without a Figure, your very Dear Friend. Since I came into the Countrey I have read Irenicum Magnum,†2 with great pleasure and satisfaction. The weakest part of the Book seem's to me, to be p. 120. There is yet another Argument etc to the end of the Answer to that Argument. I wil not trouble you with what occurred to me when reading It, both as to the Instances mentioned before we come to his Answer, and as to some of the things He answers. I am apt to think that if the Author had added p. 120, after, Determining, Magisterially, He would not have apprehended the Argument very considerable. And without that addition I conceive It doth not reach the matter in hand. I have not read over Dr Whitby on the Epistles,†3 But so far as I have gone, He appears to me to be the best I have mett with, tho I have different sentiments from him as to the meaning of many passages. He writes some things in opposition to the Reasonableness of Christianity,†4 but what He offers gives me no other satisfaction, than that as some others, He did not comprehend what He thought to answer, And so hath published several things not at all to the purpose. What He hath writ against your words, which He quotes, relating to the Resurrection of the same
― 137 ―
Body, I have two plain objections against.
1. That He might have found a very ful and satisfactory Answer in the same book from whence He hath taken your words, if He had read It with due care and Attention, and had been mindeful to distinguish betwixt popular, and strictly philosophical expressions. 2. That what He offers for Arguments wil not consist with what He asserts to be His own Notion about the Resurrection of the Body. I think He would have done wel in asserting the Resurrection of the same Body to be an Article of Faith, to have taken notice that It is so, only to those who admit of his Interpretation of scripture, or who do interpret It to the same effect, tho upon other grounds. I have several other considerations to offer with relation to what the Doctor hath said on this matter, with one that respects the Doctor's not having dealt so fairly and candidly in this matter as I expected from him, But tho I spare you the trouble of reading them, I intend to acquaint the Doctor with them, the first time I see him, or have an opportunity to write to him.†1 My publick discourse to the people of my parish was lately upon this subject; How sinners may be satisfied that upon their hearty consenting to, or faithful complying with the Terms assigned in the Gospel they shal partake of the Blessings there tendered to them? My Answer was By a due consideration of the person who does offer those Blessings there to them; viz. Jesus Christ. This did lead to another question, viz. who this Jesus Christ is? which I answered in the words of the Creed: He is God's only Son, and our Lord. Then I tooke notice That the phrase God's only Son, did signify 1. That He was a person of very great account with God, and with whom God was wel pleased. mat: 3:17. 2. That He is the person God did qualify and appoint or commission to be the saviour of sinners. or that He is the Messiah or Christ, the person God had promised of old to send into the world for this purpose; The person who did fully answer the signification of that Name by which He is commonly known, and eminently distinguished from the rest of Mankinde, The signification of Jesus christ, being A person anointed, or qualified and commissioned to fulfil all that God had ordained in order to his being the saviour of sinners. This is the ordinary sense in which the phrase The Son of God is used in the four Gospels. 3. That He is the person who
― 138 ―
hath actually accomplished all that the Messiah was to fulfil for the purpose spoken of. Rom: 1. 4. Our Lord. notes that He is the person who having fulfilled all that was appointed him, and being solemnly owned by God to have done so, by his raising him from the dead, is invested with the Authority designed for Him, hath all power committed to Him, and is constituted Judge of quick and Dead. (Here by the way, give me leave to place one query, viz. whether when Christ after the Judgment is over, hath resigned up the Kingdom to the Father, God wil not then unite himself to all that shal be justified and acquitted, that is, to all His Children, as He doth unto Jesus himself, and whether this may not be the meaning of that expression, That God may be all in all?) Having gone over these things again to shew that they afforded abundant satisfaction, that we might confidently expect from Jesus Christ the accomplishment of all that He had promised, provided we did faithfully acquit our selves as to what He makes our part, This question was to be considered, viz. What grounds we have to be assured that all these things are true concerning Jesus of Nazareth? This question, I purpose to answer from what is laid down in the creed, til we come to, I believe in the Holy Ghost. For How many truths soever are delivered in the Scripture, which may conveniently enough be reduced to the Heads following in the creed, betwixt what we profess to believe concerning Jesus Christ, and I believe in the Holy-Ghost, the meaning I cannot take to be, that I do explicitely believe every one of them: But what is delivered in that part of the creed, I conceive must be understood as the Grounds on which we do believe what is before declared concerning Jesus Christ. Now Sir when you happen to be very wel at leisure, you wil very <much>†a gratify and oblige me, if you please in a line or two to tell me that you think me to be in the Right, or in the wrong. one thing more I would also desire to know from you, which is concerning your way of Common placing, viz. Whether the two sides in the common place book must be reserved entirely for what may in time be mett with relating to that Head which shall have the first possession, or whether any other Heads begining with the same Letter and vowel may be inserted in the Margin?
Tho the length of my letter prove troublesom to you, yet
― 139 ―
I hope you wil interpret It a sure mark of the Confidence placed in you by
your most humble and obliged servant
SA: BOLDE.
Address (not in Bold's hand): To Jn Locke Esqr present at Oates
Endorsed by Locke: S: Bolde 9o Sept: 00 Answered Oct 7
2772. Edward Clarke to Locke, 12 September 1700 (2768, 2774)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, f. 94. Draft. Answered by no. 2774.
London. September the 12th. 1700.
Deare Sir,
By the last post I troubled you with my Desires for your Letters of Recommendation to Mr. Furly†1 etc. But understanding by your verie Kind Letter of the 10th Received yesterday, That Mr Furly intends to bee speedily in England, I resolve to suspend my goeing over with my son,†2 or sending Him into Holland, untill I can bee more certaine of haveing Mr. Furly's Direction and Assistance in Placeing my sonn there, which I hope you may Receive from his sonne that comes to you from Colchester†3 when you have Discoursed Him upon that subject, and therefore I submit your Writeing, or not Writeing of those Letters, as you have any certainty of the time when Mr Furly comes over here, my dependance being cheifely (if not wholly) on Him in the Disposeing of my sonn there, wherein I Begg the Continuance of your Freindly Advise to mee, as a matter of the greatest moment that I have at present under my Consideration, Nothing I thinke can happen more fortunately then Mr. Furly's speedy comeing over and Returning againe into Holland that I may send my son with Him as you mention, or at least have his Advise to Place Him, when ever Hee is sent over; Sir I can never suffitiently Acknowlidge your Freindship in the Concern you Expresse for my Health, and wish I were capable of Following your Advise, But my unhappy circumstances are such as I can Resolve on Nothing, And not knowing what the Proportions are of Jesuitts-Powder and steele that you would have mee take I have done nothing
― 140 ―
yet in it, for which I Begg your Pardon, Mrs. Clarke and All here with mee are Intirely yours and my Ladyes servants, But none with more Reason then
Your most Affectionate and obleiged humble servant
Endorsed in a later hand (T. Birch?): Mr. Clarke. Sept. 12. 1700
