2774. Locke to Edward Clarke, 16 September 1700 (2772, 2780)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, f. 95. Printed in Ollion, pp. 246-7; Rand, pp. 563-4. Answers no. 2772.
Oates 16 Sept 1700
Dear Sir
In answer to yours of the 12th which I received just now give me leave to say That I thought you would have advised with some physitian upon the place as I counselled you and then I needed say noe thing of the quantities of Steel and Jesuits pouder. Next I know not exactly the preparation nor quantities of the ingredients of Dr Sydenhams preparation of steel with extract of Gentian, I have only heard of it and think it a good one but never prescribed it, nor know how to prescribe it till I know it more particularly. Farther I think not that this prescription is sufficient of it self to remove your distemper without rideing joynd with it. These are the reasons why I enterd not farther into particulars but only pointed at this method as that which I upon my best consideration thought proper for you. If you would have me prescribe the preparation above mentioned you must furnish me, from Mr Maltus, with the discription of it and tell me you are resolved and fitted to ride. Half methods never produce whole or any cures. And health is worth all that we can doe. My swelling is not yet gon. it goes but slowly. It has kept me quiet, and I have not been on horse-back ever since I first
― 142 ―
mentioned it to you. I count it a great loss to me now winter is at hand, and there by my time of rideing near an end. For though I rode but gently a mile or two when it was fair after dinners, yet that airing and exercise (which is all that I have) I thought did me good
Mr Furlys son whom I have looked for and doe still every day is not yet come. As soon as I see him you shall hear from me. I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
My humble service to Mrs Clarke my wife and the Batchelor
My Lady and the rest here give you there their humble service

2775. John Hardy to Locke, 17 September 1700
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 142-3. The writer was the son of an Anglican clergyman; he became a Presbyterian and attended Owen's academy in Shrewsbury; minister at Sempringham, Lincs., and later in Nottingham; conformed and took Anglican orders about 1727: Calamy, Life, ii. 500-3.
Salop. Sept: 17. 700.—
Honoured Sir
The great distance there is betwixt your self and Me, had for ever discouraged Me from troubling You with My Impertinencyes, had I not flatter'd My Self Into the Opinion, that your large Soul would make the distance less, since (perhaps) you would not think it out of your Sphere to help even the Poorest Searcher for Truth; Truth, which is almost lost in terms of Art and unintelligible vaine Janglings of words; what should such as I do In this great Confusion! did not now and Then a Clear Reasonablenesse of Christianity Appear. Pardon Me Sir if I venture to Consult you to have My Scruples Solv'd, who have so often found satisfaction In Many points by your Works.
― 143 ―
It has been a Grand Controversie (You are not ignorant) even since the first Ages of our Religion whether Christ (for certain the Son of God by Extraordinary Birth and by having the Sperit dwelling Bodily In him) is properly God from all Eternity: I have endeavour'd to search the Scriptures, but can find litle In favour of the Affirmative at first sight, what ever wonder's other Men's quickness can Espy, in litle Phrases, and some flights of Pious Men. But the truth is, I could never yet rightly see, how the first Ch: of John Can be Expounded without forcing, to please those who have opposed the Deity of Our Lord, Le Clerc†1 has shown abundance of Judgement and Criticism, yet Methinks his Notions are not without difficultye; For, Let the Divine λογος (According to him) be Construed Reason, or Wisdom, by which God the Father made the world, is it some second Really distinct (as St John's discourse seems to Import) from God the Father and is it likewise a Selfe Conscious being? if not how comes it to be God? Honoured Sir, Can the earn'st Desires of an Unsatisfyed Mind prevail with You, to give Me Your Thoughts of as much of that Ch: as you thinke difficult. I am affraid (Poor Worm!) How I speak of My God and my Lord, I dare not be too bold with the Deity, Yet I would fain free my mind from these which much shake my Powers, and do seem to Weaken my Religion. It is my desire to serve God In Spirit and truth, Yet my Weaknesse exposes me to such difficultyes, that I know not where to fix.
If you would Indulge me In this boldnesse, I should be proud always in many difficult Things, to flye to You. You need not wonder there be No helpers for Me nearer home for all Men are Mad after partyes. If I should propose such a thing as this to any of those of the Learned World, I know they would Pity me, railly Me, cramm me with Orthodoxy, and if I would not Swallow, bid me Pack perhaps.
I have lately seen a Piece, admir'd by all Moderate Men, The Irenicum Magnum,†2 But Virtus laudatur et Alget,†3 som fear (as our Historians of Learning) that ther's a snake in the Grass.†4 other's
― 144 ―
Cry it down as wholly Heterodox. But other's admire the Authors Great, and Noble design, Grounded upon such Convincing Reasons; but they say It's impracticable. And indeed I've spent some thoughts upon it, and am affraid that such things the world Cannot bear. For, suppose a Minister of the Ch: of E. should offer to set up for a Scripturalist,†1 the Poor Gentleman would quicly be humbled by Church discipline. And if any of our Presbyte way should offer, all his brethren would certainly snarl at him, and thus would his Pious design vanish. Honoured Sir, if you are the Authour, as Most believe, I should be glad to understand, How you think such Methods may be put in practice. For aiming at that Publick office of the Ministry (for which I am now prepairing) I would willingly be furnish'd with all the requisites to keep my Conscience pure and undefiled before God in that station, and not onely Talk but act as much as possible; I'm sure you know the world and the Great Trade of Priestcraft (in fashion in every church) better, than to think that ever they will throw away all their narrow notions of Man-made-Divinity, and silly scandals by which they offend one another, and receive instead of it true and free Reasonable Religion. In short if a few could be entic'd into a design of promoteing it, I think it would be more acceptable before God, then to be sticlers for the Most orthodox opinions, and bare speculations.
This from yours Humbly to serve
JOHN HARDY
Honoured Sir if you are pleas'd to grant your Petioner for Truth's sake a few Lines be pleas'd to direct for me with the Rev'd Mr James Owen†2 at His House in Salop—
Address: For The Honoured John Lock Esquire These to be left with Mr John Churchill At the black Swan In Pater-noster-Row Bookseller London

2776. James Johnstoun to Locke, 19 September 1700 (2745, 2884)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 39-41.
Sept 19 Twittenham 1700
Sir
I confess my fault (and am penitent) in not writing to you. my Groome tells me that since the pads distemper recurrs he must evin considering his age die with it: so he was at noe loss by my not writing. I did indeed thinck to be at London and to writ to you upon another subject but nou that must be left to our meeting. to return to the pad. his wrench happened to him playing at Grass with another horse, old fool that he was. they rolled him and the Groome rod him twise 10 or 20 mile for a tryall before you had him and we thought him well or you should not have had him. If he had been well you should have payd dear for him considering his age but as he is I will neither give you him nor sell him to you he is a Lame horse. But if for his own sake you will take a lease of him (you may have it during lyfe) you will oblige both him and me. I am told he will not be worse and being strong and hearty he will doe all your bussinesse. nay I will wadger on his head that he brings you to Twitnam in a day if you be as willing as he. whither if you will come Mrs Johnson and you may agree on the yearly rent for the pad and she challenges you for some flowers or seeds she alledges you promised her and nou that you are out of bussiness she thincks you may keep your word both as to your Liberalitys and as to your coming to Twittenham her service pray and mine to Sir Francis and My Lady
I am
Sir
your faithfull humble servant
J. JOHNSTOUN

2779. Locke to Benjamin Furly, [22 or 23 September 1700] (2767, 2786)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 151. Copy by an amanuensis, perhaps only of a part of the letter. The original was sent to Clarke, who forwarded it to Furly: nos. 2780, 2784A. Printed in Rand, p. 566. According to Locke's endorsement of no. 2767 his answer to it was dated 23 September; according to Furly's answer, 22 September. Answers no. 2767; answered by no. 2786.
I could Wish for Mr Clarkes Sake that your Journey had not been put off to next Spring though Arent tells me it will be early, He has an intention to Send a Son of his into Holland.†3 Hee is about or years old and is designed for a Merchant. His father intends to Send him Speedily into Holland to Learn the Language and Merchants accounts, and in the mean time to Looke out for some honest Worthy Merchant to place him with as Soon as he is qualified for it. It is a very pretty Lad. Is forward in Latin and Speaks French very Well. I know noe body that understands these things Soe Well as you and cannot but advise my friend to doe with his Son as I would do with my owne, Send him over to you to dispose of him as may best conduce to his fathers designe which I have told you. I will not Say I Shall have the more Care of your Son because My friends is there under yours, For I Should doe what you may expect from me without any other consideration but of my friendship to you and Arent. But perhaps it may bee Some Security to a father, Whose affection to A Child has noe ordinary Measures, that your
― 148 ―
Son will not be wholy neglected here, Since you have a pledge there of no less consequence. If I were in Holland and sent over Arent to Mr Clarke I Should Say to him pray take care of him as if he were My Son. The Same Say I to you in reference to his and I thinke I need say noe More
I desire you to give my humble service to Mrs furley etc.
Endorsed by Clarke: Copy of what Mr. Locke Writt to Mr. Furley about Placeing my Sonn in Holland etc sent inclosed in mine to Mr. Furley on the 27th. September 1700.
2780. Locke to Edward Clarke, 23 September 1700 (2774, 2787)
Rand, pp. 564-5. The spellings 'Furley' and 'Guenellen' suggest that Rand printed from a copy made for Clarke rather than from Locke's original letter (Locke however has the spelling 'Furley' in the endorsements of nos. 1982, 2070, and 2122). Covering letter for the letter of which no. 2779 is a copy.
Oates, 23rd September, 1700.
Dear Sir,
You will see by the enclosed what relates to Mr. Furley. I have writ to him to take care of your son in prosecution of your design, and I think you may send him to him in that confidence, just as he has sent me his. Whether you will think fit to write to him first, and have an answer from him before you send your son over to him I must leave to you. However, I must desire you to send the enclosed to him by the next post, for he will be in pain about his son till he hears from me.†1
The writing to Mr. Furley upon a supposition that you will send him your son to take care of in prosecution of your design has hindered me from writing to Dr. <Guenellon>,†a for I do not see how you can commit him to two people's care at once. When he is once settled there somewhere by Mr. Furley to learn the language and merchants' accounts you may have advice from Mr. Furley what farther to do, and then we may apply ourselves to Dr. Guenellon as there shall be occasion. It is with this view that I have writ what concerns your son in the enclosed. If you have any other
― 149 ―
prospect or scheme in view concerning this matter I will write again to one or both of them (I mean Mr. Furley and Dr. <Guenellon>)†a as you shall direct.
I long to hear of the recovery of your health, the increase whereof I heartily wish, and am,
Dear Sir,
your most affectionate humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
My service to Mrs. Clarke, my wife and the Bachelor. The whole family here send their services to you all.
Endorsed: Mr. Locke's letter with one enclosed to Mr. Furley about placing my son in Holland. Received the 25th September, 1700. Answered the 26th, with a copy of what I writ Mr. Furley on the 27th.

B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 94-6. The postscript ('pray don't take state', etc.) is on a separate piece of paper (f. 96; Locke's endorsement is on f. 94) and is here attached to the present letter on account of its contents.
Sept. 26. 700
I have waited some time in hope of being in a humour to make good my former promis to You of a merry letter but I have such successions of cross accidents happens to prevent me, that I begin to beleive should I stay till my mind was indeed at eas from mellancholly subject's I should never have an opertunity to returne my thanks to you for your very kind letter and tho my gayety may fail from causes not in my power, yet beleive not so hardly of me to think my gratitude ever can. for I assure you I feel an equall share of that for the kindness of your letter as I doe of esteem and admiration for the author, this is all the returne I am able to make for the obligation's which on a 1000 account's I acknolledge my self to be indebted to you. I have as I told my lady Masham, very lately been extreamly troubled with my head ach's and yet more with the ill effect's of them on my Eyes, which I must own dos sometimes work up my spleen to a considerable heigh't; as did the discription you made me of the state of Your health, extreamly I am glad to beleive that tis possible for you to be under the direction of this monster, sometimes, and to hope twas by it's influence that part of your letter was indited and fancy riding is ev'ry way good
― 151 ―
for you if you can continue it, and tho you tell me your leg's take state upon them I cant beleive you idle as you say nor that Your head is not too buisy for Your health.
I cant but laugh with the thought how my accusing you of the spleen: will make you dispise me but notwitstanding I must tell you the laziness you describe (however your lungs are to blame) this has some part in. You have thought's and words in your letter so peculiar to this diseas that they can't be mistaken. You doe me but justice to beleive if twere in my power you should be as robust a knight as any in Essex but not as much sans pensé pour l'amour†a de Madame and if art did not fail me I should certainly lay a plot on a strong carkase near you and try cunningly to slip you into it and give your's to him, but what confusion would it make in your papers and his feilds, tho I hope the lady most concern'd in this change would have no cause to complain for an ill house and mellancholly seat would then goe down well enufe. You can't say I want generosity to wish so kind a thing for another, but pray tell me how would you use the then Mr Lock! for I can't think what you could doe with him except you could make him a portable barometter (this is a new word I've learn't and have never try'd it before I wish it prove right)†1 tho I fear for him his fate would be to be sent to be nurs't by Mrs Pauling. You doe not I kno desire news except I could firnish you with what is not to be had, good the faction's in this citty are buisily at Work in the Ellection of a new mayor in which I'me told their never apear'd greater heats then now between Whig and tory two of Each are candidates for the chair†2 it will pleas you to be inform'd the King continues in very good health they talk much of his marriage but of that I beleive but little,†3 the two Ellectresse's are to meet him again at the hague†4 which will retard his returne of which I can give you no certain account it is said they will bring with them the yong Princess of Hesse†5 if this proves true I shall be
― 152 ―
persuaded that some thing may have been intended tho not that 'twill Ever be concluded my Brother†1 is extreamly oblig'd to you for your kind wishes to him, I hope he'el thrive the better for it he is in very ill hands when or how he will get out of't I can't se they both give you there humble service good Mrs Ester was so kind to dine with me whom I once thought to've given the trouble of this but it being to be sent to Hackney†2 by the penny post I found it as easy to send it to Oat's. my Cosen†3 is not worse tho she complains she gives You many thanks for your concerne for her. I with truth and reason may doe what you in much affectation did end this with an excuse for its' being no more entertaining and may add one for it's length for fear you will weary with reading it. It will be no flattery to tell you nothing can be more gratefull to me then a share in Your esteem or rais my vanity higher. I will pleas my self with beleiving as much of this as is consistent with my opinion of you and my self. but if I am capable of the honour you doe me to call me your frend you may be assure'd I am that with the utmost sincerity and
Your faithfull and affectionate servant
M L
my service to my Lady etc
pray don't take state upon you and be long in answering this for I shall be impatient to hear from you. Mrs Clerk whine'd out some thing to me about a swelling let me kno if theres anything in't and if the effect's are good or ill. I had allmost forgot to say something to You from poor Mr Anderson†4 who by your favour I suppose has been named to Mr freak. if it be anything you kno of, that may be fit for him or that a Second Word would advance I kno You are so kind that You would help him. tho I confess I could wish he could some way be provided for in the way he seem's perfectly fit for and that is preaching. tho poor man he get's nothing for it it is so well like'd that there's scarce a sunday but he is imploy'd some where or other and some times twice and indeed I think improves. Could any thing be said to Dr Bently†5 that might move him to help him. I
― 153 ―
really think it would be doing good for as far as I can judge he will be one of the best preacher's has been some time. would a word from You or my lady to Dr Burnet of the charter house or the Bishop of Glocester doe any good in this. to introduce him to them. I only suggest these things. I designd this for a cover but having spoilt that designe I have allter'd my mind and Call it a note Mr Anderson is very sensible of the high obligation he has to You as he will very soon tell you himself. if I knew†a any thing left to fill up this space I would be glad but having no more
Adieu.
Endorsed by Locke: M Lockhart 26 Sept 00 Answered 1 Nov:

2784. Samuel Locke to Locke, 27 September 1700 (2704, 2842)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 210-11.
Honoured Sir
Mr. Bonville hath don mee the kindnesse to Impart the Contents of your obliedging Letter of 26th. august on my behalfe: wherein for the favour of your Remembrance of mee and my family doe give you our humble and verry hearty thanks. particularly for the honnour you doe my son John in inquyreing what advyse from him; who I doubt not (God spareing his Lyfe) will be Carefull to answere (per the ship norris) your most Esteem'd Letter sent him in August 1699 per the Rook friggat:†1
In the meantyme I am glad I can advyse you Sir that the 2d instant Came to my hand the inclosed Letter from him dato 25 January and 17 february from Swally Hole (the Port of Suratt) where they were blessed be God aryved the 19th: January. after a long and dangerouse voyage of neer 10 months; be pleased Sir to Excuse my presumption to Tyre you out in Reading it. which I finde was pen'd in haste and hurry, his head and hands being fill'd with the Company theyr affaires. and had not gain'd Tyme to know the affairs of the Country being but just stept on shoare. Sir Nicolas Wayte our president and Consull had Conferr'd on him the Secretaryship of the factory. and gives him an Extraordinary Carracter. as doth som other letters which I have recieved from thence;
our Company now hath a Rich ship the De Grave.†2 aryved from the Bay of Bengall, vallewd at neer £200 000 sterling at the Candle and hourely expect another the Antelop†3 of a farr greater Vallew: haveing among other good about 300 Bails†a Raw silk. we Expect dayly the Norris from Surrat which Sir Nicholas writes will be dispatcht in Aprill Last. and one or two from China and Borneo:
India Goods continue still in demaund and this weeke sold high by the old Company:†4 the 14th next month wee sell the De graves Cargo: and this next season shall Imbark for our severall factorys to
― 155 ―
the vallew £500000 sterling which with what wee have sent abroad about 700000£ as you will see by the inclos'd paper; amounts†a to about £1200000. wee hope wee shall be able to weather the Point with the old Company when the yeare 1701 comes in and will be Confyn'd to 315000£ stock:†1
I wish I had anything to Impart to you worth your peruseall: I am glad to heare wee shall have the honnour to see you here before the Cold weather Comes in. My wyfe and family give theyr due Respects and most Respectfully doth salut you
Sir
Your most humble servant and kinsman
SAM: LOCKE

2784A. Edward Clarke to Benjamin Furly, 27 September 1700
Rand, p. 565. Covering letter for the letter of which no. 2779 is a copy.
27th September, 1700.
Sir,
By the enclosed letter from Mr. Locke you will find that I shall depend on your friendly assistance in placing my second son, John Clarke, where you think most proper to learn merchants' accounts and the Dutch language (the French he has already). I had thoughts of accompanying him into Holland and putting him into your hands, but my health will not (I fear) permit me, and therefore I am enquiring who is going thither that I may entrust him withal. And when I can find a person to whose care I can commit him I purpose
― 156 ―
to send him, and shall address him to you, and beg that you will according to your accustomed goodness afford me and him your help in this affair, which shall always be acknowledged and returned in all the ways of gratitude that shall be in the power of,
Sir,
your most affectionate friend and servant,
E. C.
Pray give my hearty service to your sons.

2785. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 1/12 October 1700 (2698, 2854)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 135-6. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 117-19.
A Amsterdam le 12 d'Octobre 1700.
Il y a déja bien du temps, Monsieur, que je vous dois et des réponses et des remercimens, que je n'ai renvoyez d'un Ordinaire à l'autre, que par accident, et par malheur. Comme je ne suis pas maître de mon temps, il arrive souvent que j'emploie à autre chose celui que j'avois destiné à écrire à mes amis. Outre cela, il faut vous avouër que la petite lettre de Mr. Guenelon,†1 que vous trouverez ci-jointe, s'étoit égarée sur ma table, et que j'ai tardé à vous répondre jusqu'à ce que je l'eusse retrouvée. J'ai crû que vous me pardonneriez plus facilement, si je vous l'envoiois tard, que si je la supprimois.
Pour parler d'autre chose, je vous dirai que nôtre Magistrat n'a jamais parlé depuis de la Dédicace, et que mon Ami ne lui en a rien dit non plus, quoi que le Libraire ait eu soin de lui en envoier un exemplaire.†2 Il ne croit pas que vous puissiez avoir eu aucune part là dedans, parce que mon Ami ne lui en dit rien du tout, et se tut dès qu'il le vit refuser sérieusement. C'est un homme qui ne lit rien du tout depuis longtemps, et qui n'a jamais <guere lû.>†a †3 Hors de ses Mathematiques et de son Cartesianisme, il ne s'informe de rien, excepté des affaires politiques de la Ville. Ainsi je ne m'attends
― 157 ―
pas qu'il le lise. Vous m'avez demandé quelles preuves j'ai que la Langue Hebraïque étoit la même que la Phenicienne.
Vous les trouverez, dans la I. Dissertation des Prolegomenes de la Genese.†1 L'Evêque de Bath et Wells semble n'y avoir fait aucune attention, car il mattaque encore là dessus, dans son livre contre les Juifs,†2 où, contre le sentiment de tous les plus habiles interpretes, il prétend prouver la Trinité par םיהלא ארℶ.†3 Il parle aussi assez mal, dans la Préface de mon explication du Schiloh.†4 Il y a là dedans du zele Theologique, c'est à dire, bien de l'entêtement et de l'iniquité. Son livre est d'ailleurs si peu de chose, que je n'ai pas envie de le tirer de la poudre en y répondant à part. Dans la 2. Edition de mon Pentateuque†5 j'y répondrai en peu de mots, sans le nommer, non plus que le grossier Allemand, à qui il donne tant d'éloges.†6 Je traiterai de même, lors que l'occasion s'en présentera le Docteur Whitby, qui me met ridiculement en contradiction avec S. Paul, en m'introduisant comme un homme qui a dessein de contredire cet Apôtre. Cet homme m'auroit dû remercier, puis que je suis cause qu'il a transcrit et revû une partie considerable de cet ouvrage; mais au lieu de cela, il m'accuse, contre toute apparence, de favoriser les Ariens, sans en donner aucune preuve.†7 Quand je pense à ce Docteur, au Sieur Edoüard†8 et à quelques autres, je dis quelquefois en moi même: est-il possible qu'il y ait des hommes de ce naturel, dans un païs, ou il n'y a point de loups? Les loups n'y sontil point métamorphosez en Druides? Si j'étois d'humeur de faire des vers, il y auroit là de quoi faire une Fable pour ajoûter aux Metamorphoses d'Ovide, et je ferois déscendre ces gens-là tout droit de Lycaon.†9 Mais, raillerie à part, après avoir répondu à un ou deux de ces Messieurs, je m'en tiens à ma Dissert. de non respondendo Calumniis Theologorum.†10 Je les abandonne à leur mauvais
― 158 ―
génie. Je suis occupé à un second Tome du Parrhasiana,†1 que je ne manquerai pas de vous envoier avec mon Hesiode,†2 qui s'en va fait. Cela n'égalera pas la valeur des livres, que vous m'avez envoiez, mais j'espere que la reconnoissance que j'aurai toujours, pour vos honêtetez, sera contée pour beaucoup et qu'elle suppléra à tout. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Mr. Coste trouvera ici mes civilitez et m'excusera si je ne lui réponds pas à present. Je le ferai à la premiere occasion. Sa Version est géneralement approuvée, et a donné lieu à une infinité de gens de lire un Ouvrage, qu'ils souhaitoient de voir depuis longtemps. J'espere qu'il fera de fruit ici, et en France. S'il s'imprime en Latin à Londres, il en faudroit faire passer nombre d'exemplaires ici d'abord; autrement il ne manquera pas d'être contrefait.†3 C'est de quoi il faudroit avertir le Libraire, qui feroit peutêtre encore mieux, s'il le faisoit imprimer ici à ses dépends, pour le donner à meilleur marché. Nous remercions ma femme et moi Mr. Coste, pour le présent qu'il nous a fait d'un exemplaire de sa version. Nôtre petit garçon n'est pas mieux. Sa plaie rend toûjours beaucoups de liqueur blanchâtre, sans que rien puisse arrêter ce flux, et les Medecins ne nous conseillent nullement de faire ouvrir l'endroit, qui est justement au dessous de l'emboiture de la cuisse, dans l'endroit le plus épaix des muscles. L'eau de chaux simple, ni mêlee de sel armoniac infusé dans du cuivre, ni a rien fait. Cependant l'enfant tombe dans une maigreur extraordinaire, quoi qu'il dorme et mange passeblement. Il ne peut point remuer la cuisse, sans douleur, et il semble tout à fait que le mal est dans la jointure. Dieu veuille avoir pitié de ce pauvre enfant, nous ne savons plus qu'en penser.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings over against the plough in little Lincolns inne fields London.
Postmark: OC 11
Endorsed by Locke: J. le Clerc 12 Oct. 00

2786. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 1/12 October 1700 (2779, 2832)

Rotterdam 12 October 1700
Deare Sir
yours of the 22 past under covert of mr. Clarkes, I have, when his son comes I shall take the same care of him as of my owne. I have a great many sons at that schoole, (where mine all learned,) from Ireland, from England, from france, I have paid the master within a year about £200 stg.†1 I am often chargd with such kind of Commissions, from men that will afford me no other, and yet I have hitherto refusd none, and some from men I never saw, and how they come by my name I scarce know: from some I receive thanks, from others not a line, and one dyed in my debt, after I had paid the master, so that I am the common drudge, and unfairly taxt above and beyond my neighbours: It seems, Sir, you are to pay the score, by taking care of my son Arent, which I am much obliged to you for; as to the 6 shilling a week, they shall have it without grudging, and a thousand thanks to boot and I rest obliged to you and to my Lady for providing a place so near you. I hope he will ans<wer m>y†a care for him, and make the best of his tim<e and n>ot†a trifle and saunter it away. And I doubt n<ot b>ut†a if mr. Francis†2 will frequently speak french to him he will learn french. I live in dayly hopes to get out of this bridewel, where I have now labourd almost 7 years, out of which I shall no sooner be delivered, but I shall God willing set my face towards Oates, in which voyage my dearest will very readily accompany me, if the indisposition of her sister shall not detain her. In the meane while, with tender of her and my, and my sons humble service to yourself Sir Francis, my Lady and all the branches of the family, I am
Deare Sir
Your most affectionate friend and humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY

2790. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 14 October 1700 (2788, 2797)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 77-8. Answers no. 2788.
Oates 14 Oct 1700
Dear Cosin
Yours of the 5th I received in bed three or four days since and in bed I now write you this answer. Not that I am confined to my bed by any great increase of my old distemper. that I thank god the spending this sommer in the country has made as tolerable to me as I could expect. age I know will not mend ill lungs, and therefor my old disease of my brest must goe on as it does its old train. But there is a new maladie has lately befallen me and has obleiged me for sometime past to spend most of my time in my bed. A humor has fallen down and made me a sore leg. Being up I find increases the pain and spreading of it, against which I take sanctuary in my bed as one of the best remedies I can use. When I shall be able to returne to my former liberty of liveing I cannot tell, much lesse when I shall be able to take a journey. I therefor send this lettre to meet you in town as soon as you come, and to put in you minde of your promise that as soon as you returnd out of the West you would come down hither. It would be very acceptable to me to see you here as soon as you come to London and possibly noe disadvantage to your self. I should be glad then if your occasions would permit you to come out of town in the Bishop Startford Coach the next Tuesday after your arrival which (according to your reconing to be in London the 18th) will be to morrow seventh night i e 22th: If you come to town Friday, as you designe, pray let me hear from you by Saturday nights post. I shall be glad to heare of your safe returne, more to see and <talk>†a with you here of many things, for I would not have you looke on it as a journey of complement. I am
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate cosin and humble servant

Dear Sir
Yours of 17th and your other of a former date I received both just now with the inclosed in them and have only time to tell you that my enquiry concerning your journey into the country was not bare curiosity. I concluded by that time you would see what effect Sir R Bs prescriptions†1 had upon you and that if you found good by them you would continue the same method, If not that then you would probably leave them off because of the difficulty of haveing the Spaw waters. Upon such a resolution I intended to advise you to adde to each dose of his pils gr xv: of Jesuits pouder and soe to take them only in the mornings and ride upon them and soe spend your days in rideing. For then your excuse about not haveing a horse (which at best I thought noe very good one) I concluded would be at an end. Sir If it were in my power I would make drinking a dish of Coffee or Chocolate every day a perfect cure for you But all that I can doe for you being to tell you what I think will or will not restore you to your former health, I cannot forbeare under the earnest concerne I have for it to tell you, that as far as I can guesse. Neither steel nor any other medicines I can think of will doe it without the exercise I propose. which is the only method of physick†2 I can expect a cure from. of physick I say, for what nature it self may doe I say not. 2795. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 19/30 October 1700 (2742, 2857)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 139-40. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, ff. 211-12. Printed from the copy in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 464-5. The letter was apparently enclosed in a parcel containing the copies of the Vita Episcopii; this parcel did not reach Locke before November 1701: pp. 505-7; see also pp. 238-9, 251.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Hac æstate binas ad te literas dedi, quas ad manus tuas pervenisse spero. Dolerem si aberrassent. Nunc ad te mitto vitam Episcopii, ante plures annos, uti nosti, à me linguâ Belgicâ scriptam, et præfixam aliquot Episcopii concionibus, quarum exemplar illo tempore
― 168 ―
ad te misi. Quoniam nunc Latino sermone prodit, à nostro Marco Teute cum in Angliâ esset versa, illius ad te duo mitto exemplaria, quorum alterum filio Dominæ Masham trades, alterum ut benigno à me recipias vultu rogo.†1 Videbis ibi specimen aliquod persecutionis in patriâ nostrâ, libertatis asylo, institutæ; unde quomodo erga integras ecclesias, et ingenuos veritatis confessores passim sævitum fuerit, facile colliges. Utinam et hodie omnes hanc sævitiam detestentur! Verum quâ nunc fruimur quietem non moderatioribus Ecclesiastarum consiliis, sed Magistratus prudentiæ ac benignitati debemus; quæ nisi igneum illorum zelum compesceret, eadem nos hodie, quæ olim majores nostros, procella obrueret.
(English) Jam magnam libri tui eruditissimi partem maximâ cum voluptate legi. Omnia mihi mirificè placent. Verum quoniam non tantam linguæ Gallicæ quam Latinæ cognitionem habeo, aliquando ut vim phrasium Gallicarum intelligam, atque mentem tuam distinctè percipiam, bis terve quædam mihi relegenda sunt: quod lectionem mihi aliquanto tardiorem reddit. Verum molestiam hanc dilucidâ veritatis explicatione, argumentorumque quibus eam adstruis pondere, abundè compensas. Quando ad finem pervenero, Lib.II.
― 169 ―
Caput.XXI. De la puissance, ubi prolixè de voluntate, ac hominis in volendo libertate disseris, relegam: Quædam enim ibi habes nova, quæ attentum requirunt lectorem. Ego totum ubi perlegero candidè meum tibi judicium scribam. Verum vix credo me in quoquam à te dissensurum, adeo omnia quæ legi mihi probantur. Vale, Vir Amplissime, et salve à me ac meis: Salutem etiam officiosissimam dices Dominæ Masham totique familiæ.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS À LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 30 Octobris
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I wrote you two letters this summer; I hope that they reached your hands; I should be sorry if they have gone astray. I now send you the life of Episcopius, written, as you know, by me some years ago in Dutch and [p. 167] prefixed to some of his sermons; I sent you a copy at that time. Since it now appears in Latin, translated by our Marcus Teut while he was in England, I send you two copies of it; please give one of them to Lady Masham's son and kindly accept the other from me.†1 You will see in it a considerable example of persecution set on foot in my country, the refuge of liberty; from it you will readily gather how cruelly whole churches and frank confessors of truth were treated everywhere. Would that today also all men detested this cruelty! But we owe the quiet that we now enjoy not to more moderate counsels of the clergy but to the prudence and benignity of the magistracy; if that did not restrain the clergy's fiery zeal the same tempest as formerly overwhelmed our predecessors would overwhelm us today.
(Latin) I have now read with very great pleasure a large part of your most erudite book. Everything pleases me wonderfully. But since I do not have so great a knowledge of French as of Latin I have to reread some passages two or three times in order to understand the import of the French phrases and to grasp your meaning clearly; this makes my reading rather slow. But you make abundant amends for this trouble by a clear exposition of truth and by the weight of the arguments by which you establish it. When I reach the end I will reread bk. II, ch. xxi, 'De la puissance', where you discourse at length [p. 168] about the will and the freedom of a man in willing; for you have there some new points that call for an attentive reader. When I have read through the whole I will candidly write you my opinion. But I scarcely think that I shall disagree with you about anything, so greatly do I approve of everything that I have read. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and good wishes from me and mine. Please give my best respects to Lady Masham and the whole family.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 30 October 1700
Address: Amplissimo Consultissimo Doctissimo Viro D. Joanni Locke.
Endorsed by Locke: P: Limborch 30 Oct. 00

I am satisfied that Buckhill was let to Joseph Barnes for four and Twenty pounds for the Year 1695.
Hanny hath given a bond for 4l.10s.00d. which is the mony due from him, and promiseth payment when he is able, but he is not now worth a farthing.
As to Gullock there is no difference as to the account between Mr Locke and Mr Lyde, he hath paid Mr Lyde eight pounds since Mr Lockes letter, and there is about 5l. arere for rates and taxes, which he promiseth to pay on Mr Lockes renewing his lease, which will be expired Lady day next—Gullock is responsible, and Mr Lyde adviseth to let him have a farther lease, because it will be a means to have in the taxes—Gullock desires a lease for 21 years, sed quære, whether advisable to make so long a lease, and whatever the lease be it will be Convenient to have a proviso therein, that for nonpayment of the taxes the lessor may reenter and avoid the lease.
John Veales Barne will do well enough with a little mending without taking down a tree, but there is a necessity to thatch the

outhouses and the dwelling house, and the wall of the Barn must be mended, all which I have ordered.

2802. Laurence Hackett to [Locke?], 28 October 1700
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, f. 131. Identifiable as the letter forwarded to Locke by Samuel Locke on 18 July 1701: p. 381. Samuel Locke thought that it might be intended for Locke, in which case the letter of 29 August mentioned by Hackett would belong to 1699. Alternatively the letter may have been intended for John Lock at Surat, and sent by him to his father.
The writer matriculated from Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1693; B.A. 1697: Foster. He came to Surat as chaplain of the Norris (p. 154, etc.) and was appointed chaplain of the factory. He was now attached to Sir William Norris's embassy, and was at Brahmapuri on the river Bhima with an advance party conveying part of the New East India Company's present to Aurangzíb. He appears to have left India shortly after his return to Surat: Das, Norris Embassy, pp. 66, 256-7; Anderson, English in Western India, pp. 147, 156-7.
Generous Sir
Yours of the 29 of August received not till 20 of October last past wherin find so much generosity and good nature that I should worthily be branded with the title of ingratitude if I should not grant that request which ought first submissively to have desir'd, to wit, a constant correspondence, and since you tell mee you hope every fault will produce a letter I cannot find any in this unless it bee too much flattery which ile call so rather than deny myself the satisfaction of answering, or rather returning so great a complement and favour which I could not have expected from any but Mr. Lock and for whome I shall conserve a due respect and
― 176 ―
freindship and shall not be wanting in my Generall, but more especially particular prayers for him.
How the Court may be chang'd at the Arivall of his Excellency†1 I know not, but I wish he were here or very near coming, for things begin to look with a dismal aspect and I fear will rat<her>†a put on the squalid and direfull robes of sorrow and confusion, than light and aery ones of Mirth and serenity, for the News is the Mogull is sick†2 and not able to appear without being carry'd in the arms of his weomen and so set in his throne, and immediately returnd, all our hopes are tis not so bad as reported, for when men lifted up to such state as he is doe but complain the whole Empire groans and if his finger does but ake the whole nation is sick at heart, but I rather fear poison or a dagger may end his days, it being so very remarkable from History that few or none of those mighty Emperors who have set themselves above the rest of mankind by parricide and such unpardonable crimes descend into the grave in peace or end their days by a naturall exit.†3
The Enemy is very bold and has threatned the Lascarr†4 unless bought off with two lack of roupies and on Saturday next tis reported they will come and demand their mony.
Sir I must now begg pardon for dividing my sheet of paper but its by an accident hapening on the other half, and really time will not give mee leave to transcribe, I therefore Crave leave to Subscribe my self
Your Most Obleiged Servant
LAUR: HACKETT Cler:
<Barampore>†b October 28 1700
Address: To Mr Lock These.

2803. Dr. John Covel to Locke, 30 October 1700 (2799, 2808)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 174-5. Answers no. 2799; answered by no. 2808.
Christ College. Cambridge. Oct. 30. 1700.
Worthy Sir
I do designe, if God give me Life and Health, to print the Poran, and adde some notes and reflections upon it; but I assure you, should I speak my mind of things freely in them, it would not please many of our men who are so violently set upon their old Mumsimus.†1 I am apt to fancy, that the Banyans religion is older much then some of our Learned Authors would make it; and that their Cosmogonia and Theogonia in the Poran is very antient, I dare not say older then our sacred history; but it is so odde and quite out of our way, that I cannot believe that he that wrote it, had ever seen Moses's writings, for he would have made it more probable, and refin'd it; as the Greeks and Ægyptians trim'd those storyes which they have seem'd to have borrow'd from the Scriptures.†2 There seem to be in the Poran many hints, from whence many Eastern Opinions, and Greek fables sprang. Particularly the Æones; and the four Ages in Ovid; Phaeton; and that there was a deluge; The Dii supremi, medioxumi, and Infimi, and the Genii of the Platonists, seem to be the same with their Dewta's;†3 and much more of the same nature is very observable. Now to print the Poran plain, would be but a dry businesse; and to make an Edition of it, requires something to be said; but what, requires more then ordinary consideration. I suppose you know that the Banyans†4 are down right Pythagoreans, and they (that is, the Brachmans,) being recorded in all antient story as famous for their learning, I am apt to believe that Pythagoras learn'd from them, and not they from him.†5 Upon these and some other thoughts I must keep the
― 178 ―
Poran a while longer, though Mr Lock should sooner prevayl with me to publish that (or any thing else agreable to his desire and mature Judgement,) then any man alive.
I am much obliged to my worthy freind, My Lady Masham, and all her worthy family; but I have plaid the Truant so much this Summer, (having rambled above 700 miles) as I cannot as yet be absent. I must be forced for a few dayes to goe to Sanford Hall, but I know not when it will be; I have not been there this thre or four yeares, and I have some affaires of concerne that will force me thither. I assure you my heart and thoughts are often with you, but at present I must beg of you all to accept my true and hearty Respects; and so soon as I can Come, (which I fear cannot be till the Spring) I will certainely kisse your hands.
Worthy Sir,
Your ever Affectionate and most faithfull servant
JOH: COVEL.
Address: These To John Lock Esq. at Sir Franc Masham's house at Oates. To be left at Bishopstafford.
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Covel 30. Oct. 00 Answered Nov. 3

Oates 3 Nov. 1700
Reverend Sir
If in what I proposd to you I had noething in view but my own particular satisfaction, I must be a very unreasonable man if the great civilitys of your letter of the 30th of Oct did not fully afford it me, since the esteem and freindship of such a man as Dr Covel are of much more use and value to me then the old Bramines and their poron can be. But yet I cannot but be under some mortification
― 183 ―
that solliciting as I doe for the <publick>†a good I cannot prevaile with one who professes himself soe much disposed to comply with me. Your not consenting to the publishing of the Poron now has soe good a reason in your designe, that if what you intend some time or other to adde to it could be hinderd by its being in print I should be perfectly for that delay you mention. But there are two things I confess I cannot get over in the case. The one is that you are mortal, and if you publish it not in your life time it may possibly be quite lost, tis certain it will be lost to the publique at least for some time. I know you have had it in your hands many years and I doubt not have kept it there with those good intentions you mention to me in your letter. But yet interveneing occasions and business that time brings with it self has I see hitherto frustrated those good intentions, and soe I fear it will continue to doe on and the world will be deprived of the text and notes too. Give them the one now, they will not at all be thereby hinderd from your giveing them the other, when time and leisure will give you the oportunity to obleige them with the other. For it shall be printed under what termes you please. And if there be any scruple against your letteing the originall goe out of your hands (which I always allow to be a very reasonable one). the copying of it shall be by whomsoever you shall think fit to employ and he shall be paid for it. For if Mr Churchill. (who is printing the collection of voyages I speake of) will not doe that, I have noe more to say.
As to the doctrine of the Bramines I think with you it is very ancient and therefor am the more desireous to see what it Contiens and to understand as much of it as I can concerning their Dewtas and particular Brama. The Poron I grant to be one of their ancient books and therefor of the greater value to me and though it would be but a drie thing without notes and therefor I wish very much we had it with yours: yet if we should chance not to be soe happy.†b the great commerce that we have now in those countrys, might give an oportunity of geting greater light: And men of ingenuity and letters that goe now frequently thither might be the better furnishd to enquire and informe themselves, if they had but the book it self whereon to discourse with the Bramines there. I cannot but wonder to finde any one of opinion that Pythagoras was teacher of the Brachmans and that they borrowd their doctrines from him. They who talk soe seem to me to talk very idle and therefor
― 184 ―
I am perfectly of your minde that what opinions he held in common with them he borrowed from them. But as to this, and a great many other things I should be glad to talke with you about, you put me in pain, by delaying my hopes of seeing you here till the spring. I have for some time been confined within dores by a lame leg, and now am under the Blockade of my old enemy Winter. Your conversation would be a great releif to the prisoner. This I beg you to beleive and that I am with a very particular respect
Reverend Sir
your most humble and obedient servant
J LOCKE
My Lady gives you her humble service
Address: For Dr John Covel master of Christs College in Cambridg
Endorsed by Covel: Mr Lock.
2809. Edward Jocelyn to Locke, 3 November 1700 (2161)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 23-4.
Sir
I beg your pardon for sending this dirty paper, tis the very same, that lay under the weather glass all the last moneth. Sending my man in haste I had not time to write it over. I think you'le understand it being according to your own direction. Seven a clock at night was the time. the degrees are soe many above the figures 29 etc. If I am not mistaken you told me there were 20 degrees between every inch: by my brass there are but 10. If, Sir, you make by this any new discovery, pray let the world know what assistance you had from
your worthy friend in the Rothings
E. JOCELYN
Nov. 3d. 1700.

2810. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 5 November 1700 (2806, 2815)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, f. 81. Answers no. 2806; answered by no. 2815.
Oates 5 Nov: 1700
Dear Cosin
I herewith send you a bill on Mr Churchill for £950 as you desire. Whether sealed Bank bils will yeild anything more than barely the principal and use due upon them you can easily informe your
― 186 ―
self For this money lyeing most in Bank bils I would part with them at the current rate. This I must desire of you that at your first conveniencie after the receit of this you would goe and speake with Mr Churchil and setle the matter with him about this money soe that the bank bils may be disposd of to the best advantage and the whole matter soe orderd that you may have the money in that manner as may best suit your ease and convenience. To this purpose your talkeing with him before hand I think will not be amiss that you may not be in any hurry when the time comes that you shall have use of the money. When you come to execute the writeings pray take care to have good substantiall witnesses. all the rest I leave to you, only remember, what you mentioned to me here, to make the deeds, if it may be, for 6 per Cent with an abatement of one per cent for prompt payment within a month after the interest due. I thank you for the news you sent me and the other things I find by your letter you have donne for me. But I have not time now to enter upon other particulars. Only give me leave to aske whether there be now noe money to be received out of the East India company for the annuity or Interest. My Lady and others here give you their humble service. I am
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE

2812. Locke to Edward Clarke, 5 November 1700 (ii) (2811, 2817)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, ff. 100-1. The two leaves appear to have been torn apart and rejoined. Printed in Ollion, pp. 250-1; Rand, pp. 571-3. Locke apparently wrote most of it before, and completed it after, writing no. 2811. Answers no. 2804.
Oates 5 Nov. 1700
Dear Sir
My leg is now I thank god soe well that it confines me noe longer to the lazy lying much in bed which I was quite weary of soe that that maladie of a soar leg I look on now as quite over whether I am much to rejoyce in it I doe not well know. For though the setleing of a humor in my legs be not a very desirable thing in one of my age, and has usualy trouble and danger enough in it, yet if I doe not mistake, my lungs were much easier whilst the soars were runing, than they were before. This I said and thought I felt then. But this I am sure that I breath much worse now then when my leg was ill. Whether it be the comeing on of Winter alone that causes it, or whether the alteration be oweing in part to the vent of the humor ceaseing in my leg or wholy to the cold and foggy weather I cannot be positive. Tis noe thing but what I ought and doe expect. Every winter is of course to bring a greater load upon me till at last it put <an>†b end to my breathing at all. I am very sorry your health finds noe amendment yet, as it might and ought to doe if those strong principles of life which are in you were a little roused and excited. I concerne wish it were donne that you might be perfectly restored to your former vigor
― 188 ―
My Lady Masham returns you her thanks for your care and trouble about her businesse. She did not intend it should have cost you soe much pains. But the calling in that <m>oney†a or mending the security she thinks necessary. For the grandsons marrying tis <t>hought†a will breake his father heart.†1 I return you also my thanks for complying soe readily with my desire.
And now I must beg your assistance for a man, whom I am sure if you knew as well as I doe, you would doe all you could without my askeing
Your Cosin Hopkins,†2 I am informed, leaves Convent garden lecture at Christmas next, and I know not a fitter man to succeed him than Mr Anderson. I take him to be a very honest good man that designes to doe all the good in his calling. I have heard him preach more than once and know not where to goe if I were in town to hear better sermons than his. That therefor which I beg of you for him is, that you would get your Cosin Hopkins to use what interest he has in the Parish for him or at least to favour him as often as he can with his pulpit dureing this time of probationary preaching. I think the man really deserves assistance and encouragement and therefor I earnestly beg yours for him to your Cosin Hopkins or any one else you know of that Parish. I have this day sent Mr Anderson a letter to you which may serve to introduce him to you and if there be any farther particularitys in the case to give him an oportunity to explain them. Pray give my most humble service to Mrs Clarke and to my wife. I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate and most humble servant
J LOCKE
Not being able to rely much on my man James's†3 memory whether it be the globe or the ball in Hungerford market where†b Mr Johnstowns waterman uses to call†4 I must beg the favour of you to send the inclosed to that ale house by one of your servants.
― 189 ―
who will easily finde the house where his waterman cals whether it be the signe of the Globe or the Ball

2813. Robert Pawling to Locke, 7 November 1700 (2807, 2896)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 235-6.
Lincolns Inn Nov: 7 1700
Sir
I thank you for your Bill of £10 on Mr Bonville. I had not time to go to Mr Clarks†1 about your Black suit. I caried the Cheese presently to Mr Freke†2 and the 3 Apples to my Lord President†3 who returns you his thanks. I said, what you writt, they were the same Apples of which you sent his Lordship Grafts; he told me they were the Apples to be dryed. I thank you for giving me the opportunity of waiting on his Lordship who received me kindly, and, no one being present, he caused me to sit with him by the fire a long time. I turned my discourse chiefly to give his Lordship an Account of the progress of the buildings at, and other affairs relating to Greenwich Hospitall, my Lord was pleased to renew his former assurances of being my friend there. I gave his Lordship my humble thanks for his care of me when he joyned with my Lord Chancellor†4 in rebuking Bridgman†5 for stoping my pay, letting him know, that, though the Queen†6 was dead that promised me that place, they would be so far her Trustees as to se that I should enjoy what her Majestie promised; whereupon all my arrears were paid, though Sir Matthew Andrews†7 snarls at me every foot
― 190 ―
pray present my Service to my Lady and let her know her bill was sent the 5th of this instant but I being from home sent it to her this morning. the inclosed to Sir Francis concludes all at present from
Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING

2814. Edward Fowler, bishop of Gloucester, to Locke, 7 November 1700 (2294, 3501)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 145-6.
Sir,
I Embrace this Opportunity to Enquire after your health, in Oates's sweet air; and to tell you I cannot but hope you will get much more by parting with, than you could by keeping your 1000 l a year. I am in my Old winter dispensation already; having been in London just a moneth yesterday.†1 I know you were sensibly affected with the loss of your and my old Friend mr Hodges;†2 I pray God prepare us to follow him. Hoping this will find yourself and all the good Family in health, with our humble services to yourself, Sir Francis and my Lady, and the pritty Gentleman, and his sister,†3 I remain,
Sir
your Affectionate, Humble Servant,
E G
Nov. 7. 1700
I am next upon writing to Mr Willys, to let him understand that he must expect from you an Answer to his letter.
The News of this day is, that the French King has declared, he will Close with the K of Spains Will; which I believ will be generally wellcome. It is thought that the Treaty†4 was onely in Order to
― 191 ―
affrighting the Spaniard, into the gaining of that will; which places the Crown on the Duke of Anjous head, obligeing him to resign it, if the Crown of France falls to him, or reject that Crown: And if he dyes without issue it goes to Berry; and if he dyes without issue, to the Grand Duke; and if he, to Savoy.†1 But 'tis like you knew this before.

2817. Locke to Edward Clarke, 11 November 1700 (2812, 2824)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, ff. 103-4. Printed in part in Forster, pp. 63-4; in full in Rand, pp. 573-4.
Oates 11 Nov. 1700
Dear Sir
The trouble you were at with my letter to Hungerford market was more than either the matter of it required or I intended you and therefor I ought not to passe it without a particular acknowledgment which I joyn to my thanks for your soe readily favouring Mr Anderson, whom I take to be a man that you will as little repent assisting as any of his calling. The very day I writ to you last in confidence that my soar leg was as good as well, my other before night began to be out of Order and between the one and the other of them I am not yet free from pain and trouble but I hope I shall in a little time <g>et†a over it. In the meane time I have one inconvenience now the cold weather comes in which, if my legs should remain in the state they are, would make me very uneasy. You know that I have but one way to keep my feet warm that are apt to be without a fire icy cold. But now if I approach the fire the only remedy for my cold feet, the soars that yet remain on my legs <as>†a soon as they feel any warmth from the fire doe soe burn and shoot, that the pain is intolerable. This obleiges me to spend a great part of my time in bed a way of liveing I doe not much like: Though when I consider it well I think I ought to be content that I am at all amongst the liveing. Tis not the spleen that suggests this thought but the news I heard this post that my old friend Mr Hodges is dead.†1 He, Dr Thomas and I were intimate in our yonger days in the University.†2 They two are gon and who could have thought that I much the weakest and most unlikely of the three should have out lived them?
I am sorry you continue to give me noe better account of your health. I heartily wish it and that I could say any thing to you about it more effectuall than my wishes. I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate and most humble servant
J LOCKE

2821. William Popple to Locke, 23 November 1700 (2740, 2868)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 244-5.
London. November the 23th: 1700.
Sir,
I am obliged to you for your letter of the 18th, and more particularly for the account which you therein give me of your health. You do me justice in believing my concern for it. I do heartily wish the establishment of it, and that those lungs which you have managed some years so artificially may continue to performe their function many more, and inable you still to be instrumental in contributing one way or another to the good of Mankinde. I shall be mindful of what you desire me about Mr Halsey†2 when I see him: Though even without any speaking I believe those matters are of themselves in such a method as can not possibly occasion you any trouble: But however, I say, what you desire shall be done. In the mean while I return you here inclosed his Receipt for your Taxes in 1699 which was left in my hands, because of the obstruction in the Exchequer, which for the time past is removed:†3 But whether any thing of the like kinde may be
― 197 ―
renewd for the year now running I can not tell; Yet hope it will not be long before an Order for some further payment will give occasion for the resolution of that Doubt. I bless God my family are in such a degree of health as we usually enjoy: And all of them do with me present their best respects and service to you. As for News, I know none <but>†a the Death of the King of Spain and succession of the Duke of Anjou to that Crown, abroad; And the talk of a New Parliament at home; But that Talk seems yet to be onely conjectural. The next week will probably decide the point one way or other. I am
Sir,
Your most obedient humble Servant
WILLIAM POPPLE.

It was the 23d. day of November whereon†a- I have made Received the 950 l from Mr Churchill—I will bring my Ladys writings with me when I come to Oates,-†a which shall assoon as my affairs will permit me, being very desirous to see you, I was this week at Mr Frekes,†1 where talking of my design to see you at Christmass, Mr Clark said, that unless he was forced to go then into the West, he would see you likewise—I have let My Cosin†2 know My Ladys and Your kindness to him, he returns his hearty thanks, and hopes at Christmass to do it personally with me—My Lord Chief Justice Treby is much out of Order, He went yesterday to the Gravel pits,†3 where he still Continues, he had an ill night last night, but this morning was somewhat better, his principal distemper is an Asthma, I do very much fear how it will go with him, I wish He may recover, and that the Hazard was not so great, as it seems to be— At the Council Last Thursday night Nothing was done about the Parliament but My Lord M—h and G.—n.†4 did talk of the Dissolution, as matter of news about Town, which makes all people to Conclude there will be a new Parliament, and It is Probable that the writs will issue out just after Christmass.†5

2824. Locke to Edward Clarke, 9 December 1700 (2817, 2826)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 152. Printed in Rand, pp. 575-6.
Oates 9 Dec. 1700
Dear Sir
How much better had it been that you and the two ladys you mention had surprised me last week in my bed, than to let a kind intention you had to me come to noe thing? I hate bustle and pudder that hinders me from the enjoyment of my freinds. However the good intentions of ones freinds deserves thanks, which therefor pray return to our wives though they have orderd the matter soe as to hinder their execution. I know by experience that men who have been long prepareing for a journey into the country, have yet much to doe just before <they>†a leave the town and therefor I cannot but excuse this in Ladies who have more trinkets to provide, more penyworths to buy, and more visits to make the last weeke of their being in London
Whether the declaration upon which your accompanying them or not depends will be before this day seventhnight or noe I doe not know, but I am firm in the same opinion I have been a good while that it will certainly be soe.†1 If the delay of it leaves you in town past monday next†2 what hinders but you may afford us your
― 200 ―
company and take a little country air here for a few days. where I can more at large tell you that my thoughts perfectly agree with yours and that I am
Sir
Your most affectionate and most faithfull servant
J LOCKE
My Lady gives her service to you Mrs Clarke and my wife and bids me tell you she hopes you will all three keep your resolution of obleigeing her by your company before you goe into Somersetshire. and pray tell the ladyes from me that I am now in a better posture to receive them and enjoy their conversation than for some weeks back in which I have spent my time in bed not riseing till after candle light, this my soare legs obleiged me too. But now I thank god they are soe well that for this day or two I rise before dinner and sit up till ordinary bed time, and hope they are now in a way to be quite well
You see your neighbour Pawling sometimes I understand. The inclosed is of noe great hast therefor I venture to trouble you with the inclosed to be <deliverd>†a as he comes in your way

2828. Martha Lockhart to Locke, [c. 16 December 1700] (2782, 2941)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 97-8. The date is shortly after 12 December, when Rochester was appointed Lord Lieutenant. Clarke did not need to wait for the proclamation of 19 December (p. 199, n. 1) to decide to go to Chipley; William declared at the cabinet council on 15 December that parliament would be dissolved, and this was common knowledge by the 17th: Luttrell.
what I have to say for my self in excuse for my not answering Your two last letters is first my indisposition not only my head ach's but for some days I was so ill that I fear'd a feavor or Rhumatism, and this succeeded my being at the birthday†2 where I suppose I got cold ever since I've been nursing, and gosoping and tho the good success I have had has made me great amends, Yet beleive me I found it troublesome Enufe. I hope It's not too late to returne you my hearty thanks for Your kind letters especially the invitation you gave me to se you which you may be sure I am allways very glad to have from a place to which I have so much inclination, but the weather, and some other cares which I have upon me at this time, will not permit me to think of it. I find by
― 204 ―
Mrs Clark (who I was to take my leav on t'other day the wholl familly being to goe into the countrey) that you are still making complaints of the humour in your leg's I can't help naming to you a remidy I have known made use of in the like case as I have heard yours describ'd except that consideration which in your case I suppose must be had of your lungs.
It is, a pint of milk turn'd with a peice of allum to a posset and with peice's of fine cloath dip't in it bathd for an hour or more at a time, as often as they cool to be warm'd in the posset and if in any part of your leg the skin be broke to lay the warm Curd upon it as hot as You can bear it, during the time of the fomentation. I imagin the nature of this remidy is drying and healing whither these quallity's are fitting in Your case, you your self I beleive are the only best judge. I suppose the town news I mean the print's†1 are sent to you and they have allmost all that I kno. my Lord Rochesters being declare'd Lieutenant of Ireland†2 is they say but for a little time till this new turne of affairs settle and that it's for the duke of Ormond†3 that he holds it. I find some are very much discontented (whom they call of his sentiment's) at his promotion and are not to be persuaded to draw in the same plough†4 with him. I have at last tire'd my self out to be of the opinion that your advice and I beleive example might long since have taught me, to inquire after no news but the wellfare of my frends and if they are well and kind to me, to rest satisfied for the world I find will be the world. I am very much oblig'd to Your kind concerne for Mr Anderson and he poor man is allmost as much delighted with the notice you have taken of him as if it had procure'd him preferment (tho I suppose it Can't last so long). Mr Clark on your account has been Extreamly kind to him tho nothing Yet seems very like to doe towards his preferment. I must tell you Mrs Clark made many kind reproaches to you for not seing her before she left the town. I did the best I could to persuade her it was not in your present circumstances to be expected of You and so did Your wife but I'me affraid neither of us could sufficiently satisfie her but that it proceeded from less then former kindness to her and more then ordinary or Enufe to some newer acquaintance. accept the humble services of all this
― 205 ―
familly and of my wishes that Ev'ry good thing may be for Ever Yours. beleiving me allways
Your faithfull servant
M L

2830. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 21 December 1700/1 January 1701 (2757, 2836)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, f. 224. Answered by no. 2836.
+
Samedi. ce 1. 1701.
Voila, monsieur, la premiere letre que j'ecris en ce nouveau siecle, et les premiers vœux que j'y forme sont pour votre prosperitè et parfaite santé. A mon egard le plus grand bien que j'y souhaite c'est de pouvoir vous embrasser, et que l'injustice des hommes me permete au comencement d'un siecle cequ'ele m'a refusé à la fin d'un autre. Tout ceque j'ay essuyé de facheux dans le precedant pendant un long tems, seroit entierement efacé par la douceur de vous embrasser un moment dans celui-ci. cete esperance me soutient lors que je suis sur le point d'entrer dans de nouveles peines pour sortir des premieres. Il faut tout esperer du Seigneur qui est plus puissant que les puissances qui me traversent. Parlons de choses plus agreables.
L'ouvrage pour lequel vous vous etes si fort interessé,†2 poura parêtre avant la fin du dixhuitiême siecle, ceque les conjonctures ont empeché dans le dissetiême.
M. l'Abé du Bos est à Rome,†3 et je suis exemt de l'y aler joindre
― 207 ―
comme tout le monde m'y condamnoit, si un savant Cardinal qui a rendu publique la bienveillance dont il m'honore, avoit eté exalté.†1 Vous m'avez mandé que vous aviez eu quelque vüe pour la reformation du calendrier, et que vous n'y aviez pas trouvé de disposition dans les esprits de votre païs. J'ay aussi depuis long tems une vuë pour cela, et je suis seur qu'ele est diferente de la vôtre. Il n'y a qu'une seule regle dans ceque je voudrois proposer, et si le nouveau Pape vouloit y entendre, il y auroit lieu d'esperer que les Protestans ne s'en elogneroient pas. Il est plus eclairé qu'aucun de ses Predecesseurs dans tout le Siecle passé, et son Pontificat ne pouroit être plus glorieux que par un calendrier qui seroit accepté par tous les diferens partis.
Je me doneray l'honneur de vous ecrire une autrefois plus au long, celecy est seulement pour ne pas diferer à vous assurer des sentimens avec lesquels je suis, monsieur, Votre

2832. Benjamin Furly to Locke, [c. 26 December 1700/6 January 1701] (2786, 2889)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 167-8. Locke's endorsement, 1701, gives the year in which he received the letter. There were dissolutions of parliaments on 19 December 1700 and 11 November 1701. The remarks about the general European situation suit the earlier rather than the later period; Furly's desire to visit England also belongs to the winter of 1700. Harwood could scarcely bring news of the dissolution before 22 December/2 January. On 11/22 January 1701 Shaftesbury at Wimborne St. Giles acknowledges a letter from Furly 'which came by Mr. Crellis': Forster, p. 113; this letter must have been written before 6/17 January. As the present letter was written the day after Furly learnt about the dissolution, and apparently before it was reported in the Dutch newspapers, a date early in the available period seems most appropriate for it.
Dear Sir
Having so good an opportunity by the bearers, two Brothers of the Family of the Crelliusses,†1 who, in their passage to London, designe to visit you, I could not omit to salute you, and the honourable family where you reside.
And withal to acquaint you with a strange thing happend to a friend†a of mine lately in this towne: who having been in Zeeland at the East India sale, came home just as his wife lay adying. as he came into the chamber, she with a clear voice told him she had longd to see him before she dyed and now she had her desire, she told him her nether parts were dead, but that she had some things to recommend to him, which done she soone after dyed.
― 209 ―
Great grief there was in house, the yong folk dwelling in her fathers house, A while after he would go into the chamber to his wife, but the father labourd to divert him, what he could, but nothing would serve but he must go and kisse his wife for the last time. And there coming he recited what love had been betwixt them, how great his grief was, wishing that she could give him some token that she understood what he said to her, and what state he was now in: but said it was not to be expected, and so bowed himself to lay his lips to her lips, upon which blood gushed out of her, which spouted in his face, into his throat, and upon his cloths, upon which he fell down backward with the fright; And was forc'd to be let blood, The dead blood he said was in his throat so cold as if ice had been conveyed into his body.
This is so strange an accident as I ever heard of: and is worthy to be recorded; and to be considered by your Royall Society, whether the principles of their Philosophy, can explain it.
I am informd by Dr. Harwood†1 who past this Towne yesterday to go to the Hague that his Majesty has dissolved this Parliament.
God send him another that will take care of the Protestant interest, and the cause of universall liberty as men and christians, for now, if ever, there is need of vigourous and unanimous councils, amongst all that are heartily concerned for Liberty, against Priestcraft.
I know nothing that can tend to the stopping of that overflowing deluge, with which all Europe seems now, more than ever, threatned, but a hearty conjuction, and union betwixt these two nations, upon a Nationall bottome, this may prove a basis for a further alliance that may give check to that design which france seems to have, of extirpating heresy, that he may have the Glorious Title of Restorer of the Churches unity, and treader down of her enemies.
And yet when alls done, they will have difficulty enough, except God sends a spirit of Jealousy, and division betwixt the Spaniards and the French.
Some flatter themselvs that the Emperors son, has a party among the Grandes, and is gone to Spain.†2 But I feare 'tis night with him. else, it were better the whole should be in his hands, than the partition; Spain being too weak already for france.
― 210 ―
Which (by the loosing the Kingdoms of Naples, and Sicilia etc— And the annexing them to the Crown of france, which already is too great for Europe) would be made much weaker than it is.
In fine, things looke black, and a day of tryal sharper than ever seems to draw nigh, for all that cannot fall down and worship the beast and false prophet, from whence Libera nos Domine—
I am still in the briars with my wives and sisters affair, tho still in hopes to get through this winter—and that I shall have the happyness with my wife, of seing you in the spring or summer. Which concludes this, from
Deare Sir
Your most humble servant and cordiall friend
BENJAMIN FURLY
[Note by another writer on cover]: Sir Mr. Daniell Crellius who brought this letter from Holland, hopes to have some other opertunity of wayting on you himself.
Address: For John Locke Esquire at Sir Francis Masham's At Oates per Amy Q D G.
Endorsed by Locke: B: Furly 01
2833. Locke to Dr. (later Sir) Hans Sloane, 27 December 1700 (2640, 2838)
B.M., Sloane MS. 4038, ff. 113-14. Printed in Forster, pp. 69-71. Answered by no. 2838.
Oates 27 Dec. 1700
Sir
It is not fit I let the year goe out before I return you my thanks for the many favours I have received from you in it particularly for the philosophical transactions. whereof those of July and August came but lately to my hands. Those of April. May and June I thank you for as well as the rest, though I have them not yet, which I impute to the forgetfulnesse of Mr Churchils men who have with care laid them aside for me, and there I shall have them when I send for them and therefor pray receive my thanks for them all. And give me leave to owne to you that I am ashamd to be soe much inrichd by you in philosophical knowledg without furnishing any thing to your collections, I came into the country with a designe of imploying some part of my leisure in
― 211 ―
lookeing over some papers I have with an intention to offer you anything I should finde in them that I might presume you would think worthy to appear amongst those observations which you continue to obleige the world with. But soar legs that seized on me soon after my comeing hither and that have ever since made me spend the greatest part of my time in bed have kept me from that and several other things I proposed to my self. I thank god my legs are now pretty well again. But my old evill of my breast (as is to be expected from every years increase of age) sits heavier upon me than it was wont to doe formerly in country air. I have read physick enough to think it not at all strange that it should doe soe, and therefor am not startled at it. The tenement must some time or other fall to dust†1 and mine has held out beyond expectation. Whilst I stay here I would be willing to doe that little that I can. and if I have an oportunity make some acknowledgment to you. I have a register of the weather for ten years past of the same kinde with those†a you may remember of mine published in Mr. Boyles history of the air p. 104 etc.†2 I know not whether it will be fit to clog your transactions with such things as those. Be you judg of that. This I know that I did not keep this register for my own sake alone. and that if I had any thing of more value than this I should not refuse it you if you thought it worth the haveing†3
A Diabetes is a disease soe little frequent that you will not think it strange that I should aske whether you in your great practise ever met with it. You will doe me the favour to tell me the pathognomonick signes of it and if you have cured it or known it cured you will obleige me in instructing me in the methode. I wish you a merry Christmas and an happy new year and am
Sir
your most humble servant
JOHN LOCKE
When you doe me the favour to write be pleased to direct your letter to me at Oates. To be left at Mr Samuel Joclins in Bishop Startford
