Je vous prie de salue Mr l'Abe du Bos quand vous lui ecrivez. Cui <prospera>†a omnia et Cis et Trans Alpina opto†2
(Latin) May God grant an end to this also,†1 so that hereafter, with all your affairs in order, you may enjoy much ease and rest, and I the most heartily desired sight of you. The evils of age as it grows more burdensome, pressing more sharply on me every year, warn me to think of my departure. For two months and more a fluid [humor] which was falling into my legs, and, with breaking of the skin, inflicting pain, kept me in bed almost whole days, so much so that what time remained for me was not enough for correspondence. By God's good will this trouble is now becoming somewhat less, and I hope that He will shortly restore me to my former and more courteous manner of life. There is nothing that I may say or promise about my lungs. Their weakness, a usual evil of old age, is never made good again by the increase of time and years. Nevertheless the hope of seeing you sometime and enjoying your company flatters me and, if strength were not wanting, the wish to visit you in Paris is certainly not wanting.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Toinard chez Monsieur des Noyers devant l'Espèe royale dans la rüe Mazarin à Paris
Postmark: IA 13
Endorsed by Toinard: 1. <1701.>†b
2837. J.-B. Du Bos to Locke, 1/12 January [1701] (2748, 2900)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 238-9. Printed by G. Bonno in Revue de littérature comparée, xxiv (1950), 506-8. Year from Locke's endorsement, etc.
A Rome le Mercredi 1/12 de Jan.
Je ne crois point monsieur quil soit besoin dexcuser mon silence et vous me rendé trop de justice pour ne lavoir pas atribué a lembaras du voyage plutost qu'a ma negligence.
vous conoisé trop bien LItalie pour que je veille vous en rien aprendre et je vous entretiendré seulement de quelques livres nouveaux les quels peuvent nestre point encore parvenus a vostre conoisance.
un Napolitain nommé Gemelli vient de faire imprimer les derniers volumes de la relation dun voyage quil a faict autour du monde et dont il nest retour que depuis deux ans. Son livre est composé de six gros volumes in 8 et parmi beaucoup de choses
― 216 ―
triviales et scues de tout le monde il en contient de tres singulieres.†1 Je ne puis m'empecher de vous en ecrire une que jay lue ce matin. Gemelli raconte quil a vu a Pekin un Jesuite Espagnol le quel avoit entendu en confession une esclavé que les tartares avoient enlevee dans le golfe de la Californie et la quelle disoit estre tousjours venue par terre.
Je devois vous dire d'abord que cet autheur a faict le tour du monde a rebours et contre le vent. il a esté aux Indes Orientales par terre, de la a la Chine et aux Mexique par les Philippines. come il a vecu parmi les Espagnols il dit beaucoup de choses nouvelles <de>†a leurs decouvertes et de linterieur dun payis dont nous n'avions point eu de nouvelles, depuis celles que nous donna vostre Thomas Gage il i a pres de soixante ans.†2
un pere Bonani Jesuite a donné une histoire des papes par leurs medailles en deux gros volumes in folio.†3
le frere†b Pozzi Jesuite va publier la seconde partie de la perspective.†4 cest un habile peintre et un peintre habile je veux dire quil peint viste et assez bien.
voici monsieur ce que jay pu aprendre de nouveautez Litteraires depuis que je suis a Rome. a ce que jentends dire elles ni sont point fort abondantes et sil est vray que les sciences fassent leur tour dOrient en Occident come le soleil on peut craindre quelles ne soient ici a leur couchant il en de meme des beaux arts et si lon voit a Rome les plus beaux tableaux, les plus belles statues et les plus magnifiques batiments du monde, lon ni trouve plus ni peintres ni sculpteurs ni architectes.
vous nestes point le seul qui soié chagrin de la lenteur de nostre ami mr Toinard a publier ses ouvrages: il i a deux jours que jeu la dessus une grande conversation avec le Cardinal Noris qui ne scauroit se lasser den parler.
Le procez des Jesuites contre les missionaires de la Chine va durer lontemps sil est vray que ces premiers veillent franchir le
― 217 ―
pas come le bruit court quils i sont resolus et soutenir que les Lettrez Chinois ne croient ni la providence ni limmortalite de lame. ils faut quils soient a bout pour si resoudre, car ce sera donner un dementi bien positif a cent de leurs escrivains qui nous ont proposé ces lettrez come des Chrestiens a qui il ne manquoit que le baptesme.†1
Si je puis vous servir ici, ou je resteré jusques aux mois de May, adressé vos lettres a Paris a mr Paul Foissin†2 banquier rue des petits champs St Julien.
Je vous prie de faire mes compliments a mr Robert Cuninghuam†3 et de me croire
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
DU BOS

2838. Dr. (later Sir) Hans Sloane to Locke, 2 January 1701 (2833, 2956)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 122-3. Answers no. 2833.
London Jan. 2. 1700.
Sir
I received Your very obliging letter and am very sorry Your health has been so indifferent I am hopefull now Your leggs are better you will find some papers and observations you have by you that may be very much for the advancement of knouledge if so I shall be very glad of the favour of them and of the Register of the weather you speak of. I need not tell you that many things may be deduced from that which may be of use to the publick. I have given orders the transactions should be sent you from time to time as they are published had I better materials I would take care you should have better there, but such as they are I take it as a favour that you do me the kindnesse to accept of them.
As to what you write to me of a diabetes I can say only this in answer. I have been many times consulted in cases where people
― 218 ―
have thought they had a diabetes but I was of another opinion. There is nothing more ordinary then for Hysterical or Hypochondriac persons upon their making great quantities of water, which is a symptom of their disease, to have an opinion they have a diabetes. That being a dangerous distemper is the rather in their apprehensions who seem to be allways industrious in finding out somewhat to disturb themselves. Another kind of people are affraid of this disease and those are such who drink much of small bear, or other liquors, and especially coffee and tea, which being drunk prove diuretic and give them subject of uneasinesse not reflecting at the unusuall quantity of liquids they take at or between their meals. Upon the whole of many scores of people that have come to me on this account I never saw but one woman that had a true diabetes. There there was a great discharge of thick water like to honey and water mix'd, it was heavyer much then ordinary urine and with it was a very great dejection of the spirits restlessnesse dry black tongue drougth and other symptoms of a lurking malignant feaver. I try'd for severall days all those med'cines that are or have been famous in that disease, as gumms, Lime drinks, crocus martis adstringens, sanguis draconis etc. but without any manner of advantage: For the distemper seem'd to affect her head and nerves more and more and though her pulse did not seem to be more feaverish yet it grew weaker. In this condition another physitian was called to her. He promised great things from theriaca Andromachi which having opium in it I was affraid of, but being willing to see the successe of this method, though I was not concerned in it, I was resolved to observe what followed, which was that it seised her head more and more and in some few days from her first being taken ill she dyed. This is all I can call to mind of this very uncommon disease which is the only one I ever saw. I have indeed heard of many but in my opinion there are very few such diseased persons to be found and they are rather of the first or second kind I have mention'd. I have tired you long enough and will not say any more to you at present but that I am with great sincerity
Your most obedient and most humble servant
HANS SLOANE
Address: To Mr. Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: IA 2
Endorsed by Locke: H: Sloane 2 Jan. 00/1 Answered Jul. 14

Sir After a Long promise, This day I have sent by Lenham 1/2 cwt of Orenges,†a I gave them into his owne hand. pray Sir Axept of them, and I pray God Every one of Them particulerly may Contribute too your health, I hope They are good, and I hope there Is the whole number, This I speak because I got one of my Neighbours to buy them for me, for my Deare wife have been very bad, to that Extremitie, That she have spett bloud, she have been bleeded 3 times by the Advice of A Docter and now we have sent her Into the Cuntry and sinc that she have sum releef, for sinc the Cough have Abated she Is very short winded, All her cry was That her Lungs was hot as fier and A great paine In her back: she doe follow the Doctor directions and This day, I bless god, I heare, she Is sumthing better, Deare Cousin, I had stated our Account before This, but I must Beg A Little Longer Time Tell it pleas god to Rayes my wife Againe, for by This providenc, it has occausened This Omission, I Heartley wish you many happy Nue Yeares. I am Deare Cousin
your Faithfull Kinsman and Humble Sarvant

2844. Peter King, later first Baron King, to Locke, 14 January 1701 (2841, 2845)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, f. 119. Answers nos. 2840-1; answered by no. 2845.
London. January. 14. 1700
Honoured Sir
According to Your Order I have sold Your Stock in the East India Company at 133 l. I have indeed 133 1/4 but the Quarter I give for brokeridge, so not to puzle our account, I give you credit for it after the rate of 133 l, The books are not yet open to make the transfer, so cannot have the mony as yet till the transfer be made, assoon as I have the mony I shall follow Your Orders therein— Stock is falling and now under 133, without doubt you have good reason for what you do, but I have 200 l there of my own, which I Intend to run the risk of, the Colledge is very sanguine, that by May it will be worth 150 l per Cent. I can't learn any thing here which should make it fall, except the apprehensions of a war— No news here but of Elections, The Poll at Westminster is not yet over, but Vernon and Cross have yet the majority, The Kings Servants Poll for Vernon and Cross, but the Servants of Somebody else for Vernon and Sir Walter Clarges, who was distanced last Saturday by 1400 or 1500,†1 —Sir W. Yong, My Lord Spencer,†2 Mr Bere,†3 Mr Clark are chosen—I am sorry for what you write me
― 224 ―
about Your Lungs and Legs, I wish the weather may relieve you, and do hope that by your next I shall hear that you are recovered again—Pray Sir Give my service to Sir Francis, for whose good success I now wish at this instant, and to My Lady and the whole family—The Elections hitherto are not worse than heretofore, but rather better.†1
I am Sir
Your most affectionate Cosin and Servant
P. KING.

2846. Locke to [Richard King], 20 January [1701] (2843, 3322)
The Remains of John Locke, Esq;, 1714, pp. 15-16. The reasons for the identification of the person addressed are (1) a letter to Curll, dated Exeter, 10 July 1714, and signed R. K., and prefixed to the Remains; the writer sends Curll five letters written by Locke, of which four are addressed to himself; (2) Desmaizeaux, reprinting these four letters in A Collection of Several Pieces, 1720, identifies the person addressed as the Revd. Mr. Richard King; (3) the relationship with extant letters from King to Locke and with other letters in the correspondence.
Date: the letter answers no. 2843, which is dated 1701 by Locke's endorsement; and there are mentions of a letter from Locke to King at this time in nos. 2845, 2847, and 2849. Further a cousin of Peter King's was expected to visit Oates this December: no. 2823, etc.; nothing appears in the extant correspondence to show that Richard King visited Oates about January 1704.
Oates, 20 January 170 3/4.
Sir,
The small Acknowledgments I was able to make, for the Honour of your Visit, and Enjoyment of your Company here, left the Debt on my side, and deserve not the Notice you are pleas'd to take of them.
In your obliging Letter of the Thirteenth, you do me Favours, and you thank me too. If you intend by this, a perfect Acquisition of so inconsiderable a thing as I am, your Worth and Virtue dispose me to be as much at your Service as you please; I wish I found any thing in my self that might promise you any usefulness from me. That defect I shall endeavour to make up the best I can, with a perfect Esteem, and a Readiness of Will; which must supply the want of the Abilities of doing.
I thank you for the printed Paper you sent me, and am very glad to see such a Spirit rais'd, for the Support and Enlargement of Religion. Protestants, I think, are as much concern'd now as ever, to be vigorous in their joint Endeavours, for the Maintenance of the Reformation. I wish all that call themselves so, may be prevail'd with by those whom your Paper intimates, to imitate the Zeal, and persue the Principles of those great and pious Men, who were instrumental to bring us out of Roman Darkness and Bondage. I heartily pray for good Success on all such Endeavours.
If I may guess at the Intention of the Society, by the only Man you let me know of it, I may be confident that the Glory of God, and the Propagation of True Religion is the only Aim of it. May
― 226 ―
God eminently prosper all Endeavours that way, and increase the number of those who seriously lay it to heart.
Sir Francis, my Lady, and the rest of this Family, return you their Humble Service. I am,
Sir, Your most Humble and most Obedient Servant,
JOHN LOCKE

2849. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 24 January [1701] (2848, 2851)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 96-7. Year from King's endorsement and contents. Answers no. 2848; answered by no. 2852.
Oates 24 Jan
Dear Cosin
I thank you for your pains and concerne in my business. Had I foreseen your being chosen Parliament man I had taken quite other measures. Whether you shall put the money into Bank bills or East India bonds I leave it to you to doe just as you would doe with your own only I would have it soe as I might have it at command to buy again when it is sunk to the lowest which I am apt to think will not bee till tis seen not only what resolutions will be taken about peace or warr but also about the two companyes themselves†1 in this parliament. For I beleive it may be suspected that this parliament will not be much friends to the New Company and soe may perhaps shake it. I never loved stock jobing†2 and therefor sold not with any such view. But now I am out, though I intend to buy again, yet I would stay till it is at worst, as I beleive you would advise me, and therefore I desire you to mention in your lettres how the rate goes, and when you write anything that requires a quick answer direct it to be left at Mr Harisons at the Crown in Harlow. The list also of the Parliament members will as it grows compleat be able to give you some guesse at the temper of the house which I should be glad to know as also what the College thinks. One thing only give me leave to caution you of, that is that I would not have you let any one know that this is my money or that when you purchase again it is for me. What views I had that made me, when I gave you order to sell out, not like to be in, I shall hereafter at more leisure explain to you. It is probable that I shall in a little time receive £500 out of the Exchequer pray think how to dispose of that. I trouble you with my concernes but it is because I think you doe not take it amisse but think me nearer to you in freindship than relation. I writ to you the last post and therein inclosed one to your Cosin King. I guesse by your silence concerning it that a long lettre I writ to you the same day you went

from hence never came to your hands.†1 The business will now keep cold and I shall not now trouble you with it again. I am
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant

2852. Peter King, later first Baron King, to Locke, 28 January 1701 (2851, 2855)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 122-3. Answers no. 2849; answered by no. 2855.
London January 28. 1700.
Sir
I Received your last letter,†1 and as to the long letter which you writ me the same day I came from Oates,†2 I did receive it, and I thought I had given you an account thereof, If I did not, it was my forgetfulness, It Relates wholy to Francis Carpenters busyness, and I will take care to do what is fitting to be done therein, assoon as I go to Sutton, I think nothing can be done in it before—I this day spoke with Mr Conyers about the transferring Your Thousand pounds in his hands, he was very easy, and said that he was not willing to transfer it to another, but if you would have your mony, You should have it whenever You would, I told him, that I had only orders to ask him that Question, and that I would you write thereof,—I think the best way will be to let it ly where it is, till I find a Conveniency for the disposal thereof, I will mind both that and the 500 l., which you expect out of the Exchequer—My
― 231 ―
Attendance In Parliament will not hinder me from minding any of Your Concerns, and I hope that Neither that, Nor any thing else will prevent You from letting me serve you here, wherein I can—I desire you with my service to my Lady to let her know, that I have Received her letter, and thought to have writ her this post, but had not time. Two Dutch Mails came in too day, and what they have brought in particular, I cannot tell, only in general great probabilitys of a war, which hath tumbled down all stocks this evening to the written prices on the margent of the paper herewith sent you†1 —New East India bonds are 2s. 6d worse than mony, And old about 10s. all things are now So Uncertain, that my Cosin Freke thinks to get an iron Chest, and put his mony therein for some time—he doth not like the Bank, but however I will get 5 or 6 or 7†a Bank bills for an 100 l. each too morrow, and stay three Or four days for the rest, to see how matters will go—I will do for you in the same manner as I would do for my self, I wish now that I had sold out my 200 l. too, but the Colledge prevented me— The Colledge is very sanguine, That this will be a good Parliament, Assoon as the List is printed, I will send it you—I writ you in my last about my going the Circuit, I believe that the other Lawyers will go, however I shall give that deference to Your Opinion as to be guided by it, if my affairs will in any measure permit it, which I hope they will—I desire you to be free with me in all matters relating to this point, I would not neglect my own particular interest, and on the other hand let that sink or swim, I will prefer the publick to it, for seing I am unexpectedly brought in, I look upon it to be a particular effect of the divine providence, which I ought to improve and answer—I am Sir
Your Most affectionate Cosin and Servant
P. KING.
Address: For John Locke Esquire [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford] Frank. P. King.

2854. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 28 January/8 February 1701 (2785, 2924)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 137-8. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 119-21.
A Amsterdam le 8 de Fevrier 1701
J'ai appris, Monsieur, par une lettre de nôtre Ami Mr. Coste, que vous aviez été incommodé pendant quelque temps, mais Dieu
― 233 ―
soit loüé que le chagrin, que cette noüvelle m'auroit causé, ait été adouci en apprenant en même temps que vous étiez guéri. Les gens comme vous mériteroient d'avoir une longue et heureuse vieillesse, que je vous souhaite de tout mon coeur. Pour moi, par la grace de Dieu, je jouïs d'une santé assez égale, et la coûtume, que j'ai contractée de travailler, depuis la jeunesse, est comme changée en nature. Je vous en donnerai des preuves, par quelques petits Ouvrages, que je vous enverrai par la premiere occasion.†1 Il y a assez long-temps, que je pris la liberté de vous écrire qu'il y avoit deux Demoiselles de mes Amies,†2 qui cherchoient une condition en Angleterre, et de vous demander si Madame vôtre Hôtesse n'en sauroit point. Comme elles avoient, en quelque sorte, changé de vuë je ne vous en parlai plus. Mais elles ont repris à présent ce dessein, et je viens vous refaire la même priere. Ce sont deux soeurs, qui sont toutes deux fort au dessous de trente ans, qui savent le Flamand, et qui ont sû l'Anglois, de sorte que je suis persuadé qu'elles le rapprendront sans peine, le François étant d'ailleurs leur langue maternelle. Elles ont, ce me semble, toutes les qualitez, que l'on peut demander d'une Demoiselle, dans une maison de condition, et je croi qu'elles pourront même satisfaire des gens assez délicats. A l'égard des moeurs et de la bonne conduite, et pour le passé et pour l'avenir, j'en puis répondre comme de moi même. Ce n'est que la mauvaise conduite et la bizarrerie incurable d'un Pere, qui les oblige à se tourner de ce côté là. Je ne vous cacherai pas, Monsieur, qu'elles sont si proches à ma femme, qu'elles ne peuvent pas l'être davantage, et que par conséquent je m'interesse si fort dans tout ce qui les regarde, que si elles étoient mes filles je n'y prendrois pas plus d'intêret. Je vous supplie donc de vous informer si quelque Dame de qualité de vôtre connoissance n'auroit point besoin d'une, ou de deux Demoiselles Françoises. Si elles pouvoient être ensemble, ce seroit mieux, mais comme cela est difficile, elles ne feront pas difficulté de se séparer. Je vous aurai, Monsieur, une très-grande et très sensible obligation, si vous voulez bien prendre la peine de vous informer parmi vos Amis et vos Amies. Mr. Limbourg nôtre Ami se porte bien, quoi qu'il se fasse un peu vieux. Il ramasse, comme vous savez, le Martyrologe des Héretiques brulez par ceux qui se sont séparez de l'Eglise Romaine.†3 Je lui ai fait avoir les procès de deux brulez à
― 234 ―
Geneve. On a tiré ces procès des Registres du Conseil de cette ville.†1 S'il ne publie pas cet ouvrage pendant sa vie; il sera au moins prêt, pour ceux qui lui survivront. Faites nous part, s'il vous plait de vos occupations, si tant est que vôtre santé vous permette d'enrichir le Public de quelque chose de nouveau. Pour moi, l'Ecriture sainte m'occupe entierement, à quelque petites distractions près, que je ne puis éviter. J'ai fait une Préface au Lexicon Philologicum de Martinius, qui est imprimé il y a quelques années à Utrecht, mais qui a été acheté depuis peu par un Libraire de cette ville.†2 Si vous avez cette édition et que vous souhaitiez d'avoir la préface, je pourrai l'avoir du Libraire. Je suis, Monsieur, de tout mon coeur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC

2855. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 31 January [1701] (2852, 2856)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 100-1. Printed as far as the subscription in King, pp. 253-4. Year from King's endorsement. The later part answers no. 2852.
Oates 31 Jan
Dear Cosin
Haveing noe time but for a few words the last post†3 'tis fit I now answer the other particulars of your lettre which I then was forced to omit. Your staying in town the next vacation I look upon as resolvd and the reasons I finde for it in your own lettre now that I have time to read them a little more deliberately I think sufficient to determin you should, though I say noe thing at all. Though
― 235 ―
every time I think of it I am more and more confirmd in the opinion that it is absolutely necessary in all respects whether I consider the publique or your own private concernes neither of which are indifferent to me.
Tis my private thought that the Parliament will scarce sit even soe much as to choose a speaker before the end of the terme.†1 But when ever he is chosen tis of noe small consequence which side carys it, if there be two nominated or at least in view, as tis ten to one there will be espetialy in a Parliament chosen with soe much strugle. Haveing given all the help possibly you can in this which is usualy a leading point shewing the strength of the partys, My next advice to you is not to speak at all in the house for some time, what ever fair oportunity you may seem to have. But though you keep your mouth shut I doubt not but you will have your eyes open to see the temper and observe the motions of the house and diligently to remarke the skil of management, and carefully watch the first and secret beginings of things and their tendencys, and endeavour if there be danger in them to crush them in the Egg. You will say what can you doe who are not to speak? Tis true I would not have you speake to the house, but you may communicate your light or apprehensions to some honest speaker who may make use of it. For there have always been very able members who never speake, who yet by their penetration and foresight have this way donne as much service as any within those walls. And here by you will more recommend your self when people shal observe soe much modesty joynd with your parts and judgment, than if you should seem forward, though you spoke well. But let the man you communicate to be not only well intentioned but a man of Judgment. Methinks I take too much upon me in these directions. I have only this to say in my excuse, that you desird it more than once and I advise you noething which I would not doe my self were I in your place. I should have much more to say to you were you here, But it being fitter for discourse and debate than for lettre I hope I may see you here e're long Sir Francis haveing already proposed to me your stealeing down sometimes with him on a Saturday and returning monday. The Votes you offer me will be very acceptable if I <mistake>†a not the members
― 236 ―
have more than one copy gratis and for sometime at least dureing this busy season I would be glad you would send me every post the three news papers viz Postman Post boy, and Flying post. But when you begin to send them you will doe me a kindeness to stop Mr Churchil from sending me any more of them. For he sends them now but it is by the Butcher and they come very uncertainly. But when you send me these papers doe not think you are bound always to write to me. Though I am always glad to hear from you, yet I must not put that penance upon you. Things of moment I doubt not but you will let me know. I am
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
Sir Francis my Lady etc give you their service
Since the concludeing the above written I have received yours of 28th. I thank you for all the rest but am troubled to finde you say you will stay in town if your affairs will in any measure permit which you hope they will. I know they will permit if you will order them soe. And therefor I earnestly beg you that you would. And I think you may trust me in what I said to you in reference to your interest. But I can say noe more now. I doubt not but as to the disposeing of the mony in your hands you will doe as for your self. Though in my opinion Bank bills are the better security. I am not covitous of growing rich, though I am not willing to loose the little I have. which makes me think whether your Cosin Frekes be not the best way for some time. Think well of it. Ready mony by one, is a good commodity if perilous times threaten
My Lady thinks her self obleiged by your intention to answer her lettre. But says you ought not to trouble your self to doe it, noething in it requireing an answer

Dear Cosin
I am glad to find by yours of Jan. 30 that you are resolved to stay. Your own resolution in case of unforseen accidents will always be in your own power. Or if you will make me the complement that you will not goe without my leave, you may be sure that in any unforeseen presseing occasion that may happen that may make it necessary for you, you will not only have my leave but my perswasion to goe. What you write me of Mr Justice Powis I am glad of for his sake and for yours.
Though you sold out of the East India Company yet give me leave to minde you that you are to have the Interest or dividend for Christmas quarter for that which you sold as well as that you did not sell it not being sold till after Christmas
This I mention that amongst your other much business it may not be forgotten and soe neglected and lost.
If you received my letter concerning Francis Carpenters businesse,†1 there needs noe more to be said. It will keep cold

Tis said the two East India companys will unite is there anything in it?

2857. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 7/18 February 1701 (2795, 2866)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 141-2. I have not found van Limborch's copy. Printed apparently from his copy in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 466-8, omitting the passages relating to van Limborch's son. Answered by no. 2866.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Prælegit mihi hisce diebus Guenellonus noster epistolam tuam, quæ te cum astmate graviter conflictari nuntiabat. Equidem valetudinem tuam afflictam ex animo doleo, eamque tibi firmiorem precor. Sed non sine admiratione ex literis tuis intellexi, te binas tantum hoc anno à me accepisse; cum circa finem mensis Octobris tertias scripserim, quibus addidi duo vitæ Episcopii, à Marco Teute latinitate donatæ, exemplaria, unum tibi, alterum Francisco Masham Cudworth, unà cum literis ad ipsum, quæ jam dudum tibi
― 239 ―
reddita nullus dubitabam.†1 Fasciculus quatuor comprehendebat exemplaria, quorum reliqua duo destinata erant Rev. Episcopis Salisburiensi, ac Bathoniensi et Wellensi. Filius meus per epistolam bibliopolam Churchil monuerat, fasciculum per nautam, cujus nomen indicabat, esse missum, et de omnibus instruxerat. Nauta redux filio retulit, fasciculum bibliopolæ Churchil esse traditum. Nunc autem, cum ex literis tuis ad Guenellonem cognoscerem, exemplaria hæc ad tuas non pervenisse manus, nauta denuò à filio meo rogatus, respondit, duos se habuisse fasciculos, eorum alterum ab eo ad quem destinatus erat è navi suâ esse petitum: alterum autem, quem bibliopola petere neglexit, in telonium esse delatum: ignorare autem se, uter eorum filii mei fasciculus fuerit. Jam metuo, ne noster sit fasciculus qui in telonio asservatur. Posset moneri Churchil, ut eum inde repetat, et unicuique suum exemplar tradat. Inscriptio præfert nomen Episcopi Salisburiensis; additum autem erat, tradendum esse fasciculum bibliopolæ Churchil. Doleo interim etiam epistolam meam aberrasse, in quâ scripsi, magnam me libri tui partem legisse, omniaque maximoperè mihi probari.†2
― 240 ―
Postea retulit mihi amicus, se Cartesii quosdam sequaces, à quibus aliquot e prioribus capitibus lecta erant, convenisse: illis maximè displicuisse duo, quæ ego verissima duco; nullas videlicet dari ideas innatas: et animam non esse nudam cogitationem.†1 Verum quid aliud à Cartesii sequace exspectes? Alios audivi magnoperè librum tuum laudantes, et sententiæ tuæ applaudentes. Ego summâ cum delectatione eum legi, et etiamnum illius lectionem continuo. Verum quoniam non tam exactam linguæ Gallicæ cognitionem habeo, ut phraseon quarumdam Gallicarum vim primâ lectione assequar, præsertim in materiâ subtili et arduâ, cogor nonnumquam, ut distinctè mentem tuam percipiam, lectionem aliquoties repetere. Gratissimum foret, si librum tuum latinitate donatum†a conspicere†a quandoque detur; tum facilius quæ scripsisti intelligerem, et fortasse de quibusdam, quæ de hominis in volendo libertate scripsisti, tecum conferrem. Valde quæ ibi scribis mihi probantur. Video te terminos aliquot obscuros aut ambiguos in illâ materiâ elucidasse: Sed nescio an ubique mentem tuam perceperim: Relegam integrum caput; et si quid occurrat ad quod hæsito, ingenuè ac rotundè ad te scribam; planè persuasus dilucidâ tuâ explicatione omnem, si qua sit, obscuritatem disparituram.
― 241 ―
Sed et ingenuè tibi confiteor, mærorem ex filii mei infortunio,†1 ex quo difficulter emerget, quodque non leviter rem meam familiarem afflixit, sæpe meditationes meas, quas studiis consecravi, turbare. Verum dabit Deus his quoque finem.†2 Ego ut honestâ et non inutili occupatione mæroris mei tædium diluam, incepi Commentarium in Acta Apostolorum conscribere, sed novâ quadam ratione ac methodo.†3 Criticos egerunt Grotius,†4 aliique; quorum laboribus mea diligentia nihil addere potest. Itaque omissâ criticâ, aliam mihi interpretandi methodum præscripsi: ut ex historiâ Apostolorum, variisque illius circumstantiis, ac præsertim eorum concionibus, religionis Christianæ veritatem ac divinitatem asseram, et quâ methodo Apostoli contra Judæos eam adstruxerint ostendam. In hisce explicandis prolixior paulò sum: reliqua huc non spectantia obiter tantum attingo. Quibus alia contra Judæos disputandi methodus placet meum laborem non probatum iri, facile prævideo. Sed veritati litandum est, et Apostolos duces sequi præstat, quam homines affectibus ac præjudiciis nimium indulgentes. Vale, Vir Amplissime: Deus pristinam tibi restituat sanitatem, ut, quoad vivis, egregiis tuis laboribus publico
― 242 ―
inservire possis. Salutant te quam officiosissimè uxor mea liberique. Salutem à nobis dices Dominæ Masham, totique familiæ.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS À LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 18 Februarii
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
The other day our friend Guenellon read to me your letter, which informed us that you were grievously afflicted with asthma. I am heartily sorry that your health is troubled and pray that it may become steadier for you. But it was not without surprise that I learnt from your letter that you had received only two letters from me this [last] year, since I wrote a third about the end of October, adding to it two copies of the life of Episcopius [p. 238] translated into Latin by Marcus Teut, one for you, the other for Francis Cudworth Masham, together with a letter to him; I had no doubt that these had long since been delivered to you.†1 The packet contained four copies, the remaining two being intended for the reverend bishops of Salisbury and of Bath and Wells. My son had informed the bookseller Churchill by a letter that the packet was sent by a mariner, whose name he gave, and had instructed him [Churchill?] about everything. On his return the mariner reported to my son that the packet had been delivered to the bookseller Churchill. But now, when I learnt from your letter to Guenellon that these copies had not reached your hands, the mariner, being questioned anew by my son, replied that he had had two parcels; one of them had been fetched from his ship by the person for whom it was intended, but the other, which the bookseller had neglected to fetch, had been conveyed to the custom-house; but he did not know which of them was my son's packet. I am now afraid that it is our packet that is being kept in the custom-house. Churchill could be advised to fetch it thence and to deliver his copy to each of those concerned. The address shows the name of the bishop of Salisbury, but it was added that the packet was to be delivered to the bookseller Churchill. Meanwhile I am sorry that my letter also has gone astray; I wrote in it that I had read a large part of your book and very greatly approved of everything in it.†2 A friend told me later that he had met some followers of Descartes [p. 239] who had read some of the earlier chapters; they were very greatly displeased by two things that I regard as most true: namely, that innate ideas are denied; and that the soul is not bare cogitation.†1 But what else would you expect from a follower of Descartes? I have heard others greatly praising your book and applauding your opinion. I have read it with very great pleasure and am still continuing to read it. But since I do not possess so exact a knowledge of French as to understand the import of some French phrases at a first reading, especially in subtle and difficult matter, I am sometimes compelled to repeat the reading several times in order to grasp your meaning clearly. It would be most welcome if it were some day given [to me] to see your book translated into Latin; then I should more readily understand what you have written and perhaps discuss with you some things that you have written about the liberty of a man in willing. I thoroughly approve of what you write about it. I see that you have elucidated some obscure or ambiguous terms in regard to that subject; but I do not know whether I have grasped your meaning everywhere. I will reread the whole chapter, and if anything occurs at which I am at a stand I will write to you frankly and roundly; fully convinced that all obscurity, if there is any, will disappear [p. 240] with your clear exposition. But I frankly confess that grief for my son's misfortune,†1 from which it will be difficult for him to extricate himself, and which has seriously injured my private means, often disturbs my meditations, which I have dedicated to studies. But God will grant an end to these things also.†2 In order to allay the irksomeness of my grief by a worthy and not useless occupation I have begun to compose a commentary on the Acts of the Apostles, but on a new plan and in a new way.†3 Grotius†4 and others commented as critics; my diligence can add nothing to their labours. Therefore, omitting criticism, I have prescribed for myself another way of interpreting: so as to declare from the history of the Apostles and its changing circumstances, and especially from their sermons, the truth and holiness of the Christian religion, and to show by what way the Apostles established it against the Jews. I set forth these things at some length; I only touch by the way on the rest that have no bearing on them. I easily foresee that those who are satisfied with another way of arguing against the Jews will not approve of my work. But truth must be served and it is better to follow the Apostles as leaders rather than men who are over-indulgent to passions and prejudices. Good-bye, excellent Sir. May God restore your former health to you, so that as long as you live you can serve the public by your [p. 241] excellent labours. My wife and children send you their warmest greetings. Please give our respects to Lady Masham and the whole family.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 18 February 1701
Address: For John Locke Esquire at Mr. Pawlings overagainst the plough in Little Lincolns Inne feilds London

2859. Locke to Edward Clarke, 10 February [1701] (2826, 2861)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, f. 105. Printed in Ollion, p. 252; Rand, p. 577. Year from Clarke's endorsement.
Oates 10 Feb
Dear Sir
When Sir Francis went to town I desired him to give you my service and to let me know whether you were there that I might write to you as soon as I knew you were in London. Your kind lettre of the 8th gives me an assurance of that, though it be too silent of your health which was an other part of my enquiry by Sir Francis. I will hope, hearing noe complaints from you, that it is pretty well reestablishd. This is not a time to be ill in. I cannot yet get my legs well. They soe much inconvenience me when I am up, that they make me spend most of my time in bed, wherein I have noe great satisfaction. As to my lungs they keep their ordinary course, and feel the effects of winter. I long to hear this days success†1 by which I shall make some guess of the future. Pray give my service and thanks to all that rememberd me at Chipley. I shall write more at large in my next. This is only in short to welcome you to town. For though in this place out of the world I am in noe hurry yet the messenger makes me in hast. I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate friend and humble servant
J LOCKE
My service to the Batchelor
My Lady and this family give you both theirs

2860. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 14 February [1701] (2858, 2862)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 106-7. Two paragraphs and part of the postscript are printed in King, pp. 255-6, as interpolations in the rendering there of no. 2870. Year from King's endorsement.
Oates 14 Feb.
Dear Cosin
I thank you for your two of the 6th and 11th and the papers annexd. I shall not repete any thing that I writ to you of before, you say you will mind it and soe I looke upon it as donne. By what I can observe things have not a tendency to a war. the temper of the two houses and the leading men in it will give you a better judgment of that matter. If there be not like to be a war and the East India stock begin to rise again I would have you buy again, for I know not why mony in the continuance of peace will not be as safely lodgd there as any where else and will always be at command more than in land security. I desire you to consider this and doe as if it were your own. your Cosin Freke and the Colledg will give you as much light as you can have any where. in case there is not like to be a war I am for buying, (if you have noe very strong objection against it) and that before†a- it rises-†a to the rate you sold at.
When you goe to the meeting of those gent you mention†1 I think you should say little as to publick affairs, but behave your self rather as one unversed and a learner in such matters. And your other business in the law will be an excuse if you are not there every night and you may always learne the next day (if you have a mind to it) what was debated there the night before.
You will doe me a kindness to send me word what is donne in the house of Lords, and which way at any time they move with regard to publick things on foot. I should enlarge to you in another postscript but that you answerd not my questions concerning the two pamphlets concerning the succession of the Duke of Anjou.†2 I would gladly know who is suspected to be the author or of what kidny he is thought to be. and how he is approved or disapproved by the partys. And †b- the answer that I find is to it against a war.-†b†3 I have besides several other questions to aske you and indeed the
― 245 ―
whole matter of my postscript is fitter for a discourse than a postscript. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
The transactions also of the convocation are worth observeing.†1 Pray tell me is Dr Kennets answer to Mr Atterbury†2 worth the reading if it be pray speake to Mr Churchil, when he comes in your way, to send it me.
My legs trouble me again and I write this in bed

Oates 14 Feb 00/1
Dear Sir
I returne you my thanks for yours of the 11th instant with the heads of the speech in it. I have since seen the speech it self, and though all the rest are†a fit for the consideration of the great counsell
― 246 ―
of the nation yet there is none but the second that seems at present fit to take up your time and thoughts. for unlesse that be soe well considerd as to provide a security for us and the rest of Europe what makeing a stir and provisions about the rest will signifie I confess I doe not see.†1 But tis like I may mistake and you will forgive these melancholy visions of a man out of the world who lies abed and dreams.
The inclosed†2 I send you open that you may either send it forwards, or back to me to be amended as you see cause. For in this you know I must continue to be governd by you. And tis not barely answering the letter with affection and all the prudent advice I can give unlesse it be suited to some particular turne which you know how to direct to make it as I would have it most serviceable to you both.
You must excuse me to my wife for not writeing to her tis with much adoe that I get time for this and the inclosed, my untoward legs made me keep my bed all day yesterday, and I think I shall doe the same to day for I am not yet up and it is now past two in the afternoon
Mrs Smithsby has lately laid out some mony for me and I have writ to her by this post to buy me some other things. I have directed her to you for money. I have not given her a bill nor mentiond any sum to her not knowing what she has or will lay out. I am

2863. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 18 February [1701] (2862, 2865)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 110-11. Year from King's endorsement.
Oates 18 Feb.
Dear Cosin
You will wonder to find in me soe great a varietie or at least
― 248 ―
uncertainty of mind. The partial and affrighting views of affairs may easily suggest several measures on a suddain to one who at a distance scarce sees any thing but confusion. Upon a more sedate recollection I am come to reason thus. If we enter into a war The companys actions†1 will tumble yet down and sink much lower. If we shal be soe fond of the name of the Peace of Europe as to sit still and loose the oportunity of alliances that now offer them selves is not this the way for Europe to be swallowed peice meale every one in his turn, and to give up our selves to the mercy of a neigbour who has none? <In>†a which case the companys actions will not only come to be of little value but none at all. Soe that whatever may happen I am upon second thoughts inclinde to be of opinion that your Cosin Fr's method†2 may be best; and last, that it is best to sit still, and looke about you a while before you buy. and in the mean time to reduce (as you were goeing) what you have by you into as little a room as you can. Besides there is an other thing that perhaps one may think convenient to see what will come of, before one medle, and that is whether S S's case of bribery may not be laid hold on as an handle to Shatter that company.†3 But the main considerations I offer to you are those above. ponder them a little and pray tell me your opinion whether I reason right. I am at a distance and soe see but little scraps of the scene: And I lie all day a bed and may have uncouth visions. However I think fit to send them you as matter of consideration the best I have. This is all I can doe. For the matter is (as is most reasonable) left to you upon the place to doe as you would doe with your own. Only I think it is best at present to sit still and looke about a while. That one may have what one has as much in ones reach as may be what ever may happen. Gain is not worth ones aim but security and that I think should cheifly govern you in this affair. I long mightily for an hower or two's talke with you. Tis possible Sir Francis and you may light of a convenient oportunity
― 249 ―
to steal down of a Saturday and return on the monday. I should be very glad of it. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE

Oates 22 Feb 1700/1
Vir Colendissime
Ex ultimis tuis, 18 præsentis Februarii datis probe sentio quam firma quam <immutabilis>†a sit tua erga me amicitia, cum tribus ante missis ad me silentem literis quartam addere non dedignatus es, sine reprehensione aliquâ tantæ et tam criminosæ taciturnitatis. Ignoscis video ideoque valetudinis incommoda non causabor. Penultimas tuas cum fasciculo librorum vel amissas vel in itinere malè hærentes maxime doleo quod crediderim te sensum tuum de
― 252 ―
libro meo jam tum cum scriberes perlecto liberius explicuisse. Quod de iis quæ de libertate hominis in volendo†1 scripserim aliquantum hæsitas non miror. Totum illud argumentum in prima editione penitus <omittendum>†a censui sed noluerunt amici,†2 quicquid ego de rei ipsius et novitate et subtilitate contrà afferrem ne lectores aliis assueti ratiocinationibus, non probe perspecto ubique animi mei sensu offenderentur, et ea quæ in isto parergo commentatus sum vel tanquam novatoris paradoxa, vel tanquam inconsultè errantis sphalmata negligerent si non plane condemnarent. Nec me eventus penitus fefellit, cum plures inter amicos familiaresque meos de hoc uno subjecto mecum seruere sermones quam de omnibus reliquis totius libri capitibus.†3 Fateor adhuc neminem fuisse cui scrupulum, quo detinebatur, non exemi si modo dabatur otium sensim et pedetentim integram materiem a capite ad calcem mecum perpendendi: quod quidem rei veritati, non meæ quantulæcunque mediocritati tribuendum censeo. Quod si tibi novâ recensione, ut promittis, recurrenti aliqua obiicienda occurrunt,
― 253 ―
persuasum tibi sit nihil acceptius mihi fore quam errores meos amicâ manu detegi eoque ipso evelli. non enim famæ, nec opinioni, sed veritati solæ litandum censeo. Quicquid demum fuerit, disputationes nostras in unam eandemque sententiam terminatum iri pro certo habeo. cum utrique unam eandemque illibatam veritatem studiose quærimus
(English) Vulnus†a- rei tuæ familiari inflictum dolui magnopere et ad huc doleo, tantoque impensius quod graviter animo tuo insidere video. Optimi filii tui Industria diligentia fides resarciet damnum illud cum laude, ne desperes, non suâ culpâ sed aliorum fraude passus. Quod si <amitteretur>†b prorsum opum pars non contemnenda an aliquod in mærore tuo quæris remedium? Quæ possidemus non nostra sunt sed illius supremi moderatoris qui nutu suo omnia gubernat et melius nobis providet quam nos nobismet ipsis, qui, quicquid nobis reliquum fecerit, id <omne>†c in vitæ jucundæ utilitatem trahentes, grato animo illi acceptum referre debemus et in lucro ponere.-†a

(Latin)
Oates 22 Feb 1700/1
Honoured Sir,
From your last letter, dated the 18th of the present February, I well perceive how firm and unchangeable is your friendship towards me: since to three letters previously sent to me without response you have not disdained to add a fourth, without any rebuke for so great and so criminal a silence. I see that you forgive me, and so I shall not plead the troubles of ill [p. 251] health. I am very sorry about your last letter but one, with the packet of books, that is either lost or sticking badly on the way, because I think that you, having read through my book at the time when you wrote, may have more freely set forth your opinion about it. I am not surprised that you are rather at a stand at what I have written about the freedom of a man in willing.†1 I thought that that whole subject ought to be altogether omitted in the first edition, but friends disagreed,†2 whatever I brought forward to the contrary about the novelty and subtlety of the matter itself; fearing that readers accustomed to other processes of reasoning, if they did not discern my meaning properly in all places, might be displeased and might disregard, if not wholly condemn, my meditations in that by-work as either the paradoxes of an innovator or the stumblings of an ill-advised wanderer. Nor has the event wholly deceived me, as among my friends and intimates more have entered into discussion with me about this one subject than about all the remaining chapters of the whole book.†3 I grant that so far there has been no one from whom I have not taken away the difficulty that held him, provided only that leisure was given for pondering with me, little by little, the whole matter from beginning to end: which I deem should certainly be [p. 252] attributed to the truth of the thing and not to my mediocrity, how small soever. But if anything objectionable meets you when, as you promise, you revert to a new examination, please be assured that nothing will be more acceptable to me than to have my mistakes revealed by a friendly hand and thereby plucked out; for I hold that not fame or opinion, but truth alone is to be served. Whatever the outcome, I am sure that our discussions will end in the one and the same opinion, for we are both earnestly seeking the one and the same unimpaired truth.
(Latin) I was greatly grieved by the injury inflicted on your private means and am still grieved, and so much the more because I see that it sits heavily on your spirit. Do not despair: your excellent son's industry, diligence, and trust-worthiness will repair that loss, and that with esteem, he having suffered it not by his own fault but through other men's fraud. But if a not contemptible part of your wealth is entirely lost do you seek some remedy in your grief? What we possess is not ours but belongs to that Supreme Ruler Who governs all things at His will, and provides better for us than we for ourselves; and whatever He has left us we, bringing it all to the furtherance of a happy life, ought with a grateful spirit to acknowledge our debt to Him and to count it as gain.
(Latin) But to what end do I say these things to you who are so pious and prudent? [p. 253] This alone I know for certain, that cares and vexations of the spirit neither lessen present evils nor provide against those to come.
(Latin) I am glad that you are considering a commentary on the Acts of the Apostles and such a way of interpreting it as does not stick in critical observations or the husk [cortex] of words. As it seems to me, the object [scopus] and spirit of the Christian religion are nowhere more apparent than in that history. For what can show us the genuine and sincere meaning of the Gospel better than those first preachings of the Apostles, by which they converted unbelievers, Gentiles as well as Jews, to faith in Christ?
(Latin) To come at length to your previous letters: I commend your resolution in deeming that no reply should be made to Burmannorum Pietas. The reproaches of such wranglers are altogether despicable.
(Latin) Our press is in a ferment and we see scarcely anything coming out except political and ecclesiastical disputations. I do not know what will finally become of it. I see what the storm threatens; I do not see the end. As much as I can I seek tranquillity. May God Almighty preserve the freedom of the Reformed Churches and of all Europe. So prays your most regardful
J LOCKE
(Latin) Lady Masham sends her warmest greetings to you and yours, especially to [p. 254] your son. Please give them all my best respects, together with the Veens, the Guenellons, and the rest of our friends.
Lady Masham wrote to your son a few days ago.
Address: Mÿne Heer Mÿne Heer Limborch op de Kaisars Gracht bÿ de Remonstranse Kerck t'Amsterdam

Dear Cosin
You need not make apologies for not precisely answering my letters I can easily conceive your hands full of late. When you see my Lord Shaftesbury again pray with my most humble service let him know That though the honour of a visit from him be what I could not in good maners aske, yet there is noething I have for this good while more earnestly longd for than an oportunity of kisseing his hands, and since he owns soe favourable an intention as that of comeing hither My Lady Masham (who looks on her self as mightily obleiged by it) and I are in an impatient Expectation of it. And yet I find some here wonder that whilst the King of France makes such a mighty collection of forces in Flanders just over against us we hear not of raising any Land soldiers on this side the water, espetialy since the printed papers mention transport ships drawn togeather about Calais and that way,†2 and if his fleet should be ready before ours (which god forbid) what will your thirty thousand sea-men†3 signifie? I am Dear Cosin
yours

Dean: March 19th: 170 1/0
Sir
A Gentleman lately seeing me in the unhappy Circumstances of my health, related at my Table what wonderfull Benefit you had found by leaving off Wine and malt liquours. This Sir with the Honour of a former Acquaintance I had with you, has encourag'd me to give you this present trouble, knowing that you are very communicative and have as great Judgment in Physick as in Phylosophy and Politicks; and therefore I shall presume to give you a short Abstract of my Case. I have been ever since King James his Reign troubled with Hypocondriacal and Rheumatick Pains; and finding little or no Benefit by Remedies prescrib'd, I used to resort to Laudanum as my Ultimum Refugium; which by taking twice or thrice did use to put them off for a month or six weeks. In May last I went to the Bath where though I drank the Waters (without bathing) I lost my Appetite and Sleep, and have
― 267 ―
ever since found my Strength decline, and a gradual Constriction of my Nerves, and Stiffness and Numness of my Limbs from my Hipps downwards, and a kind of Lumbago or Weight in my Back increase upon me, notwithstanding (according to Advice) I used the Exercise of Riding. this oblig'd me in November to quit my horse and take my Coach, and at last I cou'd not goe without being led by two Persons. At the Begining of November I took Advice of several Physicians who all agreed that I had a Palsie comeing upon me which they call Paralysis Scorbutica, and that Steel-Wine with Bitters was my proper Remedy; This I took without any apparent Benefit for two months; and fearing to loose my left Ancle I did by Advice of a Physician take 40 drops of Laudanum in a day; not omitting my Steel Course. With this (though very much decry'd by others) I can (I thank God) now walk with the single Assistance of one Person. Before I took Laudanum, I usually took a Pint of Canary at Bedtime to warm my Limbs, and to make me easie and sleep; the drinking of this Sack made some People fear it might bring a Hectick†1 upon me. I have now quite left it; drinking onely 3 or 4 Glasses of the best Red or White Wine I can gett at Meals, and as much toasted Water; and I find my Appetite increasing (though not very good) Since I left off taking crude Steel in Powder, and take it by Infusion. Now Sir I begg your Opinion, whether or no finding my health increasing I shall continue the same Course I am in? or whether I shall leave off Laudanum (which I am sure I shall very much miss) guttatim? Whether I ought to drink Spawe or Tunbridge Waters and leave off totally the use of Wine by degrees? Whether Balsamick Mum may not be drank some times? which I do. In short Sir Your Opinion of the whole Matter, as to the Nature of the Disease and the Method of its Cure wou'd be very acceptable. Whether it might not be conduce much to my health to spend the next Winter in a warmer Climate. Not knowing Sir where you live I send this by my Friend Mr Day, who will wait upon you at your leisure for your answer, the Favour of which will very much oblige
Sir
Your most humble and Faithfull Servant
JAMES OXENDEN.

THE LETTERS CONCERNING THE HUMAN WILL: nos. 2881, etc.
Van Limborch received a copy of Coste's translation of Locke's Essay when, about May 1700, it was published and intended to read it about August (pp. 101-2). Late in October he wrote that when he had finished reading it he would return to II. xxi, Of Power, in which Locke treats the Will and the Liberty of a Man in respect of Willing, and would send Locke his opinion on the subject (pp. 168-9, 240). The subject was important for him as it was a principal issue in dispute between Remonstrants and Calvinists. He set out his opinion in March 1701 in the course of no. 2881. This led to a discussion running through parts of nos. 2925, 2953, 2979, 3010, 3043, 3055, 3192, and 3200. As a result of the discussion Locke added a passage to § 71 and made further additions to, and alterations in, the chapter.
The translations are to be regarded not as substitutes for, but as aids to the reading of, the Latin texts. In these passages therefore I have kept close to the Latin regardless of English style or idiom. In rendering words I have generally avoided variation where only one meaning is concerned (where a word is used in two senses, as Mens, I have used the appropriate English words). I have retained Latinisms (accede, inevident, both on § p. 693) where the meaning is clear and avoidance would necessitate a periphrasis. For what are more or less technical terms I have used Locke's words and what I consider to be the English representatives of van Limborch's. The two men held different views on the act of Willing and were writing with different texts in mind; these divergences influenced their choice of words and I have tried to represent them in the translations.
Locke's vocabulary is mainly that of the fourth edition of the Essay; part of it is clarified by the addition to II. xxi. 71. His English usage presents the chief difficulty. He seems scarcely to differentiate between Mind and Soul: so I. ii. 5 or II. i; for the usages see O.E.D., Mind, sb.1 17; Soul, sb. 2. He prefers Mind, in Latin Mens, and I have rendered Mens accordingly. But in these letters he occasionally has Anima, the Soul, where he is repeating or echoing van Limborch's words; for these occurrences I have used Soul (for the exceptional Animus in no. 2979 see below; Locke uses the word elsewhere, but not as a technical term in the present discussion). 'The two great and principal Actions of the Mind ... are Perception, or Thinking, and Volition, or Willing. The Power of Thinking is called the Understanding, and the Power of Volition is called the Will' (II. vi. 2; elaborated in II. xxi. 5). The Latin words are Intellectus and Voluntas (with velle). Intellectus is always the Understanding and never the Mind as Locke uses the latter word. Other words present little difficulty. Locke varies between Liberty and Freedom, with a marked preference for Liberty; I have used it to render Libertas in all passages relating to the Will from no. 2881 onwards. Where Locke has Abstinere I have rendered it by Abstain from; his English word would probably have been Forbear. In no. 2925 he changes from Desiderium to Cupido. He perhaps took the latter word from van Limborch's Theologia Christiana, p. 130, § 21; there is little difference in meaning between it and Desiderium.
Van Limborch knew no English and read French only with difficulty. What he commented on is not Locke's text of the Essay but until no. 2953
― 269 ―
Coste's translation of it; thereafter Burridge's translation, with some help from Coste's. That Coste's was defective, despite Locke's supervision, emerged when, after it was published, Coste read it again to Locke (Coste to Leibniz, 20 April 1707, in Leibniz, Phil. Schriften, ed. Gerhardt, iii. 391); Burridge made his without assistance from Locke. Van Limborch discussed the Will and Liberty in his Theologia Christiana, II. xxiii, 'De Intellectu et Voluntate hominis' (in third edition pp. 126-30; quotations below are from this edition, and all citations in the notes to the letters on this subject are of it by page and paragraph). He is concerned with Anima, the Soul. Coste renders Locke's Mind by both Esprit and Ame (the seventeenth-century spelling of Âme): so II. vi; there is little difference in meaning in the sense in which he uses the two words (I cannot find any principle to determine his preference on any occasion). Van Limborch's usual word is Anima. In his Theologia, p. 125, § 5, he recounts its creation, citing Genesis 2: 7. He opens II. xxiii with 'Animæ humanæ duæ sunt facultates, seu potius actus essentiales, Intellectus et Voluntas'. While his Anima and Locke's Mens apply to the same object, the two words have different implications, for the one its religious, for the other its psychological, aspect. I have therefore rendered Anima by Soul. Van Limborch uses Mens occasionally in the Theologia (by my soundings rarely). He provides no definition and there may be some looseness. He parallels Mens and Voluntas (pp. 131, § 5; 345, § 4; 359, § 8); this perhaps arises from the power that he attributes to the Will, more extensive than that attributed to it by Locke. He distinguishes Mens and Intellectus (p. 393, § 1; less obviously p. 404, § 2). On p. 450 below he brings Anima and Mens together, preferring Mens as he is concerned with the psychological aspect. Wherever the word occurs in the present sense in the Theologia Mind is an, if not the only, appropriate rendering; in the letters it is the only appropriate rendering. Intellectus and Voluntas are Understanding and Will as with Locke, but with different powers.
The word Animus on p. 367 appears to be a slip; for van Limborch it comes close in meaning in one sense to Anima; for Locke, who repeats it on p. 407, to Mens. I have explained why van Limborch uses Intelligens where it occurs on p. 276.
On pp. 461-2 there are two short extracts from Burridge's translation (they are adapted to fit the context). The renderings here are translated from the extracts without recourse to Locke's text.
The absence in Latin of the articles provides a problem of which there is no satisfactory solution. When Locke writes about man in connection with his mind he prefers the indefinite article: 'so far as a Man has power to think'. Coste preserves this at the beginning of II. xxi, but increasingly lapses into 'l'homme'. I have found nothing to show what van Limborch had in mind. I have taken it that Locke would assume the indefinite article in most cases. I have therefore adopted it throughout, although this may falsify van Limborch's reading of Locke's letters and intention in his own. Further I have generally preferred 'the liberty of a man' to 'a man's liberty', and the same form in similar phrases, as being that closest to Locke's usage.
Locke and van Limborch underline words, phrases, and sentences, sometimes for the titles of books or chapters, sometimes as quotations, sometimes
― 270 ―
to distinguish them as the subjects under discussion. I have found it impossible to differentiate between those for quotations and those for distinction. I have therefore italicized the titles of books and chapters and used inverted commas for the rest. I have also occasionally italicized a word where it is indicated as a subject for discussion.
Le Clerc discusses Locke's treatment of Liberty in II. xxi in Bibliotheque choisie, xii. 82-105, part of his notice of the fifth edition of the Essay; it is mentioned also in his notice of Some Familiar Letters, ibid. xvii. 234-41.
2881. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 19/30 March 1701 (2866, 2921)

(English) Amplissime Vir
Redit ad vos filius meus. Amici aliquot, quibus sinceritas ac fides ejus probata est, autores nobis sunt, ut in Angliam redeat. Pollicentur illi operam suam adeo benignè, ut iter hoc gradum ipsi ad priorem, imo meliorem conditionem, divinâ annuente gratiâ, futurum sperare ausim. Ille coram de omnibus prolixè tecum aget, omnia enim literis credi non possunt. Credo consilium nostrum tibi probatum iri. Ego commendo Tibi viscera mea. Scio, si Deus Tibi vitam continuet, ipsi directionem tuam non defuturam; et si consilio tuo illi aliquâ in re inservire possis, Te illi me absente alterum fore patrem. Non eum multis Tibi commendabo, ne affectui tuo vel minimum diffidere videar. Experimento jam disco, grave
― 271 ―
esse patri seni liberos à se peregrinas in oras dimittere. Verum et hoc quicquid est levius redditur, quando considero affectum tuum erga eum verè paternum, et, si filii saluti consultum velim, hanc mihi occasionem non esse negligendam. Ego Tibi me filiumque devinctissimum profiteor, et Dominæ Masham impromerito favori plurimum debere. Res suas filius Londini aget, ibique assiduus esse debet. Deus, quem semper præ oculis habiturum spero, iter ejus secundet, ut omnibus ex voto peractis sospes ad nos redeat. Quando filius in Angliam venerit, non dubito quin exemplaria vitæ Episcopii,†1 si adhuc lateant, sit recuperaturus. Si verò perierint, alia mittam. Doleo hoc inexspectato casu ea tardius ad vos pervenire.

(English) Relegi magnâ cum attentione cap.XXI. lib.II. tractatus tui de Intellectu humano. Expendi voces ac phrases quas in materiâ hac controversâ adhibes. Puto me jam plenè mentem tuam percepisse, à quâ ego non dissentio.†a Optimè doces, Intellectum et Voluntatem non esse duas facultates reverâ ab animâ distinctas, sed mentem ipsam humanam immediatè per seipsam intelligere et velle. Inde infers, non recte voluntatem dici liberam, sed hominem.†2 Recte etiam meo judicio definis libertatem. Verum quando dicis § 24. libertatem consistere in potentià agendi, et non agendi,†3 et quidem in eo solo; non puto te id restringere ad solas actiones externas, sed et extendere ad internas, seu cogitationes nostras;
― 275 ―
illæ enim non minus quam actiones externæ subjectæ sunt arbitrio nostro: idque consentaneum est iis, quæ in sequentibus capitis illius scribis. Porro jam inquiris, quod præcipuum est, quid sit illud quod hominem ad hoc aut illud agendum movet. Ego hactenus ita me explicui, bonum jucundum seu voluptatem esse id quod hominem allicit; illique oppositum dolorem esse malum quod homo aversatur; adeoque quodcunque homo vult, id ab eo considerari ut jucundum; quod vero aversatur ac fugit, ut molestum. Non negas tu illud, quin imo id etiam urges § 41. et seqq. Verum ut distinctius ostendas, quâ ratione voluptas aut dolor hominem moveat, doces § 29 et seqq. voluntatem determinari ab inquietudine quam homo in se experitur aut ex præsentià doloris, aut ex absentiâ boni seu voluptatis, in quâ vel totam vel partem saltem suæ beatitudinis collocat: quamdiu enim homo in statu suo acquiescit, nullam illius mutationem quærit, sed solummodo quando in statu suo non acquiescit, seu quandam inquietudinem sive ex præsentiâ doloris, sive ex absentiâ voluptatis, quam ut fœlicitatis suæ partem considerat, in se sentit. In his facile tibi assentior. Inde rectè deducis, bonum in nobis excitare desiderium, non tamen inde sequi majus bonum semper majus in nobis desiderium excitare. Quod verissimum est, et tu rectè probas. Unde porro deducis, libertatem
― 276 ―
hominis in eo consistere, quod possit suspendere impletionem cujuscunque desiderii sui, plenamque habeat libertatem unum post aliud considerandi, objecta eorum examinandi, eaque ab omni parte observandi, ac inter se comparandi, antequam se determinet ad agendum. Et hoc tecum agnosco. Inde jam infers, indifferentiam†a quæ non possit determinari per ultimum judicium quod homo fert de bono et malo cujus electionem sequendam credit, esse summam naturæ intelligentis†1 imperfectionem. In Remonstrantium scriptis sæpe vox indifferentiæ†a occurrit, quando de libertate hominis agitur: Verum ea nunquam hoc sensu à nobis accipitur, quod posito illo ultimo judicio, in quo propriè actus volitionis consistit, nihilominus hominis potentia agendi sit indifferens, et per voluntatem non determinetur: sed quod ante illud voluntatis decretum homo libertatem habet se in hanc vel illam partem determinandi, et non ad unum tantum oppositorum determinatus est: accedente autem voluntatis decreto, seu volendi actu, indifferentia illa tollitur, et potentia ad agendum aut non agendum determinatur.†2 Et hic etiam puto nos consentire. Reliqua
― 277 ―
capitis iis quæ jam recensita sunt magis illustrandis ac confirmandis inserviunt. Puto me hic sententiam tuam de libertate hominis recte percepisse. Nec est quod illi quicquam opponam: imo quædam distinctius, et clarioribus quam hactenus à nostris factum est terminis ac phrasibus posse exprimi didici. Si non bene perceperim, aut si quid omiserim, quod ut sententia tua plenè percipiatur omitti non debuit, rogo ut me erroris admoneas; nolim enim in sententiæ tuæ explicatione, quam prout eam accepi etiam meam esse agnosco, à mente tuâ aberrare. Si in quibusdam dissentimus, quod ego ignoro, amicè tecum conferre gestio, ut exiguus qui forte restare posset dissensus tollatur. Plures tecum de hoc capite contulisse non miror. Materia est intricata, et diversis Philosophorum ac Theologorum sententiis†a agitata.†a Primus, meo judicio, Episcopius in tractatu de libero arbitrio, et contra Cameronem,†1 eam clarius explicuit, ostenditque Intellectum et Voluntatem non esse duas facultates reverâ inter se et ab animà distinctas uti hactenus in Scholis creditum fuit; sed animam immediatè per seipsam
― 278 ―
intelligere ac velle. Porro licet non iisdem tecum vocibus ac phrasibus utatur, in summâ tamen rei, quantum ego percipio, est consensus. Gratias interim Tibi ago, quod multa me libri tui editione docueris. Ego eum iterato evolvere statui; secundâ enim lectione multò distinctius eum intelligo. Deum precor, ut diu Te nobis incolumem ac prosperâ fruentem valetudine conservet. Uxor ac filia Te salutant. Salveat quam officiosissimè à me, uxore, ac filia, Domina Masham ejusque liberi. Vale.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS À LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 30 Martii
