(Latin) Excellent Sir,
My son is returning to your country. Some friends, who praise his integrity and trustworthiness, have advised us that he should return to England. They promise him their services so kindly that I venture to hope that this journey will by God's grace be a step for him towards his former, indeed towards a better condition. When with you he will discuss everything with you at length, for everything cannot be entrusted to a letter. I think that you will approve of our plan. I commit my child to you. I know that if God continues your life your guidance will not fail him; and that if you can be serviceable to him with your advice in any matter you will be a second father to him in my absence. I shall not commit him to you with many words lest I should seem to show the very least distrust of your affection. I am [p. 270] now learning by experience that it is grievous for an aged father to send his children away from him to foreign shores. But this, however heavy it may be, is rendered lighter when I consider your truly fatherly affection for him, and that, if I want to provide for my son's welfare, this opportunity is not to be neglected by me. I acknowledge that I and my son are very greatly obliged to you, and are very much indebted to Lady Masham for her undeserved kindness. My son will carry on his business in London and ought to be diligent there. May God, Whom I hope he will ever have before his eyes, prosper his journey, so that he may return to us safe and sound with everything accomplished according to our prayers. When he comes to England I do not doubt that he will recover the copies of the life of Episcopius†1 if they are still lying hidden; but if they have perished I will send others. I am sorry that through this unexpected mischance they are rather slow in reaching you.
(Latin) The people of Overijssel have recently furnished a truly detestable example of altogether inexcusable severity in the cause of religion. A certain Mennonite minister, now fifteen years ago, was suspected of Socinianism by the Synod and was accused of that heresy before the States of Overijssel by ministers of the Public Church. He was accordingly suspended from the performance of his office, so that for about two whole years his church was [p. 271] without the public exercise of religion. After lengthy proceedings, since the ministers could not make good their accusation, he was sent back to his church and enjoined to beware of teaching Socinian dogmas, under pain of such punishment as might be thought fit. Three years ago he published a booklet, of very small value, in which he urges union between the Christian denominations, even with the Socinians. On this occasion he rather unwisely wrote some things in favour of the Socinians; there also occur some stinging remarks directed against the cassocked tribe. If this booklet had been disregarded it would scarcely have found readers. But you know that that holy tribe is readily provoked by the very smallest affront. Accordingly information against him was anew brought before the bailiff†1 of the district of Vollenho. The bailiff sends him to the Synod. The Synod puts to him, for him to subscribe, five articles containing a confession that he had published that booklet contrary to the States' order, that he repented of that disobedience, that he would suppress all copies of it; and other things. He refused to subscribe. Some of the ministers kept pressing, indeed entreating [p. 272] him to do so. But he steadily refused. It is said to have been discovered later that they had desired it so ardently in order to have a confessor to an accusation [reum confitentem] and so by his own confession liable to such punishment as might be thought fit. This took place in the midsummer of 1699. In the following January he was cast into prison by the bailiff and, after an imprisonment lasting nine or ten months, by the judge's sentence there was at last imposed on the penniless man—emaciated by scanty victuals and the long continuing filthiness of the prison—a fine of a hundred silver ducats, which make about thirty of your pounds sterling;†1 nor was he to be discharged from prison unless the money was paid. Since he was unable to pay, as being penniless, he was thrust into a foul, stinking, and dark underground prison; after he has sustained life there for a fortnight on bread and water, at length last November he is given another order, forbidding him to spread abroad the errors contained in his booklet on pain, should he do so, of public exposure [catasta]†2 and exile, without any further form of trial; and so he is discharged from prison. The wretch has now been reduced to extreme indigence; all his household stuff, which, however, could in no wise make up the fine to which he was condemned, having been sold. I cannot excuse his imprudence; [p. 273] yet I cannot but detest this cruelty, especially when in the enlargement of the sentence the Imperial laws are brought from the Code as the props and foundations on which this rigorous sentence rests. Thus little by little we are sliding back to that detestable tribunal of the Inquisition.†1
(Latin) I have reread with great attention bk. II, ch. xxi of your treatise concerning the Human Understanding. I have pondered the words and phrases that you use in this controversial matter. I think that I have now fully grasped your meaning, and I do not disagree with it. You show excellently that Understanding and Will are not two faculties in reality distinct from the soul, but that the human mind itself understands and wills immediately of itself. Thence you infer that it is not rightly the will that is said to be free, but the man.†2 In my opinion you also define liberty rightly. But when you say in § 24 that liberty consists in a power to act and not to act,†3 and indeed in that alone, I think that you do not restrict this to external actions only, but that [p. 274] you extend it to internal actions also, that is, to our cogitations; for they, no less than external actions, are subject to our choice; and this is consonant with what you write in the following parts of that chapter. Next you inquire, and this is the principal question, what it is that moves a man to doing this or doing that. Hitherto I have expressed myself thus: an agreeable good or pleasure is what attracts a man; pain on the other hand is the evil that a man shuns; and so much so that whatever a man wills is considered by him to be agreeable; but what he shuns and flies from, to be troublesome. You do not deny that; indeed you urge it in § 41 and the following paragraphs. But in order to show more clearly in what way pleasure or pain moves a man you declare in § 29 and the following paragraphs that the will is determined by an inquietude that a man experiences in himself from either the presence of pain or the absence of a good, or rather pleasure, in which he places the whole, or at least a part, of his felicity: for as long as a man is satisfied with the state that he is in he does not seek for any change in it, but only when he is not satisfied with it or feels some inquietude in himself, whether from the presence of pain or from the absence of a pleasure that he considers part of his happiness. In this I readily agree with you. Thence you rightly deduce that a good rouses desire in us, but that it does not follow thence that a greater good always rouses greater desire in us. That is very true and you prove it well. You then deduce thence that the liberty of a man consists in [p. 275] this: that he can suspend the fulfilment of any of his desires and has complete liberty to consider them one after another, to examine their objects, to observe them from every side, and to compare them one with another, before he determines himself to acting. This also I acknowledge with you. You now infer thence that an indifferency which cannot be determined by the last judgement that a man makes of the good and evil by which he thinks his choice would be followed, is the highest imperfection of an understanding nature.†1 The word indifferentia occurs frequently in the Remonstrants' writings when the liberty of a man is being discussed; but it is never taken by us in this sense, namely that when that last judgement, in which the act of volition properly consists, has been made, nevertheless a man's power of acting is indifferent and is not determined by the will; but that before that decree of the will a man has liberty to determine himself to this or that side, and is not determined to one only of opposites; but when that decree of the will, or act of willing, is added, that indifferency is taken away, and the power is determined to acting or to not acting.†2 And here also I think that we agree. The rest of the chapter serves to making clearer and to confirming those [p. 276] things that have already been surveyed. I think that here I have correctly understood your opinion about the liberty of a man. Nor is there anything that I oppose to it: indeed I have learnt that some things can be expressed more precisely, and in clearer terms and phrases, than has hitherto been done by our writers. If I have not well understood your opinion, or if I have omitted anything that ought not to be omitted if your opinion is to be fully understood, please tell me of my error; for I should wish not to stray from your meaning in the exposition of your opinion, which, according as I have understood it, I acknowledge as my own also. If we disagree about some things, and I do not know that we do so, I eagerly desire a friendly discussion with you, so that any small disagreement that could perhaps remain may be taken away. I do not wonder that a number of people have discussed this chapter with you. The subject is intricate and is discussed with diverse opinions by philosophers and theologians. In my opinion Episcopius, in his treatise concerning free will and against Cameron,†1 was the first to set it forth more clearly and to show that the Understanding and the Will are not two faculties in reality distinct from one another and from the soul, as had hitherto been believed in the schools; but that the soul understands and wills immediately of itself. Moreover, although he does not use the same [p. 277] words and phrases as you, yet in the main, as far as I perceive, there is agreement. Meanwhile I thank you for teaching me many things by the publication of your book. I have decided to read it again, for I understand it much more clearly on a second reading. I pray God long to preserve you for us safe and sound and enjoying good health. My wife and daughter send you their greetings. Mine, my wife's and daughter's best respects to Lady Masham and her children. Good-bye.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 30 March
1701
Address: Amplissimo Consultissimo Doctissimo Viro D. Joanni Locke amicâ manu.
Endorsed by Locke: P: Limborch 30 Mar. 01. Answered May. 21

Si nous avons eté joyeux de recevoir une lettre de vótre part, le recit que vous nous faitte des douleurs que vous avez si long tems souffert au jambes, nous a saisi le cœur, et nous voudrions trouver quelque moyen de vous soulager. vous nous dite pas si pendant

cette fluxion, vous avez moins souffert au poumons, si votre douleur a eté principalement au jointures. Monsieur Hop secretaire de cette ville,†1 (que je soigne dans ses Maladies,) apres avoir eté menacé de ptysie par une tou fatigante et opiniatre, s'est trouvé tout d'un coup soulagé par des attaques de goutte, il en est mesme entierement gueri depuis que ses gouttes ont augmentées. notre zele pour votre santé et la prolongation de votre vie, nous fait esperer que si vous souffrez au jambes la poitrine en sera plus elargie. nous nous faisons un plaisir de chercher ce qui nous peut flatter la dessus, et augmenter nos esperances. notre Cousin Limburgh†2 qui a bien voulu se charger de celle cy va s'etablir a Londres pour quelques temps. vous scavez (a ce qu'on ma dit) la perte quil a souffert. cela nous a tous affligé, il est tres honneste homme. jespere quil reussira mieux dans ce nouveau dessin. tout ce prepare icy pour la guerre, et quoy que tout le monde soit fort animé et content de sacrifier une bonne partie de son bien pour conserver le reste, neanmoins il y a beaucoup a craindre pour nous, nous aurons les ennemis a la porte, et je m'imagine que leur premiere furie sera terrible a essuyer. toute la famille vous presente ses treshumbles respects. Monsieur veen commence a dechoir fortement. il luy prend souvent une grande surdité. il est subject au vertiges, et crache encore quelquefois du sang. ma femme continue, graces a Dieu, a se bien porter. notre fils pierre fait son devoir, et le cadet ne manque pas de courage et de genie. il a cela de particulier, que la passion forte quil a pour dessigner, a tellement eveillé son imagination, quil fait toute sorte de figure de son invention, mieux cent fois que son aisné, quoy quil n'aye encore eu que trois mois un maitre. je suis avec un tres profond respect,
Monsieur
Votre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON

Dear Cosin
Though I took the liberty to give you the same advice that I would have given my son had I one in your circumstances yet I doe not pretend to governe you; and though I pressed you soe far in what I thought and think still your interest as to obtein a promise from you, yet you may be sure I shall not make such an use of it as to hold you by it to any thing against your will: and therefor notwithstanding that, when ever you will you must be at your own disposal. But since you still desire my thoughts freely in the case, I shall tell you freely. that they are just the same they were when I first mentioned them to you. For notwithstanding what you say I see noething in the case alterd with reference to you and your interest, and if I mistake not the matter presses now more than ever. And therefor I am still postively of the opinion, and as much as ever, that you should not stir. I dare say you doe not think I would oppose any thing that should be to your advantage. And had I not demonstration that this cannot be to your loss I should not give you or my self the trouble of one word more about it. You must excuse me for this once. You have again desired my advice and I here again sincerely give it to you. I am
Dear Cosin

2889. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 26 March/6 April 1701 (2832, 2919)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 169-70.
Rotterdam 6 April 1701
Dear Sir
I have not of a long time wrote to you nor received any from you, because of my frequent writing to and hearing from my son Arent, whom I find, if he be the enditer of the french letters he writes, very much improved in that language.
But having the present oportunity by mr. Fr. van Limborch, I cannot omit to write directly to yourself, who, tho you are retired from the noise of secular affairs, cannot, so long as you live in the world, but be concernd for the good of those that are in it. We are now brought to the Brink of war, and would to God, say I, that we were heartily ingaged in a good and smart war, but not such a lingering one as that of the last. For tho, I, being no friend to war, as you know, delight not in war, yet I think, if we and others do now sit still, and suffer the french man to settle himself in spain, and those 2 nations to become in a manner one, by being governed by one and the same Council, actum est de libertate communi,†3 and the world must bow to french Tyranny, and see their wives
― 286 ―
ravisht, their children torne from them, themselvs dragoond, and if they cannot own a piece of bread, (consecrated by the polluted fingers, and worse heart of a sodomitic Priest) for their God—be sent to the Gallyes, to be better instructed by stripes and cruelty: And yet if your fleet be not reformed, your armies better payd, and managd than in the last war, even the war, which is the onely visible means to deliver us from the utmost ruine, will ruine us with a Witness.
The proceedings of the Commons, tho their zeal was quasht by the ministry, or Court,†1 gave life to men here for a while, and brought over Amsterdam, who first began to bestir themselvs, I know not by what infatuation, against a war, are now, they say, fully bent to adhere to England, and the Emperor, and are for exerting all the force they can, to bring the war to a short issue. The passages in the house of Lords censuring the Partition Treaty, and perfidy of France, and addressing against all treating with him but upon sufficient caution,†2 confirmd us, that both houses were fully agreeing one with another—
Yet a breath from the Hague, some think conveyed over the seas, begins to infect our people, and some of our Rulers do begin to tax England, as designing to drive them into a war, and themselvs to sit still. As looking upon themselvs sufficient to defend themselvs against all the world.
They say, they have, as wise men, taken care to bind their kings that shall next succeed, but as for the common cause they do nothing, they neither raise men at home, nor give mony to raise or pay them abroad.
Whether these discourses proceed from a pure zeal to the common cause, and fear that we, after all our great zeal, in words, to drive that son of a — french man out of spayne, will contribute nothing, nor men, lest they should be continued in time of peace (by the next Prince, in case his present Maj: should dy, whom God long preserve, for the sake of Europe) nor mony to raise and pay foren troops.
Or whether there be not a great mixture of malice in it, and that they proceed from an evill heart of unbelief, and drawing back from the common cause—I cannot, I confess, determine.
― 287 ―
But when I hear that they also decry the Emperor for a prince that has no mony, and demands such excessive sums, of England, and this state that are not to be raisd, it makes me incline to fear the worst—
In fine except the Parlament do speedily, whether the K. demands it, or not, franckly offer in case of a rupture to furnish or pay 30 a 40 thousand men to make a short end of the war, I see not but all will be lost—I had almost forgot to add that, 'tis reported, and that by none of the meanest of our rulers, that the Parlement have refused to furnish the 20 ships and 10000 men, till attacked, which 'tis true, is conformable to the words of the Treaty of 1677.†1 But not applicable now, where both Nations are equally concerned to enter into, and be hearty in the war—
But I stopt this report, by assuring the Gentlemen that I had read the Votes, and that there was nothing relating to that affair in them. And that it was in its self ridiculous they having consented to it, upon the first demaund, and would have gone further, had they not been checkt by Sir Ch—†2 and told no more was required of them, but the fulfilling that Treaty—
Yesterday news came from the Hague that Monsieur D'Avaux was packing up his pipes†3 to be gone, but whether it be not a copy of his countenance, to see if we shalbe frighted out of our wits, upon that bravado answer that the Demand of his Maj. is impertinent and that the States must moderate theirs, or he must return, And that if he sees that we wish him good speed, he will not, as formerly, receive orders to stay a little, I know not, but this I know, I wish him wel gone, Tho', I must confess we shall have the heavyest end of the staff.†4 Yet I spake with one yesterday who saw a letter writ from mastricht, by the Commander there to the Earl of Athlone,†5 that they were now in good posture, and able to make a vigorous, and honorable defence if attackt.
This, is all I can write you about the state of affair's here, save that we hope one way or other within 2 or 3 weeks to have effectively 100000 men in our cuntry, if we get your 10000; they are
― 288 ―
labouring hard on the ships of war. But I hear a certain person in A—†1 had shewd that good affection to the cause, that he has assignd those ships, that require longest time to fit out. So that it seems impossible to have all men equally earnest for a good cause. I hope you, with Arents help wilbe able to read this writ in so much hast—I am with dearest love and deepest respect to your good self, Sir F. my Lady, and all the family—from myself, wife, and sons
Sir
your most humble servant
B F
Address: For John Locke Esquire at Oates

2893. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 5 April 1701 (2892, 2894)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 128-9. Excerpt printed in King, p. 257. Answers no. 2892; answered by no. 2898.
Oates 5 April 01
Dear Cosin
I thank you for sending my letter and a bill for ten pounds to my cosin Peter Stratton
As to the East India company I thinke it not convenient to buy till the books are open again for transfers, because I doe not think it safe as the world goes to pay the money till the transfer be made. And when their books are open again I think it ought to be considerd whether there be not like to be a warr. I confesse I doe not see if we stick to our proposals which the Dutch and we have given in how a warr can be avoided. And if we doe not obtein that security the Dutch and we must be lost. The house of Lords in their Address†1 are clear in that point, and I think every body sees
― 291 ―
it. The good K of France desires only that you would take his word and let him be quiet till he has got the west Indies†1 into his hands, and his Grandson well establishd in Spain, and then you may be sure you shall be as safe as he will let you be in your Religion property and Trade. to all which who can be such an infidel as not to beleive him a great friend?
I am glad my Lord Shaftesbury and you talke of comeing at Easter, there will be then some time of Vacancy. When the resolution is taken and the time fixed between you, I would desire you to make a visit to Mrs Lockhart, as from your self, to let her know you are comeing hither, and aske what commands she has to Oates; and it will not be amiss to let drop, as by chance, who comes with you. This Visit to Mrs Lockhart I doe not put you upon as a bare civility, though that will not be amiss in you, But soe managed there is business in it, which you shall know when I see you, and therefor pray doe not neglect it. I am
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
JOHN LOCKE
my Lady etc gives you her service
I doe not doubt that you commonly write in great hast and therefor took noe notice of the first lettre that came without date. But now that you have omitted dateing your lettres two or three times I think it convenient for your sake to mind you of it

2896. Robert Pawling to Locke, 5 April 1701 (2813, 2911)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 237-8.
Lincolns Inn Aprill 5 1701
Sir
Captain Robinson†4 was with me yesterday to enquire of your health; and being to go to his Ship on Monday, and not having
― 294 ―
time to write to you himself, intreated me to write to you. his request to you is to intreat you to favour him with a few lines to my Lord President, who is now the chief at the Admiralty Board;†1 presuming that my Lord at your request will easily be prevaild with to remove him to a Ship of larger Size; becaus he hath but 8 seniors among the Captains and no one will question his valor, honesty, or Conduct; he is now in the Dunkirk;†2 His family is great and 4s a day wilbe a good addition towards their maintenance; If you think it proper to send to my Lord in his commendations; I shalbe very glad to be the messenger to deliver it and of the opportunity to wait on his Lordship having had so kind and respectfull a reception the last time, when I caried the Apples; but this is not of my seeking, but at his earnest request that I give you this trouble.
I thank God we are all in good health; my Wife and Daughte Justice†3 <are>†a at Headington†4 and my Daughter Christian†5 goes to them the next week, my Daughter Susanna†6 is come from Hampsted; her year being up at our Lady day; she is very well at present and hopes she may have her health here; but if not, she goes for Headington. we are now 6 in family and all drink onely from my Tavern.†7 the maids cant be hired to drink any malt drink. I hear of an other family, larger than mine, that doth the same; the Master of the family his Wife and Children have drank it for some time, and when he hires new servants, he gives them 20s per annum the more to bring them to it; but will take in none that will not be prevailed with on those terms; but that I keep as a secret
I should be glad to see you here but while the wind is in this cold corner we cant expect you. Sir Thomas†8 keeps close to his fire side and if he be tempted to go out, which is but rarely, he comes home very short breated a little while; but while he is at the
― 295 ―
fire he is easy and chearfull; here I will end lest you complain of my longwindedness. I am
Sir
Your very humble Servant
ROB PAWLING
Sir Thomas, I know, would have bid me present his service to you, had he known of my writing

2900. J.-B. Du Bos to Locke, 8/19 April [1701] (2837, 2982)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 240-1. Printed by G. Bonno in Revue de littérature comparée, xxiv (1950), 508-10. Year from Locke's endorsement and contents.
A Rome le 19 d'Avril
avant de partir de Paris Monsieur, javois recu le voyage de Fryske†2 et je croiois vous en avoir remercié. jacepte avec plaisir les livres que vous m'offré et je vous les demanderé dès que je seré de retour a Paris. je fais mon compte di ariver a la fin du mois de Juillet par la route de Venise et de Milan estant venu ici par celle de Gennes et de Florence.
Je mettré le voyage de Gemelli entre les mains de monsieur Josselin†3 qui sest chargé de vous le rendre. c'est un gentilhomme
― 298 ―
Anglois fort galand homme et de qui jay recu ici beaucoup dhoneteté. il est officier dans la compagnie des gardes du duc d'Ormond et il ma dit quil avoit lhonneur de vous conoistre.
Jay Impatience de lire le livre de vostre escrivain qui fait de la foy un baume dimmortalité,†1 pour voir coment il aura respondu a une objection quil a du prevoir. que les apostres aux quels asurement la foy na point manqué sont morts come les autres.
Je nai pu decouvrir d'autres relations imprimees depuis vint ou trente ans et qui vaille la peine que lon en fasse mention que lhistoire des dernieres guerres du Bresil entre les Hollandois et les Portugais imprimee en 1698.†2 un Pere Espagnol fit imprimer en 3 volumes in folio il i a quinze ans une histoire du Pérou, mais elle ne contient que des etablisements d'eveché et des fondations de monasteres.†3 les autres voyages sont des voyages de la terre sainte. Si je suis plus heureux dans les autres villes dItalie qu'a Rome je vous donneré part de mes decouvertes.
Don Livio Odeskalki neveu dInnocent onze entreprend de deseicher LAufente Paludé, ce sont les anciens marais de Minturne. ces marais qui empechoient la continuation de la voye Appiene come il le paroist par la satyre dHorace egressum magna me capit Aricia Roma, furent deseichez par Trajan et par Hadrien et nous en avons meme une medaille de ce dernier avec linscription Tellus stabilita. le deseichement naiant pas esté entretenu les marais sont redevenus en leur premier estat et cest a les deseicher de nouveau que lon va travailler. lingenieur don se sert don Livio est un mr. Meyer Hollandois qui sest acquis beaucoup de reputation en faisant ici quelques digues pour areter linondation du Tibre. il a deux ans quil publia ici un traitté de lart de rendre les fleuves navigables.†4
― 299 ―
cet ingenieur ne trouvera po<int>†a les choses si faciles ici quen Hollande ou le payis est plat et sans montagnes les quelles dans les fontes de neiges envoient des torrents qui endomagent bien les digues et les canaux.
Baglivi medecin conu dans vos quartiers et membre de vostre Societé fait imprimer une lettre de fibra motrice et morbosa nec non de experimentis ac morbis salivæ bilis et sanguinis.†1 ce monsieur Baglivi a le sort de la plus part des medecins qui ecrivent sur leur profession de sacquerir beaucoup de reputation dans les payis etrangers et fort peu dans le payis ou ils pratiquent.
Le Pere Bonani Jesuite va nous donner un receuil de coquillages.†2
l'affaire des Jesuites et des missionaires de la Chine s'examine aux Saint Office les jours que la congregation se tient devant le pape. on escrit tousjours de part et d'autre mais plus lon escrit plus il me semble que le fait sembrouille.
il est difficile que mr Robert Cuninghuam nait point encore recu le livre que je lui ai adressé pour vous. il i a plus dun an que je lay mis entre les mains de mr Stivenson son corespondant a Paris
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
DU BOS

2901. Henry Fletcher of Saltoun to Locke, 10 April 1701 (2908)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 125-6, with enclosures ff. 123-4, 127-8. Henry Fletcher, d. 1733, was a younger brother of Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun (no. 1756); for him and his wife see no. 1851. The letter is answered by no. 2908.
Sir
I wrote to my brother at a venture, not knowing whither he would think fit to speak to you of my wifes condition, or whither
― 300 ―
you would take notice of it. when one is ready to perish, they lay hold on evry thing they think can save them, without considering what trouble they give to others; you perceived my distress, and have generously offered your assistance, which I hope will be as beneficial to her as it was formerly. I was unwilling to trouble you twice, and therfor I delayed to write, to see what turn her sickness would take, becaus it varyed very much. I am
Sir
Your most obliged humble servant
H. FLETCHER

― 302 ―

2905. Francis Limborch to Locke, 15 April 1701 (2606, 2910)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 183-4.
London 15 April 1701.
Honoured Sir.
I begg that these few rude lines may serve to render my Most hearty thanks to your worthy self and the Lady masham, for all the Civiliteys and favours they have againe been pleased to favour me with. Yesterday j had the honour to waite on Sir Francis, who did me the favour to bring me to My Lord Shaftsbury, who was mighty civil to me and told me that on my fathers account he would doe me all the service possible, j was sorry j could but just see his Lordship, but hope j shall have an other opportunity to pay my humble respects to him. I waited also on the Lord bishop of Salisbury, who received me with a greatt tendernes and protested if j knew anything wherein he could be servicable to me and j did nott tell him, he should take itt very ill, he was so good as to order that I should come next week one day or other before eight a clock to him, alsoo he would have a little more time to see me, as long as he pleases to favour me with the honour of his presence, j think itt nott unfitt to accept of itt. j had yesterday nott the time to discourse so fully of my intentions with Sir Francis as I desired, therefore j pray Good Sir be so kind as to discourse a little thereabout with him, and when he comes to towne againe j shall take the liberty to waite on him; the letter My Lady Masham hath been pleased to write to me is miscarryed, by whatt means I doe not know. Pray Sir be soo good as to present my humble respects to My Lady and Madam Masham and all the gentlemen and Mr Coste and be soo good as to beleeve that j am with all my heart
Honoured Sir

2908. Locke to Henry Fletcher, 23 April 1701 (2901)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 42-3. Draft. Answers no. 2901.
Oates 23 Apr 1701
Sir
I†b- have received yours of 10th instant and with it the account you have sent me of your Ladies case-†b
Any one that reads it will easily see that her distemper has mightily broken her constitution and disorderd the whole Economy of her body. which though it would require much to be donne to set it right again, yet the present circumstances of her breeding
― 306 ―
gives but little roome for medecins, espetialy vigorous and effectual ones. All that I think can rationaly be aimed at now is to support her till she is brought to bed. That which seems most to threaten her with danger before that time is want of breath and want of strength
The first of these however painfull and terrible It be yet I imagin will not put an end to her life within that time because I am of opinion that symptom is not from any decay in her lungs but is produced by the disorder in her humors and animal spirits: though yet noething is to be neglected in her asthmatic fits which may give her present ease and breath.
As to her weakness which threatens most. It is in my opinion impossible to stop the increase of it and hinder her from sinking unlesse her stomach be taken care of that her appetite may be recoverd and digestion performed and this the rather because what increase of strength can be got this way will also help to lessen her short breathing
To this purpose I propose a diet of such wholesome nourishments as are most acceptable to her stomach and she can most easily digest. To know what her stomach will best close and best deale with her stomach must be consulted, for noebody else can tell only I think her diet should be as little medicinal as may be but her pallate and appetite humord as much as possible with what goes easily off her stomach.
In the next place seeing she has tried Ens veneris since her being with child and has always found benefit by it and seems now to have a longing after it I am of opinion she may now take it again, proceeding to larger doses as she grows nearer her time. espetialy after soe many drops as she has taken of Elixir proprietatis
And for the better strengthening of her stomach I propose that a large plaister of Caranna with a little balsam of Peru should be applied regioni ventriculi to which her†a- physitian may perhaps as she approaches near her time may think fit to add a little Galbanum.-†a I mention her physitian for I would have all this course (if you think fit to follow it) managed under the direction a physitian upon the place who may observe all occurrences and accomodate it to the accidents and symptoms which cannot be foreseen at a distance; nor can it be said beforehand which of them will or
― 307 ―
which of them will not deserve to be considerd though I think a great many of them may at present be neglected if the method usd does increase her strength and none should have any particular application to them but such as threaten imminent danger, for she is in my opinion too weake to bear many medicines, which if multiplied her stomach will not have time to demand or digest food sufficient for her support till child birth
If the faintings you mention often returne I think hot cordials whose basis is the spirits of distilld vinous liquors by noe means proper but instead of those a pretty large does of good orange flower water a litle sweettend with Syrop of Clove July flowers may doe better. or instead of that syrop Venice treacle dissolvd in it to make it more effectuall if need
If sweet smels as you say comfort and releive her let her by all means use them and those which she finds most agree with her, for noe thing but trial in this case can discover which is best. though a tincture of Ambergris seems to me to be as likely to be good as any. by all means let her burn wood in her chamber and though she cannot walke abroad yet if she could be caried abroad in a chair when the weather is favourable I gues the fresh open air would much releive her. I hope by such a method as this under the direction of a skilfull physitian on the place she may be supported till her lying in which is all that in my opinion can be proposed at present. I wish good success to this or what ever else may be used for her releif and am
Sir
Your most humble servant
J L
Marked by Locke: JL to H: Fletcher 23 Apr 01

Dear Cosin
I writ to you yesterday by the post and in my letter returned the bill you sent me. The bearer here of Mr George Burrell an Attorney has been with me here this morning to borrow four hundred pounds for Mr Robert Lay a Shopkeeper of Bishop Startford. The estate he will mortgage he says is worth £40 per annum. I know noething of the value but what he tels me and therefor I must beg you to enquire into that as well as into the title. He will give but 5 per Cent but says he will be punctuall in paying the interest, to secure which punctualnesse pray let it be made as Sir R: Gipps†1 for 6 per Cent with abatement of one per cent for prompt payment if payd within twenty days after every 6 months or if you allow thirty days it matters not soe you can obtain this condition, which I would have to secure the interest every half year without duning. Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and servant

2917. Samuel Locke to Locke, 10 May 1701 (2873, 2961)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 216-17.
Honoured Sir
I have Continued for som tyme debtor to your favour of 24 march last; and therein one from you to my son John.†1 which I sent the 27th ditto per the Susanna Captain Engledew for Suratt. I am verry much obliedgd to you Sir for your repeated instructions and favourable advyse to him for the preservation of his health: I know he will put a due Regard on such Regularitys which you so affectionately lay before him: I pray God hee may live to Returne, and you, to receive his personall acknowledgments for them: But while he lives in India he will not faile to furnish you from thence with the occurences of those parts
about 8 days since our Company received an ample letter of 4 sides dato 16 August 1700 (of which my son was the penman
― 315 ―
and as one of the Councill signed it) it came by way of Allepo. advyseing that all was well. and that our shiping would be dispatcht in tyme; also that the Mogul Aurange Zeeb was liveing. and that our Ambassador†1 had orders to come to Court or Camp: though the old E. India Company by theyr Agents had bin practiseing to make wrong Impressions there: also that the said Company theyr agents at Suratt had bin newly detected of foule or corrupt practises there, by bribeing the Governor to smother the debts owing by them to the inhabitants of Surat to the Vallew of nine hundred thousand pounds sterling. heerwith I presume to sende you the Clause out the originall letter:†2
by which and such like, you may see the great Reason wee have not to Joyne with such a Company; upon the foot of theyr old, Imbroyled. indebted, and but Immaginary stock.
I shall be glad when your Indisposition will permit you to be in London: where I shall hartely Esteeme the favour to see you at my house and where mr Bonville this weeke acquainted som of my people of your ordring down som wine, whence I hope your good health increaseth, which that it may. is the prayer off.
Sir
Your most affectionate Cosin and servant
SAM: LOCKE
London. 10 May 1701
2 days since I saw Sir Francis Massum in good health.

2919. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 14/25 May 1701 (2889, 2932)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 171-2. Answered by no. 2932.
Rotterdam 25 May 1701.
Dear Sir
I received your most acceptable letter of the 16/27 past, and was very glad to see it, and to understand that you are gayning ground of your weakness, my Lord Shaftesbury assures me that he left you as well as he had known you—onely that of late you have had a humour in your legs.†1
I see you are not onely got out of all administration of publike business, but also become a great stranger to what passes. Yet I am glad to understand that tho you indeavour to keep your thoughts from medling where they can only disturb you, without doing good to any; that you cannot but conclude that if the Ballance and with it, the Liberty of Europe be not kept, we are
― 317 ―
not like to live undisturb'd by our growing, and restlesse neighbour —This is my thinks so evident, that he must be blind that sees it not. And is so melancholy a prospect, to see men, so unconcernd or deluded with vain hopes, that the same causes, will not now have the same effects they ever had, that I can have no pleasure in thinking upon the measures some are taking, to make themselvs, and all Europe dependent upon France.
I speak it with regret enough, I see not how I shall break out this summer to come and visit you, in England, which I ought to do, and to go to Scotland to, to see if I can get something for my children: So that if you desire any books to be sent you, let me know what, and I shall do my best to have them securely conveyed to you—
And seing it is so, that I shall not, I fear, be able to come to you for your good advice, how to dispose of Arent, I must intreat it of you by letter—
When he went hence, he was much inclin'd to be with mr. Leers, desirous of being always conversant with books—
Some would have me bring him up to Physic—but I am afraid to trust him, among the wild <youth>†a of any of the universities.
Others would have me let him study the Law, at lest, the Introduction to it, for a year, as a meanes to give him a good method of thinking.
You know his capacity, and I know have an affection for him and me, and will advise us both to that which may be for his good. And I shalbe willing to do for him to the utmost of my power.
Your thoughts upon this subject I humbly desire, and when it may be seasonable to have him home in order to what may be Judged best for him.
For I cannot conceive any settlement for him on that side the water—
If he should settle to the calling of a bookeseller, I think it wilbe better here than in England, because they keep their books mostly in Quires, and so have no stock lying dead in the bindings.
I have not seen mr. Bayle a good while, when I meet him I shal do as you direct. This goes by mr. Wrights 2 sons†1 which have been here at school to learn french and Dutch—
― 318 ―
My dearest, myself and sons have our humble service to your self, Sir Fr. my Lady and the rest of that noble family; which concludes this from
Dear Sir
Your most humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
I would have Arent see Kensington, Hampton Court, Windsor and Oxford. and when he returns have those Historicall Tables of Monsieur von Helmont†1 back: if no body will print them—
Address: For John Locke Esquire These at Oates
Endorsed by Locke: B Furly 25 May 01 Answered 30

2921. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 16/27 May 1701 (2881, 2925)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D. 16, f. 215. Copy by van Limborch. The original was transmitted through Francis Limborch; Locke received it on 21 May: pp. 323, 342. Answered by no. 2935.
(English)
D. Joanni Locke
Amplissime Vir
Propensissimum ac verè paternum, quem erga filium meum testaris affectum, nunquam pro meritis estimare possum. Abest ille a parentibus: Verum in Te alterum parentem repperit, qui affectu, consilio ac operâ commodis illius consulit. Ego me Tibi, ac Dominæ Massam, cujus erga se amorem verè maternum aliquoties in literis suis deprædicat, perpetuo devinctum agnosco. Ita nimirum divinæ providentiæ placet dum res illius afflictæ patriâ illum excedere suadent, alteram illi quasi patriam parare, animumque illius gravi illâ calamitate saucium per vos reficere, illumque inter homines ignotos vestro potissimum consilio dirigere. Hac vestrâ benevolentiâ fretus, subinde in rebus dubiis ad vos confugere audeo, vestrumque consilium, quod mihi oraculi vice est, nonnumquam exposcere. D. d'Aranda filio meo autor est, ut sibi in suâ negotiatione socium adjungat, hominem Anglum, nummis non destitutum, ac in Anglicis†a negotiis ac legibus versatum, qui simul cum ipso negotia curet; qui quod filius meus majore labore ac
― 320 ―
sudore præstat, à suâ parte nummis, sine quibus negotiatio exerceri nequit, compenset: Sic tutiorem fore negotiationem, et cum pluribus posse intercedere. Placet mihi id consilium, si talis socius reperiri possit: eaque de re ego ad D. d'Aranda literas dedi. Idem si tibi ac Dominæ Massam probetur, rogo, ut paucis verbis D. d'Aranda id commendare digneris, ut, si possit, hac in re filio meo operam suam commodare non gravetur. Ita me nòvo beneficio tibi obligatum habebis. Prolixius hac de re ad filium scripsi, rationesque quæ me consilium illud amplecti suadent illi aperui. Ignosces si in negotio, quod me maxime sollicitum habet, ad Te tanquam amicum certissimum subinde confugio. Non dubito quin jam duo vitæ Episcopii exemplaria per filium acceperis, quorum alterum D. Francisco Cudworth Massam detur rogo. Addidissem literas ad ipsum: Verum quia hodie plures mihi exarandæ fuerint, in proximi tabellarii discessum eas differre cogor. Salutant te uxor, ac filia; imprimis ego
Tui amantissimus
P. A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 27 Maji 1701.†1
(Latin)
To Mr. John Locke
Excellent Sir,
I can never value as it deserves the very great and truly fatherly affection that you show towards my son. He is away from his parents; but in you he has found another parent, one who takes thought for his advantage with affection, advice, and practical aid. I acknowledge that I am forever obliged to you and Lady Masham, whose truly motherly love towards himself he celebrates from time to time in his letters. Thus surely, while his troubled affairs urge him to leave his native land, it pleases divine providence to provide him with as it were a second native land, and through you both to restore his spirit, wounded as it is by that grievous calamity, and above all, he being among strangers, to guide him by your advice. Relying on this goodwill of yours, I venture from time to time to resort to you in doubtful matters and sometimes to beg for your advice, which is like an oracle to me. Mr. D'Aranda has suggested to my son that he should associate a partner with himself in his business, an Englishman not lacking money and experienced in English business and laws, who together with him would look after their affairs and who on his side would counterbalance with money, without which [p. 319] business cannot be carried on, what my son would provide by greater toil and sweat; thus the business would be safer and could be between several persons. This plan pleases me if such a partner can be found, and I have written about it to Mr. D'Aranda. If you and Lady Masham approve of it please be so good as to recaommend it to him in a few words, so that, if he can do so, he will not be loth to give my son his help in this matter. You will thus put me under an obligation to you by a fresh kindness. I have written about this at greater length to my son, and have disclosed to him the reasons that urge me to embrace that plan. You will forgive me for resorting from time to time, in an affair that causes me very great anxiety, to you as a most assured friend. I do not doubt that you have now received through my son the two copies of the life of Episcopius; please let the second be given to Mr. Francis Cudworth Masham. I should have added a letter to him, but since I had to write several today I am compelled to put it off until the next departure of the post. My wife and daughter send you their greetings, as do I,
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 27 May 1701†1

2923. Francis Limborch to Locke, 19 May 1701 (2910, 3098)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 187-8.
London 19 May 1701
Honoured Sir.
Your two most agreable letters of the 29 past and 9 May I both received this past seavennight, and j should have answhered 'm sooner, but because j received last tuesday the exemplars of the life of Episcopius (where of two goe herewith one for your worthy self and one for Mr Francis Cudworth Masham) j thaught itt better to trouble you butt once; I can nothing Sir but render you my fathers and mothers (who j advised of your extraordinary favours) and my most hearty thanks for the same, according the liberty you please to give me j shall take the fredom to desire your advise of what Mr D'aranda proposed me;†1 he had heard that had suffered a greatt losse, and sayde he was very sorry for itt, and that he considered j came now over with the same intention hither, as he came over for holland, that is sayde, with a small stock, and whereof sayde he j am nott ashamed, and to make his fortune there, whereon j replyed thatt itt was my intention, so immediatly he proposed to me whether itt should nott be best to look for a partner for me, who had a stock to beginn with, and was already in businesse heere, because (sayde he) credit is att present so mighty scarse heere that merchands who are already knowne finde work enough to maintain itt; but sayde he further if you doe nott like that I'll doe all for you what's in my power, and in case you want to draw any money for holland I'll endeavour to procure you the necessary creditt; whereupon j replyed as to the first that I had no greatt inclination to itt, because j could nott beleeve Any Merchand who was already in businesse and had a stock should admitt a personn with him who hath nothing, or that itt must be for his owne intrest, onely to know my friends and when he was acquainted with them to leave me againe, and secondly that if such a man might admitt me in partnership and j should share equally in proffitt and losse, and he might gett once a misfortune of an important summe I should nott be able to bear itt, but remaine alwayes poor and a slave, and that for my part if he would be so kind as to procure me some creditt and acquaintance amongst old
― 323 ―
and creditable merchands, j did nott doubt butt with the godly blessing j should strive well enough; and att last says j, Sir if you know a merchand who seeks his ease and will leave of his businesse and you can gett me with such a man im partnership that j may write my name with his to become so acquainted in the world I shall share in no proffitt or losse but he shall onely give a summe of money a year I'll doe all his busines that he needs to doe nothing but to be att ease, jll gladly accept off itt, butt in case I cant finde that I should rather ramaine alone; j wrote about itt to my father and told him my meaning so as heere, he is to answhere me thereabout per the very first, and desired me to entreate your advise thereabout to, which also j humbly begg, and alsoo j fear itt may be to much trouble to you sir to write so much j'll willingly come once downe one saturday morning or Other to receive your advise thereabout as alsoo about some other particular affaires; I thank god I received severall commissions and if j had beene able to perform all, itt had been above 10£ in my wayes already; but when the Verginy fleet arrives I doe nott doubt butt I shall be able to doe itt; I have had neither time nor occasion yett to waite on Sir Francis but hope to doe itt this week, and shall with much respect accept of the favours he pleases to bestow on me, jn the meanwhile I humble crave leave for the liberty I take and desire you to beleeve me to be without any reservation
Honoured Sir
Your most oblidged humble servant
FRANCIS LIMBORCH

2924. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 19/30 May 1701 (2854, 3080)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 139-40. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 121-2.
A Amsterdam le 30 Mai 1701.
J'espere, Monsieur, que Mr. Daranda vous aurez fait rendre le paquet, dont il voulut bien se charger, pour vous l'envoyer, et que j'avois donné d'abord au fils de Mr. Limbourg, qui l'oublia par accident. Cest le second Tome des Parrhasiana, où je débites bien des moralitez communes, mais pourtant si négligées, qu'il semble que l'on les ignore, de sorte que j'ai crû qu'il n'étoit pas inutile de les renouveller. J'avouë qu'on n'avance pas beaucoup par là, mais si l'on ne fait pas des réformations dans le monde, on empêche qu'il ne vienne à un trop grand excès de dépravation, en y entretenant certaines idees de droiture et de justice. Le goût du siecle n'est pas d'ailleurs éloigné de cette espece d'écrits, si l'on en peut juger par le débit. On a fait une seconde édition du premier Tome, mais je n'ai presque rien ajoûté. Je suis présentement fort occupé au Nouveau Testament en François,†1 et à la revision des Oeuvres d'Erasme,†2 dont on verra dans peu deux volumes. On a publié depuis peu le commencement d'un Journal à Trevoux, capitale de la principauté de Dombes, qui est au Duc de Maine, où l'on m'a très-mal traité, et où l'on ne vous a pas non plus épargné.†3 Ce sont des Prêtres passionez et ignorants qui le font, et qui n'observent aucune regle de justice ou d'honêteté. Je les ai un peu relancez dans un article, que j'ai fait mettre à la fin dans l'Edition, qui s'en est faite ici, et il y aura moyen de le faire davantage dans la suite, s'ils continuent.†4 Je vous l'envoyerois, si je
― 325 ―
n'apprenois que Mr. de la Mothe l'envoÿe à Mr. Coste, car c'est un livre qui ne mérite pas qu'on le garde. J'attens une réponce du Dr. Whitby, qui m'a fait quelques excuses de la maniere dont il a écrit contre moi, et à qui j'ai écrit par la voye de l'Evêque de Salisbury, qui m'avoit fait tenir sa lettre. Il a promis d'effacer des paroles injurieuses dans la seconde Edition de son livre, qui doit paroître à présent, si je ne me trompes. Celui qui doit porter cette lettre qui est Mr. de Vaux, ami de Mr. Coste aussi bien que le mien, et qui est un fort honête homme, ne me donne pas le temps de vous en dire davantage. Je suis, Monsieur, de tout mon coeur vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
 
J LE CLERC. 	
Mes civilitez, s'il vous plait, à Mr. Coste.

2925. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 21 May 1701 (2921, 2935)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 258 m. Printed in part in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 478-81; omitted passage, postscript, and address, in Ollion, pp. 221-2. Answers no. 2881; answered by no. 2953.
(English)
Oates 21 May 1701
Vir Amplissime
Gratissimus erat nobis omnibus (de hac familiâ loquor) filii tui adventus mihique inprimis, eoque magis quod illum mihi a te tantâ fiduciâ concreditum video, siqua est in me fides, opera, gratia, consilium, quibus illi utilis esse possum non frustra concreditum dices. Laudo tuum in eo mittendo animum, laudo consilium quantum ego rem capio. Non dubito quin ejus industria
― 326 ―
probitas peritia, fides, amicos negociumque facile et certo parabit, si a tenui exordio sensim crescentis spei moras patienter ferre possit, mercatoribus enim solum mutantibus <idem>†a accidere arbitror quod arboribus in aliam terram transplantatis, quæ primo anno satis agunt si radices tantillum agant, incrementa et fructus futuri sunt temporis. Non multum mihi cum mercatoribus commercium, jamque minus ex quo me procul ab urbe procul a negotio in hunc secessum avocavit valetudo. Quibusdam tamen quibus fidem habendam censui et Domina Masham et ego illum commendavimus. Siquidem donec nostrorum hominum mores probe noverit, non tam familiarium numerum et frequentiam quam probitatem et fidem quærendam esse censui. Quando <Londinum>†b proficiscar, quod spero propediem futurum, quid ultra conveniet videbimus. Interim id filio tuo penitus insidere velim, ut maximopere caveat ne temere fidem habeat iis quorum integritas non probe nota sit et perspecta et fama ultra dubium stabilita. Hoc illi facile persuasum iri credo experientiâ nimis sumptuosâ in limine, quod doleo, edoctus. Quod tamen in ejus commodum aliquando cessurum minime dubito. Virtuti enim et probitati sua semper certa, etiamsi
― 327 ―
aliquando tardior, merces. Me quod attinet Tibi filioque tuo penitus persuasum velim, me illi quacunque datâ occasione certum et paratum esse amicum et adjutorem.
(English) Magno honori mihi esse duco quod tu tantum lucubrationibus meis tribuas ut in iis perlegendis bonas tuas horas locare velis, Et eas tibi veritatis amatori non displicuisse gaudeo. Cum ego libertatem consistere dico § 24 Cap.xxi lib. 11 in potentia agendi et non agendi,†1 nequaquam id restringo ad solas actiones externas uti constat ex §.8 38†a aliisque illius capitis locis. de hoc igitur inter nos convenit. Quando vero dicis quod quicquid homo vult ab eo consider ari ut jucundum metuo ne Voluntatem, cum Desiderio confundas. Quod a plerisque factum video, qui hoc argumentum tractant, non sine magno veritatis vel saltem perspicuitatis incommodo. Desiderium fertur in jucundum fateor sed Voluntas fertur solum in actiones nostras et ibi terminatur. Sed quia Voluntas raro agit nisi ducente Desiderio, ideo pro uno eodem actu plerumque sumuntur cum toto cælo distent. § 30.40†b Cupido enim passio est mota a bono absente. Volitio autem actus Voluntatis vel animæ†2
― 328 ―
imperium exercentis in potentias <hominis>†a operatrices. Has†b duas†b operationes animæ sc: illa quâ cupit aliquid, et illa quâ determinat vel imperat aliquid agendum nisi distinguantur probe, nihil dilucide ut mihi videtur de voluntate humanâ statui potest: Ideoque spero ignosces mihi quod de ista loquendi formâ te monitum velim, cum de summâ rei a me omnino non dissentias. In usu vocis Indifferentia quod a Vestris differam non mirum est, cum in his scribendis nec aliorum placita secutus sim, nec vel scripta omnino consuluerim, sed quæ res ipsæ me, quantum indagatione et meditatione assequi poteram, docuerint, ea verbis quam potui aptissimis explicuerim. de terminorum igitur usu nulla inter nos erit disputatio, modo de re ipsa constet. Quamvis ut libere dicam ista antecedens indifferentia hominis qua homo ante determinationem sive decretum voluntatis supponitur libertatem habere se determinandi ad alterutram partem oppositorum non omnino videtur mihi spectare ad <quæstionem>†c de libertate. quia libertas unice consistit in potentia agendi vel non agendi secundum determinationem voluntatis. Disputare autem an homo ante ultimum judicium intellectus libertatem habet se determinandi ad alterutrum oppositorum mihi videtur omnino de nihilo sive de re impossibili disputatio. Quis
― 329 ―
enim rogaret, vel quorsum attinet rogare, an homo potest ad alterutram partem oppositorum se determinare in statu, in quo se non potest omnino determinare? nam ante Judicium intellectus non potest se omnino determinare, ideoque frustra quæritur an in illo statu libertatem habet se determinandi in alterutram ubi in neutram omnino partem potest se determinare. Ideoque omnes illæ lites quæ agitantur de libertate se in alterutram partem determinandi ante judicium intellectus mihi videntur, (ignoscas fatenti) nullo modo pertinere ad quæstionem de libertate: quæ ne supponi quidem debet nec potest, in statu in quo manifestum est quod homo ut agens liberum non potest agere, cum libertas ut dixi consistat in sola potentia agendi vel non agendi consequenter et congruè ad determinationem voluntatis. Ita autem sæpe usu venit. Disputantium fervor et partium studium rebus per se claris nubem et caliginem obducit, dum undique conquisitis <laqueis>†a alter alterum innodare et absurdis involvere conatur. Vides quam liberè tecum agam, eandem a te libertatem vicissim expectans, si enim tu meæ, vel ego tuæ opinioni assentior, perinde est veritatem quærentibus, dummodo illius potior habetur sententia quæ verior, et in ea consentiamus. In aliis libri mei partibus, dum
― 330 ―
percurras, siquid minus recte dictum vel cogitatum invenias moneri imo et redargui a te cupio. Vale Vir Optime et me ut facis ama tui amantissimum
J LOCKE
(English) Uxorem filiamque tuam meo nomine salutes reliquosque nostros
Domina Masham te officiosissime salutat
(Latin)
Oates 21 May 1701
Excellent Sir,
Your son's arrival was most welcome to us all (I speak of this family) and especially to me, the more so because I see that he is entrusted to me with such great confidence; if there is any trustworthiness in me, if any practical aid, friendship, and advice, with which I can be of use to him, you will say that he has not been entrusted to me in vain. I praise your spirit in sending him, I praise the plan so far as I understand the matter. I have no doubt that his industry, honesty, skill, and trustworthiness, will readily and surely [p. 325] provide friends and business, if he can bear patiently the delays of hope growing little by little from a small beginning; for I think that the same thing happens to merchants who leave their country for another as to trees that are transplanted into a different soil: in the first year they do well enough if they take root ever so little; growth and yield are for the future. I have not had much intercourse with merchants, and have less now that ill health has called me far from the city and from business to this retreat. Nevertheless Lady Masham and I have recommended him to some whom I deem trustworthy, since I think that, until he knows well our men's ways, a large number of friends is not so much to be sought as honesty and trustworthiness. When I go to London, which I hope will be soon, we shall see what further is fitting. Meanwhile I should wish it to be thoroughly fixed in your son's mind that he should be very earnestly on his guard against rashly trusting those whose integrity is not well and clearly known, and whose reputation is not established beyond question. I think that, taught at the outset by too costly an experience, for which I am sorry, he will readily be persuaded of this. Nevertheless I have no doubt that this will at length turn to his advantage. For there will always be a sure, if sometimes rather tardy, reward for virtue and honesty. For my part I should wish you and your son to be thoroughly convinced that on any occasion I shall be a sure and ready friend and helper for him. [p. 326]
(Latin) I hold it a great honour for me that you value my lucubrations so highly as to be willing to bestow your good hours on reading them through, and I am glad that they have not displeased you who are a lover of truth. When I say, bk. II, ch. xxi, § 24, that liberty consists in a power to act and not to act,†1 I by no means restrict this to external actions only, as is evident from §§ 8, 38, and other places in that chapter. On this, then, we are agreed. But when you say that 'whatever a man wills is considered by him to be agreeable' I fear that you are confusing Will with Desire, as I see is done by most of those who treat this subject, not without great damage to truth or at least to perspicuity. I grant that Desire is directed to the agreeable, but Will is directed only to our actions and terminates there. But since Will rarely acts unless Desire leads, they are therefore generally taken to be one and the same act, whereas they are perfectly distinct from one another. §§ 30, 40. For Longing [Cupido] is a passion moved by an absent good; Volition on the other hand is an act of the will or of the soul†2 exercising command over the operative powers of a man. Unless these two operations of the soul, viz. that whereby it longs for [cupit] something and that whereby it determines or commands [p. 327] that something must be done, are properly distinguished, nothing, it seems to me, can be clearly established about the human will; and therefore I hope that you will forgive me for wishing to warn you about that way of speaking, since you do not disagree with me at all about the main thing. It is not surprising that I should differ from your writers in the use of the word 'Indifferency' since in writing about these things I have neither followed other men's opinions nor so much as consulted any writings at all, but have set forth in the most suitable words in my power what the things themselves have taught me, so far as they could be compassed by investigation and meditation. There will then be no arguing between us about the use of terms, provided that we agree about the thing itself. Although, to speak freely, that antecedent 'indifferency' of a man, by which he is supposed, before the determination or decree of the will, to have liberty to determine himself to one or other of opposites, seems to me not to have any bearing at all on the question of liberty, because liberty consists solely in a power to act or not to act according to the determination of the will. Moreover to argue as to whether a man, before the last judgement of the understanding, has liberty to determine himself to one or other of opposites seems to me to be arguing about nothing at all or about an impossibility. For who would ask, or what does it avail to ask, whether a man can determine himself to one or other of opposites when [p. 328] he is in a state in which he is altogether unable to determine himself? For before the judgement of the understanding he is altogether unable to determine himself, and so it is idle to inquire whether in that state he has liberty to determine himself to one or other alternative when he is altogether unable to determine himself to either. And therefore all those disputes that are carried on about liberty to determine oneself to one or other alternative before the judgement of the understanding seem to me (forgive me for saying so) in no respect to pertain to the question of liberty: which should not and cannot even be supposed in a state in which it is manifest that a man as a free agent cannot act, since liberty, as I have said, consists solely in the power to act or not to act consequent on, and according to, the determination of the will. But so it often happens. The fervour of disputants and partisan zeal spread cloud and darkness over things clear in themselves, while everywhere one tries to entangle another in snares that he has sought out, and to involve him in absurdities. You see how freely I deal with you, expecting the same freedom from you in turn, for whether you agree with my opinion, or I with yours, is all one to seekers for truth, so long as that one's judgement that is more true is held to be preferable, and that we agree in it. If, while you are running through my book, you should find in other parts of it anything wrongly stated or ill considered, I desire it to be pointed out, and indeed confuted, [p. 329] by you. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and continue to love me your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
(Latin) Please give my greetings to your wife and daughter and to the rest of our friends.
Lady Masham sends you her warmest greetings.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch t'Amsterdam

Sir
I speak it ingenuously, I would not presume to give you this trouble, if I thought it would last any longer than the reading, and if my experience did not assure me that you will not grudge me the good advice it comes for. 2927. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 25 and 26 May 1701 (2922, 2928)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 146-7. The letter appears to have been carried by Mr. Burrell: pp. 334, 336.
Oates 25 May 01
Dear Cosin
Mr Burrell (Mr Lay accompanying him) brought me yours of the 22th that afternoon, Upon discourse with them Mr Lay told me the particulars that he now would morgage to me were worth £900. But I am informed since that they are worth about £600 and that they were morgaged lately to one Mr Tooke for £300 who now cals in that £300 for a purchase that he is makeing. You say noething to me of that morgage, and soe I know not whether they have discoverd it to you, for by what is said to me that Tooke desires his mony for a purchase that he has made, it seems to be still in being.
As to the deed of Settlement on his daughter I desired Mr Clarke of Hollingbury†2 a good understanding man to goe to Mr Lay and
― 332 ―
see whether any of the particulars offerd me, were in that deed of Settlement upon his daughter. Mr Lay told him there was such a deed but that those writeings were kept either by Mr Kendale a trustee for the same and now dead or by his son in law he doth not know which, so that he could not give Mr Clarke a sight of them, only he did averre, that noe part of the Lands in that settlement were any of those in my morgage. and he offerd to give Mr Clarke an account of the Lands soe setled upon†a his†a daughter which Mr Clarke did not think worth the takeing, as being altogeather insignificant towards my satisfaction. I doe not see how this agrees with his telling you Mr Burrel should see the deed at Startford, nor with his telling me Mr Burrell should take the particulars out of the deed and bring them to me tomorrow morning, when he has promised to call on me as he goes to London then I shall be able to say more to you. at present methinks it looks not very well.
As to your purchaseing in the East India company since you did not doe it when I writ but delaid though it were riseing I wish you had informed me a little in the particulars of that matter which would have given me some view without losse of time as it now stands. My goeing on or not goeing on with this Morgage ought to have had noe influence upon your buying or not buying For you might have been sure if you had bought as I desired you at that time when I concluded it would rise, if you thought it fit to purchase at all yet, that I should have found money for this Mortgage or else have mentiond to you the doeing of the one as a condition of forbearing the other. But perhaps it is best that you did not buy, only I would be glad to know your opinion upon that matter. whether there is a probability of a war or whether the old company being soe gently laid by†1 may not attack them again by some new and more passable proposals.
The weather and my legs togeather have not yet favourd my comeing to town though I desire it as much as you. If there be
― 333 ―
any particular business for which you would have me there pray let me know it for I shall neglect noe occasion to serve you. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
Pray send the inclosed to Mr Churchill
26o May between twelve and one
Mr Burrel came to me about an hour since and Mr Lay with him and though the deed of Setlement be not produced and he pretends he has noe counter part nor knows where the deed is yet he seems very earnest for the money and proposes expedients without clearing this point. He†a- denying that they were setled on his daughter,-†a I asked him besides whether he had never conveyed the lands offerd to me nor any part of them to any body else since they were his. He†a- denyd that he ever had.-†a This is contrary to the intimation I have had that they were morgaged to Mr Tooke: I must desire you to presse Mr Burrel upon that point, for Mr Lay haveing absolutely denyd any conveyance of any part of these lands to any body since they were his I could not aske Mr Burrel before his face concerning that matter. Upon the whole I doe not like this matter it has not a fair appearance, and therefor you must not part with the money till every part be cleard and we are satisfied that there is noe manner of incumbrance and that all this has been rather mistake than any unfairness intended. By talkeing farther with Mr Burrell you will be able to see what is fit to be donne for I must refer my self to you in these cases. I am
Yours

2932. Locke to Benjamin Furly, 30 May 1701 (2919, 2946)
B.L., MS. Eng. letters c. 200, ff. 18-19. Answers no. 2919; answered by no. 2946.
Oates 30 May. 1701
Dear Friend
I am very sorry we are not like to enjoy your company this year here in England and what is like to be after this year I have not soe promiseing a prospect of as to build much upon it. I have ever since you gave me the hopes of seeing you here promised my self much satisfaction in converseing again with you for some time face to face. But disappointments in this world are noe strange things to a man that has been soe long in it as I. And 'twill be well if what I imagin is one great cause of your stay at home produce not greater mischeifs than our not seeing one an other.
You aske me one of the hardest questions I know when you aske me how you should dispose of your son Arent. The like has been demanded of me by persons of several conditions, and I have seldom found my self able to propose any thing that I could fully satisfie my self in. This when I examin into the causes of it I impute to the great corrupsition and dissoluteness which has overspread this part of the world and of late years got into all ranks and professions of men. and seems to me the certain forerunner of that ruin confusion and disorder which seems to threaten all Europe. Without a stop to the overflowing of vice, and a reformation into better manners tis easy to see the several communities in this part of the world will very hardly be able to subsit. for vertue is the very strength and cement of Societie without which it cannot stand. Such reformations have seldom if ever been brought about in the world without great and publick calamities. Old as well as yonger boys are seldom amended without scourging. and noe thing but overturnings bring depraved <hearts>†a from fashionable and growing immoralitys. But hold I see my apprehensions (for fear is the common doteage of old men) have caried me away from the subject I was upon, and I wish we were togeather to debate particulars the better to come to a resolution about your son. I have talked with him more than once since the receit of your letter. I find as I imagind before that he has an inclination to learning and
― 338 ―
knowledg and wants not capacity for it.
But since speculations of the head will not fill an empty stomach, his study if he makes study his business must be applied to some particular calling that may afford a lively hood as well as information. Divinity he has noe mind to and therefor of that I shall say noe thing. Law in England enough to bring a man to the bar and pleading is very chargable to get and requires his being of one of the Inns of Court and at last all that learning when gotten is of noe use or improvement any where but in England. The under trade of Solicitors and Atturnys has soe many temptations to corruption both in the attainment and practise that I cannot imagin you should ever have a thought that way. The law you speak of that some have advised he should study for a year I imagin is the civil law or that of Holland. But the studying of law for a year in order to any other calling is what I cannot understand or that he should study law for any thing else but to be a Lawyer. but what state that is in on that side the water I am ignorant and soe can say noe thing. Physick is the freest of all studys and is not tied to any particular place a good physitian being welcome every where. But against that you have made an objection which I cannot answer, and your son Arent an other as hard to be over come which is a natural aversion in him to see soars bloudletting and other such unpleasing objects as often occur in the practise of physick, this at first was his objection to me and some instances he gave of such an antipathie in himself as I think may be hard to conquer and at least will clog his progress in this study, Though after we had discoursed togeather he told me he thought that might be no hindrance But the reason of that I found to be that if he studys physick England must be his residence, and there he ownes he had rather be than in Holland But besides his and your objection which are both <strong>†a against the study of physick I have an other thing to adde which is that if I mistake not the practise of physick is goeing to decay apace in England. Besides that I beleive the faculty is overstockd and there be many amongst us that make a hard shift to live. Upon the whole therefor I think his first was his most natural and the best choise. For to a bookseller the languages he has will be usefull, and the calling it self will afford him books which he has a love for, and oportunitys to improve his knowledg. I think his first choise of a calling not only right but the place also I mean Rotterdam
― 339 ―
under your eye, and the man Leers if his temper be as good as his skil in that trade seems to be. Holland certainly is much better for that trade than England where they print Latin and French in aboundance and fill all Europe with books of all kinds from their presses, and as I hear men from small beginings quickly grow if they have skill and care into great trade stock and credit. Our booksellers for the most part are but a company of pittiful pedlers, few of them get anything, but by their dear and ill printing they have shut themselves out from sending any of their commoditys into forain parts and have noe commerce with the rest of the world.†1 Thus you have what appears reasonable to me upon this matter
You aske me farther when it may be seasonable to have him home. My thoughts are that what ever course of life you shall designe him to it is now time he should be entering upon it. His years require it, and he wants not capacity, and tis I imagin better to setle his thoughts one way than to leave him floating under different views which may make him stick the lesse close to that which shall be his proper business. For noe thing more contributes to make men thrive in their callings than the observeing of that rule which says Hoc age†2
You see with what freedom I have let my thoughts run to you in this matter even†a- <beyond> the-†a utmost bounds of a letter. I wish Arent good successe in whatever course of life you shall choose for him. He comes not short in his parts of the expectation I have had of him from a little one, and one may promise that there be few will out goe him in this way if he be set right and kept steady, which those of quick parts have as much or more need of than those who are slower. I am
Dear Friend
your most affectionate friend and servant
J LOCKE
My service to your wife and sons. My Lady with the rest of this family give you and them their service
― 340 ―
I think all Vossius s works have been lately reprinted in folio.†1 Pray tell me how many volumes they are and what they will cost in quires
Address: For Mr Benjamin Furley an English merchand at Rotterdam

May 30
Dear Sir
I was very glad to hear from Sir F.M.†2 of the amendment of your health, and that you were pleased to have me at all in your thoughts; I beg your pardon that whilst I was for near 4 months in Oxford, I did <not>†a write to you to inquire after your health, I hope you will not impute it to any forgetfullness of what I have so great a Concerne for, but as it really was, partly out from†b the business I was and am still engaged in, and partly because I hoped to have bin in Towne a month agone, and then I should not have faild to have satisfyed my self of what I so much desired to know, yet could not be so happy till now: I should be glad to know when you think to be in Towne, that I may order my affairs to be there at that Time, since I have many things to discours with you, both in relation to my past, and future small Performances: as to my Poor Family I suppose Sir F.M. told you that my Daughter is marryed to a yong Gentleman in Berkshire, one Aldworth,†3 of much the same Age, and Fortune with her self, James†4 is in Towne, but will go either for Ireland, or Germany within a few weekes, the latter will be on an Affair of which you shall know more if holds. my Father†5 is pretty well, but often in paine with his Legs, and wind from the spleen. I make bold to trouble you with these domestic Concerns, since I suppose they may not be unpleasant to you; I have not yet condoled the loss of our good Freind Mr: Hodges, whom I saw at Oxford about 6 weekes before his decease;†6
― 341 ―
and he was then indisposed, and as I hear was never well after his coming to Norwich. he dyed much richer then I expected and has given (as I hear) considerable Charities to the workhouses at Glocester, and the Place last mentiond; I beg your pardon, that I must be for some time longer in your debt as to that small sum I owe you, my Daughters weding puting me more behind hand; tho when I have done all I can, I shall never discharge my self of that lasting obligation of being not onely your Debtor, but real Freind, and humble servant
J TYRRELL.
