Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 258 n. Printed in part in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 481-2; omitted passage, postscript, and address, in Ollion, p. 222. Answers no. 2921; answered by no. 2953.
(English)
Oates 1 Jun 1701
Vir Amplissime
Eodem die quo nuperrimè ad te manè scripsi literas tuas 27 Maji datas vesperi accepi. Filius tuus qui jam hic apud nos est de societate (de qua mentio fuit) de rerum suarum præsenti statu, deque consilio suo abundè coram mecum egit. Laudo ego illius cautam prudentiam, quod spes vanas vel fallaces, qui juvinum plerumque mos est, non avide nimis amplectatur: Laudo moderationem quod lentiores quæstus festinationi non raro cæspitanti præferat. De re de qua ad me scribis nihil amplius movendum censeo: Nec ut societatem cum quoquam ineat temere suaserim, nisi forte oblata sit iis conditionibus quæ vix expectari possint, et etiam tum demum a molestia, a lite a periculo vix tuta erit. Suas res ut secum agat consultius fore crediderim. Industria sedulitas, constantia, fides parva initia ad majora cum tempore promovebunt certissimè. Cognita illius diligentia et probitas, modo expectare tantisper velit, mercatorum negotia attrahent. Quaeruntur enim ubique imo et
― 343 ―
desiderantur viri intigri et fidi quibus res suas tuto credere possint mercatores. Inter hos tuum filium brevi eminere nullus dubito.
(English) Vitam Episcopii summâ cum voluptate perlegi. Historia placet, res gestæ plane displicent. Doleo sane Reformatos tam propere mores pontificios, de quibus tam graviter questi sunt, imitatos. Sed scire juvat quod cognitum laudare non possis. Inquisitionem quæ in Ecclesia Romana lentius succrevit uno quasi nixu inceptam et pene perfectam hìc conspicere mihi videor. An has protestantium inter se inimicitias et mutuas persecutiones jam castigaturus sit deus nescio. Hoc saltem credo Theologorum ambitiosa dissidia et invicem dominandi in fratres cupido orbem reformatum antiquis hostibus denuo obruendum objecit et in tantum periculum adduxit, Avertat deus O M omen, nec ad persecutionem tam proclives animos persecutione catholicâ puniat. Unum est quod in libro tuo desidero, nempe articulos illos quinque Remonstrantium, <quorum>†a tam frequens est mentio. Hos vel quòd in properâ lectione non observatos præterierim, vel quòd eos tu historiæ tuæ non inseruisti, ignorare me fateor. Rogo igitur ut mihi indicare velis ubi <eos>†b legere possim, magnam enim lucem ut mihi videtur præbebunt
― 344 ―
causam Remonstrantium penitus cognoscere cupienti. nam iterum credo perlegam hanc tuam historiam. Maximas pro hoc dono gratias ago. Vive diu utilis Religioni Christianæ. Vale et me ama
Tui amantissimum
J LOCKE
(English) Versionem Latinam novam bibliorum a Schmidio ni fallor Germano nuper factam audio.†1 An quid in eâ dignum notatu præstiterit aveo scire. Versio Latina tractatus mei de Intellectu humano jam typis impressa est.†2 Bibliopolæ scripsi ut exemplar filio tuo tradat tibi transmittendum ut siquid in Gallica translatione hæreat versio Latina lucem fæneretur
(Latin)
Oates 1 Jun 1701
Excellent Sir,
In the evening of that same day on which, in the morning, I recently wrote to you, I received your letter of 27 May. Your son, who is now here with us, has discussed with me at length the partnership of which there was mention, the present state of his affairs, and his plans. I praise his wary prudence in not too eagerly embracing vain or deceptive hopes, as is commonly the way of young men; I praise his moderation in preferring slower gains to speed that often stumbles. I think that nothing further should be attempted in the matter about which you write to me, nor would I urge his rashly entering into partnership with anyone unless it were offered on such terms as can scarcely be expected, and even then it will scarcely be secure from trouble, dispute, and risk. I should think it more advisable for him to conduct his affairs by himself. Industry, assiduity, steadfastness, and trustworthiness will most certainly in course of time advance small beginnings to greater things. His diligence and honesty, when they are known, if only he is willing to wait so long, will attract merchants' business, for upright and trustworthy men, to whom merchants can safely entrust their affairs, are everywhere [p. 342] sought for, and indeed are needed. I do not doubt that your son will shortly stand out among them.
(Latin) I have read through the life of Episcopius with very great pleasure. The narrative pleases, what was done thoroughly displeases. I truly grieve that the Reformed [sc. the Calvinists] so quickly imitated the Pontifician ways of which they complained so bitterly. But it is pleasing to know what one cannot praise when it is known. I seem to see the Inquisition, which in the Roman Church grew more slowly, here started and almost brought to perfection as it were by a single effort. I do not know whether God will now chastise these hostilities of Protestants among themselves, and their mutual persecutions. This at least I believe: that the self-seeking(?) dissensions of theologians, and their longing to lord it over their brothers in their turn, have anew exposed the reformed world to being overwhelmed by its old enemies and have brought it into such great danger. May God Almighty avert the omen and not punish with Catholic persecution spirits so prone to persecute. There is one thing that I feel the want of in your book, namely those five articles of the Remonstrants of which there is such frequent mention. I confess that I do not know them, whether because I passed them unnoticed in a hasty reading or because you have not inserted them in your narrative. Please, therefore, be so good as to inform me where I can read them, for, as it seems to me, they will supply great light to one who wants to know thoroughly the Remonstrants' case; for I think that I shall read your narrative [p. 343] through again. I give you my best thanks for this gift. May you live long to bear service to the Christian religion. Good-bye and love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) I hear that a new Latin version of the Bible has recently been made by Schmidius, a German if I am not mistaken.†1 I wish to know whether he has provided anything worthy of note in it. The Latin version of my treatise on the Human Understanding has now been printed.†2 I have written to the bookseller to deliver a copy to your son for transmission to you, so that if anything sticks in the French translation the Latin version may lend(?) some light.
Address: Mÿn Heer Mÿn Heer Limborch t'Amsterdam

June 21 701
If you are not so far out of charity with me that you will not receive it I would by this tell you that in this only I can pretend to be like You (viz) that I am allways hinder'd doing those things I propose which as You may easily beleive is most commonly that which one likes best to doe. and it is from the influences of my
― 349 ―
cross star's that it has hapn'd that you have been so seldome troubled with my letters nor have not before this seen me at Oat's. should I hear repeat the many accidents that has follow'd me since I saw you it would be a long inventory of misfortunes, Sore eyes, a sick familly etc with a long continuence of spleen or that uneasiness of mind and body that is commonly calld so. but the last week when I thought I had broke thro' most of my incumberances and was thinking nothing but mustering up all the good humour I have left and to pack my self up in the first stage coach that would cary me within reach of You I was surprizd first in the print and afterward's to find it true that Mr Masham†1 was dead, which I did think would be an improper time to come to You, besides I did not kno but the funerall might be there. I sent to Martha Br.†2 who could give me no information in this matter. I in the mean time desire You'le as a token of forgivness to all my faults (that is if You will call my misfortunes so) let me kno if my lady and you will receive me and if so the time I may be the least troublesome; this I shall wait for with impatience for many reasons amongst other's if You should not baulk my fancy whither some thing elce may not fall out here again to hinder me. for news Expect none from me 'till things grow better which will be the greatest we have heard for some time. I shall take care to send to Mr Bonvill before I se You to pay my Years intrest due at Lady day. I have a very ill hand at condoling complement's for in cases of reall afflictions I think speaches are intollerable and in formallity they run heavily. You may if You pleas think this an ill excuse for want of an accomplishment that is now I must tell you quite out of fashion. I hope however that I shall never be wanting in taking a very sincere part with what ever happens well or ill to my frends and I don't kno but according to the hearty concerne that my Lady Masham has for Sir francis his familly this change may be afflicting to her and Mrs Hester†3 to whom I wish every thing that is good, pray be so kind to say what you think fit for me on this occasion and to your self say I am in the usual manner a very much obliged and
faithfull servant
M LOCKHART
― 350 ―
my Cosen†1 and all our familly give there service to my Lady Your self and all with You.
Address: For Mr Lock [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]

2942. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 23 June 1701 (2940, 2943)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 164-5. Answers no. 2940.
Oates 23 Jun 01
Dear Cosin
I have received all your letters and packets since my last to you in their due order and return you my thanks. My Lord Havershams words I see have given you great offence.†2 Pray in your next send them me. I see the Epithites you give them but can not yet learne what they were. that I would gladly know. I that never loved bustle all my life and am soe utterly unfit for it now am not much delighted you may think with the noise of it. But yet how fond soever I am of peace I think truth ought to accompany it, which cannot be preserved without Liberty. Nor that without the Balance of Europe be kept up which I am glad to find mentiond in your last Fridays votes.†3
I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
Address: For Peter King Esqr Member of Parliament. To be left at Mr Potmans in the Middle Temple London Frank.

2943. Peter King, later first Baron King, to Locke, 24 June 1701 (2942, 2944)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 142-3. Answered by no. 2944.
London June. 24. 1701.
Sir
This day the parliament was prorogued to the 7th. of August next, I could not hear the Kings Speech, but, as I am told, He thanked the Commons particularly for their supplys, and assurances to stand by and support him—The House of Lords were much displeased with the Votes of the Commons last Friday, and in Requital Voted Yesterday the Resolutions herewith inclosed, the last whereof is a Censure of those lords, who refused yesterday to be present at the trial of the Earle of Orford, All those Lords who did not like the proceedings in my Lord Somers's trial absented themselves Yesterday from the trial of the E. of Orford, so that he was acquitted Nemine Contradicente. The†a- first five hundred pound New East India Stock bought for You cost 110 l. 15s. 00d. per Cent. and the Second five hundred pound Stock bought for you cost 117 l. 10s. 00d. As it hath hapned, It would have been more for Your Advantage to have bought sooner, but no man can foresee all Events, I followed the Opinion of the Colledge in delaying, which hath not succeeded to my desire—I have taken up One hundred and fifty pounds of Auvmsham†b Churchill.-†a—You did write me the other day something about a Morgage, If you have any other Mony to lay out that way, If you will let me know what the summ is, I believe that I may in a little time find a Conveniency to dispose of it, I have had a letter from Devonshire, and believe, that assoon as I shall be in that Country, I shall receive the Interest of the 2000 l—Assoon as I can find a security which I like, I intend to take in the 1000 l from Mr Coniers as You formerly Ordered me— I have Nothing more to say, than that I hope You will be here Shortly, which is much desired by all your friends, and most particularly by Sir
Your Most Obliged and affectionate Cosin and Servant
P. KING
Endorsed by Locke: P: King 24 Jun 01 Answered 27

2944. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 27 June 1701 (2943, 2948)

Oates 27 Jun 01
Dear Cosin
I measure the obligations of my friends by the intention and not the event, and as long as you meant for the best your purchase to me is for the best only this last £500 stock being bought before Midsomer day I make account I am to have the Midsomer dividend for this latter £500 stock as well as for the former. A security for £2000 or any summ under I beleive I shall be able to compass only I would not have you doe any thing about the £1000 in Mr Conyers name till you and I have talked and therefor say noe thing of it till then. I have not time now to enter upon these matters with you haveing company with me here and it will be fitter for a discourse than a letter. I am
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE

2945. John Shute, later Barrington, later first Viscount Barrington, to Locke, 27 June 1701 (3074)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 95-6. John Shute, 1678-1734, was a nephew of Samuel Shute, sheriff of London 1681-2, and was probably a connection of Lady Masham, his mother's sister being wife of Sir Thomas Abney, a brother-in-law of Damaris Andrews (no. 731), Lady Masham's half-sister. In 1711 he inherited property at Little Baddow, Essex, under the will of Francis Barrington (no. 2609), who had married a first cousin of his; and in 1716 he changed his name to Barrington. He was created Viscount Barrington of Ardglass (Ireland) in 1720: D.N.B. At the time of Lady Masham's death he wrote of his great affection for her: Esther Masham's letter-book, pp. 323-7.
Sir
You must forgive me, that I have not discharg'd a promise, I remember I made at Oates, of sending you Mr de Vries's Miscellanies†1
― 353 ―
long since. For as my want of timely notice, when Sir Francis made his elopements†2 in the winter hinder'd me from being as good as my word then; So the earlier informations, I have gott, of his leaving the Town to morrow, has given me the first oportunity of keeping it now. Else I shou'd have taken care, to have suited the entertainment better to the season; and to have sent you Mr de Vries's abstracted thoughts, when the Winter lockt you up from good company, and the agreable objects of Sense; rather than now, when the Season invites to Meditation and Discourse.
You are hardly capable Sir of being inform'd in matters, where our Reason does not want the assistance of mechannicall operations and instruments, or of long experience and observation, the onely things that can bound your knowledge; Such as are the abstracted Subjects of which this Author treats. Informations of this kind, you must wait for till you gett into the other world: Or expect 'em here from your own thoughts and studys. But tho' new discoveries in the World of Spirits may not be your entertainment in the perusall of our Author; Yet I'm persuaded you'll find a great deal of Satisfaction, in seing an effect which Truth allways has upon the minds of Men, that search for it with the same desires and the same application, in making 'em think alike in different Countrys and distant times. For you'll find Mr de Vries in many things, and some of'em principall ones too, to entertain the same opinions, which you have advanc'd with so much strength and so much success.†3
And tho' the observation has given me a great deal of pleasure, yett I must own at the same time, that it has done me some prejudice. For by being hardly brought to forbear, thinking it time mispent, to enquire into matters, which two persons, so unbyass'd and so earnest in the pursuit of truth, have agreed in: I use my self too much, to that Servile Spirit, which the Freer Thinkers of the last Age, have so justly reproach'd. Indeed Sir when I consider your Reasons, they have that force and clearness,
― 354 ―
that like a sudden light, which strikes us, they <leave>†a no room for doubt or farther consideration: But the mischeif is, that I pay so great a deference to both your Judgements separately, but especially where they concurr, that I can hardly suspend my Judgement so long, as is necessary to consider those reasons cooly, upon whose authority alone I know you challenge my assent.
And as Truth has form'd your notions alike; so Vertue has made your Tempers and your practice to agree too. For Mr de Vries has a great deal of that chearfullness, that willingness to oblige, that easiness and compliance, that affability, that candor, that communicativeness which as it makes you, so it renders him too a mighty ornament to Learning; freeing it from the Objections of Sullenness and Pedantry; and rendring it agreable as well as usefull: And tho' I must own Sir, that these mighty qualifications want no other argument to sett the Person, that possesses 'em as high as may be in our Esteem, yett I cannot forbear to say, that the particular share Mr de Vries gives me in his affections and the mighty share he has in my best esteem adds this to their vallue in you Sir that they represent Mr de Vries to me, who I thought, before I had the honour to see you, the best Man and the best Thinker of this Age.
I cant forbear here Sir returning you abundance of thanks for the light you have given me in the nature of my own indisposition; and the remedys you have directed me to: which have been of great use to me. Whatever Suspicions you may entertain of me, yett I'll assure you Sir I'm become a sincere Convert to Water-drinking; and I hope in a little time to reach perfection. Like a young Convert, I'm very zealous to propagate the Doctrine; and have had no small success in making Proselytes. I onely wish my zeal may be as lasting as tis vigorous, and that by naming you to give creditt to the opinion, I dont procure you the trouble of some consultations, which some have threatned you with. But if it shou'd, I'm sure your goodness and your willingness to serve Mankind, will engage you to forgive this fault, as well as the others, and particularly the hast of
Sir
Your most obedient Servant
JOHN SHUTE
London June 27. 1701.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Shute 27 Jun. 01

2946. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 27 June/8 July 1701 (2932, 2960)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 173-4. Answers no. 2932.
Rotterdam 8†a July 1701
Dear Friend
Ever since receit of yours of the 30th may, for which I am extreamly obliged to you, and in which I concur with you in all points, I have been labouring with all my might to break lose, and come over for some time, because I very much long to see, and have some converse you, ere we are separated for good and all. I have spoke with mr. L——s†1 who tells me, sub Rosa, that he is in treaty with one to take over his shop, because he intends, if that proceeds, to keep himself onely to the books of his own printing, and then my son may be with that person. I told him it was not all one to me with whom I intrusted my son, and that he must be a solid and sober person, and family in which I would place him, he replyed, that he was such a one in whom he was sure I would be satisfyed.
Mr. Joseph Wright writes me that his 2 sons go morning and afternoons to learn the mathematicks in order to give them a generall knowledge of things, I am apt to think that may not be amisse for my Arent to spend the rest of his time in that he may stay in England till I come, (which I hope maybe within a month,) and shalbe ready to returne again, which may be after 2/m stay there. But this I perfectly submit to your better Judgment. If you approve of it, and mr. Wright shall write to him, or if he goe as (I had ordred him, and mr. Wright was expecting him, and they should incline to it)—If you think it convenient, I say, he may learn with his 2 sons.
We are much alarm'd at the clashing of the 2 houses, and that that keeps his Maj. longer there than he intended; whose arrivall we long for, not doubting but things will soone come to action, and this summer not be wholly lost.†2 But what wilbe done, or can be done against France, now they say, that by a courier to†b D'Avaux†b not onely the certain news, Of†c A†c league offensive and
― 356 ―
defensive betwixt france, Spain, and Portugal is concluded,†1 but also copy of it, they say, is in the Hague in the hands of mr. D'Avaux: which if true, I feare he has seen more reason for it than we are aware of. And then we may bid good Night to the Ballance and liberty of Europe.
Meanwhile Mr. Stanhope has declared to mr D'Avaux and Don Quiros that his Master had commaunded him to tell them that he could not treat with them, without the Baron Goes the Imperiall Ambassodor, who must have satisfaction.†2 This Don Quiros calld a Declaring warr—It makes me think often of Sir William Petty's Text, What shall we to all these things?†3 Pray give my and my wives most humble service to Sir F. my Lady and all that worthy family whom I hope now shortly to have the honour of seing, and in the mean while do remaine
Dear Sir
Your most humble servant and affectionate friend
BENJAMIN FURLY
Mr. Baile†4 came the other day while Mr. Clark and mr. Chadwick (who are gone to Aken†5 and Spaa) were with me, to give me a visit where I had occasion to speak with him about your booke, which he said, his great occupations had hindred from reading it through.†6 but so far as he had read it he had read it with great delight, and admired the depth of Judgment he found in it, desiring me to give his humble service to you when I wrote you.
All Vossius'es things are not yet out, the last Volume is now soon expected.
Address: For John Locke Esquire etc. etc. etc. These at Oates
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 8 Jul 01 Answered Jul:

2949. Elizabeth Clarke to Locke, 5 July 1701 (2317, 2996)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 157-8. Printed in Rand, p. 580.
Chipley July the 5th (1701)
Sir
I long to renew our conversation (tho if I mistake not it is on your side it rest's,) therefore amongst the concourse of Visiter's that wellcom you to towne, Lett me tell you that I am much pleased at your being there Master of So much more health, then you are used to bee; and I know nothing could add to the pleasure I received with the News, but its being confirmed by you when your Leasure will permitt; for you daily have my best wishes, I being devoted to you, by gratitude as well as by inclination.
Perhaps you may grumble a Little at this Letter, concludeing that I might as well have desired my Father to make my Service acceptable to you? 'tis true Sir, and I Still must beg his assistance,
― 359 ―
for it is impossible for mee alone to thanke you for your great favour's, or to express my Selfe as I ought,
Your most obliged freind and humble Servant
E CLARKE
My Mother and Sister†1 send you their Service.
I hope you left the family at Oates well. I'll answer Mrs Masham's Letter very Soon.
I have read Telemaque,†2 and La Fontaine with as much pleasure (lately) as at the first time; I could almost envy the difficulty's of that young Man, Since it procured him So much Wisedom!
Address: To John Locke Esqr at London
Endorsed by Locke: E: Clarke 5 Jul 01 Answered Aug. 13
2950. Mrs. Elizabeth Burnet, formerly Berkeley, to Locke, 6 July [1701] (2879, 2980)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 232-3. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Salis: July: 6:
Sir
I was first afraid to trouble you too soon either with my complaints for complements I had so litle right to, or my thanks for the very much estemed favour of hearing from you; after I flatered my self with hopes of seeing you before I left London, but had the mortification of knowing you would not be there 'till a few days after, as it was a very reall lose, so I confess I was truely concerned at my misfortune, and had I at all known my Lady Marsham I should have ben tempted to have come to see both her Ladyship and your self but that is past; may I say how wellcome you would be here: if it might be no injury to your health or better imployments to take such an easy journey; I can only assure you of a most harty wellcome from all that have intreast here and then leve it to your own inclenation; as to what you are pleased to say about the papers you sent, I know very well they are not worth your second perusall nor indid your first for other cause then the giveing you an opertunity to corect my erors; which has often tempted me
― 360 ―
to trouble you, and which I cant repent of, having gained so very much by it and I hope has don you no other injury then the expens of time that might have ben imployed on more capable larners.
I do not wonder you should not understand some parts of those papers, for in some places I cant find my own meaning, tho I gess I had some obscure one when I writ them; you may be sure you have a right to command any thing of this Nature, but you must not think me so foolishly vain as to beleeve any thing but your too great cevelity makes you desire them. I am in great hopes by your being in Town that your health is better, and then I am sure you are not Idel, but†a I wish what I have heard prove true that you will comunicat some more of your studys to the world, it is great pety if not want of charity to hord up truth while there is so great a dearth, but perhaps you think it is under such prohebetions that the free venting of it is neither safe, nor likely to do the good you desire; however truth has this advantage that it never loses of it reall value, the stamp may make it current but cant add to its waight, and one time or other it will pass for payment; I have not ben very well this spring my old illness of my stomack returns allways at that time of the year, and a sort of unreasonable sadness and hevyness on my spirits, I now begen to be a litle better if the weather is clear; I think indid the strang heats of this winter, and the litle regard to justice charity or truth affected me too much, tho I see such things so often I am allways surprised and griveed at them and cant help it; can't you now in Town convince those who want it of the danger and Fooly of such violence and partiallity to partys right or rong, surely wee have enemies enough abroad, and 'tis madness to quarell at home, when truth and liberty will fall by it; but I know you'll say 'tis to no purpose; but you cant be sure of it, I never knew you write without success and conviction and why not now; pray forgive this liberty which I run into before I was aware; if you have read Mr Norises Book of the Ideal world†1 I should be glad in a line or tow to know your thoughts which without your leve shall go no farther; the Bishop with his service bids me tell you, the nearness of L Saftburys will he hopes be a motive, he will send his Coach a days journy to meet you, and when you desire it to Carry you to
― 361 ―
my Lords if you please to accept it;†1 I suppose you have heard how unkind some have ben in the readyness they have showd to find the faults of his books,†2 but where wee are secure of acting from an honest intention the ill usages wee meet with are easely supported; I forget I am robbing you and will not turn again my paper, I am Sir Your obliged servent
E B
Endorsed by Locke: E: Burnet 6 Jul. 01 Answered Aug. 9

2952. Awnsham Churchill to Locke, [7 or 8 July 1701] (2947, 2962) enclosing Charles Hatton to Awnsham Churchill, 7 July 1701
B.L., MSS. Locke c. 5, ff. 138-9, and c. 11, ff. 150-1. The date in Locke's endorsement is too late. Locke left London on Tuesday 8 July: p. 373. The letter was written probably before his departure.
Charles Hatton was the younger brother of Christopher Hatton, first Viscount Hatton (D.N.B.). He was sometime lieutenant-governor of Guernsey; a captain in the army 1687-8; apparently a Jacobite; committed to the
― 362 ―
Tower 1690: Dalton, English Army Lists, vols. i, ii; Luttrell; etc. Letters from him in Hatton Correspondence show his interests in learning and culture, in horticulture and in voyages (he met Dampier). He approved of Locke's conduct in the controversy with Stillingfleet: ibid. ii. 224.
Sir
Whilst I was reading the note from you which the Bearer hereoff brought. mr Hattons man brought me the Enclosed, to which I returned an answer vizt. That you seldom went out before 10 in the morning, and was usually at home by 8 in the Evening.
I beleive mr Hatton has not ben able to goe abroad from some time. Sir
Yours at Comand
A CHURCHIL.
I shall mind your Directions about mr Clarks bond
Address: To John Locke Esqr present
Endorsed by Locke: A: Churchill 9 Jul. 01
[Enclosure:]
July. 7. 1701
I have for severall month's Sir by most violent paines in my head been confin'd as a Prisoner to my House But Last saterday†1 I unfortunatly went into Berkely street in my Neighbourhood and in the Interim the Great and Incomparable Mr lock was pleased to call at my House which I looke on as a greater Honour than had the Emperor himself given me a visit For I justly revere Mr locke as the Glory of our Nation and the Ornament of this Age
Had I been at home the reception of the Honour he design'd me wou'd have so reviv'd my spirit I am most certaine it wou'd have made me for some time totally to forget my paines if it had not perfected a cure on me which the vexation of being unhappily deprived of the obliging favour intended me hath retarded But that I may in some measure repaire my loss and may endeavour to make my acknowledment to that great and deservedly renowned man for the high obligation he hath Lay'd on me. Good Sir doe me the favour to let me know in a line or two by this Bearer Where Mr Locke lyes and what time of the day you Judge most
― 363 ―
seasonable for me to waite on him so as I may be the least troublesome to him. I am
Sir
your Humble servant
C: HATTON
Address: For Mr Churchill at the Black Swan in Pater-Noster-Row London
2953. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 8/19 July 1701 (2935, 2979)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 145-6. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, ff. 216-18. Printed from the copy, less the first paragraph and the last two sentences, in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 483-90. Answers nos. 2925 and 2935; answered by no. 2979.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Binas tuas literas accepi, amoris tui ac propensissimi erga filium meum affectus testes omni exceptione majores. Ego sententiæ tuæ penitus acquiesco, et tuâ toties probatâ amicitiâ confisus filio scripsi, ut in negotiis ambiguis aut perplexis à tuo consilio totus pendeat. Interim me tibi maxime obligatum agnosco, quod eam pro filio meo in te curam susceperis, ut licet à patre absens paterno tamen consilio non sit destitutus. Ego beneficiorum tuorum memoriam gratâ semper mente recolam, donec spiritus hos reget artus.†1
(English) Vitam Episcopii tibi, summi judicii viro, non displicuisse, est quod mihi gratulor. Multa exteris ignota ibi esse præterita, quia
― 364 ―
nobis notissima, nullus dubito. Quinque autem articulos nostros, quorum decidendorum causâ Synodus Dordracena convocata fuit, nulli ignotos credebam. In explicatione sententiæ Arminii pag.6. in vita Episcopii ego eos brevi in compendio exhibui. Exstant autem in Remonstrantia Ordinibus Hollandiæ anno 1610 oblatà, quam reperies in Epistolis præstantium Virorum à me editis, no. CXLV.pag.254.†1 vel in Historiâ Quinquarticulanâ Petri Heilini Anglicâ, cap.V.pag.50.†2 Si altera vitæ Episcopii editio aliquando prodeat,†3 possem illi quinque illos articulos, aliaque quædam non sine Episcopio gesta, aut ipsum ipsiusve consanguineos spectantia, hic illic inserere, quæ ad historiæ nostræ cognitionem penitiorem haud exigui futura sunt momenti. Continuavit Brantius noster senior historiam usque ad finem anni 1623, in quâ gravis illa contra nostros persecutio exactè describitur.†4 Verum illa hactenus lucem non adspexit; et præ metu ne edatur Synodus Hollandica jam ab aliquot annis Deputatis suis in mandatis dedit, ut sollicitè invigilent ne illa alicubi imprimatur. Nolunt enim mysteria illa iniquitatis
― 365 ―
revelari. Utinam historiam suam continuasset ad annum usque 1632, quo persecutioni ubique ferè in patriâ nostrâ finis est impositus, nobisque palam in cœtus†a convenire non fuit prohibitum!†1 Ex illius lectione deprehendere posses veritatem dicti cujusdam monachi, quod Marnixius refert in epistolâ ad Casparum Verheiden, inter Epist. select. à Belgis vel ad Belgas, anno 1617 à Baudio et Heinsio editas, Cent.II. epist.51.†2 haud æquè diu Reformatorum ollam calefactam fuisse, atque illorum quos tantoperè incesserent: Videre se planè, antequam par sæculorum intervallum labatur, parem utrobique imperii ecclesiastici fore rationem. Scripta est hæc epistola ult. Mart. an. 1577.
(English) Legi, relegi, et seriò expendi quæ de libertate scribis.†3 Sed non deprehendi illum inter nos esse consensum, quem lecto illo de potentiâ capite credidi. Quia uterque unicè veritatem quærimus paulò distinctius terminos quibus usus sum explicabo, et si qui aptiores sint, illis lubens utar; amo enim perspicuitatem, et in veritatis inquisitione omnem verborum ambiguitatem, quantum
― 366 ―
fieri potest, vitandam judico. Putas non rectè dici nos velle jucundum: illud esse desiderium, non voluntatem: desiderium enim ferri in bonum absens; volitionem autem esse actum voluntatis, vel animæ, imperium exercentis in potentias hominis operatrices. Facilè ego hoc discrimen admitto, et ut perspicuitatis causâ unicuique verbo suam tribuamus significationem, utile esse existimo. Verum ego puto nos duo velle, finem, et media quæ ad finem ducunt. Multa desideramus, quæ tamen non volumus. Est enim desiderium aliud completum, aliud incompletum, sicut et voluntas alia est completa, alia incompleta, quam barbaro vocabulo in Scholis velleitatem†1 appellant, quâ designamus non quid homo propriè velit, sed quid vellet. Prudentis est, ex multis desiderabilibus illud eligere, sibique omnium actionum suarum finem proponere, quod undequaque est perfectum, et in quo concurrunt omnes rationes quæ rem desiderabilem faciunt. Atqui illa electio non fit sine determinatione voluntatis, quâ homo decernit hoc bonum, quod omnibus aliis præferendum judicat, sibi omnium actionum suarum finem proponere. Ita ego credidi, rectè posse dici, hominis voluntatem in bonum ferri, idque bonum semper ab ipso apprehendi ut jucundum. Si verò credas, actionem quâ ferimur in bonum illud
― 367 ―
impropriè dici voluntatem, sed debere appellari desiderium, quia fertur in bonum absens, de termino non contendam, modo de illius significatione constet. Ut ergo omnis ambiguitas vitetur, dicamus desiderium ferri in bonum, voluntatem dirigere actiones. Sed caveamus ne quævis desideria confundamus, et desideria completa distinguamus ab incompletis, quæ velleitates, voce in scholis usitatâ appellari solent; si vero aliud aptius vocabulum indicare possis, eo lubens utar, ut omnis, quantum fieri potest, obscuritas et ambiguitas in sermone nostro vitetur.
(English) Quod attinet vocem Indifferentia, certum est nostros eâ non rarò esse in hac materiâ usos. Verum eam non adeo deperimus, quin si commodior nobis offeratur eam repudiaturi simus: eoque magis, quia videmus Philosophos Cartesianos eâ sensu à nostro planè alieno uti.†1 Illis enim Indifferentia est fluctuatio judicii, quando mens ex rationum pro utraque parte æquilibrio incerta est quid sibi eligendum sit. Nobis vero Indifferentia est vis illa animi,†a †2 quâ†3- positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis potest agere vel non agere.-†3 Verum in totâ hac de libertate disputatione video sæpe ludi verbis
― 368 ―
ambiguis, aut saltem in ambiguum sensum detortis. Optandum foret, omnia verba eodem significatu ab omnibus accipi: multæ inanes disceptationes et λογομαχίαι vitari possent. Nunc quoniam in significatione verborum convenire non possumus, necesse est ut quisque explicet, quo significatu unaquaque voce, de quâ contenditur, utatur. Circa rem ipsam video nos dissentire. Dicis: <Ista†1- antecedens Indifferentia>,†a quâ homo ante determinationem sive decretum voluntatis supponitur libertatem habere se determinandi ad alterutram partem oppositorum, non omnino mihi videtur spectare ad quæstionem de libertate: quia libertas unicè consistit in potentiâ agendi vel non agendi secundum determinationem voluntatis.-†1 Mihi planè contrarium videtur, libertatem unicè consistere in potentiâ quâ homo actionem volendi potest determinare, vel non determinare:†2 et si eam homo ante voluntatis determinationem non habet, quod non sit liber, neque ullus status concipi possit in quo liber dici queat. Quia enim voluntas actionum nostrarum domina est, easque pro arbitrio moderatur, si determinatio voluntatis non sit libera, nec in actionibus nostris nulla
― 369 ―
erit libertas, quia actiones voluntatis nostræ determinationem necessariò sequuntur. Quare vix capio quid velis, cum dicis, ante ultimum judicium intellectus homo non potest omnino se determinare. Verum antequam hic sententiam meam explicem, quid per ultimum intellectus judicium significetur, propius explicandum est, ne†a propter†a ambiguitatem vocis aliqua in oratione nostrâ sit obscuritas. Communiter ultimum intellectus judicium vocant, quo homo decernit quid sibi faciendum sit: idque vocant ultimum judicium practicum intellectus.†1 Verum hoc judicium non est tam actus intellectus, quam voluntatis, vel saltem actus mixtus, ad cujus complementum voluntas concurrit. Judicium autem quod solius intellectus actus est, non ulterius procedit, quam, hoc oportet facere, hoc oportet omittere. Ulterius si procedat intercedit aliqua actio voluntatis. Quæ duo tamen à multis <confunduntur>.†b Jam mea est sententia, hominem, quando <rectæ>†c rationi consentaneè agit, semper velle, quod intellectus judicat oportere fieri: posse tamen etiam contra rationem agere, et voluntatem in <c>ontrariam†d partem determinare: quin et, antequam intellectus post accuratum rationum examen judicaverit quid facere oporteat, posse bruto
― 370 ―
impetu†1 agere <non>†a quod rationi consentaneum est, sed quod concupiscentia dictat. Hic si homo non habeat libertatem se determinandi, aut non determinandi, et actionem suam suspendendi, videre nequeo in quo libertas consistat. Eandam esse tuam putabam sententiam, idque colligebam ex § 47. capitis supra nominati; ubi inter alia ais; Animam, quæ habet potentiam suspendendi impletionem cujuscunque desiderii sui, sicut evidenter patet per experientiam, consequenter etiam habere libertatem ea successive unum post alterum considerandi, eorum objecta examinandi, ea ex omni parte observandi, et inter se comparandi: Et in hoc consistere libertatem hominis; Omnemque erroris ac vitiorum originem inde arcessis, quod præcipitemus judicium, voluntatemque nostram cito nimis determinemus, et actioni nos accingamus antequam bene examinaverimus quid agere nos oporteat. Hæc aliaque quæ ibi addis verissima esse judico, iisque plane assentior. Verum hæc cum iis quæ in epistolâ scribis, quod homo ante judicium intellectus se non potest omnino determinare, conciliare non possum. Fortasse mentem tuam non bene percepi. (Latin) Excellent Sir,
I have received your two letters, unexceptionable witnesses of your love and very great affection towards my son. I am thoroughly satisfied with your opinion and, trusting to your so often proven friendship, have written to him to rely entirely on your advice in doubtful or intricate affairs. Meanwhile I recognize that I am very greatly obliged to you for having taken on yourself such care for him that, although absent from his father, nevertheless he will not lack fatherly advice. I shall recall the memory of your acts of kindness with an ever grateful mind as long as 'breath shall move these limbs'.†1
(Latin) That the life of Episcopius has not displeased you, a man of the greatest judgement, is a matter on which I may congratulate myself. I have no doubt that, because they are very well known to ourselves, many things unknown to [p. 363] foreigners are not mentioned in it. But I believed that our five articles, which the Synod of Dort was convoked to decide upon, were known to everybody. I gave them in brief summary on p. 6 of the life of Episcopius when setting forth Arminius's opinion. They are to be found, moreover, in the Remonstrance presented to the States of Holland in the year 1610, which you will find in my edition of the Epistolæ Præstantium Virorum, no. cxlv, p. 254,†1 or in Peter Heylyn's Historia Quinqu-Articularis (in English), ch. v, p. 50.†2 If another edition of the life of Episcopius should some day appear†3 I could insert in it here and there those five articles and some other transactions in which he took part or which relate to him or his kinsfolk; these will be of no small importance for a more intimate knowledge of our history. Our Brantius the elder has continued the history down to the end of the year 1623; that grievous persecution of our people [sc. the Remonstrants] is exactly described in it.†4 But so far this history has not seen the light; and for fear of its publication the Synod of Holland some years ago gave orders to its Deputies to watch carefully lest it should be printed somewhere. For they wish those mysteries of iniquity not to be revealed. Would that he had continued his [p. 364] history down to the year 1632, when an end was put to persecution almost everywhere in our country and we were not forbidden to assemble openly in congregations.†1 By reading it you could discover the truth of a certain monk's saying that Marnix reports in a letter to Caspar Verheiden, no. 251 in Epistolæ selectæ à Belgis vel ad Belgas, published in 1617 by Baudius and Heinsius:†2 that for a long time the Reformers' pot had not been heated as much as that of those whom they attacked so fiercely; he saw clearly that before a like interval of time had elapsed there would be a like form of ecclesiastical rule on both sides. This letter was written on the last day of March 1577.
(Latin) I have read, reread, and seriously pondered what you write about liberty.†3 But I have not perceived that there is that agreement between us which I believed there was when I read that chapter 'Of Power'. Since we are both seeking truth alone I shall set forth a little more clearly the terms that I have used, and if there are any more suitable I will gladly use them; for I love perspicuity and deem that in the search for truth all ambiguity of words ought to be avoided as far as may be. You think that it is not right to say that we [p. 365] will the agreeable: that is desire, not will: for desire is directed to absent good; volition on the other hand is an act of the will, or, rather, of the soul, exercising command over the operative powers of a man. I readily admit this distinction and think it expedient for the sake of perspicuity that we should give every word its signification. But I think that we will two things, an end and the means that lead to an end. We desire many things which nevertheless we do not will. For there are complete desire and incomplete desire, just as there are complete will and incomplete will, which last is called in the schools by the barbarous denomination 'velleity',†1 by which we denote not what a man wills, properly speaking, but what he might will. A prudent man will choose from many desirables, and set before himself as the end of all his actions, that one which is perfect in all respects and in which are joined all the reasons that make a thing desirable. But that choice is not made without a determination of the will by which a man decrees that he will set before himself this good, which he judges to be preferable to all the rest, as the end of all his actions. I have accordingly believed that it can rightly be said that the will of a man is directed to a good, and that that good is always apprehended by him as agreeable. But if you believe that the action by which we are directed to that good is improperly called will, but ought to be called desire, because it is directed to an absent good, I shall not [p. 366] contend about the term, so long as we are agreed about its signification. In order therefore to avoid all ambiguity let us say that desire is directed to a good and that will governs actions. But let us take care not to confuse all sorts of desires, and let us distinguish complete desires from the incomplete, which are wont to be called 'velleities', a word much used in the schools; but if you can point out another more suitable denomination I will gladly use it, so that, as far as may be, all obscurity and ambiguity should be avoided in our language.
(Latin) As regards the word 'Indifferency', our people [sc. the Remonstrants] have certainly used it not seldom in treating this subject. But we are not so strongly attached to it that we would refuse a more appropriate word, were one offered to us: and the more so because we see that the Cartesian philosophers use it in a sense manifestly different from ours.†1 For Indifferency is for them a wavering of the judgement when the mind, on account of an equal weight of reasons on either side, is uncertain which it ought to choose. For us, however, Indifferency is that energy of the spirit†2 by†3- which, when all requisites for acting are present, it can act or not act.-†3 But in all this discussion about liberty I see that play is often made with ambiguous words, or at least [p. 367] with words twisted into an ambiguous sense. It were to be wished that all words were taken by everyone with the same significance; many unprofitable disputes and logomachies could be avoided. Now since we cannot agree about the signification of words it is necessary for each of us to set forth with what significance he uses every word about which there is contention. I see that we disagree about the thing itself. You say 'That†1- antecedent Indifferency, by which a man is supposed, before the determination or decree of the will, to have liberty to determine himself to one or other of opposites, seems to me not to have any bearing at all on the question of liberty: because liberty consists solely in a power to act or not to act according to the determination of the will'.-†1 It seems to me, altogether to the contrary, that liberty consists solely in a power by which a man can determine, or not determine, an action of willing;†2 and that if a man does not possess that power before the determination of the will he is not free, nor can any state be conceived in which he can be called free. For, because the will is master of our actions, and governs them according to its choice, if the determination of the will is not free neither will there be any liberty in our actions because actions [p. 368] necessarily follow the determination of our will. Wherefore I scarcely understand what you mean when you say, 'Before the' last 'judgement of the understanding a man is altogether unable to determine himself'. But before I set forth my opinion about this, what is meant by the last judgement of the understanding ought to be more nearly set forth, lest there should be some obscurity in our language by reason of the ambiguity of a word. The last judgement of the understanding is the name commonly given to the judgement by which a man decrees what he ought to do; and it is called the practical last judgement of the understanding.†1 But this judgement is an act not so much of the understanding as of the will, or at least it is a mixed act, in the completion of which the will joins. Moreover a judgement which is an act of the understanding alone proceeds no further than 'This ought to be done, this ought to be forborne'. If it proceeds further some action of the will intervenes. These two things are nevertheless confused by many people. Now my opinion is that when a man acts in accordance with right reason he always wills what his understanding judges ought to be done; nevertheless he can also act against reason and determine his will to the contrary; more than that: before his understanding, after a careful examination of the [p. 369] reasons, has judged what ought to be done he can by brute impulse†1 do, not what is in accordance with reason, but what carnal desire dictates. If a man does not have liberty herein to determine himself or not to determine himself, and to suspend his action, I cannot see in what liberty consists. I thought that your opinion was the same, and gathered as much from § 47 of the chapter mentioned above, where you say, among other things, that the soul, which has the power of suspending the fulfilment of any of its desires, as is evident from experience, consequently also has liberty to consider them successively one after another, to examine their objects, to observe them from all sides, and to compare them one with another; and in this consists the liberty of a man; and you derive the origin of all our mistakes and faults from our precipitating our judgement and determining our will too quickly, and in our preparing ourselves for action before we have properly examined what we ought to do. I judge these, and other things that you add there, to be most true, and I thoroughly agree with them. But I cannot reconcile them with what you write in your letter, that before the judgement of the understanding a man is altogether unable to determine himself. Perhaps I have not rightly grasped your meaning. I am not so addicted to any opinion, [p. 370] much less to any phrases or word, as not to be prepared to give way to anyone who shows me a better. For I seek truth alone; should I find it I shall triumph over error. And so I beg you, if it is not troublesome, to show me how I ought to reconcile these statements with one another, and to set forth more clearly what I have not fully grasped.
(Latin) I had written this much when a copy in Latin of your treatise on the Human Understanding was brought to me; I am most grateful to you for this notable gift and thank you for it. I have decided to read it through from beginning to end and to compare it with the very fine French version, which without doubt will sometimes lend(?) light to the Latin. And when I have read through the whole treatise I will candidly write you my opinion, not because it is necessary but because you ask it of me and I recognize that I owe it to you when you ask for it. But, so far as I have perceived from reading the French version, you will have my approval of your opinion; if, however, I should be at a stand about anything I will candidly point it out to you, so as to draw from you a fuller exposition of it. I pray God to continue your life and strength, so that you can further benefit the learned world by your excellent labours. My wife and daughter send you greetings. Please give our best respects to Lady Masham and the whole family. I make no answer at present to her letter, or to that of her son Francis, except to say this one thing: That I shall always be under obligation to her, and if I can be of use [p. 371] to her in anything my service will never fail her. I pray God to grant her all things prosperous and salutary. Good-bye again.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 19 July

Oates 11 Jul. 01
Dear Cosin
I got safe and well hither on Tuesday†1 But when your health amongst others was enquired after I was blamed for coming away without bringing with me a promise from you of comeing down hither before you goe your circuit. Upon reflection I think I did ill to let the many other things I had to talke to you about croud that soe far out as to make me not presse you on that point soe much as I might and as I think it reasonable now to doe. I conclude you will have at least a weeks leisure before you leave the town and you cannot doe better than to come and spend it here. It is as much for your health to come hither, as it is contrary to mine to come to town and you know we have many things to talke of. Send me our account by the next post and I shall looke it over against you come that we may then adjust it. All here give you their humble service. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant

Rotterdam 25 March 1701
Yesterday I had at my house a Young Lad of 17 Year old, that can neither read nor write, that out of his head will reckon any of the most difficult sums you can give him even to the utmost fractions: I gave him an avarage†2 to make of a ship run a shore to save ship and goods: belonging to 7 persons the ship and goods saved were worth f13679:14:— The charges on the Salvage was f2931:16:— I askt him how much that was per Cent. he told me after a little talking to himself that it was 21 gilders 9 stivers and a small fraction and so it is. I askt him what f4943:3:— f2848:4:— f2244:7:— f2194:7:— f544:19:— f351:18:— and f52:16:— must pay respectively. he told me exactely to so many <stivers>†a and 270/1000. I askt him how he came by that knowledge, he said by selling sea
― 375 ―
snayles (Aly kreucken)†1 and mussles: for which he received nothing but deuts†2 and so he brought his father home so many deuts but could never tell how much money they amounted to, till he askt his father how many deuts made a Gilder, and being 160. then he reckoned how many in f10. and f100. and so from one thing to another; he has a table of multiplication in his head of half a Yard long or more, I tryed him by a table I have and he answered me as readily, as you can upon the ordinary table of Multiplication, And he wanders from town to town to see who has any thing to cypher and so gets some money, but would fain learne to read and write. This I mention because it is so prodigious, and he devides almost with as much ease as he multiply's and reduces things to the least denomination in fractions. I have a great mind could I be assured of his fidelity to take him into my house and learn him to read and write and cypher.

D'Amsterd. ce 28 jul. 1701.
Monsieur,
Je me suis pas hasté a vous respondre, pour avoir assez de tems pour mediter la responce que je vous doibs sur une affaire aussi importante comme est votre santé, si utile au public, et si chere a vos amis, dont je prens la liberté de me conter du nombre. j'ay consulté ce que j'ay d'amis icy parmis les Medecins reputez. nous sommes tous, Monsieur Veen en teste d'accorde avec ceux de Londres quil seroit dangereu d'arrester les fluxions au jambes par quelques topiques ou autrement, puisque il y auroit a craindre, que cela retomberoit sur vos poulmons. mais cela n'empesche qu'on puisse corriger l'acrimonie de votre sang, qui se manifeste si evidemment de toute parts. votre age ne permet pas de faire de grandes evacuations. dans un corps plus robuste la seignée ne seroit pas hors de propos, la quelle en diminuant la quantité du sang, fait succeder un meilleur chyle a la place qui pouroit porter avec soy la vertu de quelque bon medicament.†a nous sommes tous d'opinion qu'une decoction de chine et de salseparille seroit convenable, dont il semble que la vertu principale consiste a emousser l'acrimonie du sang. je me souvien d'avoir gueri une demoiselle de cette ville, agée de vingt et cinq ans, laquelle pendant 3 a 4tre annees consecutives avoit eté fortement attaquée de semblables pustules avec imflammation au jambes, au bras et au visage. elle s'estoit servie inutilement de plusieurs bon remedes sous la direction de deux de nos premiers medecins. ce fut environ cette saison quelle m'appella a son secours, apres quelques evacuations generales, je la fit prendre pendant un mois entier tous les jours quatre onces de succ. recent des herbes, lapathum acutum, Cochlearia, portulaca et becabunga exprimez. et clarifiez par subsidence. ensuitte sur l'automne je luy fis prendre les eaux de Spa encore pendant un mois, une bouteille par jour le†b- matin a june.-†b elle fut exempte de son mal la méme année qui avoit coutume de la prendre avant l'hyver. je luy fis faire le méme regime l'année suivante il y a 8 ans, et depuis elle n'a eu aucune recidive et se porte parfaittement bien.
― 378 ―
je ne doubte pas que les antiscorbutiques ne vous soient utiles. mais d'en prendre le suc ainsy cru, je craindois que cela offenseroit vótre estomach. mais on pouroit infuser chaudement ces herbes sur la decoction de chine et de salseparille et se servir principalement du lapathum acutum soit de l'herbe ou de la racine a son deffaut. vous pouriez joindre a ce remede dont vous boiriez souvent une verrée par jour un benin laxatif a prendre une foi la sepmaine le quart de cette ordonnance

jay vu souvent de fort bons effets de mercure doux. un nommé Monsieur André dans son livre des vers quil a nouvellement publié†1 croit que ces pustules naissent par des vers que le sang y porte. cela ne manque pas de probabilité, et c'est peut étre en tuant ces vers que le mercure agit. nous serions tous d'avis que quand méme ces pustules viendroient a vous quitter, quil seroit utile de porter une cautére a la jambe pour y attirer ce quil y auroit d'impur dans votre sang, et d'en guarantir vos poulmons.
Comme vous avez de grandes lumieres vous ne scauriez manquer de bien choisir sur tout ce que vos amis vous peuvent conseiller. tousjours Monsieur, soyez persuadé que nous voudrions de tout nótre cœur vous pouvoir donner quelque soulagement. toute la famille vous presente ses treshumbles respects, ma femme continue tousjours sur le bon pied. elle est presentement a se divertir a la campagne de Monsieur Veen. Monsieur le clerc y passa un jour de la sepmaine passée. Monsieur son frere le medecin de Geneve vient de publier son histoire de la medecine avec un second tome qui comprend la vie de Galien.†2 il seroit a souhaitter quil voulut continuer jusqu'au medecins de notre tems. il marque beaucoup d'erudition et d'exactitude.

nous croyons icy la guerre en bref. 2960. Benjamin Furly to Locke, [c. 17/28 July 1701] (2946, 3030)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 166. Written apparently shortly after Furly learnt about the memorial presented by Avaux.
Dear Friend
I am in such a stand in myself, as to my coming over, being in dayly expectation of a war, that I cannot determine what to do: If a war should break forth, my wife will never consent to my going, and without it I can't resolve: So that I think it best that Arent goes to London, and see what's there to be seen, and hampton court, and Windsor if he can get good company to guide him, and then go downe to colchester to see my relations, and so home thence directly or by the packet from Harwich—I have just now been with mr. Leers, but he puts me off yet 8 or 10 days before he can tell me any thing. Passing through Leyden last week, I discourst Vander Aa†2 about my son, who advis'd the placing him with Wetstein. If mr. Leers should refuse, as he said, he beleevd he would, because he had understood that he intended to bring up his wives son†3 to that trade, and then would not be so ready to teach my son the most mysterious part of it. I told him Amsterdam was too far
― 380 ―
off, and askt him if he wanted not a yong lad, telling him how well qualifyed he was, which pleasd him well. So he told me that not above 4 days before he was pressed by a friend†a of his, that had been the occasion of his being put to that calling, and so claimd a right to have him take a yong man of his acquaintance. That he had not yet seen the yong man, nor treated about him much less: That if they did not agree, he would take my son, and treat him as his owne; with a great deale of affection; saying that he had been a soldier of fortune, and began with nothing. But now has a good estate, and a great printing house—
This memoir†1 tels the States, that his master saw their mixing themselvs with England, was not done with an intention <to>†b continue the peace, and would produce a war, that he did not yield to treat with England and Holland jointly without foreseeing that it would be demanded that the Emperor should be joind in the Treaty. That if they did really beleev themselvs in so much danger as their letter to the K. of England expresses; they had the means in their own hands to have deliverd themselvs from those fears; without arming themselvs so, buying allyes at such dear rates, drowning their lands etc as in the greatest wars. That he should abuse his master if he should give him any hopes of effecting anything by these conferences at the Hague. That it would be in vain for his master to continue him longer here. That if he had had any design to have made any conquest upon them, he had had oportunity enough to have kept their Troops and Attackt them when at their weakest. That he knew which of their places were without defence. That he had a long time seen the game they were playing, and winkt at the affronts offerd to his flag both by English and dutch. And yet had born, and dissembled all this nor out of any diffidence of his power, but onely not to give the lest shadow of breaking the Ryswyc peace. Not doubting but if it come to that, that God would bless him, in the Just defence of his Grandchilds right, as he had all along done throughout his glorious reign—
yet som think that all this is but the Copy of his countenance because he concludes that there is yet time for them to form Resolutions
― 381 ―
to their advantage. I am, with humble service to your self and that Honourable family
Sir your humble servant
B FURLY
Address (written by an amanuensis): For John Locke Esquire These per Courant†a
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 01

Honoured Sir

Sir you have one doz. quarts and 2 doz. pint bottles sent you of the Clarret of last vintage which seems to drink the freshest: though I have trespast on your order and added halfe a dozen bottles of the Clarret of last vintage was twelve†b month†b that you may see which you like best. heerewith you have Sir the account I have of the Salop: which I hartily wish may succeed to your good likeing: you may please to command a supply:

Address: To The Honorable John Locke att Oates
Endorsed by Locke: S: Locke 18 Jul 01 Answered Oct 9
― 382 ―

[Enclosure:]
Sir
The Salop†1 grows in several parts of the World vizt.
At Bursa†2 in Asia 8†a days Journy frome Constantinople—
In Anguyry in Asia and at Almada at the bottom of the Apple Hill—
In Persia from whence came that which you have
It is a Roote Like an Onyon; grows wilde in the fields and when gather'd Is cleane wash't; Strung and hang'd up adryeing; It is esteemed to be very good for the Lungs; and against the Tyssick and comfortable for the Stomack—It is pounded in a morter or ground to Powder and Cyfted, and makes a kind of Jelly, which as I am inform'd is by†b the†b takeing 3 pintes of the best Spring (no Pump) water, Sett Over the fyre in a pure clean vessell of earth or any other; very clean from grease and when the water boyles put in halfe an Ounce of the Salop: and keep it continually Stiring and boyling for about 3 or 4 minutes. then put in About 11/2 Ounce of the fynest Powder Sug<er>†c or Other fyne white Suger keep it Stiring till disolved then Adding a few dropps of Rose water take it off and when pour'd Out and Setled. please to drink of it a dish or 2. as you doe Tea:—Som in the morning and Some an hour or two after dinner, and before be<d>†d tyme the Armenians whom I have talkt with cry it up very much—
I send you an Ounce Powder'd to try it—

As for East India Stock I know not what to Say, It fell Yesterday to 105, is now come up again to 1061/2. That which makes it fall is peoples apprehension of a war, some people of Consideration think we shall have, others are of another mind, but all agree, that we shall know in a little time, I cannot tell what to advise you, If I could, I would, I cannot meet with any man, who can give me any advice herein to be relied on—I am
Sir
Your Most Obliged and affectionate Cosin and Servant

― 386 ―

Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant

2967. William Popple to Locke, 26 July 1701 (2877, 2971)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 251-2.

Sir
I suppose it will not be unacceptable news to you to hear that the Treasury have ordered your quondam Office†1 a Six months payment, in which you are concerned as others that remain in.
I have the Orders already in my hands: But Mr Lowndes's Letter of Direction for the payment is not yet writ, though we expect it will be shortly. The Commissioners have therefore begun to contribute (as usually) towards the Charges: And you may accordingly if you think fit send me a Bill for 26 or 28£ to be made use of as occasion requires. It will be necessary also that you send a Blank Receipt, which must be upon a paper folded in four, according to the form that I have marked on the back of this. My wife and all mine present their most humble service to you. And we beg the favour of you to present our most humble services to Sir Francis, my Lady, and Mr and Mrs Masham. I am
Sir,
Your most obedient humble Servant

― 389 ―
More quiet then the Persons under the same Roofe with you and I am to impartial not to be equelly troublesome, I fancy you will say this is a very prety Letter because it tends to nothing, but if you would have me write Properly and upon a Subject pray give me one and instruct me how to doe it. 2974. —— Pilliod to Locke, 5 August 1701
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 160-1. I have failed to identify the writer.
Monsieur
Vous serés sans doute surpris qu'un homme qui vous est aussi incognu que je le suis et qui l'est presque autant au monde ait la temerité de vous escrire. j'ose cependant croire que le motif qui my a porté vous paroistra excuser en partie mon hardiesse et vous engagera a la pardonner. Il y a environ huict ans que Mylord Evesque de Clogher†1 me fit venir dans ce Royaume et que par ces recommandations on my a confié l'Education de quelques jeunes Gentilhommes ce qui ma fait rechercher avec soin tous les livres qui pouvoient m'estre de quelque secours dans cest Employ pour que je ne donna pas lieu a mon Patron de se repentir de m'avoir trop honoré mais il faut que j'avoue que je ne trouvai dabord que des traittés bornés et imparfaits sur ce sujet qui quoy qu'ils fournissent quelques bonnes et judicieuses maximes ne m'en apprenoit cependant pas assés pour me satisfaire. Et ce n'est (souffrés Monsieur que je le dise) que depuis que j'ay le bonheur de cognoistre vos pensées la dessus que je puis dire que je suis une juste methode et que jay un guide parfait aussi ay je acquis quelque repution dans ce genre d'employ par l'usage que jay fait de vos directions n'estant pas possible de ne pas reussir si on veut les estudier et les suivre. Il seroit seulement a souhaiter quelles fussent plus generallement suivies. On auroit le plaisir de voir un Assemblage d'hommes plus sains de corps et d'Esprit, On verroit des Esprits plus droits plus dociles et moins effeminés aussi bien que des corps mieux proportionés et plus robustes. Nous Verrions moins de Maladies, moins d'Entetement et moins d'opiniatreté et par consequent moins de disputes et moins de partis, plus de gens raisonables et moins de tesmoins emportés des sentiments dautruy. En un mot nous vivrions dans un plus agreable Societé. Car qu'on forme tant qu'on voudra des desseins de reformer nos Societés si les membres qui la <composent>†a nont pas eté eslevés selon vos regles on ne reussira jamais puis que cest la le fondement qu'on
― 395 ―
doit poser et sans lequel ce ne seroit jamais qu'une Republique imaginaire. Je ne sçaurois donc voir un Ouvrage aussi precieux que l'est Vos pensées sur l'Education et me sentir quelque capacité d'en faire part a ma Patrie (qui est le pais de Vaud en Suisse) sans me Croire tres coupable si je ne fais mes efforts pour le leur communiquer, ne croyant pas qu'il soit encore traduit en françois mais quoy que je me fasse un devoir de le leur donner en cette langue, je ne m'en <fais>†a pas moins un de ne l'entreprendre qu'apres que vous m'en aurés donné la permission, que si je l'obtiens et n'en donne quune foible traduction (comme je dois le craindre) elle servira au moins d'emulation a d'autres qui en recognoitront comme moy le pr<ix>†b mais qui seront plus capable de rendre justice a vos pense<es.>†b Voyla Monsieur la cause de ma temerité que je vous prie de pardonner nayant eu dautre dessein que celuy de vous temoigner quon ne peut estre avec plus de respect que je le suis
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
PILLIOD
Si vous m'honorés d'un mot de responce mon adresse est To Mr. Raymond†1 fellow in the College Dublin
A Dublin le 5e Aoust 1701.

2975. James Tyrrell to Locke, 7 August [1701] (2933, 3071)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 143-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Okeley Aug: 7th:
Dear Sir
I am allmost ashamed to acknowledg, that I have received your kind letter of June 1, and have left it 2 months unanswerd, yet I hope I may obtaine your Pardon, when I tell you, that within three
― 396 ―
or four days after I receiv'd it, I was obliged to go out of Towne in some hast, about 3 miles beyond Bury to peruse some historical Manuscripts†a in Sir Simmonds Dews's Library,†1 and from that Freinds who had the loane of those I needed, went to Cambridg for the same Purpose, in both which Places, I spent about a month, and at my returne to Towne found (to my great disappointment) that you had bin there and after a few days stay not finding the Air to agree with you were gone downe again; but they told me at your Lodgings that you were expected again in Towne within a fortnight or three weeks, so that the hopes of seeing you there, together with the continual Hurry I was then in, made me deferr writing till I came hither, where I have bin ever since the begining of this month to enjoy my new son,†2 and daughters company, who intend to pass some time longer here, and upon shewing her your kind concerne for her happyness she desires me to present you with her humble service and thankes for that favour.
I was as sorry to hear of the sharp humour that fell into your Leg, as I was pleased with the good news of its being gone, I hope you gaind this advantage by it, that it carryed away a great deal of the like matter from your Lungs; if it returne againe, the best advice I can give is to draw it out by the application of yong Cabbage or Colewort leaves, which have had so good an effect upon somewhat the like humour in my Fathers legs, that by the Constant use of those Leaves, and a dyet drink he has arrived to an extreme tho uneasy old Age. as for what you desire to know in relation to the disease, and Fortune of our deceasd Freind,†3 the Account I can give you is but imperfect, having not spoke with any body that was with him at his death; onely I hear at second hand: that the disease he dyed of was cheifly Cholical paines and decay of Appetite, he complaind to me about this Time 12 month at Oxford, that his Hypocondries†4 were so filld with windy matter
― 397 ―
and were so much upon the stretch, that he was very uneasy with it, which symptomes it seems increasd still upon him till his departure, tho' by what I can find, he might have bin releived, and his life saved, had he had ever a skilfull Physitian with him, but I cannot hear he used the advice of any, nor did think himself in danger of death till it was too late, as for the Fortune he left I am told it was in Land money worth above 5000 l: which shews how much a Batchelor (tho he lives handsomly) may lay up from a moderate Income by prudent mannagement: he has given an 100l. apeice to the Citty Stock of Norwich and Glocester for Employment of the poor, and somwhat but how much I have forgot for the repair of the Cathedral of norwich, the rest of his Estate he has left to his nephew who is a sickly decrepite yong man, so that it will in Time all come to that persons sister and her children, all which circumstances considerd I wish he had performd what he promisd me when I last saw him at Oxford, that he would bestow much on publick uses. but he is gone and thereby gives us this warning that even Codicils to Wills are not to be deferd to the Last.
Since I am now come beyond my first designe to the last side of this paper I will now fill it up with an Account of the advancement of the Res Litteraria in both our Universities. at Cambridg there is in the presse a fine new Edition of Suidas, with notes and corrected from the best Manuscript†a Copies; by a Germane one Custar who calls himself Neochorus:†1 in oxford besides Mr: Dodwells new Chronolical Miscellanies that came out lately†2 there is still in the Presse a new Edition of Dionys: Halicarnas: with notes,†3 and allso of Justine Martyr.†4 my Lord Clarendons history of the civil war goes on but slowly, so that I beleive the first volume will scarce come out till the next spring.†5 I am now upon finishing a
― 398 ―
third volume of the Eng: History. conteining the Reignes of the three Edwards and Richard the second:†1 I should be glad if either your self or the Ingenious Lady have perused my last performance to have your censure of it, that if there be any thing in the composition that does not well satisfy you I may mend it in this I am about. and therefore desire to be treated as to that point with the same plain historical Freedom, with which I endeavour to performe that work.
I have nothing more at present to add, but that I have now spoke with my daughter about the third volume of Herodotus which you want,†2 and assures me she never saw more then those 2 volumes of it which you have: which way the third came to be lost I know not, but hoped when you last asked me about it that my daughter had it: which since it is not so, I am ready to procure you the third volume if it may be had in London: but I will stay till my son comes back who perhaps may have borrowd it unknowne to me. so hoping this may find you still†a in Towne; and praying for your health and our happy meeting remaine
Your most humble and obliged servant
J TYRRELL.
I praay present my humble service to that worthy Couple, with whom you commonly are
Address: For John Lock Esqr at Mr: Pawlings house over against Plough stables in the New buildings near Lincolns Inne London.
Postmark: AV 12
Endorsed by Locke: J Tyrrel 7 Aug 1701

2976. Robert Pawling to Locke, 9 August 1701 (2970, 2989)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 46-7.
London Aug: 9 1701
Sir
I†a- this morning paid Mr Clark £10 as you will find by the inclosed Note; I could not prevail with him to abate more than the 4d.-†a
I delivered your Letter to my Lord Aversham who presents his service to you, and intends to write to you and will send his Letter to me. I was with his Lordship about half an hour and he desired me to come down and set with him; which I intend to do; he rememberd me ever since he was at the Office to have his pattent for his Lordship; he looked over my books then while I got his Pat: stamped, and was well pleased with my methods etc.†1
The 2 doz 1/2 were delivered to Mr Bonville sealed; and I hope they will come safe to you.
Mr Clark the Taylor hath lost his onely child and is very impatient under the affliction; I met him some days before she dyed in Fleetstreet, like a distracted man, railing against his Doctors, calling them a pack of K: and Rogues.
Mr Robinsons wife dyed†2 of a Fever about the time my Daughter Christian was ill; she was ill about 17 days and the Apothecary by the direction of the Doctors poked her Soul out of his body with his ingredients; he followed her so close with his Stuff that his Bill in that time came to £15.
God be thanked, I had no Apothecary for my Daughter; she was almost a quarter of a year before she walked abroad, but all her Phisick, except Milk water,†3 which we had at the best hand, and of the best sort, from the College;†4 came not to 5s, but some will say I take a course to starv apoth: and Brewers and hinder the Kings revenu; yet still I persist; and have brought my 3 Clarks at the Office to drink water too; at this rate we may, in time, be a majority. I see children dayly drinking at our Pump, as well as men and weomen; we shall never see a thorough reformation in England till that
― 400 ―
becomes the chief drink; twill cure men of Drunkeness and many other vices, and if it really clenses from these sins and vices it will, by being taken inwardly do more than when outwardly applyed in Baptisme unless the thing signified be really found in the persons so outwardly sprinkled or dipt. I am
Sir
Your very humble Servant
ROB PAWLING
Address: J L For Sir Francis Masham a member of Parliament [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Frank
Postmark: AV 9

2977. John Bonville to Locke, 9 August 1701 (2972, 3001)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, f. 111.
London August the 9th 1701
Honoured Cousin
Sir Last†a- Thursday morning I went to Madam Lockhart, but she was not Att home, but her Sarvant, Asked my name, and presently conducted, me to A Gentlewomans house hard by, And she paid me 15 l pounds, I parseve Madam Lockhart received my Letter,-†a because was Exspeted, and provition, for my Coming. I have This day sent by Lenham, 30 bottles of wine, 6 of Them are flatt don with Twygs. Them I packt upright, I hope They will all com safe I nue Tide downe and seld the flatt bottle, for I found They ware but badly don before, Sir I hope you have received my sonns Letter, It will be A Inexspresable satisfaction to me, was he In settled busines, now he Is Capable, for Anything I find the busines which he Is now upon will soone be at An end, we All give our Humble Sarvis To you,
I Am Deare Cousin your Faithfull Kinsman and Humble Sarvant

2978. Sir John Thompson, first Baron Haversham, to Locke, [9? August 1701] (3029)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 165-6. The date in the endorsement is probably that on which Locke received the letter. It may have accompanied no. 2976 of 9 August, a Saturday; 11 August is also possible.
John Thompson, c. 1648-1710; created a baronet 1673; Baron Haversham of Haversham 1696. He was a whig until about the end of 1701, and then a tory, and equally reckless throughout: D.N.B.
Sir
I Received the favour of your Letter by Mr Pauling in behalfe of Cap Tho Robison†1 and doe not find he is in so much dainger of goeing to the West Indies as he may apprehend, but he is very right in that what ever is in my power Dr Lock may Command it. I must adde my obligation for your good opinion of me. I can pretend to no more but to indeavor to deserve it tis a dificult thing to know what the right notion of a true English man is and much harder to practice those notions. My wife has soe great a desire that My Lord Anglesey should wait on you that I must beg the favour to let me know when you are in towne she intends to git him to come to Towne at that time. he is very Consumptive and wee both promise ourselves great advantage to my Lord if you will favour him with your advise.†2
I am with great sincerity and respect
Sir
your assured humble servant
