2979. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 12 August 1701 (2953, 3010)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 258 c, and Some Familiar Letters, pp. 501-4. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 490-504; the omitted paragraph, in Ollion, p. 223. The manuscript of the addition to the French translation of the Essay is missing; it must have been on a separate piece of paper (the part of the letter in Latin covers the whole of four pages), and
― 402 ―
presumably bore the address; it is here reprinted from Some Familiar Letters. Some errata (p. 464) are also missing. Answers no. 2953; answered by no. 3010.
(English)
Oates 12 Aug 1701
Vir Amplissime
Quod pauca illa benevolentiæ meæ erga filium tuum officia quæ adhuc præstare mihi datum est tantopere prædicas, id factum existimo potius ut morem geras animo tuo in gratitudinem proclivi, quam quod credas, me mihi aut amicitiæ nostræ satisfecisse in iis quæ illius causâ facere mihi hactenus contigit. Tibi pro certo sit me ad omnia, quæ illius utilitati inservire possint paratum esse. Si consilio, re, operâ, gratiâ illum quovis modo juvare possim, non deero. Verbis opus esse ut hoc tibi persuadeam non credo. De amicitiâ nostrâ inter nos convenit, Proinde ad ea procedendum est de quibus inter nos non videtur tam plane convenire
(English) Quod omnis obscuritas et ambiguitas in verborum usu sit vitanda tecum plane sentio. Verum liceat mihi adjicere, quod hoc sæpe non fit etiam a volentibus evitare obscuritatem. Ideæ quæ obversantur hominum mentibus præsertim eorum qui veritatem attentius quærunt multo plures sunt quam voces cujusvis linguæ quæ ad eas exprimendas paratæ sunt. Hinc fit quod homines (quibus integrum non est nova vocabula quoties opus est ad novas Ideas significandas ad libitum procudere) eâdem voce pro diversis Ideis, præsertim si cognatæ sint, identidem utuntur: unde oritur non raro
― 403 ―
sermonis obscuritas et incertus sensus, quando ad præcisiones accuratas veniendum est, quo non solum audientium sed et ipsorum etiam loquentium mentes implicantur. Inter illa quæ proposui lib iii Cap xi huic malo remedia illud mihi præcipuum videtur, sc: ut diligenter colligamus omnes simplices Ideas quæ ingrediuntur compositionem cujuslibet Ideæ complexæ cujus nomen usurpamus, easque eidem voci affixas sedulò in animo teneamus. V.g. In argumento quod præ manibus habemus, Si Voluntas significat potentiam quam homo habet incipiendi sistendi, vel vitandi aliquam actionem mentis vel corporis sui, ut ego fusiùs explicui lib ii Cap xxi. §. 5 etc: In quo tu etiam acquiescere videris. Si hæc inquam sit Idea quam vox Voluntas significat; eamque præsentem in animo habemus quando de Voluntate loquamur, nihil certius esse potest quam quod Voluntas terminatur solummodo in actionibus nostris nec potest ulterius extendi ad rem aliquam aliam, nec ferri in bonum remotum et absens. Adeoque si Contendis Voluntatem ferri in bonum ut finem recedis ab eâ Ideâ quam huic voci assignavimus, aliamque substituis, unde fit quod Tu et Ego diversas res designamus quando de Voluntate loquimur, nec omnino possumus inter nos de Voluntate disserentes quicquam proficere donec tu Ideam indices cujus apud te Vox Voluntas signum est, ut de sensu vocis i e de re de qua disserimus conveniamus
― 404 ―
(English) Distinctio de Desiderio completo et incompleto sive de Voluntate completâ et incompletâ quam affers, nihil mihi videtur argumentum tuum juvare. Sive enim aliquod sit incompletum desiderium, vel incompleta voluntas, quod sane dubito, id nunquam efficiet ut sit verum, quod Voluntas fertur in bonum. Dico me dubitare an aliqua potest esse incompleta Volitio;†a Voluntas enim hic, ni fallor, sumitur pro actu Voluntatis i.e. pro Volitione. Volitionem inefficacem facile agnosco, ut cum paralyticus manum paralysi solutam movere velit, inefficax fateor et sine successu est ista Volitio sed non incompleta. Actus enim volendi hoc in casu æque completus est, ac olim quando manus volitioni obsequebatur. Itidem desiderium alicujus propositi boni quod, propter majus bonum incompatibile, prosequi negligimus, non est incompletum desiderium nec incompleta Voluntas sed desiderium completum brevi terminatum eousque non procedens ut nos impellat ad volendum actiones quibus obtineri possit illud bonum in quod ferebatur breve illud desiderium: nec incompleta dici potest voluntas ubi nulla omnino est volitio, etiamsi scholæ Velleitatem appellare ament. Quod si breve illud desiderium eousque procedat ut nos ad volendam aliquam actionem excitet, Voluntas illa non est incompleta, sed completus actus volendi etiamsi omissâ ulteriore inefficax sit ad obtinendum bonum propositum
― 405 ―
quod cessante desiderio negligitur. In his et hujusmodi mentis actionibus, adeo celeres sunt motus animi, et inter se conjuncti, ut non mirum sit, quod sæpe, uti fit confundantur, quæ attentius consideranti distinguenda sunt ut recte conceptus nostros formemus. Vis libere dicam quid hac de re sentio. Homo fertur in bonum absens sive finem. Multis simul intellectui obversantibus bonis non subordinatis nec consistentibus homo unum neglectis aliis sibi proponit ut finem i.e. ut prosequendum, hoc facit voluntariè adeoque voluntas fertur in illam actionem mentis qua unum præ reliquis sibi proponit ut finem, et in eâ actione terminatur, eodem modo quo terminatur in computatione quando vult numerare, vel in motione pedum quando vult ambulare. Ob hanc voluntariam propositionem istius boni ut finis fateor non rarò dicitur vulgo quod voluntas fertur in eum finem vel in id bonum, an propriè et ut philosophicam decet ἀκρίβειαν tu Judices.
(English) Quanta sit vis consuetudinis in usu verborum quæ irrepit subinde nobis insciis patet ut mihi videtur in iis quæ in Epistolâ tuâ sequuntur. In priore Epistolâ†1 libens et apertè mecum consentire videris, quod actiones sunt Agentium sive Substantiarum, et
― 406 ―
non Potentiarum sive Facultatum: et tamen hic usitatâ loquendi formâ te abduci pateris, dicisque quod Voluntas est actionum nostrarum domina easque pro arbitrio moderatur†1 et similia passim in toto illo epistolæ tuæ paragrapho: Quod ni fecisses nulla arbitror tibi mecum lis esset. Hoc non dico quod adeo delicatulus sim ut hujusmodi loquendi formulas nullo in loco pati possim: Earum usus in sermone familiari, si rectè intelligantur, non omnino vituperandus. Quando vero in disceptationibus philosophicis pro fundamentis argumentorum, quasi iis inniteretur rerum veritas omnino rejiciendæ sunt metaphoricæ et tralatitiæ hujusmodi locutiones, ne nos in errorem inducant; resque ipsæ uti reverâ sunt propriis et non figuratis vocabulis exprimendæ. V.g. Dicere quod Voluntas sit actionum nostrarum domina easque pro arbitrio moderatur et inde <arguere>†a quod nisi Voluntas sit libera nulla erit in homine libertas, est, ut mihi videtur ex vi metaphoræ illius nos in errorem conjicere. Libertas apud me est potestas hominis agendi vel non agendi secundum suam voluntatem: scilicet si homo potest agere hoc, si vult agere hoc; et abstinere e contrà ab agendo hoc quando vult abstinere ab agendo hoc, eo in casu liber est homo. Hanc esse veram Libertatis notionem videtur mihi constare ex iis quæ a me
― 407 ―
dicta sunt §. 8. etc: Quæ si vera sit inde omnino sequitur Libertatem nullo modo competere Voluntati uti monstravi. §. 14. Imo inde sequitur, quod illa antecedens indifferentia ante decretum Voluntatis nullo modo, ut dixi,†1 pertinet ad quæstionem de Libertate. Si enim Libertas sit potentia agendi actionem quam homo vult, et vicissim abstinendi ab eadem actione si ab eâ homo vult abstinere quid facit rogo ista antecedens indifferentia ad Libertatem quæ est potentia agendi vel non agendi consequenter ad Voluntatis determinationem?
(English) Quandoquidem verò inciderit quæstio de istâ vestrâ antecedente Indifferentia cui vos omnem inniti Libertatem contenditis, de eâ liceat mihi paulo distinctius inquirere. Hæc Indifferentia definitur a te Vis animi qua positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis potest agere vel non agere.†2 Jam hic rogo, an intellectus judicium vel cogitatio sit unum ex requisitis ad agendum?
(English) 1° Si dicas quod intellectus judicium vel cogitatio sit unum ex requisitis ad agendum, Vestra Antecedens Indifferentia nunquam efficiet ut voluntas sit libera (quamvis eum in finem ut inde astrui possit Voluntatis libertas excogitata et introducta videtur) quia, ut dixi, aliquâ actione semel intellectui propositâ Voluntas non est in
― 408 ―
statu in quo potest agere vel non agere; (in quo, ut mihi videtur consistit libertas) necessario debet agere; nec potest abstinere ab agendo, i.e. a volendo actionem illam scilicet, vel illius <omissionem>.†a Imo verò Voluntas eo in statu non est indifferens ad alterutram partem oppositorum, nempe ad actionem propositam, vel ejus omissionem, quia determinatur a præcedente intellectûs judicio actionem illam vel ejus omissionem preferente
(English) 2° Si dicas quod intellectus judicium sive Cogitatio non sit unum ex requisitis ad agendum. Videas quæso, dum hominem hoc modo liberum reddere velis annon Agentem cæcum plane efficis? et ut liberum facias ab eo intellectum removes, sine quo nec esse, nec supponi potest Libertas ulla. Ad res enim cogitatione et intellectu destitutas nulla omnino attinet libertas. Perpende igitur quæso et tecum cogita an libertas hominis recte fundari potest in ejusmodi statu qui excludit cogitationem, redditque lapidem æquè capacem Libertatis? An illa Indifferentia pertinere potest ad quæstionem de Libertate, quæ sepositâ cogitatione nullum locum in subjecto relinquit Libertati
(English) Hæc omnia ita se habent ex meâ Libertatis notione, quam fusiùs traditam invenies. §. 8-13. Quod si tu aliam isti voci sensum tribuas
― 409 ―
forsan hæ omnes evanescent difficultates. Sed tunc rogandus es ut tuam Libertatis definitionem ad me mittas si de diversis rebus sub eodem nomine disserentes nollumus sine fructu disputare
(English) Ex his quæ supra dixi mihi constare videtur quod libertas nullatenus consistit in Indifferentia hominis, sed solummodo in potentia agendi vel non agendi prout volumus. Exemplo forsan res clarior erit. Homo v.g. amat vinum; Judicat sibi bonum esse; ex voluntate suâ bibit: Nulla hic Indifferentia est, et tamen libera prorsus est hæc actio, quia si modo mutaverit voluntatem potest abstinere. E Contrà homo vinum nec amat nec aversatur, nec judicat sibi bonum aut malum esse, supponamus quantamlibet hominis Indifferentiam: Ex voluntate abstinet a vino in carcere ubi vinum non permittitur. Hæc actio nempe abstinentia a potione vini est voluntaria fateor, sed non est libera: Quoniam homo ille si mutet voluntatem, vinum tamen eo in casu bibere non potest. Vides igitur quod Indifferentia potest esse sine Libertate, et Libertas sine Indifferentia, et actio Voluntaria sine utrâque. Hæc me res ipsæ per se planæ docere videntur. Imo vero res ipsæ melius forsan et simplicius nos docerent multa Si scholarum subtilitas in procudendis facultatibus, distinctionibus aliisque speciosis inventis mirè acuta non obduceret sæpe rebus in se claris operosam et doctam obscuritatem.
― 410 ―
(English) Dicis porrò quod Libertas consistit in potentia qua homo actionem Volendi potest determinare vel non determinare.†1 Si per actionem volendi determinare vel non determinare significas Velle aut non Velle. Libertas in eo consistere non potest: Quia aliquâ actione homini propositâ homo non potest abstinere a Volitione, debet necessario Velle aut actionem illam propositam, aut abstinentiam ab istâ actione. quantumvis levis et instantanea præcedat mentis cogitatio semper et necessario sequitur actus Volendi, quo actio proposita vel eligitur vel negligitur: et ita Voluntas præcedente cogitatione semper determinatur ad agendum: i.e. ad volendum scilicet existentiam vel non existentiam actionis propositæ. Quod si per potentiam qua homo actionem volendi potest determinare vel non determinare significas potentiam quicquid temerè volendi, vel sine præviâ cogitatione vel contra intellectus judicium, uti sequentia verba videntur innuere, ubi dicis, nisi determinatio Voluntatis sit libera, et loqueris de bruto impetu: Libertas in hujusmodi potentiâ non potest consistere. Quia ut dixi libertas supponit cogitationem. Ubi enim nulla est cogitatio nulla esse potest Libertas, uti fusius explicui §. 8 et 9. Porro libertas non potest consistere in potentia determinandi actionem volendi contra judicium intellectûs,†a quia homo non habet hujusmodi
― 411 ―
potentiam. Actio enim volendi hoc aut illud semper sequitur judicium intellectus, quo homo judicat pro hic et nunc hoc esse melius. Ex quo facile est intelligere, quid velim, cum dico, Ante ultimum judicium intellectûs homo non potest omnino se determinare. Hocque facile conciliare possis cum iis quæ citas ex § 47 de suspensione impletionis cujuscunque desiderii, si modo memineris quod ante unamquamque volitionem præcedit semper judicium aliquod intellectûs de re agendâ Judiciumque illud quod immediate præcedit volitionem sive actum volendi est eo in casu ultimum judicium intellectûs. Quod te in diversum abripuit mihi videtur hoc esse, nempe quod ultimum judicium intellectûs videris confundere cum maturo et recto judicio, si recte capio sensum istius sententiæ ubi hæc verba lego Intellectus post accuratum rationum examen judicaverit quid facere oporteat etc: Sed id non est ultimum judicium de quo ego loquor. Loquor ego de eo judicio quod in omni volitione immediatè præcedit Volitionem, quod revera est ultimum judicium sive bene expensum sit et matura deliberatione recoctum, sive extemporaneum et subito impetu enatum, et æquè voluntatem determinat, sive sit sive non sit rationi consentaneum
(English) Si meum sensum in his satis rectè et clarè exposui non apparebit credo tibi hæc relegenti tanta inter nos opinionum distantia,

Je sai que certaines gens font consister la Liberté dans une certaine indifference de l'homme, antecedente à la détermination de sa volonté. Je souhaiterois que ceux qui font tant de fonds sur cette indifference antecedente, comme ils parlent, nous eussent dit nettement si cette indifference qu'ils supposent, précede la pensée et le jugement de l'entendement aussi bien que le decret de la volonté; car il est bien mal-aisé de la placer entre ces deux termes, je veux dire immediatement après le jugement de l'entendement, et devant la détermination de la volonté, parce que la détermination de la volonté suit immediatement le jugement de l'entendement: et d'ailleurs, placer la liberté dans une indifference qui précede la pensée et le jugement de l'entendement, c'est, ce me semble, faire consister la liberté dans un état de ténebres où nous ne pouvons ni voir ni dire ce que c'est: c'est du moins la placer dans un sujet incapable de liberté, nul agent n'étant jugé capable de liberté
― 414 ―
qu'en consequence de la pensée, et du jugement qu'on reconnoit en luy. Comme je ne suis pas délicat en matiere d'expressions, je consens à dire avec ceux qui aiment à parler ainsi, que la liberté est placée dans l'Indifference; mais c'est dans une sorte d'indifference qui reste après le jugement de l'entendement, et même après la détermination de la volonté: ce qui n'est pas une indifference de l'homme (car après que l'homme a une fois jugé ce qu'il est meilleur de faire ou de ne pas faire, il n'est plus indifferent) mais une indifference des puissances actives ou operatives de l'homme, lesquelles demeurant tout autant capables d'agir ou de ne pas agir, après qu'avant le decret de la volonté, sont dans un état qu'on peut appeller, si l'on veut, indifference: et aussi loin que s'étend cette indifference, jusques-là l'homme est libre, et pas au delà. Par exemple, j'ay la puissance de mouvoir ma main, ou de la laisser en repos; cette faculté operative est indifferente au mouvement et au repos de ma main; je suis donc libre à cet egard. Ma volonté vient à déterminer cette puissance operative au repos, je suis encore libre, parce que l'indifference de cette puissance operative qui est en moy, d'agir ou de ne pas agir, reste encore; la puissance de mouvoir ma main n'étant nullement diminuée par la détermination de ma volonté, qui à present ordonne le repos; l'indifference de cette puissance à agir ou ne pas agir, est justement telle qu'elle étoit auparavant, comme il paroit si la volonté veut en faire l'epreuve en ordonnant le contraire. Mais si pendant que ma main est en repos, elle vient à être saisie d'une soudaine paralysie, l'indifference de cette puissance operative est détruite, et ma liberté avec elle: je n'ay plus de liberté à cet égard, mais je suis dans la nécessité de laisser ma main en repos. D'un autre côté si ma main est mise en mouvement par une convulsion, l'indifference de cette faculté operative s'évanouït; et en <ce>†a cas-là ma liberté est detruite; car je me trouve dans la nécessité de laisser mouvoir ma main. J'ai ajoûté ceci pour faire voir dans quelle sorte d'indifference il me paroit que la liberté consiste précisement, et qu'elle ne peut consister dans aucune autre, réelle ou imaginaire.
(Latin)
Oates 12 Aug 1701
Excellent Sir,
I suppose that you praise so highly those few services belonging to my goodwill towards your son that it has as yet been in my power to perform, rather in order to comply with your proclivity to gratitude than because you believe that I have satisfied myself or the claims of our friendship in what it has so far befallen me to do for his sake. You may be assured that I am ready for anything that can be to his advantage. If I can help him in any way with advice, substance(?), practical aid, or friendship, I shall not fail. I think that words are not needed to persuade you of this. We are agreed about our friendship; we ought therefore to proceed to those things about which we seem not to be entirely agreed.
(Latin) Just as much as you I think that all obscurity and ambiguity in the use of words are to avoided. But let me add that often they are not avoided even by those who wish to shun obscurity. The ideas that are present in the minds of men, especially of those who seek truth more heedfully, are many more than the words that are provided in any language to express them. Hence it happens that men, who are not at liberty to fashion new denominations at pleasure as often as there is need to signify new ideas, often use the [p. 402] same word for different ideas, especially if the ideas are akin; whence, when precise and accurate statements are to be made, there not rarely arise obscurity of language and uncertain meaning, in which the minds of not only the hearers, but also those of the speakers themselves are entangled. Among those remedies for this evil that I have proposed in bk. III, ch. xi, that seems to me the principal: namely, that we should diligently collect all the simple ideas that enter into the composition of any complex idea whose name we use, and carefully keep them in mind affixed to that same word. For example: In the argument that we have on hand, if 'Will' signifies the power that a man has to begin, to stop, or to forbear any action of his mind or body, as I have set forth at greater length in bk. II, ch. xxi, § 5, etc., in which you also appear to acquiesce: if, I say, this is the idea that the word 'Will' signifies, and if we have it present in mind when we speak of Will, nothing can be more certain than that Will terminates solely in our actions and cannot be further extended to anything alse or directed to a remote and absent good. And so, if you contend that Will is directed to a good as an end, you are receding from that idea that we have assigned to this word and substituting another, whence it results that you and I denote different things when we speak of Will, nor, when discussing Will with one another, can we make any progress at all until you make known the idea of which the word 'Will' is the sign for [p. 403] you, in order that we may agree about the sense of the word, that is, about the thing that we are discussing.
(Latin) The distinction that you bring forward of 'complete and incomplete Desire' or of 'complete and incomplete Will' seems to me not to help your argument in any way. For if there is any 'incomplete desire' or 'incomplete will', which I greatly doubt, that will never make it true that Will is directed to a good. I doubt, I say, whether there can be any 'incomplete Volition'; for, if I am not mistaken, 'Will' is here taken for an act of the Will, that is, for a Volition. I readily recognize ineffective volition, as when a paralytic wills to move his palsied hand; I grant that that volition is ineffective and without result, but not that it is 'incomplete'. For the act of willing is in this case just as complete as it was formerly when the hand complied with the volition. In the same way the desire of some proposed good, the pursuit of which we neglect because of a greater good that is incompatible with it, is not an 'incomplete desire' or an 'incomplete Will', but a complete desire quickly terminated, not proceeding so far as to impel us to willing the actions by which can be obtained that good to which that short-lived desire was directed; nor, where there is no volition at all, can 'will' be called 'incomplete', even if the schools like to call it Velleity. But if that short-lived desire proceeds so far as to rouse us to willing some action, that 'Will' is not [p. 405] 'incomplete', but is a complete act of willing even though, through the omission of further action, it is ineffective for obtaining the proposed good, which is neglected when the desire ceases. In these and similar actions of the mind the motions of the spirit are so swift and so connected with one another that it is not strange that, as happens, matters are often confused that, for one who considers them more heedfully, are to be distinguished in order that we should rightly form our concepts. You wish me to say freely what I think about this matter. A man is directed to an absent good or end. When many goods, not subordinate to, or consistent with, one another, are present to the understanding at the same time, a man, neglecting the others, proposes one to himself as an end, that is, as a thing to be pursued, this he does voluntarily and so far the will is directed to that action of the mind by which he proposes to himself one thing as an end in preference to the rest, and it terminates in that action in the same way as it terminates in computation when he wills to number or in movement of the feet when he wills to walk. I grant that, owing to this voluntary proposing of that good as an end, it is not infrequently said in every-day speech that the will is directed to that end or to that good, whether appropriately, and as befits philosophical precision, you can judge.
(Latin) How great is the force of custom in the use of words, which steals in from time to time while we are unawares, is manifest, it seems to me, in what follows in your letter. In your previous letter†1 you seem readily and [p. 405] unreservedly to agree with me that actions pertain to Agents or Substances, and not to Powers of Faculties; and yet here you suffer yourself to be led away by a common way of speaking, and say that 'the Will is master of our actions, and governs them according to its choice'†1 , and similar things here and there in that whole paragraph of your letter; if you had not done this I think that there would have been no dispute between us. I do not say this as being so fastidious as to be unable to suffer such expressions anywhere; their use in familiar speech, if they are rightly understood, is not altogether to be censured. When, however, metaphorical and figurative forms of expression of this kind are put forward in philosophical discussions for the foundation of arguments, as if the truth of things rested on them, they are to be altogether rejected lest they lead us into error; and the things themselves, as they are in reality, are to be represented by proper, and not figurative, denominations. For example: to say that 'the Will is master of our actions, and governs them according to its choice', and to argue thence that 'unless the Will is free there will not be any liberty in a man', is, it seems to me, to plunge us into error by the force of that metaphor. Liberty for me is the power of a man to act or not to act, according to his will: that is to say, if a man is able to do this if he wills to do it, and on the other hand to abstain from doing this when he wills to abstain from doing it: in that case a man is free. That this [p. 406] is the true notion of Liberty seems to me to be established by what I have said in § 8, etc.; and if it is the true notion it altogether follows thence that Liberty does not in any way appertain to the Will, as I have shown in § 14. Indeed it follows thence that that 'antecedent indifferency before the decree of the Will', as I have said,†1 does not pertain in any respect to the question of Liberty. For if Liberty is a power of performing an action that a man wills, and in turn of abstaining from that same action if he wills to abstain from it, what bearing, pray, has that antecedent indifferency on Liberty, which is a power to act or not to act consequently upon the determination of the Will?
(Latin) Since, however, there has arisen the question of that 'antecedent Indifferency' of your writers on which they contend that all Liberty rests, may I be permitted to inquire into it a little more precisely? This 'Indifferency' is defined by you as 'the energy of the spirit by which, when all requisites for acting are present, it can act or not act'.†2 Now I ask you whether the judgement of the understanding, or cogitation, is one of the 'requisites for acting'.
(Latin) 1. If you say that the judgement of the understanding or cogitation is one of the 'requisites for acting' your writers' 'Antecedent Indifferency' will never prove that the will is free (although it seems to have been devised and introduced to the end that the liberty of the Will can thence be established) because, as I have said, when any action has once been proposed to the understanding the Will is not in a state in which it can act or not act [p. 407] (in which, as it seems to me, liberty consists); it must needs act; nor can it abstain from acting, that is to say, from willing that action or its forbearance. But, what is more, the Will, when in that state, is not indifferent to one or other of opposites, namely to the proposed action or forbearance from it, because it is determined by the preference of the preceding judgement of the understanding for either that action or forbearance from it.
(Latin) 2. If you say that the judgement of the understanding, or cogitation, is not one of the 'requisites for acting'. Please consider whether, while you want in this way to make a man free, you are not simply making him a blind agent; and whether, in order to make him free, you are not taking away from him understanding, without which any sort of Liberty cannot exist or be supposed to exist. For liberty does not belong in any way whatsoever to things destitute of cogitation and understanding. Please, therefore, ponder and consider earnestly whether the liberty of a man can be properly founded in a state of such a kind as excludes cogitation and renders a stone equally capable of liberty; whether that Indifferency which, setting cogitation aside, leaves no place for liberty in the subject, can pertain to the question of Liberty.
(Latin) All this is in accordance with my notion of Liberty, which you will find set down more copiously in §§ 8-13. If you should attach another meaning to that word all these difficulties would perhaps vanish. But in that case I must ask you to send me your definition of Liberty if we do not [p. 408] want to argue without profit, discussing different things under the same name.
(Latin) From what I have said above it seems to me to be established that Liberty in no wise consists in the Indifferency of a man, but only in the power to act or not to act according as we will. An example will perhaps make the matter clearer. A man, for example, likes wine; he judges it to be good for him; of his own will he drinks: there is no Indifferency here, and yet this action is entirely free because if only he has changed his will he can abstain. On the other hand a man neither likes nor dislikes wine, nor does he judge it to be good or bad for him; let us suppose as much Indifferency in him as you please: of his own will he abstains from wine in a prison where wine is not allowed. I grant that this action, namely, abstaining from drinking wine, is voluntary, but not that it is free: since that man, if he changes his will, is yet in that case unable to drink wine. You see therefore that there can be Indifferency without Liberty, and Liberty without Indifferency, and Voluntary action without either. The things themselves, plain in themselves, seem to teach me this. But, what is more, the things themselves would teach us much, better, perhaps, and more simply, if the subtlety of the schools, wonderfully acute in fashioning faculties, distinctions, and other specious inventions, did not often spread a laborious and learned obscurity over things clear in themselves.
(Latin) You say further that 'Liberty consists in a power by which a man can [p. 409] determine, or not determine, an action of Willing'.†1 If by 'determine, or not determine, an action of willing' you signify to Will or not to Will, Liberty cannot consist in it; because, when any action has been proposed to a man, he cannot abstain from Volition; he must necessarily Will either that proposed action or abstention from it. However slight and momentary a cogitation of the mind may precede, there always and necessarily follows an act of Willing, by which the proposed action is either chosen or disregarded; and thus by a preceding cogitation the Will is always determined to acting: that is to say, to willing the existence or non-existence of the proposed action. But if by 'a power by which a man can determine, or not determine, an action of willing' you signify a power of willing anything unadvisedly, either without previous cogitation or contrary to the judgement of the understanding, as the following words seem to hint, where you say 'if the determination of the Will is not free' and speak of 'brute impulse': Liberty cannot consist in such a power because, as I have said, liberty presupposes cogitation. For where there is no cogitation there can be no Liberty, as I have set forth at greater length in §§ 8 and 9. Further, liberty cannot consist in a power of determining an action of willing contrary to the judgement of the understanding because a man does not possess such a power. For an action of willing this or that always follows a judgement of the understanding by which a man judges this to be better for here and now. From this it is [p. 410] easy to understand what I mean when I say, Before the last judgement of the understanding a man is altogether unable to determine himself. And you can easily reconcile this with what you quote from § 47 about the suspension of the fulfilment of any desire, if only you remember that every single volition is always preceded by some judgement of the understanding about the thing to be done, and that that judgement that immediately precedes the volition or act of willing is in that case the last judgement of the understanding. What has led you to a different [opinion] seems to me to be this: that you seem to confuse the last judgement of the understanding with mature and right judgement, if I rightly understand the meaning of that sentence in which I read these words: 'The understanding, after a careful examination of the reasons, has judged what ought to be done', etc. But that is not the last judgement of which I am speaking. I am speaking of that judgement which in every volition immediately precedes Volition; which is in reality the last judgement, whether it has been well pondered and recast by mature deliberation, or is extemporaneous and sprung from a sudden impulse; and equally determines the will, whether or not it is in accordance with reason.
(Latin) If I have set out my meaning rightly and clearly enough in this I think that when you read it again there will not appear to you so great a difference of opinions between us as you thought. I hold it for certain that, as we are [p. ] each of us sincerely seeking truth, we cannot disagree for long about things themselves, although our expressions sometimes seem to diverge. But it will be easy for us while thinking about things themselves to dispel the mists of phraseology from which usually arise all controversies between lovers of truth.
(Latin) Well—in a rather lengthy letter I have complied as best I could with your request for an exposition of my opinion. Please forgive me for having cited my book so often; I have done this for the sake of brevity, so as not to rewrite here in a letter what you would read better in the printed book.
(Latin) About the two translations: it is proper to warn you that, wherever you find them disagreeing with one another about my meaning, you should decide from the French. For the author read through the whole of it to me, and corrected it where I discovered that it strayed from my meaning.†1 As it happens, I have not yet read the Latin. Ill health and business affairs have not allowed me enough leisure. Good-bye and continue to love
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) After I had written the above it occurred to me that it would not be [p. 412] unsuitable if I inserted in my book something to elucidate the nature of the 'Indifferency' in which liberty consists for the sake of those who value 'Indifferency' so highly in this argument that they think that, if it is laid aside or omitted, nothing can be rightly or clearly established about liberty. Here then is what I think should be added to § 71. I wrote it in English; Mr. Coste has translated it into French, and so, if you approve, you can insert it in the French translation of my book.†1

Je me haste de vous escrire monsieur en arivant dItalie afin d'avoir plutost le plaisir de recevoir de vos nouvelles. il i a trois jours que jen suis de retour en bonne santé malgré les fatigues du voyage les quelles ont esté assez grandes a cause de la chaleur excessive quil a fait cette annee. jay trouvé touts mes amis en bonne santé particulierement monsieur Toinard qui ma paru rajeuni de plusieurs annees.

showed Toinard the letter shortly after he received it, either on 17/28 August or during the next two or three days. Hence the date 18/29 August or shortly afterwards for Toinard's letter. Answered by no. 3009.
Enfin†a mon procez a eté terminé. Il y a bien du gris melé dans le jugement. On ne m'a acordé que ceque l'on ne m'a pu ôter. Les honêtes gens de la chambre ont fait Ceque la justice leur inspiroit, mais la cabale devote a prevalu. Ele etoit apuiée des gens qui aiment le sac, et par tant atachéz au President de qui depend la distribution des procez. Je contois sur le Raporteur parcequ'il a une reputation d'homme de bien, et je l'avois demandé au President. c'etoit me confesser au Renard, et l'infidelité jointe à l'ignorance a paru dans un beau jour à mes depans. Il est vray que j'ay tort de n'avoir pas assez fait d'atention sur une chose que m'avoit autrefois dite un Cardinal Prelat qui a pour Grand Vicaire un Capitene de marine;†1 c'est qu'il aimoit les gens de bien, et qu'il n'aimoit point les devots. cependant on me fait des compliments sur le gain de mon procez, et je m'en defens pas, parceque ma grande afaire est de n'en point avoir. Je nesai neanmoins si celleci n'aura point de queüe, car quoique j'aye un bon Arest contre de certains garans et parans, il y a lieu d'aprehander qu'ils n'executent pas les choses ausqueles ils sont condannéz. ce qui m'a desolé dans la sollicitation de ce procez où lon ne ma rendu ni bonne ni brieve justice, c'est d'avoir eté privé du deplaisir de vous embrasser come je me l'etois proposé. Je serois pour cela parti au printems passé, ceque les conjonctures ne me permetront peutêtre pas l'année prochaine. J'avois fait dessin de passer de là en Holande, où par je nesai queles rencontres, j'ay fait plusieurs amis que je ne connois que par letres, sans conter M. Grævius, avec qui vous pouvez bien penser que j'aurois celebré votre santé. J'ay trop de chagrin de penser à la fatalité qui m'a privé des douceurs efectives que j'aurois goutées en vous embrassant puisque la seule pensée me donnoit tant de plaisir: mais paulò jucundiora canamus.†2 M. L'Abé du B. nous a tout nouvelement regalé de sa presence, et moy en particulier en me montrant hier des nouveles qu'il a receües de vous en date du 10/21. d'Aoust.†3 J'en aye ressenti une joie que je ne saurois vous
― 420 ―
exprimer par raport à linquietude que votre long silence m'avoit donée.
J'atens d'Holande le 3. vol. de Dampier en langage chretien. Il y a du tems que je say qu'il a perdu son vaisseau, et j'en suis faché pour son interest, mais celui des curieux, est qu'il ait sauvè ses memoires.†1
J'ay eté assez heureux pour conêtre otrefois ici m. Halley, qui m'a bien apris des choses curieuses de l'Ile de ste Helene.†2 Je n'ay pas u ocasion dentretenir commerce avec lui. Il a envoié à m. Cassini†3 une carte graveé de quelques terres Australes, dont je voudrois bien par votre moyen avoir un exemplaire, et la relation s'il y en a, quand meme ele seroit en Anglois.†4 Je suis en peine de savoir quelle declainaison il aura trouveé de l'Emant en ces endroits la. Vous avez ci joint des observations faites en 1698.†5 qui renversent les hypotheses, car vous y voiez que la declinaison qui selon narbroug†6 etoit de 17. D. NE. à l'orient du Detroit de magellan, y etoit de 19. en 1698. ce qui est contraire à cequi s'observe en Europe ou l'Eguille s'est premierement raprochée du Pole, et ensuite ele a passé à l'oüest. cequi est aussi surprenant contre le systeme de Tellure magno magnete,†7 est que l'Eguille marque l'Est aux deux entrées du Detroit de magellan selon Narbroug qui en donne une mechante raison selon la traduction que j'en ay fait faire.
Otre chose surprenante est que deux habiles navigateurs m'ont assurè qu'en alant à Baye d'Hudson ils n'avoient trouvé jusques vers le 63. Degré aucune inclination de lEguille sous l'Horison
― 421 ―
contre cequi est dans les Auteurs, et que nos Basques qui vont jusques au 80. D. et par dela m'ont dit avoir observé.
J'atens avec impatience des nouveles de votre santé, et suis—

2985. William Popple to Locke, 23 August 1701 (2971, 2999)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 255-6.

Sir,
This morning, just as I received your letter, Dr Paul came in to see us: So I shewed it to him: And he will answer your Desire so soon as possibly he can. But as it happens, he is not able to do it on the sudden. For he has been out of town (at St Giles's) this month or six weeks, and is but just newly returned, and consequently not acquainted, by any observations of his own; with the circumstances of what you enquire about. But he said he would visit some of the Doctors of his acquaintance, this day, or as soon as possible, and then write to you not barely what they say but his own sense upon the information he may get from them.†1
The next week we shall make some progress in the Exchequer towards our payment: It is possible we may receive, though I dare not too possitively flatter my self with those hopes. However, in order to forward the work I must now receive your bill upon Mr Churchill, which I have not yet touched. I am
Sir,
Your most obedient humble Servant
WILLIAM POPPLE.

2986. Dr. (later Sir) Hans Sloane to Locke, 23 August 1701 (2984, 3458)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 124-5. Answers nos. 2956 and 2984.
London Aug. 23. 1701.
Sir
I received Yours this day and for answer to it can only tell you that wee have two sorts of feavers now about town one intermitting the other continuall. The first sort are of no great danger but after bleeding and vomiting generally show themselves by a considerable calm or intermission in which the bark ought to be given. The other has remissions in the morning, great headachs, deliria, and has also some spotts and miliary†1 eruptions break out after a while. The pulse is not very much disordered. In the beginning of th<is>†a I likewise bleed and vomit, and besides lay on blisters and give Serpentaria Virginiana, allow plentifull drinking and if there be a fair intermission I try the bark not omitting any thing else that I would give were I sure it were what wee commonly call malignant. There are some feavers that I verily think are such as that it may be reasonable to suppose both kinds of feavers join'd. I have seen spotts and miliary eruptions with deliria and the worst symptoms cured by the bark and other med'cines used in malignant feavers. such a one was a feaver a son of Lord William Paulettes†2 is just recover'd of wherein he had eruptions out upon him for many days so thick as a pins head could not be sett between them and yet I gave him the bark and he is recovered. I thank you for Your letter and its enclosed concerning the Dutch cypherer. 'tis a singular story, and pleasd the Company at Gresham College†3 so well that they ordered you their thanks in an extraordinary manner. I dread the effects of the hott weather wee have had of late though I think people in the Country suffe<r more>†a by it then wee in town. I believe this may proceed from their being more abroad in the open air and wee more in the shade of our houses. I am very much
Your most obedient and most humble servant
HANS SLOANE

2987. Dr. Robert Pitt to Locke, 23 August 1701 (3006)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 162-3. Robert Pitt, 1653-1713; of Dorset origin; M.D., Oxford, 1682; fellow of the Royal College of Physicians 1687; Censor 1687 and 1702; physician to St. Bartholomew's Hospital 1698-1707: D.N.B.
The Royal College of Physicians was at this time engaged in conflict with the Society of Apothecaries. By its charter (1518) and by act of parliament (1523) the College was given control of the practice of medicine in London and 7 miles about. The apothecaries at that time were members of the Grocers' Company. While a few of them traded in drugs on a large scale many of them depended on the sick or injured who sought their aid; they could not claim fees for their services, but made their living by their charges for drugs and appliances. When they were established as a separate Society (1617) their charter empowered their freemen not only to keep shop and prepare medicines, but also to 'give, apply, or administer' them. The conflict between the two bodies turned on the apothecaries' determination to exercise this power.
The fellowship of the College was limited to 80 at this time; educational requirements for members and licentiates were high; the total number of members of all classes was 136 in 1695 and 111 in 1704 (from 1712 to 1764 it was usually below 100). The apothecaries were trained by apprenticeship (they were examined by the College); no figures are available for their number; the contemporary estimate of 1,000 for the London area (p. 522) may be exaggerated, but reflects the great disparity in numbers between them and the physicians.
Attempts to reach agreement between the two bodies had failed so far and, while there was need of greater provision for the sick poor, the establishment of the Dispensary (see below) was due in part to the desire of some fellows of the College to attack the Society; the chief threat was the College's decision to establish its own laboratory for the supply of medicine, and more generally to fix the price of medicines. The principal dispute was settled in 1704 by the decision of the house of lords in Rose's case, which 'recognized the right of the apothecaries ... to practise medicine in its full range from the most trivial cases to the gravest, while they continued to make up medicines and sell them': Cecil Wall, H. C. Cameron, and E. A. Underwood, A History of the Worshipful Society of the Apothecaries of London, vol. i, 1963 (cited below as Underwood, Apothecaries); Sir George (Norman) Clark, A History of the Royal College of Physicians of London, 1964-6. The Apothecaries' charter is printed in C. R. B. Barrett, The History of the Society of Apothecaries of London, 1905.
― 425 ―
Aug. 23. 1701
Sir
In St Bartholomews Hospital we have lost not one Patient in 80, the last year and half, of Feavers, by being only treated with few Medicines, given on the apparent opportunities of assisting the Despumation†1 of the blood, and waiting, till some other occasions offer'd of doing good. The Deliria, Phrensies went of, allowing time, as in the Paroxysm of an Ague. I have Patients of the same Feaver you describe. The Urine continuing high color'd, after the bilious Vomitings with Phlegm, shews, that that matter is to be seperated cheifly by the Liver, and the glands of the Stomach and bowels. I therefore keep 'em to an Alkali Powder, which easily opens the Pores, and moves to the Kidneys, adding some grains of Creme of Tartar, and a gr. or 2 sometimes of salt of Tartar. But, upon Fernels great observation,†2 which is own'd in part by all the other rational Physicians, that the blood separates the Febrile matter principally per sedes: and that of many others, that the Febres longæ are most securely shortned, by infusions of Rhubarb etca. I appoint an Infusion of Sena and Rhubarb in Aq. Cardui,†a leni calore, with a few gr. of a fixt salt, to be given, diebus alternis. The Infusions of the common bitters are usefull to support the stomach, open the Liver, and besides move a little to the bowells. If the matter be turgent†3 in the Stomach and primæ viæ, the Carduus Vomit seems to be necessary. I have not yet given the Infusion of the Barcke, tho I observ it offers at intermissions, which probably may be after a week of great Service. Sir, I shall receiv your Commands as a great Favour to
Your most humble servant
R PITT
Our Dispensery†4 is the only method, by which Honest, Innocent, and usefull Physick can be reviv'd.
Address: For Dr John Locke in Oates to be left with Mr Harrison at the Crown in Harlow Essex
Postmarks: AV 23; London Penny Post: B SAT
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Pitt 23 Aug. 01 Answered Sept. 22

2991. Dr. [Louis?] Paul to Locke, 30 August 1701 (1449)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 208-9. For the antecedent of this letter see p. 422.
Sir
I was just come from the countrey where I had continued for a good while, when you was pleased to desire me in one of your letters to Mr Popple to give you an account of the methode, which I had found to be the most effectual in the feaver that now reighnes. Having thus been absent from that litle buisiness I have in town, I thought myself hardly fit to satisfye your curiosity and put of giving you an answer in hope to pick amongst other men's observations something to helpe my oun, and to answer in some measure your expectation, and your favourable opinion of me, but I find I have both failed in not being punctual, and missed the advantage I expected to get by it, yet in case that litle I have to say does not satisfye you I hope the good will may.
Most of the feavers I have seen or heard of for a good while, were of the inflammatory kind, apte to affecte the troath and sometimes the longs. their first violence hath been often blunted by bleeding. the sweats to which the patients were for the most part inclined, were gently promoted by supplying them with convenient liquor, whilst the stomack was defended from being clagged by it. we have sometimes used for that purpose the roots of Petasites, which they call butter burr either in posset or in decoctions.
― 430 ―
sleeping medecins given in a moderate dose and at proper times, used to favour that evacuation without any inconveniency excepte the body had wanted to have been cleaned before with a gentle vomite or some other proper medecine. when we have met with ill symptoms of the brain and nerves, or have had reason to fear them, we have used the blistering plasters as t'is usual. sometimes it happened that a kind of intermitting feaver joined with the continual, and conceal'd by it, went on unminded and made the distemper prove stubborn, but when it hath been happily discover'd or guessed at, the barke moderately given without neglecting other medecines hath been a great helpe to the cure, we have met also with very crude waters which seemed to threaten us with a very long distemper, and yet it often proved short. You see Sir that there is nothing here new to you, and that a litle time can show you more then you can heare from others, but I see you are unwilling to trust to guesses although never so sharp as long as you can go by experience. I wish Sir you should know the same way the great esteem I have for you and how truely I am Sir
Your most obedient and humble servant
PAUL
London. August the 30th. 1701.

2992. John Patrick to Locke, [c. 1 September 1701] (3002)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 200-1. The date from Locke's endorsement.
The writer (fl. 1686-1720) was one of the leading English makers of barometers at this time and was called 'the Torricellian Operator'. His shop was in Ship Court to the west of the Old Bailey: N. Goodison, English Barometers 1680-1860, 1969, pp. 178-93, 33-7.
Mr Locke
Sir
The Duke of Sumersitt†1 haveing beCome my Costomer and has Baught a diagonal†2 and a Pendent Barometer of me and he is
― 431 ―
mighttily pleased with there performance after he had the Tryall of them he was pleased To Aske me maney questiones about them which I Answred According to Experriment he seamed to be very well pleased with my discorce which was above An hour and said It was a pitty but it was followed and Carryed On. I told him the Charge was to great for me to persue the Torricillion Experriment†1 at my one Cost to Improve it further then I have done for I sattisfied him I Could if I had a Soport to Carry it on he said he wood see what Could be done in it and he said he wood doe all that he Could by sum meanes or other to promote me or searve me for the Carrying it on further, Sir I have bin thinking if you would be soe kind to be my frend to the Earle of Pembroke to Git him to Joyne with the Duke in this good Intent of his, and if they take it in to Consideration too gather I dout not but they will Accomplesh it by sum meanes or other, and I shall ever be bound to pray and ever think my selfe Idebted to you for the truble and will Studey how to Retalliate your favor, I am your Reall And Fath Full Sarvant To Command
JOHN PATRICK
I have bin very bissy of late but will Git your pendent Barometer done the furst Oppertunity I have.

3002. John Patrick to Locke, 16 September 1701 (2992, 3037)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 202-3.

Sir
I Receved your kind letter and the InClosed for which I Return you hartty thankes for the truble I have given you, and I will deliver it to the President†1 As soon as he Comes too Town, which will be a bout a fortnight hence.
To find the degrees of the Thermoeter In winter sum years a goe I tooke sum snow and salte and I berryed the globe balls of 2 thermoeters one fild with spirritt of wine the other with watter and when I perceved the watter Just to shut or frez I then marked the spirritt glass too which it sunk that was the place for Just freezing which agrees with the o upon your glass and Mr hunts†2 o and is 65 upon the scale of that glass I sent to you then my Inquierry was to know how hy the spirritt wood Rise under the line haveing sent severall abroad and haveing An Accompt from severall hands and Comparing them to gather I found they differd About 3 or 4 degrees but I took the largest Exstent which is o at tope then haveing An Accompt from a frend of mine how went a whale fishing and he saled soe far into the Ice till he gote in to 81 at green land and was there about 5 or 6 weekes he marked the lowest degrees it fell to upon the fraim then from o to Just freezing I devied in to 7 Eaquall Partes and 3 of the same Eaquall partes lower then subdevied them
― 440 ―
in to 10 Eaqual partes agin then found by Observation that the Air was at Eaqualliberam at 45 Nither to hott nor to Cold soe that at the pole it will be at bottom, and under the Equator it will be at tope, soe be pleased to Except of this my industtry till I Can be in form of a better or Meate with InCoredgment to inquier further. Sir my Room being west†1 the hotest part of the day is betwen 3 and 4 a Clock soe that it standes hyer by 3 or 4 degrees with me then at 12 a Clock or at sun sett. I keep my Jornoll at 6 In the morning at 12 and at Sun Sett
June the 30 was the hottest day in that Month it Ris to 13 degrees
July the 17 was the hottest day in that Month it Ris to 12 degrees
August the 20 was the hottest day in that Month it Ris to 10 degrees
September the 6 it Ris to 28 which was the hottest day in this part of the month
Mr Winn†2 maid your Thermoeter but by what standard I know not which is all at present from your Reall Servant To Command

3006. Dr. Robert Pitt to Locke, 27 September 1701 (2987, 3016)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 164-5.
Sept 27. 1701.
Sir
I rec'd your letter yesterday, which I perceiv is dated the 22d. I hope, you may be more easy, after you have diverted the humour, which now falls on your Legs: and will allways hold that Course, unless directed to an evacuation some other way. I presume it can be no prejudice to your Lungs, if it shall be gently remov'd by very gentle purgation, with Pil. Ruff. or such like. To repel without evacuation is dangerous: and feeble Lungs cannot bear any vehement operation of purging. But both may be us'd to advantage,
― 444 ―
if the necessary cautions are observ'd. You may at <least>†a abate the trouble, which that humour gives you, and by applying Diachylon or Melilote soon dispose the swelling to an easy digestion. I write now in haste, that I might not loose this Post. When my Cou. Freke†1 and I shall have Consulted on your Case, I will more particularly offer my opinion to you, and gain the opportunity of subscribing my self
Your most humble and affectionate servant
ROB. PITT.
Address: For Mr John Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: SE 27

3009. Locke to Nicolas Toinard, 30 September 1701 (2983, 3019)
B.M., Add. MSS. 28,836, ff. 15-17 (the letter) and 28,728, f. 11 (the enclosure). The letter is a copy, made about 1871 by a French transcriber; the owner of the original not stated; printed in Ollion, pp. 146-8. The enclosure is an original; the notes for it that Locke made on no. 2983 show that it belongs here. Answers no. 2983; answered by no. 3019.
Oates, 30 Sept 01.
Combien du temps la dernière lettre dont vous m'avez honoré étoit en chemin je ne puis pas dire précisément faute de date mais je puis vous assuré que l'aiant reçue il y a quelque temps je n'aurois pas tardé si long temps de vous en remercier si j'aurois pu plûtôt recevoir de Londres une réponse a deux ou trois lettres que j'ecrivis pour être pleinment informé touchant la carte de Monsieur Halley dont on m'assura qu'on n'en trouva pas à vendre dans les boutiques. Enfin on a trouvé que la planche ou il a fit graver la carte, il a gardée lui même ayant fait tirer autant des exemplaires qu'il destinoit pour présents à ses amis et point d'avantage. Monsieur Haly est présentement en mer aussi tost qu'il sera de retour je tâcherai d'en obtenir un exemplaire que je vous enverrai par la première occasion et la relation s'il y en a.†1 A l'occasion des variations observées en 1698 que vous m'avez envoiées j'ay parcouru le voiage de Narbrough en 1669 sur la même route. vous avez ci-joint ses observations des variations observées dans son voiage au détroit de Magelan. Sur quoy permettez-moy s'il vous plait de remarquer que la variation sur la côte orientale de la terre des Patagons en 1669 alloit en diminuant vers le Sud tout contraire à ce qu'elle faisoit en 1698. Hormis que en 1698 au dela du 47 D. deminuet et en 1669 à 52 ad 53 D. et augmenta. Ad hoc Œdipum expectus. Ego vero Davus sum.†2 En verité la variation de l'eguille est pour moy une grande mystere, mais si vous voulez je le proposerai à la Société Royale pour en tirer quelque éclaircissement. Le dernier siécle a été fort heureux en bien des découvertes. mais l'observation de ce changement de la direction magnétique dans la terre n'a pas été à ce que je m'imagine ni assez long temps ni assez universel pour en établir une parfaite histoire sur quoy fonder une hypothese
― 447 ―
assurée. Elle seroit je l'avoue de grand usage, mais l'utilité qui donne de l'empressement ne fournit pas toujours des lumières.
Je suis fort aise que votre procez est enfin terminé et j'espère qu'il n'aura point de queue. Le chagrin qu'il vous a donné et le domage qu'il ma deja fait en vous détournant de votre voyage designé a augmenté ma haine naturelle contre les procez. Dieu vous en garde pour l'avenir et vous donne l'occasion d'executer votre bonne volunté et de me rendre encore une fois heureux en vous embrassant. Venez donc animæ dimidium <meæ>†a †1 vous serois ici comme chez vous nous parlons françois touts qui nous sommes dans la maison et chasque un et impatient de vous voir pour quoi attendrez le printemps. Vous serez icy a votre aise en repos pendant le mauvais temps de l'hyver. Cela vous exemtera de la pein de m'ecrire votre jugement de mon essay ce que j'ay attendu de vous avec quelque sorte d'impatience pour corriger les fautes que vous y trouverez. Je me reglerai sur vos aviz que votre amitié auroit déjà m'accordez si votre maudit procez vous auroit laissez de moments à perdre en des bagatelles de ma façon
Je vous prie de faire mes tres humbles et tres affectiones baises mains à Monsieur l'Abé du B—†2 Je lui suis infiniment obligé de l'honeur qu'il me fit en me donnant des nouvelles de son retour en santé à Paris aprèz une si long et penible voiage dans le fort de l'Eté j'en etois fort ravi et je temoinerais ma reconnaissance par la premiere occasion
J'attend toujours de vous un petit mot musical mais dans votre dernière point dharmonie, cela me désole.
Je suis avec une ardeur sincere
Monsieur
votre tres humble et très obeissant serviteur
J.LOCKE
