3010. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 3/14 October 1701 (2979, 3043)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 147-8. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, ff. 190-3, dated 11 October (N.S.). Printed from the copy, with date 11 October, N.S., in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 504-20. There are small variations in the Amsterdam version. The difference in date may be due to the length of the letter. Answers no. 2979; answered by no. 3043.
Van Limborch discusses the will in Theologia Christiana, II. xxiii (pp. 126-30).
(English) Vir Amplissime
Quod tantum meâ causâ laborem susceperis, ut prolixiori epistolâ sententiam tuam distinctius mihi explicare non fueris gravatus, maximas tibi habeo gratias. Legi, relegi, expendi epistolam tuam magnâ cum attentione. Quantò exactius eam expendo, tantò magis observare videor, nos non†a tam sententiis, quam phrasibus ac loquendi modis discrepare, et quandoque diversas ideas iisdem, nonnunquam easdem ideas diversis vocibus designare. Respondissem citius; verum consultò responsum distuli, donec integrum tuum tractatum perlegissem. Eo jam perlecto, et cum epistolâ tuâ collato, magis magisque observare videor, omnem qui inter nos
― 449 ―
apparet dissensum, non tam circa rem ipsam, quam circa voces, ac diversam ejusdem rei explicandæ rationem versari. Quia verò non ubique phrasium mearum sensum rectè percepisse videris, et ut, quicquid fortasse adhuc inter nos restat dissensus, paucis et in compendio comprehendi possit, primò sensum vocum ac phrasium, quibus usus sum, quantâ possum perspicuitate explicabo: Deinde, phrasibus claris et ambiguitati non obnoxiis sententiam meam, quantâ possum brevitate, exponam. Tandem inquiram, in quibus consentiamus, et quis adhuc remaneat dissensus; utrumne ille in re ipsâ, an verò in vocibus ac phrasibus, et diversâ rem quam inquirimus explicandi ratione consistat. Ita puto, si fortasse nondum per omnia idem sentiamus, brevi omnem dissensum sublatum iri, nec veritatem sincerè eam quærentibus diu absconditam fore.
(English) Significationem voluntatis, quod sit potentia quam homo habet incipiendi, sistendi, vel vitandi aliquam actionem mentis vel corporis, ego tecum agnosco, et ab eâ non recedam: à voluntate etiam distinguo desiderium quo ferimur in bonum absens; neque id unquam sub notione voluntatis comprehendam. Agnosco hic me minus exactè locutum, et desiderium à voluntate esse distinguendum. Quod dixi, voluntatem etiam ferri in finem, nihil aliud volui, nisi quod tu ipse in epistolâ tuâ dicis: Multis simul intellectui obversantibus
― 450 ―
bonis non subordinatis nec consistentibus, hominem unum neglectis aliis sibi proponere ut finem, et ut prosequendum: hoc facit voluntariè. Hæc ergo electio est actio voluntatis: Quando hanc sibi electionem fecit homo, desiderio suo fertur in bonum illud quod sibi elegit; et voluntate suà dirigit actiones suas, quibus se bonum desideratum consecuturum sperat.
(English) Vox Libertas mihi designat dominium quod homo habet in actionem suam.†a Qui non est actionis suæ dominus, seu, agere non potest quod vult, non est liber. Verum ego puto hoc ad omnes hominis actiones sine ullâ exceptione extendi, tam ad internas actiones mentis, quam externas corporis, adeo ut etiam actio volendi, quæ est interna mentis actio, sit libera. Quando autem dixi, voluntatem esse actionum nostrarum dominam, nihil aliud volui, nisi, actiones nostras externas dirigi à volitione nostrâ, adeo ut faciamus quæ volumus, et non faciamus quæ nolumus; nisi intercedat cohibitio, aut coactio.†1 Utraque enim illa libertatem destruit. Semel declaravi, credere me animam seu mentem immediatè, absque ullis intermediis facultatibus, intelligere et velle.†2
― 451 ―
Per intellectum itaque et voluntatem, quotiescunque iis vocibus utor, aliud non intelligo, nisi potentiam seu facultatem ipsius animæ, quâ actionem intelligendi et volendi elicit, et quam actionem anima immediatè exercet. Et hanc significationem te etiam admittere puto.
(English) Superest ut dicam de Indifferentià. De quâ primò præmoneo, eam non esse nostram, uti tu credis; id est, à nobis inventam, aut ita à nobis adscitam, ut pro eâ, tanquam necessariò in hac quæstione usurpandâ, contendamus. Nihil minus. Nos diu illâ voce usi non fuimus: Libertatem definientes, eam ordinariè vocavimus dominium quod homo in actionem suam habet. In disputatione autem contra illos Theologos, qui Intellectum et Voluntatem statuunt duas esse facultates realiter ab animâ et à se invicem distinctas, quarum una tantum intelligit, nihil autem vult, altera tantum vult, nihil autem intelligit, hanc illorum sententiam hoc argumento oppugnavimus: Quod per eam aut omnis libertas tollatur, aut omnis actio hominis reddatur bruta ac irrationalis. Aut enim voluntas determinatur ab intellectu, adeo ut necessariò velit quod intellectus illi præscribit: atqui tum omnis actio necessaria est: quia omnis actio intellectus est necessaria: Aut non determinatur ab intellectu, sed seipsam determinat: Atqui tum omnis actio voluntatis est irrationalis ac bruta, quia supponitur voluntatem
― 452 ―
nihil intelligere, sed solummodo velle.†1 Hujus argumenti ictum ut evitent, <responderunt radicem libertatis esse in intellectu>;†a quia in intellectu <est>†a indifferentia, quâ potest quodcunque objectum quod sibi offertur apprehendere ac dijudicare.†2 Responderunt nostri, eam esse tantum indifferentiam passivam,†3 qualis est in oculo, qui etiam quævis objecta sibi occurrentia potest videre, eorumque imagines recipere; quem tamen propterea nemo dixerit liberè videre; quia non potest quin quod sibi videndum proponitur videat: sicut non potest intellectus quin quod clarè sibi proponitur apprehendat;†b aut dubitet de eo, pro quo utrimque æquè graves militant rationes. Si vero libertas quæratur in indifferentiâ, oportere eam esse activam, quâ homo dominium habet in suam actionem. Exinde, quoniam alii vocem Indifferentiæ adhibuerunt, nos, ut omnem in disputando ambiguitatem vitaremus, distinctionis causà addidimus vocem activæ, diximusque libertatem consistere in Indifferentiâ activâ, eamque residere in voluntate.†4 Vides ergo, nos non pro hac voce velle decertare, nec eam à nobis esse excogitatam; sed nos vocem ab aliis usurpatam explicuisse, et additione vocis activa significationem illius explanatiorem reddidisse.
― 453 ―
Interim non nego, nos postea quandoque etiam illâ in scriptis nostris esse usos, quia juxta explicationem nostram accepta commodissima visa fuit, et idem significare cum phrasi antea à nobis usurpatâ, dominium in actiones nostras. Idque etiam constat ex definitione hujus Indifferentiæ, quam in præcedente meâ epistolâ dedi; quod sit vis illa animi, quà positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis potest agere, vel non agere: quod mihi aliud nihil est, quam quod homo dominium habet in actionem suam, ut possit, prout ipsi placuerit, vel agere, vel non agere. Itaque inter omnia ad agendum requisita vel maximè colloco intellectus judicium, quod præcedere debet; alias volendi actio merè esset irrationalis. Quando autem dico, quod possit agere et non agere, mens <mea>†a non est, quod simul possit agere et non agere; aut, nec agere nec non agere, seu, nec velle nec non velle: hoc enim contradictorium est: sed quod potentia ad neutrum sit determinata, ac proinde ex duobus oppositis possit eligere quodcunque ipsi lubitum fuerit; imò ubi jam se determinavit ad agendum, quod actionem suam sistere possit, et se rursus in partem oppositam determinare: hoc est, quod dominium habet in suam actionem. Ubi hoc non habet homo, non est liber. Sic rectè mones, eum qui volens in carcere à vino abstinet, non libere abstinere, quia non habet facultatem vinum bibendi;
― 454 ―
nec qui volens in carcere manet liberè manere, quia non habet facultatem exeundi. Sed vero alia est ratio actionum internarum, quæ solâ mente perficiuntur: Ad illarum libertatem nihil requiritur, nisi libera determinatio voluntatis. Sic qui in carcere concupiscit alterius uxorem, eamque turpem concupiscentiam in animo fovet, eâque se oblectat, liberè concupiscit, et peccat, licet ea concupiscentia intra solam delectationem morosam,†1 uti Scholastici loquuntur, consistat; ideoque ad ejus consummationem ipse externus adulterii actus non requiritur.
(English) Per brutum impetum non intelligo actionem voluntatis sine ullâ præcedente cogitatione: sic conciperem non hominem; sed præcipitatam actionem, ante debitum et accuratum illius examen: sicuti videmus multos homines vehementi affectu sæpe abripi ut hoc aut illud agere velint, antequam omnes actionis circumstantias, rationesque ac argumenta quibus ad eam incitari, aut ab eâ deterreri possint, ritè consideraverint. Hanc ego†a tribuo libertatem homini, ut quando actio ipsi proposita est, possit vel præcipitare judicium, vel mature omnes actionis circumstantias examinare, atque ita vel bruto impetu, vel prævio maturo ac deliberato consilio agere: ejusque libertatis unumquemque sibi esse conscium credo.
― 455 ―
(English) Nec hoc omittendum, per Indifferentiam me non intelligere statum, in quo homo quasi in æquilibrio est constitutus, nec in unam partem magis propendet quam in alteram: talis enim status indifferentiæ circa actiones morales in nullo homine reperitur: semper in unam partem magis propendemus quam in alteram, in actionibus præsertim moralibus, prout vel affectibus agimur, aut consuetudo ac habitus nos erga virtutem aut vitia proniores reddidit: sed statum, in quo homo potentiam habet se determinandi in quamcunque oppositorum partem velit: licet enim magis sit propensus in unam partem, quam in alteram; non tamen dominium in actionem suam amisit, sed in alteram etiam partem se determinare potest. Verum quia vox Indifferentiæ accipi potest pro statu, quo homo in neutram partem inclinat, sed planè in æquilibrio est constitutus, licet ille sensus directe explicationi nostræ adversetur, ad omnem vitandam amphibologiam à voce illâ abstinebo.
(English) Ultimum intellectus judicium ego non confundo cum maturo et recto judicio: sed ibi distinguo ultimum judicium, quod sit vel maturum et rectum, vel pravum et præcipitatum, quod ibi vocavi brutum impetum, quia illud magis sequitur vehementem concupiscentiam carnalem, quam ductum rationis. Utrumque est ultimum judicium, quando immediatè actionem volendi antecedit, et inter illud actionemque volendi nullum aliud judicium intermedium est.
― 456 ―
(English) Ita explicatis terminis quibus usus sum, jam quantâ possum brevitate et perspicuitate sententiam meam proponam. Eam his thesibus comprehendo.
(English) 1. Homo est agens liberum, et habet dominium in actiones suas, illas vel faciendi, vel omittendi.
2. Intellectus et Voluntas non sunt duæ facultates realiter ab animâ hominis et à se invicem distinctæ, sed anima per suam essentiam immediatè intelligit et vult.
3. Homo nihil vult aut facit nisi desiderio boni, aut sensu molestiæ ex absentiâ boni desiderati excitatus.
4. Actum volendi antecedit actus intelligendi, quo homo judicium fert de actione suâ.
5. Judicium illud vel est prudens post adhibitum maturum rationum ab utraque parte militantium examen; vel est præcipitatum, et ab affectu magis quam ratione dictatum.
6. Judicium hoc, <quatenus>†a est merus intelligendi actus, non procedit ultra suasionem, hoc est eligibile, seu, hoc consentaneum est eligere; hoc consentaneum est rejicere: aut; inter <eligibilia hoc>†a magis hoc <minus est eligibile; inter>†a fugienda, hoc magis hoc minus oportet fugere.
― 457 ―
(English) 7. Judicium, quo homo decernit hoc est faciendum, est ipsa volitio, vel ad minimum actus mixtus ex intellectione†1 et volitione, et ad cujus consummationem actus volendi concurrit.
8. Actus intelligendi, quatenus merus intelligendi actus est, est necessarius, et nititur momento rationum ab homine perceptarum.
9. Actus volendi liber est, habetque homo dominium in illum, ac facultatem eum vel eliciendi, vel non eliciendi. Si quæ ergo libertas in judicio est, ea procedit non ab actu intelligendi, sed volendi.
10. Actionum internarum, quæ solâ mente perficiuntur, libertas consistit in liberâ mentis determinatione, quâ actionem volendi vel elicere potest, vel cohibere. Ad libertatem vero actionum externarum, ad quarum consummationem concurrere debent membra externa, etiam requiritur, ut homo habeat facultatem sive potentiam faciendi quod vult, et omittendi, seu non faciendi quod non vult: sive, liberum et non impeditum membrorum externorum usum.
(English) Ita paucis explicatâ sententiâ meâ, videamus nunc in quibus conveniamus, et quis inter nos supersit dissensus. Quando epistolam tuam confero cum lib.II.cap.XXI. de potentiâ, videor mihi posse dicere, nos in quinque primis thesibus convenire, nec de iis ullum
― 458 ―
inter nos esse dissensum. De ultimâ etiam nulla est inter nos controversia, nisi forte quod tu libertatem in solâ potentiâ faciendi quod volumus, et non faciendi quod nolumus collocare videris; cum ego eam etiam ad ipsius voluntatis determinationem, seu volitionis actum, extendam. De quo mox. Utroque etiam pollice amplector,†1 quod in epistolâ tuâ scribis: Quod homo fertur in bonum absens, sive finem; et quod multis simul intellectui obversantibus bonis non subordinatis nec consistentibus, homo unum neglectis aliis sibi proponit ut finem, id est, ut prosequendum: et hoc facit voluntariè: ideoque voluntas fertur in illam actionem mentis quâ unum præ reliquis sibi proponit ut finem: et in eâ actione terminatur. Eam autem voluntatis actionem sequitur desiderium finis. Hactenus ergo consentimus. Videamus quousque in reliquis consentiamus, et quis supersit dissensus.
(English) Primò, non videmur consentire in definitione libertatis. Sic enim dicis: Libertas apud me est potestas hominis agendi vel non agendi secundum suam voluntatem. Quæ definitio mihi angusta nimis esse videtur: et si ea agnoscatur, tum certum est, libertatem nullo modo competere voluntati: sicut certum est, animam nunquam esse posse sine
― 459 ―
cogitatione, si vera sit definitio, anima est cogitatio.†1 Imo si hæc genuina sit definitio libertatis, fieri posset ut libertas consisteret cum summâ necessitate, ut mox ostendam. Ego autem puto, libertatem esse dominium quod homo habet in quamcunque suam actionem, eamque extendi non tantum ad actiones quas facit secundum suam voluntatem, sed et ad ipsum volendi actum, seu volitionem.
(English) Quod sextam et septimam thesin attinet, nescio quousque in illis conveniamus,†a aut quis de illis inter nos sit dissensus. In postremâ meâ epistolâ idem jam affirmavi: Verum tu nullam in tuâ epistolâ illius mentionem facis: itaque incertus sum, quousque hic mecum sentias. Mihi evidens videtur, hominem judicium suum determinare, quia vult acquiescere rationibus quas expendit: suspendere autem judicium suum, quia nondum vult acquiescere; sed rationes aut exactius expendere, aut, an sint plures quibus judicium ejus inclinari†b possit inquirere: Atque ita determinationem ultimi judicii, quo homo decernit, hoc est eligendum aut faciendum, si non totam, maximam saltem partem esse actionem volendi.
― 460 ―
(English) Octava thesis, quâ statuo, omnem actum intellectus, quatenus merus intelligendi actus est, esse necessarium, nescio an inter nos controversa sit. Illam enim expressè asserere videris lib. IV. cap. XIII. § 2. et cap.XX. § 16. At ea distinctius paulum explicanda est, ut pateat, an aliquis de eâ sit dissensus. Hic ego observo, quod res, quas intellectus percipit, sunt vel merè theoreticæ, vel practicæ.†1 Circa veritates theoreticas actio intellectus necessaria prorsus est: propositâ veritate clarâ et evidenti, intellectus necessariò assentitur, seu homo necessario eam percipit, illique assensum præbet: Propositis argumentis verisimilibus tantum, homo necessariò opinatur: propositis utrimque argumentis æqualis ponderis, homo, seu intellectus, necessariò dubitat. Omnesque hæ intelligendi actiones nituntur momento rationum ab homine perceptarum. Circa veritates practicas actio intelligendi, quatenus mera intelligendi actio est, et nulla intercedit actio volendi, etiam necessaria est: pro rationum enim momento quas intellectus expendit, judicat quid convenientius, quid minus conveniens, quid ex usu sit facere, vel non facere. Hoc judicium ducit quidem voluntatem, sed eam non plenè determinat: est enim illud imperium tantum suasionis, cui voluntas potest non obtemperare, seu, homo potest
― 461 ―
aliud velle: Determinatio autem procedit à voluntate, quâ homo decernit, hoc est faciendum. Eaque determinatio fit, vel juxta suasionem intellectus, et tunc est rationalis: vel fieri potest contra eam; et tunc est irrationalis, hoc est, procedit ab affectu carnali, et suasioni intellectus neutiquam auscultat. Vel etiam potest esse præceps et temeraria, ita ut maturum judicium antevertat. Hic videmur dissentire: Dicis enim, hominem non habere potentiam determinandi actionem volendi contra judicium intellectus: Actio enim volendi hoc aut illud semper sequitur judicium intellectus, quo homo judicat pro hic et nunc hoc esse melius. Idem etiam affirmare videris in fine § 71. cap.XXI. Sed tamen quando hæc confero cum definitione voluntatis in tuâ epistolâ, quod sit potentia quam homo habet incipiendi, sistendi, vel vitandi aliquam actionem mentis vel corporis: et cum cap.XXI. § 47. et aliquot anteced. et seqq. dubito an multum dissentiamus, et an non magis diversitas sit in modo explicandi, quam in re ipsâ. Omnino enim mihi illic agnoscere videris libertatem quandam in judicando. Dicis enim illic, liberum esse menti appetitionum suarum objecta considerare, eas introspicere penitus, et utrum præponderet trutinâ diligenter examinare. In hoc libertas hominis consistit: et quæ ibi porro egregia habes. Addis mox: indultam nobis potestatem voluntatem
― 462 ―
revocandi à prosecutione <hujus>†a aut istius appetitionis. Hic mihi videtur fons esse omnis libertatis:†1 etc. Ex iis enim <liquere>†a videtur, libertatem etiam versari in judicio formando, imo ibi esse libertatis fontem. Unde colligo, libertatem (juxta tuam explicationem) non solummodò consistere in potentiâ faciendi quod volumus; sed etiam ante volitionis actum, imò ante judicium de actione suâ hominem esse liberum, et libertatem suam exercere. Solummodò discrimen inter nos esset, an judicium ultimum quo decernitur, non, hoc convenit facere; sed, hoc est faciendum, sit actio intelligendi mera; an verò ad id etiam concurrat actio volendi? et, an libertas resideat in actione intelligendi, an volendi? seu, an id quod in judicio, quo hominis actio determinatur, liberum est, resideat in intellectione, an volitione? Si in eo consistat discrimen, puto facile sententias nostras conciliari posse. Quamvis enim mihi perspicuum videatur, libertatem residere in actione volendi, nihilque esse liberum, quin sit etiam voluntarium; non tamen hic tantoperè videmur posse dissentire, quin facile ad consensum reducamur. Cum enim uterque statuamus, intellectum et voluntatem non esse duas potentias realiter ab animâ et à se invicem distinctas; sed hominem, seu animam, immediatè per suam essentiam intelligere et velle; satis
― 463 ―
convenimus, quando uterque agnoscimus, judicium hominis ultimum liberè determinari; Quando enim adest potentia faciendi quod ultimum illud judicium libere à nobis determinatum dictat, et non faciendi, seu omittendi, quod ultimo illo judicio non esse faciendum decernitur, homo plenâ fruitur libertate. Solummodò controvertitur, an illud judicium, quod homo liberè format, et quo actiones ejus determinantur, sit actio intellectus, an voluntatis. Sic disquireretur solummodo, utra explicatio cum Philosophicà ἀκριβείᾳ melius conciliari possit; in reipsâ autem foret consensus.
(English) Si vero dicamus, omnem actionem intellectus esse necessariam, et ultimum illud judicium practicum esse merum intellectus actum, ac per illud voluntatem determinari; non video quomodo ulla in homine reliqua sit libertas. Actiones enim omnes determinantur à voluntate, nisi homo aut cohibeatur quò minus facere possit quod vult, aut cogatur facere quod non vult; cohibitio enim et coactio, ut rectè observas, repugnant libertati: et quando nostri juris sumus semper facimus quod volumus. Si autem voluntas determinatur ab intellectu, et intellectus actio sit necessaria; omnia erunt necessaria: Nam à principio necessario, hoc est judicio intellectus, determinatur voluntas; à voluntate actiones: itaque homo ad actiones suas determinatus est: et licet potentiam habeat
― 464 ―
faciendi quod vult, et non faciendi quod non vult; potentia tamen illa per antecedentem voluntatis determinationem ad unum determinata est. Atque sic mera in actionibus hominis regnaret necessitas. Prolixior paulò fui: sed prolixitatem, ut perspicuè mentem meam explicarem, evitare vix potui. Si alicubi mentem tuam non rectè, aut non plene percepi, aut me à veritate aberrare credis, me liberè moneas et instruas rogo: Veritatem enim unicè sector. Et quoniam nunc plenius mentem meam explicui, brevius quicquid tibi non probetur indicare posses. Ut verô plenius sententiam nostram percipias, suaserim ut legas brevem Episcopii tractatum de Libero Arbitrio, qui exstat in ejus Oper. Vol. I. part. 2. pag. 198. et epistolam illius, qua judicium suum profert de loco quodam Ethices non edita,†a quæ est I&Cback;LV. inter epistolas nostras Ecclesiasticas et Theologicas.
(English) Reliqua libri tui valde mihi probantur, multumque me ex illius lectione profecisse gratus agnosco. Lectionem ejus repetere statui. Verum versio Gallica multum Latinæ præstat; eam ego subinde consulo, quando Latina obscurior est, sive interpretis, sive typographi culpâ. Quæ epistolæ tuæ inclusa sunt errata, et additamentum de Indifferentiâ, nescio an in privatum meum usum miseris, an verò ut imprimantur. Verum ego puto te sententiam nostram de
― 465 ―
Indifferentiâ non rectè percepisse, ideoque eam in hac epistolâ plenius et distinctius explicui. Sed tandem manum de tabulâ. Vale, Vir Amplissime: Uxor et filia te plurimum salvere jubent. Salutem a nobis officiosissimam dices Dominæ Masham, totique familiæ.

PHILIPPUS À LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 14 Octobris
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I am most grateful to you for having without reluctance undertaken for my sake so great a task as to set forth your opinion more precisely for me in a rather lengthy letter. I have read, reread, and pondered your letter with great attention. The more carefully I ponder it the more I seem to observe [p. 448] that we differ not so much in opinions as in phrases and manners of speaking, and that we sometimes denote different ideas by the same words, sometimes the same ideas by different words. I should have replied sooner, but I deliberately put off replying until I had read through your whole treatise. Now that I have done so and have compared it with your letter, I seem to observe more and more that all the disagreement that there appears to be between us turns not so much on the thing itself as on words and on different ways of setting forth the same thing. But because you seem not to have understood correctly the meaning of my phrases everywhere, and so that whatever disagreement still perchance remains between us can be comprised in few words and summarily, I shall first set forth, as perspicuously as I can, the meaning of the words and phrases that I have used; then I shall set out my opinion, as briefly as I can, in clear and unambiguous phrases. Finally I shall inquire into what we agree in, and what disagreement still remains: whether it consists in the thing itself, or rather in words and phrases, and in different ways of setting forth the thing into which we are inquiring. I think that thus, if perchance we do not yet hold the same opinions about everything, all disagreement will soon be removed, nor will truth be hidden for long from those who are sincerely seeking it.
(Latin) I recognize with you the signification of Will, that it is 'the power that a man has to begin, to stop, or to forbear any action of the mind or body', and I shall not recede from it; from will I also distinguish desire, by which we are directed to an absent good; nor shall I ever comprise it under the notion of will. I acknowledge that I spoke carelessly about this, and that desire is to be distinguished from will. As to my saying that will also is directed to an end, I meant nothing else than what you yourself say in your letter: 'When many goods, not subordinate to, or consistent with, one another, are present [p. 449] to the understanding at the same time, a man, neglecting the others, proposes one to himself as an end and as a thing to be pursued; this he does voluntarily'. This choice is therefore an action of the will: when a man has made this choice for himself he is directed by his desire to that good which he chose for himself; and by his will governs his actions by which he hopes to obtain the desired good.
(Latin) The word 'Liberty' denotes for me the dominion that a man has over his action. He who is not master of his action, or who cannot do what he wills, is not free. But I think that this extends to all the actions of a man without any exception, as well to internal actions of the mind as to external of the body, so much so that the action of willing, which is an internal action of the mind, is free also. Again, when I said that the will is master of our actions, I meant only that our external actions are governed by our volition, so much so that we do what we will and do not do what we do not will, unless restraint or compulsion intervenes. For either of them destroys liberty. I have declared once for all that I believe that the soul or mind understands and wills immediately, without any intermediate faculties.†2 Accordingly, by understanding and will, as often as I use these words, I understand nothing [p. 450] other than a power or faculty of the soul itself, by which it elicits the action of understanding and willing, which action the soul exercises immediately. And I think that you also approve of this signification.
(Latin) It remains for me to speak of 'Indifferency'. In the first place, I forewarn you about this that it is not, as you believe, our [sc. the Remonstrants'] [word]; not, that is, invented by our writers or adopted by us so far that we contend for it as necessarily to be used in this inquiry. By no means. For a long time we had not used it: defining Liberty, we ordinarily called it the dominion that a man has over his action. Again, in argument against those theologians who hold that Understanding and Will are two faculties distinct in fact from the soul and from each other, of which one only understands, but does not will, the other only wills, but does not understand: we have opposed this opinion of theirs with this argument: That by this opinion either all liberty is taken away or every action of a man is rendered brute and devoid of reason. For either the will is determined by the understanding, so much so that it necessarily wills what the understanding prescribes to it, and then all action is necessary because all action of the understanding is necessary; or it is not determined by the understanding, but determines itself; but then all action of the will is devoid of reason and brute, because the [p. 451] will is supposed not to understand, but only to will.†1 In order to avoid the thrust of this argument they have replied that the root of liberty is in the understanding because in the understanding there is indifferency, by which it can apprehend and judge whatever object is presented to it.†2 Our writers replied that this is only passive indifferency,†3 such as there is in the eye, which also can see any objects that meet it and receive their images; yet nobody would say on that account that it sees freely: because it cannot help seeing what is put before it to be seen; so the understanding cannot help apprehending what is clearly put before it, or doubting that for which equally weighty reasons are contending on either side. Indeed, if liberty is to be sought in indifferency, this must be active indifferency, by which a man has dominion over his action. Hence, since others have employed the word 'Indifferency', we, in order to avoid all ambiguity in discussion, have added for the sake of distinction the word 'active', and have said that liberty consists in 'Active Indifferency' and that this resides in the will.†4 You see, therefore, that we do not wish to contend for this word and that it was not devised by us; but that we have explained a word that was used by others, and by the addition of the word 'active' have made its signification clearer. Meanwhile I do not deny that afterwards we too used it sometimes in our writings because, if taken according to our explanation, it seemed most [p. 452] appropriate and to signify the same as the phrase formerly used by us, dominion over our actions. And this is also supported by the definition of this 'Indifferency' that I gave in my preceding letter: that it is that energy of the spirit by which, when all requisites for acting are present, it can act or not act: which for me is nothing else than that a man has dominion over his action, so that he can act or not act as it pleases him. And so among 'all requisites for acting' I place above all others the judgement of the understanding, which must precede; otherwise the action of willing would be wholly devoid of reason. Again, when I say 'that he can act and not act' my meaning is not that he can at the same time act and not act; or, neither act nor not act, or, neither will nor not will; for this is contradictory; but that the power is determined to neither, and that therefore of two opposites he can choose whichever he pleases; and what is more, when he has already determined himself to acting, that he can stop his action and determine himself again to the opposite: that is, that he has dominion over his action. When a man does not have this dominion he is not free. Thus you rightly point out that he who willingly abstains from wine in prison does not do so freely, because he has no power to drink wine; nor does he who willingly remains in prison do so freely, because he has no power to go out. But the case is different with internal actions, which are performed in the mind alone: [p. 453] nothing is required for liberty in them except the free determination of the will. Thus he who in prison lusts after another man's wife, and cherishes that foul lust in his mind, and delights himself with it, lusts and sins freely, although that lust stays within the bounds only of morose delectation,†1 as the Schoolmen say; and therefore the actual external act of adultery is not required for its accomplishment.
(Latin) By 'brute impulse' I understand not action of the will without any preceding cogitation: anyone acting thus I should conceive not a man; but precipitate action, before it has been duly and carefully examined; just as we see that many men are often carried away by violent passion to will to do this or that, before they have well considered all the circumstances of an action, and the reasons and arguments by which they may be incited to or deterred from it. I [therefore] attribute this liberty to a man, that when an action has been proposed to him he can either precipitate his judgement or examine maturely all the circumstances of the action, and so act either by brute impulse or with previous mature and deliberate consideration; and I think that everyone is aware of this liberty.
(Latin) Nor should this be omitted, that by 'Indifferency' I do not understand a [p. 454] state in which a man is set as it were in equilibrium and does not incline to one side more than to the other: for such a state of indifferency in regard to moral actions is not found in any man; we always incline to one side more than to the other, especially in moral actions, according as we are either urged by our passions or rendered by custom and habit more prone to virtues or vices; but I understand a state in which a man has a power to determine himself to whichever of opposites he wills; for, although he may be inclined to one more than to the other, yet he has not lost dominion over his action, but can even determine himself to the other. But because the word 'Indifferency' can be taken for a state in which a man inclines to neither side, but is wholly set in equilibrium, although that meaning is directly opposed to our exposition, yet in order to avoid any ambiguity I shall abstain from [the use of] that word.
(Latin) I do not confuse 'the last judgement of the understanding' with mature and right judgement: but I there distinguish the last judgement according as it is either mature and right or wrong and precipitate, which I called brute impulse there because it follows a violent carnal lust rather than the guidance of reason. Either of these is the last judgement when it immediately precedes the action of willing, and there is no other judgement between it and the action of willing. [p. 455]
(Latin) Having thus explained the terms that I have used I shall now set forth my opinion as briefly and as perspicuously as I can. I comprise it in these propositions.
(Latin) 1. A man is a free agent and has dominion over his actions, whether in doing or in forbearing them.
2. Understanding and Will are not two faculties distinct in fact from the soul of a man and from each other, but the soul of its essence immediately understands and wills.
3. A man does not will or do anything unless roused by a desire of a good or by a feeling of trouble from the absence of a desired good.
4. An act of understanding, by which a man forms a judgement about his action, precedes an act of willing.
5. That judgement is either prudent, after a mature examination of the contending reasons on either side has been applied; or it is precipitate and dictated by passion more than by reason.
6. This judgement, in so far as it is purely an act of understanding, does not proceed beyond persuasion: this is eligible, or, it is proper to choose this; it is proper to reject this; or, among eligibles, this is more, this is less, eligible; among things to be avoided, this ought more, this ought less, to be avoided. [p. 456]
(Latin) 7. A judgement by which a man decrees that this is to be done is itself a volition or at least an act in which intellection†1 and volition are mingled, and in whose accomplishment an act of willing joins.
8. An act of understanding, in so far as it is purely an act of understanding, is necessary and rests upon the weight of the reasons perceived by a man.
9. An act of willing is free, and a man has dominion over it and a faculty of eliciting or not eliciting it. If therefore there is any liberty in a judgement it proceeds from an act not of understanding but of willing.
10. The liberty of internal actions, which are performed in the mind alone, consists in the free determination of the mind, by which it can elicit or restrain an action of willing. But for the liberty of external actions, in whose accomplishment the external members must join, it is also requisite that a man should have a faculty or power of doing what he wills and of forbearing or not doing what he does not will; or, a free and unimpeded use of his external members.
(Latin) My opinion having thus been briefly set forth, let us now see in what we agree, and what disagreement remains between us. When I compare your letter with bk. II, ch. xxi, 'Of power', it seems to me that I can say that we agree about the first five propositions, nor is there any disagreement between [p. 457] us about them. About the last also there is no controversy between us, unless perhaps that you seem to place liberty solely in a power of doing what we will and of not doing what we do not will; whereas I extend it also to the determination of the will itself, or act of volition. Of that presently. I also welcome with both thumbs†1 what you write in your letter, that a man is directed to an absent good or end; and that when many goods, not subordinate to, or consistent with, one another, are present to the understanding at the same time, a man, neglecting the others, proposes one to himself as an end, that is, as a thing to be pursued: and this he does voluntarily; and therefore his will is directed to that action of the mind by which he proposes to himself one thing as an end in preference to the rest; and it terminates in that action. Moreover the desire of the end follows this action of the will. So far, therefore, we agree. Let us see how far we agree in the rest, and what disagreement remains.
(Latin) First, we do not seem to agree in the definition of liberty. For you say: 'Liberty for me is the power of a man to act or not to act, according to his will'. This definition seems to me to be too narrow; and if it is approved then it is certain that liberty in no way appertains to the will; just as it is certain that the soul can never be without cogitation if the definition is true, [p. 458] that the soul is cogitation.†1 Indeed, if this were the proper [genuinus] definition of liberty it could be that liberty might consist with the most stringent necessity, as I shall show presently. I myself think that liberty is the dominion that a man has over any of his actions, and that it extends not only to actions that he performs in accordance with his will, but also to the act of willing, or volition itself.
(Latin) As regards the sixth and seventh propositions, I do not know how far we agree in them or what disagreement there is between us about them. I asserted the same thing already in my last letter, but you make no mention of it in yours, and so I am uncertain how far you agree with me about it. It seems plain to me that a man determines his judgement because he wills to acquiesce in the reasons that he has pondered; again, that he suspends his judgement because he does not yet will to acquiesce, but wills either to ponder the reasons more carefully or to inquire whether there are more reasons by which his judgement may be changed; and so it seems plain to me that the determination of the last judgement, by which a man decrees that this is to be chosen or done, is, if not wholly, at least very largely, an action of willing. [p. 459]
(Latin) I do not know whether the eighth proposition, in which I hold that every act of the understanding, in so far as it is purely an act of understanding, is necessary, is in controversy between us. For you appear to affirm it expressly in bk. IV, ch. xiii, § 2, and ch. xx, § 16. But it ought to be set forth somewhat more precisely, so that it may appear plainly whether there is any disagreement about it. Here I note that the things that the understanding perceives are either purely theoretical or practical.†1 When concerned with theoretical truths the action of the understanding is absolutely necessary: when a clear and plain truth is put before it the understanding necessarily assents, or rather a man necessarily perceives it and gives assent to it; when arguments that are only probable are put forward a man necessarily forms an opinion; when the arguments put forward on either side are of equal weight, the man, or rather the understanding, necessarily doubts. And all these actions of understanding rest upon the weight of the reasons perceived by a man. When concerned with practical truths the action of understanding, in so far as it is purely an action of understanding, and no action of willing intervenes, is likewise necessary; for by the weight of the reasons which the understanding has pondered it judges what is more fitting, what less, what it is advantageous to do or not to do. This judgement certainly guides the will, but does not fully determine it: for it is a command only of persuasion, which the will can disobey, or, rather, a man can will something else. Again, [p. 461] a determination by which a man decrees that this is to be done, proceeds from the will. And this determination is made either in accordance with the persuasion of the understanding, and then it is rational; or it can be made contrary to it, and then it is devoid of reason: that is, it proceeds from carnal passion and does not in any wise heed the persuasion of the understanding. Or it can even be headlong and rash, so that it outstrips mature judgement. Here we seem to differ: for you say, 'A man does not possess a power of determining an action of willing contrary to the judgement of the understanding: for an action of willing this or that always follows a judgement of the understanding by which a man judges this to be better for here and now'. You seem to assert the same thing also at the end of § 71 of ch. xxi. But yet when I compare this with the definition of the will in your letter, that it is 'the power that a man has to begin, to stop, or to forbear any action of his mind or body', and with ch. xxi, § 47, and with some preceding and succeeding passages, I doubt whether we greatly disagree and whether the difference is not rather in our manner of exposition than in the thing itself. For you certainly seem to me to recognize there some liberty in judging. For you say there, 'The mind is at liberty to consider the objects of its desires, to look into them thoroughly, and to examine diligently which of them weighs heavier in the scales. In this consists the liberty of a man'; and further excellent things that you have there. You add later: 'the power granted to us of recalling the will from the prosecution of this or that desire. This seems to me [p. 461] to be the source of all liberty', etc.†1 For from these passages it seems to be clear that liberty is also concerned in forming a judgement, indeed that the source of liberty is there. Whence I gather that liberty (according to your exposition) consists not only in a power of doing what we will; but that even before an act of volition, indeed before a judgement about his action, a man is free and exercises his liberty. The difference between us would be only whether the last judgement by which it is decreed, not 'it is fitting to do this', but 'this ought to be done', is purely an action of understanding; or whether in fact an action of willing also joins it; and whether liberty resides in the action of understanding or in that of willing; or rather, whether what is free in the judgement by which the action of a man is determined, resides in intellection or in volition. If the difference consists in this I think that our views can easily be reconciled. For although it seems clear to me that liberty resides in the action of willing, and that nothing is free without also being voluntary; yet we seem not to be able to disagree so greatly about this but that we may easily be brought into agreement. For since we both hold that understanding and will are not two powers distinct in fact from the soul and from each other, but that the man, or rather the soul, of its essence immediately understands and wills, we agree sufficiently, seeing that we both recognize that the last judgement of a man is freely determined; for since there [p. 462] is present the power of doing what is dictated by that last judgement which was freely determined by us, and of not doing, or rather of forbearing, what that last judgement decrees is not to be done, a man enjoys full liberty. All that is in controversy is whether that judgement which a man forms freely, and by which his actions are determined, is an action of the understanding or of the will. Thus the only matter to be investigated would be which exposition can better be reconciled with philosophical precision; about the thing itself there would be agreement.
(Latin) If, however, we say that every action of the understanding is necessary, and that that last practical judgement is purely an act of the understanding, and that the will is determined by it: I do not see how any liberty is left in a man. For all actions are determined by the will unless a man is either restrained, so as to be unable to do what he wills, or compelled to do what he does not will; for restraint and compulsion, as you rightly observe, are incompatible with liberty; and when we are our own msaters we always do what we will. Again, if the will is determined by the understanding, and the action of the understanding is necessary, all things will be necessary: for the will is necessarily determined from the beginning, that is, by the judgement of the understanding; the actions are determined by the will; and thus a man is determined to his actions; and although he has a power of doing what he wills and of not doing what he does not will; nevertheless that power is determined in every case by the antecedent determination of the will. [p. 463] And thus pure necessity would rule in the actions of a man. I have been somewhat prolix: but in order to set forth my meaning clearly I could scarcely avoid prolixity. If I have not rightly or not fully understood your meaning anywhere, or if you believe that I have strayed from truth, please tell me freely and instruct me: for I pursue Truth alone. And since I have now set forth my meaning more fully you can point out more briefly anything of which you do not approve. But in order that you should understand our [sc. the Remonstrants'] opinion more fully I would recommend you to read Episcopius's short treatise on Free Will, which is to be found in his Opera, vol. I, pt. 2, p. 198, and a letter of his in which he makes known his judgement about a passage in an unpublished [book on] Ethics; this is no. 555 of our Epistolae Ecclesiasticæ et Theologicæ.
(Latin) I esteem the rest of your book very highly, and gratefully acknowledge that I have greatly profited from reading it. I have decided to read it again. But the French translation is much better than the Latin; I consult it from time to time when the Latin is rather obscure, whether the translator or the printer is to blame. I do not know whether you sent me the errata that are enclosed in your letter, and the addition on Indifferency, for my private use or for printing. But I think that you have not rightly understood our opinion [p. 464] about Indifferency, and so I have set it forth more fully and clearly in this letter. But it is time to stop. Good-bye, excellent Sir; my wife and daughter send you their best wishes. Please give our best respects to Lady Masham and the whole family.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 14 October
1701
Endorsed by Locke: P. Limborch 14 Oct 01 Answered Nov. 20

3016. Dr. Robert Pitt to Locke, 14 October 1701 (3006, 3024)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 166-7.
Oct. 14. 1701
Sir
I have frequently thought of your Case, since you did me the favour to report it to me. I suppose so easy a depletion of the humours by Pill. Ruffi cannot make any impression on your Breast. Your Stomach will be supported by it, and the increase of Phlegm prevented. By that very gentle evacuation, the Humours will not in so great Quantity, instructed with an iter melius, fall on your legs, and consequently the Ulcuscula sooner dispos'd to heal, or at least to be less disturbing to you. I desire to be inform'd, how I may send a little Pacquet of Papers to you, writt at several times, by order of the College†1 and by private hands, on the great Reformation we hope to make in Physick. The People will not give their Apothecary any Mony, he therefore pays himself for his Visiting and prattling, by the much Physick he sends in, if he cannot gett the sick to take it. This vast Charge make the People stick the closer to him, to avoid the other. He is desir'd to bring in a Doctor, when Danger appears. The Doctor must write as he will, and applaud his management. by both which the People are still more confirm'd. The Dispensary can only instruct the publick, that Medicines are cheap, and that many distempers are easily cur'd by few. It has now the universal Applause. We are never to make the least profitt by the Physick. which convinces the People, that those Phys. will never appoint a grain more then is necessary.
― 470 ―
The greatest Care is us'd in the choise†a of every Drug, and the forming of every composition. Sir, I desire you to excuse the Confidence I take to give you this trouble.
I am
Your most humble servant
R PITT
Address: For Mr John Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: OC —
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Pitt 14 Oct. 01 Answered 17
3017. Paul D'Aranda to Locke, 14 October 1701 (2899)

Sir
I intreat your excuse, that not having Mr Arent Furly's letter by me when I wrote to him, I forgot what he said to me from you, till now a letter from him, after having been at Shoram in Sussex, comes to put me in mind that I ought to have wrote him, that my Taylor is Mr. John Ward and partner Dickinson, and dwells in Hatton Garden, at the next door to the Unicorn, if you use them I hope they may please you as well in the make of your cloaths as they have done me, neer thirty years, in the punctuality to their promise, in the time of their delivering them made, as I'm confident you'l find them do with you. Sir I humbly thank you for your obliging hint to Mr Furly concerning my drinking the Water at Bath; whither I am not like to go this year, after having been hindred from going till now, that, through long exact observance of my rules in dyet, I am beyond all expectation wonderfully recover'd in about 14 days or 3 weeks, and therefore defer going till the next spring, unlesse relapse, which I hope to prevent, (if my having more of the animal than of the Rational man in me will permit) necessitate my drinking those waters sooner. whenever I go, I will observe your obliging advice, as what has prov'd to me the most beneficial of any I ever received from the multitude of Phisicians my seeming remediless indisposition forced me to

consult. I much long to hear that the best helps nature can receive may compleat your own recovery, that the remainder of your life may be as easy to your self, as the past part of it always has been, and what of it is to come certainly will be, advantagious to the rest of mankind. I am
Sir
Your most faithfull and most obedient servant
P. D'ARANDA
Shoram in Kent the 14th: October 1701

3019. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, [21] October/[1] November 1701 (3009, 3132)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 229-30. Toinard apparently omits the numeral for the first day of the month, much as he omits the month for the first month of the year. Answers no. 3009.

ce Novembre 701.
Je fus hier delivré, Monsieur, d'un extrême inquietude, en recevant l'honneur des votres du 30. Sept/11. Octbre, et je partis sur le champ pour faire part de ma joie à M.D.B.†1 Il est en bonne santé, et vous fait les remerciemens touchant ceque vous m'avez ordonné aupres de lui. Je l'accompagnay chez M. Gendron qui m'a chargé de vous marquer de nouveau sa reconnoissance pour votre Essay. Il la lu avec une parfete satisfaction, et cela lui est commun avec tous les ôtres Lecteurs, qui n'ont rien trouvé à redire dans le livre que le Titre, car il devroit etre intitulé chef d'œuvre.
M. Gendron travaille à un grand ouvrage où il tretera à fond de la connêssance de la nature humaine, et renversera bien des sistêmes.†2
― 473 ―
Il a trouvè depuis quelque tems une poudre vulnerere, qui empêche la supuration. Il s'en est servi avantageuzemant dans pluzieurs cures importantes. cete poudre est un veritable secret. Ele coûte peu, se fait aizemant, et se garde toujours, et s'employe à diferantes maladies. ne dites point que je vous aye mandé cela.
Je vous diray avec la derniere sincerité que je ressens un deplaizir inexprimable d'être dans une conjoncture qui ne me permet pas d'aler goûter la plus grande douceur que je pûsse esperer dans tout le reste de mes jours. Vous entendez assez que c'est de vous embrasser. J'ay ancore à mon âge assez de santé pour entreprendre un voyage d'outre mer, mais une hydre renaissante de divers contretems me prive de ce bonheur. Il y a de facheuses queües du maudit procez qui m'empêcha de faire du Printems dernier la plus belle saison de ma vie: et cela ne poura se reparer tout au plûtôt que l'année prochéne, si meme les afaires generales ne vienent à être d'intelligence avec les particulieres, qui m'ont jusques à prezant desolé sur ce point. Je vous prie, monsieur, de ne pas prendre pour une Parodie ceque vous alez lire sur ce sujet, mais d'etre tres persuadé que c'est une pure verité originale.
Me si fata meis paterentur ducere vitam
Auspiciis, et sponte meâ componere curas:
Londinensem urbem primùm, dulces quoque Locki
Amplexus peterem, et pax utcunque maneret,
Londinum celeri peteretur nave per æquor.†1
On m'a fort instruit, monsieur, de l'aimable compagnie que vous avez dans votre campagne: mais aucun magnetisme ne peut m'y atirer si puissanmant que l'ardant dezir que j'ay de vous voir.
A propos de magnetisme, il faut selon l'Extret que vous m'avez envoié du Voyage de Narbrough, que je ne vous aye pas bien fait entendre ma pensée touchant l'augmentation de la Variation de l'Eguille vers le Sud. comme ce voyage n'est pas en Langage Chretien, j'en ay fait traduire ceque j'ay jugé m'etre necessere sur ce fait, et j'y ay trouvé une chose tres singuliere, c'est qu'il a observé
― 474 ―
que l'Eguille nordeste à la côte oriantale des Patagons aussi bien qu'a l'occidantale.
ceque je vous ay ecrit touchant l'augmantation de la variation n'a rien de commun avec les variations qu'il y a depuis le 35.D.o. jusques au 53.52'. entre lesquels espaces du Nord au Sud, les variations diminuent presque toujours, (quoiqu'irregulierement et improportionelement) alant au Sud; puisqu'au 35.D. on a observé 18.D.20'. et au 50-10'. seulement 16-37'. comme au 52-26'. on a trouvé 17.D.
J'ay voulu parler d'un ôtre Phænomene magnetique plus particulier, m'atachant à un seul lieu. c'est qu'en 1668. l'Eguille nordestoit de 17.D. à l'embouchûre oriantale du Detroit de magellan selon Narbrough, et en 1698. de 19.D. selon le voyage de De Genes, et l'année derniere de 20.D.
Donc de 1668. à 1698. augmentation de deux D. en dix ans, et de 1698. à 1700. ôtre augmentation d'un.D.
Il ne faut pas tant admirer la disproportion qu'il y a de deux Degrez en dix ans à un Degré en deux ans, que l'augmentation continuele vers l'Est: parceque dans tous les ôtres endroîs du monde, où l'on a observé la variation de la declinaison, on a trouvé qu'ele se reformoit par le mouvement de l'Est au Nord dans les lieux où l'Eguille Nordestoit, où bien qu'aiant passé à la bande de l'oüest apres avoir eté en direction au nord, ele augmentoit de tems en tems vers l'oüest. Il y a à Paris prezantemant variation d'environ huit D. au Nordoüest. Ele etoit d'environ 8.D. aussi en 1610. au Nordest. L'Eguille a donc avancé de 16.D. en 90. ans de l'Est tant au Nord qu'a l'Oüest, et de même en 1580. ele etoit de 11.D.30'. à Londres. Il n'y en ut ocune en 1667. et depuis ce tems la ele a passé de plusieurs degrez au Nordoüest.
J'estime, monsieur, que ces deux exemples vous peuvent sufire pour vous faire connêtre que c'est le contrere de cequi est arivé depuis trente deux ans à l'embouchûre Oriantale du Detroit de Magellan, où la variation etant selon Narbrough de 17.D. Nordest en 1668. ele devroit être diminuée depuis ce tems de quelques degrez en se tournant au nord, comme ele a fait à Paris et à Londres, au lieu quele a augmenté vers le sud, et aparemmant augmentera encore, puisqu'en 1698. ele etoit de 19.D. et en 1700. de 20.
c'est cete diferante marche qui doit doner de l'etonnemant, principalemant proche d'un grand continant, comme est la terre des Patagons, où ele devroit plutôt Nordoüester, que nordester:
― 475 ―
car la terre devroit y atirer à soy l'aimant, comme ele fait vers la côte occidentale depuis le meme Detroit jusques au Chilé.
Je vous dirois ici bien au long cequi m'ariva en 1667. à Lisbonne sur ce sujet, si je ne croiois vous l'avoir otrefois dit de vive voix. Je le repeterai seulement en peu de mots. J'assistay à une observation que j'avois solicitée. Ele se fit par les deux mêmes personnes qui en avoient fait une pareille et avec les mêmes instrumens en 1639. et la variation avoit eté trouvée de 7.D.30'.NE. Je voulois faire gageure qu'ele passeroit au nordoüest. Tout le monde se moquoit de moy, mais pas un ne voulut toper au pari. La scene etoit dans le chateau, où fûrent prezans tous les prisonniers Espagnols, dont il y en avoit bon nombre et de bien qualifiéz. Le marquis de Liche, fils de Dom Louis de Haro,†1 etoit le plus habile de la troupe. Enfin il se trouva qu'ele passoit de 19.m. nordoüest, et c'etoit assez pour me faire gagner. ce pronostic me donna plus de consideration que la choze ne valoit, mais c'etoit assez d'etre dans un païs où il n'en faut pas tant pour etre estimé tout au moins demi-magicien.
Puisque nous voila sur l'Emant, je vous diray une otre chôze qui m'a surpris par raport à son inclination sous l'horizon à mezure que l'on aproche de l'un ou de l'otre Pole. c'est pour cela que nos navigateurs Basques qui vont à la pesche des Balenes jusques au 80.D. et par dela, comme j'ay vu dans leurs Journaux, lorsque j'etois à st Jan de Luz, chargent de cire d'Espagne le bout meridional de l'Eguille de la Boussole pour la tenir en suspension horizontale à mezure qu'ils s'avancent vers le Pole, et empêcher que le bout septentrional qui porte la fleur de Lis, ne frait sur le bord de la boussole, cequi feroit perdre la connessance de sa direction. neanmoins mr d'Iberville,†2 criole de monreal en canada, aussi bon observateur que brave oficier, m'a assuré qu'il n'a trouvé aucune inclination de l'Eguille au 63.D. et mr de Serigni†3 son frere, à qui j'avois recommandé la choze l'année derniere, lorsqu'il aloit à la Baye de Hudson, m'a confirmé ceque m. d'Iberville m'avoit dit. La valeur de ces deux freres n'est pas ignorée des Anglois qui ont interest à la Baye de Hudson. Ils sont ensemble prezentemant en
― 476 ―
mer pour la Riviere de mississipi.†1 L'un d'eux m'a fait prezant d'une peau de sibola,†2 dont j'ay conmancé à me couvrir la nuit depuis quelques jours, en la metant sur mon lit. c'est un de ces sortes de beufs, dont je vous ay envoié de la laine.
Voila assez vous rompre la tête. Il faut pour vous rejouïr, vous dire un scrupule que j'ay d'avoir oté aux Basques un repos d'esprit qu'ils avoient touchant l'inclination de l'Eguille emantée. Leur en aïant demandé la cause, l'un des principaux, et qui avoit eté plus avant vers le nord que pas un ôtre, me dist, en se frotant les mains, Quant à nous, nous croions que c'est le froid qui la resserre: et la troupe paroissoit fort contente de la reponse que leur savant avoit donnée. mais ce ne fut pas plus cela apres que je leur us demandé, que si cela venoit du froid, pourquoi il la resserroit de ce côté la plutôt que de l'otre: car ils parûrent fort atristéz, et toutes les fois que j'y pense, je ressens de la peine de leur en avoir fait, et de les avoir troubléz dans leur heureuse ignorance.
Pensez vous que la variation de l'Eguille vers le parage de la côte des Patagons, puisse faire juger d'un grand continent vers les terres Australes à l'Est du Detroit de magellan? cela seroit suivant les ancienes hypotheses, ou tout au moins qu'il y oroit beaucoup d'Emant dans les terres voizines vers l'Est.
Je suis parfaitemant, monsieur, votre—
Noted by Locke (f. 229, head): Toinard Nov: 01 Answered Mar. 7

3024. Dr. Robert Pitt to Locke, 27 October 1701 (3016, 3045)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, f. 168.
Sir
I need not give my Opinion of the Purgatives you mention: its almost indifferent, what sort of the Gentle ones are to be us'd. I thinke Pil. Ruffi very easy, and supporting to the Stomach, and Cordial. I have sent our Farrago of Papers by a Gentleman going to Cambridge. I desire you at your leisure to entertain your selfe with them. The design is great, and has principally the publick service in veiw. The Hard words do not exceed the truth, or the importance of the Debate. The Power is gone so far one way, that its much more difficult now, then in Dr Sydenham's time. so many of the College running in to their present and great advantage the other way.†1 I shall please my selfe to debate this matter with you by letter, which may probably give you a more pleasant amusement then the Votes†2 after a month or 2. I will expect your first Thoughts as soon as you please. I hope you have read Sir Will. Temples Posthumous Miscellanys.†3
Sir I am
Your most humble servant
R PITT.

3025. Locke to Edward Clarke, 30 October 1701 (2988, 3058)
Venice, Biblioteca Marciana, MSS. Latini, cl. 7, no. 22, colloc. 3116. Given by Ayshford Sanford to Rawdon Brown (D.N.B.), who gave it to the Marciana. Transcribed from microfilm. Answers no. 2988.
Oates 30 Oct 1701.
Dear Sir
I was very glad to be assured lately by my cosin King that he saw you not long since at Chipley in a pretty good state of health and he left Mrs. Clarke and all the good family well. I hope since the country†a has gaind soe far upon your distemper the air and exercise you have there will perfect your recovery by your longer continuance in it. My lungs continue on their old course and make all motion painfull to me unlesse it be on horse back, but that way I take the air when the weather permits though now my old adversary winter approaching begins with its cold to confine me to the chimny corner which I find more comfortable to me than I expected, by a way I have found out to fence my legs from the heat of the fire, which used to put my soar legs into a rage when ever I approached it. but now I thank god they are not soe troublesome as they were wont to be this last year, only they make me lie much a bed and soe wast a good deale of my time. This account of my self I think I am obleiged to give one who expressed soe much kindeness and concerne for me as you did in your last letter for which I am mightily obleiged to you. If I knew any thing to adde to my former advices to you for the restoring your health I should certainly send it to you, but stiring in the open air espetially on horsback being the best that I know. I can only repeat that and with it send my wishes that you may come to town soe well fortified by it as to be able with vigor to bear up and goe through this next winters fatigue. Pray give my service to Mrs. Clarke my wife and her sister. My Cosin King told me he heard your son was returnd.†1 If he be I desire you to give him my service and let him know I congratulate his safe return. I am Dear Sir
your most humble and most faithfull servant
J LOCKE

Sir
I delivered both yours yesterday to the Lords; my Lord Hav.†1 intends to answer his the other presents his service to you and enquired of your health, I answered that you wrot nothing of it; but I said I guest by your manner of writing that you was in good health. I did, as you directed, enquire of his, his Ladys, and Childrens health, as from you; who bid me write you word that they were all in good health and my Lord presents his Service to you and gives you many thanks for your kind enquiry.†2
The account I had of the Oxford, I mean the University Address,†3 I had from Mr Freke; who saith that a Letter was read in the Greecian Coffee-hous†4 from a Doctor in that Univ: that the Vicech: having called a Convocation said he called them on a Silly account; but seeing the Nation played the fool; he thought they must do so too; whereupon an Add: was drawn up, and sent by one of the Beedles to the D of Orm: their Chan,†5 to be presented to the Lords Justices; who when he understood who he was, returnd him the Add: and said if they thought not fit to come up with it themselvs, he would not deliver it. as near as I can remember these were the words; if not, they were to this Effect.
I enquired of my Lord whether the University Address were come to their hands. Sir

3028. Locke to Esther Masham, [7 November 1701?] (3003)
Newberry Library, Chicago: copy of the original by Esther Masham in her letter-book, pp. 153-4. Transcribed from microfilm. Printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 493, with date as 7 November; in Newberry Library Bulletin, 2nd ser., no. 4, July 1950, pp. 134-5, by Professor Maurice Cranston, who associates it with Esther Masham's letter of 20 September to Locke (no. 3003). In the letter-book the copy follows immediately a copy of a letter from Francis Cudworth Masham to Esther, dated Oates, 7 November 1701. The two copies are enumerated as a single item, 'LXVII Lettre'; this, in view of Esther's care in compiling the letter-book, implies a close connection. The proposed date fits the contents of the letter; the chief objection is that Francis hears 'no likelyhood' of Esther's return to Oates. The letter perhaps acknowledges no. 3003. The explanatory note was written by Esther.
Deare Dib
Your Johannes has been long indebted to you for a kind Letter and tho' he has desired others to give you his thanks, yet he thinks not that enough, nor can he consent to defer it to a personal view, since you so long prefer the delights of the Town to the Country
― 485 ―
company here. Give me leave therefore to return you my acknowledgments with my own hands for that favour and to tell you that though I find your Letters good which I owe to your absence yet they the more persuade me that your Company is better, and that I shall always be desirous to change the one for the other. Tis talk'd here that you are preparing to satisfie my wishes in this matter, and that you give some hopes that we shall in a little while see you here again. I have one favour to beg of you before you come out of Town and that is that when you call at Mr Churchills, which I presume you will do, you would call upon him for a folio Bible in quires which I have spoke to him for,†1 and that you would let it come down amongst your Cloaths, where it will lye very quiet and inoffensively being unbound. I should not trouble you with it but that I am afraid to venture it by the Butcher for fear, as it often falls out, it should in that way be wett or sulli'd, and this is a book which I am at the charge for only to have it a very fair one. I am
D D
your most faithful and obedient
†a JOHANNES

P S
Just now we received the acceptable newes of the Imperialists being past the Adda and got into the Millanese which take as follows
Milan 31 October
This morning about an hour before day are the Germans passed the Adda very strong with their fieldpieces an houre on this side Lodi near Trocazono: Just as last summer at Carpi, they surpriz'd the Army, so that the horse had not time to mount and were very ill treated: Colonel Monroy with a Lieutenant Colonel and his wife are taken prisoners: The regiment of Valde Fuentes is totally ruined; The Germans are now on this side the Adda neare Albegnano, Cassano and Vaprio, and do not at all molest Country people. We are in Great confusion in the Towne about this affaire. The Allies are now rallying all their forces on all hands, so that we are shortly like to heare of some considerable action
De la Suisse 9 Novembre 1701
Dans ce moment vient d'arriver un Expres de l'armée Imperiale en Italie avec la bonne et grande nouvelle, que le jeune Prince de Vaudemont avoit le prime†a de ce mois passé la riviere d'Ada avec quelques Milles cheveaux a Cassano, et qu'ils y avoient entierement defait les regimens de Cavallerie ennemie, sc. de Monroy de Neapolis et de Valde fuentes avec 2 Compagnies de la Cavallerie Allemande del stato, qui y estoit pour garder le passage de cette riviere: Que le generael de la Cavallerie Espagnole il Duca del Sesto, qui commandoit les troupes, au lieu de le secourir, y avoit tellement pris l'epouvante qu'il estoit courru jusques dans le Milan, sans reguarder derriere luy; Que le Colonel Monroy, le major de son regiment, 2 Capitaines et 55 Cavalliers avoient esté fait prisonniers: qu'on ne sçavoit pas encore le nombre de tuéz, Onze
― 488 ―
Cornettes, une paire des Tymbales, cinq Cent cheveaux et tout le bagage des officiers, et que les Imperiaux, avoient pris poste au de la de L'Ada: et ainsi les voila dans le Milaneze.
[Benjamin Furly:]
Rotterdam 18 November 1701
Dear Sir
My son having acted the laudable part of a Gentleman, shews that he has been bred at the feet of Gamaliel: give me now leave to go my old marchant road, and to return you my most humble and hearty thanks for all the favours you have heaped up upon him, which I hope he will have the grace never to forget, tho it may be out of his power, any other way ever to express his gratitude, to your self, and that worthy family that so often admitted him to converse therein. I find, as you wrote me, that he is grown in stature, And, not a little, which is the chiefest, improved in the indowments of his mind, and manners, according to his years, which is chiefly owing to your good care over him.
He has in one thing mightily neglected the orders I gave him, viz. to mind his writing, and cyphering, which now he is recovering, I hope with courage. I have oft told him, I have no estate to leave him, that he can live upon without a stile†1 in the world, by meere study. A Hireling†2 I would not have him, that's the vilest of trades that I know of in the World, to make marchandise of the soules of men. A Lawyer is not much better, to get estates by bawling and lying, and to a Doctor now he has no inclination;
yet I find his mind hanckering towards your Canaan, and some body had put it into his head to seek to get to be an under Clark in the Navy, Treasury or Admiralty, where he might, by merits, rise to be a secretary etc—
He tells me he spake of it to a good friend†a and acquaintance of yours and mine, who is a secretary where you was a Commissioner,†3 and that he thought it might be wel; could he but once get in.
I told him that was not the onely, tho' no small, difficulty, I having no friends at Court. He replyed doubtless I had divers, and named yourself and my Lord Pembrook, and some others.
― 489 ―
But the grand difficulty was his present incapacity in the English tongue, which would cost him labour and time: and his time went away apace.
Besides, if he should get†a in†a by any present Interest, when his friends were layd aside, which often befals Courtiers, he might fall also, and that it was but a sorry stay, to depend upon the breath of a courtier—
I then propounded to his brother Benj.†1 and him, his entring upon my Comptoir, in order to, carry on that post in Company, they intirely loving each other, and might be a support to each other. This seemd very agreeable to them both and I would contrive a way in a year or 2 to lett them into Company with me.
But after having maturely thought of it, he came and told me very judiciously, that he had considered of that Proposition of joining with his Brother and could not see that he should be fit for it: that his Brother writing so well, and being so neat, he feard he should not be able to pleas him, and that might breed difference, tho' he would do his best to learn to write well. And in fine that he did not like companyship. that he that was in Company was not free; That his mind should always be to study and books; that that, and marchandise would not well go together. That he might be a hinderance to his brother or himself. etc.
And said, if he must stay in this Contry he should have most likeing to that stile he first made choice of, and which yourself so well approvd. But there presents†b a difficulty, which I cannot well see through. That person†2 would have me enter into a Contract with him, after 3 or 4 years service, to take over his shop, and all the books in it: Because he resolves to give over, and not to sell any thing but what he prints himself: And so whoever he takes, must take all the books he shall then have at a certain price, and further be obliged to take some quantity of the things he shall print.
This gives me trouble in this affaire, which I had not expected; so that I feare that I shall not get him in there. I am concern'd for him, and would do any thing, in my power, to give him the utmost satisfaction, in which he may have occasion to prosecute his studies:
― 490 ―
which he thinks in some such office he would have, they being bound to give attendance but certain hours in the day.
I humbly request your thoughts upon this Subject, as one that I am confident dos bear a true love to us both.
We have this day received the welcome news of the Imperialists having masterd the passe at the Adda, and got into the Milanese, where they have fixed themselvs. Both armies lye incampt, and neither dares rise first. This gives us courage; And is capable to give no small disturbance to NOTRE Grand Monarque, as the french, even Refugiez, do frequently speake. They say he is sometimes as a man besides himself, to see the affaires of Italy go so. The courant yesterday, says, that theyl trust no more spaniards to keep any place of consideration.
I am, dear Sir, with due respects and Salutation from my wife self and family to yourself, and that honourable family
Your most humble servant and affectionate friend
BENJAMIN FURLY
