3043. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 19 November 1701 (3010, 3055)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 258 p. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 521-4. Answers no. 3010; answered by no. 3055.
(English)
Oates 19 Nov. 1701
Vir Amplissime
Gratissimam Epistolam tuam 14 Oct: datam legi relegique et te Auctore perlegi etiam Episcopii tractatum de Libero arbitrio. Non tam magnificè de me sentio ut audeam in tantorum virorum scriptis quicquam reprehendere: Fateor tamen nonnulla et in illius dissertatione et in tuâ Epistolâ occurrere quæ si coram tibi adessem, explicari a te peroptarem ut melius perspicere possem quomodo inter se et cum rei veritate consistere possint. Sed si singula quæ in hoc argumento†a in†a aliorum scriptis suboriri possunt dubia persequi velim, et pensiculatius ad trutinam revocare, in volumen abieret epistola: nec meum est aliorum opiniones convellere,
― 502 ―
(quarum ignarus in scribendo nec aliorum sententiam fugi, nec authoritatem secutus sum) sed solum mea cogitata quantum ex rebus ipsis perspicere possum rebus ipsis conformare. Hæc causa esse potest, quod inconsultis auctoribus, et mea mecum meditatus, terminis et loquendi formulis hoc in subjecto familiaribus non sum usus. Hoc mihi ignoscendum postulo.†1 Nec Episcopii acutissimi, cujus memoria summâ apud me in veneratione est, mentionem hic fecissem nisi te suasore tractatum ejus de libro arbitrio perlegissem quem tuum fecisti, tuamque per omnia sententiam continere mihi notum fecisses
(English) Hæc a me præfanda erant ne forsan videar aliorum scripta qui me in hoc argumento præcesserunt insolenter nimis negligere, vel non satis eorum authoritati tribuere. quod a meo animo et a meâ mediocritate et est et esse debet remotissimum. Fateor ego non sector nomina sed ubique veritati litans, eam quacunque ducit unice sequor: ideoque gratias tibi ago maximas quod me ubi errasse existimas in viam reducere conaris
(English) Primum et præcipuum quod in novissimâ hâc tuâ Epistolâ culpare videris est mea definitio Libertatis quam dicis nimis esse angustam. An tua laxior est quam illa quam ego L.2.c.xxi § 8. et 12 tradidi
― 503 ―
tum videbimus cum tu illam proferes. nam quod dicis Libertatem esse dominium quod homo habet in quamcunque suam actionem Hoc mihi non videtur esse definitionem Libertatis quum nihil aliud dicit nisi hominem habere dominium in actiones suas quod habet, quod huc tantum redit, Libertatem esse libertatem quam homo habet in quamcunque suam actionem; quo <evenire>†a potest ut nulla omnino sit hominis libertas, scis enim esse aliquos qui negant hominem ullum in actiones suas habere dominium, sed omnia præstituto et ineluctabili duci fato. Quod si dicas te supponere hominem habere dominium in actiones suas et in eo consistere Libertatem. Tunc rogo quid sit Dominium hominis in actiones suas. <Dominium>†b enim sive sit vox tralatitia sive ob aliquam aliam causam mihi videtur æque si non magis obscura quam vox Libertas, ideoque non minus eget definitione. Et sic pergam rogando donec perventum erit ad simplices Ideas ex quibus conflatur Idea Libertatis
(English) Video ex hac tua Epistola quanta sit vis consuetudinis, et quâ constantiâ non cogitantibus, etiam et invitis irrepit. Fateris, et candidè fateris, Voluntatem esse animæ facultatem, et facultates non esse Agentes: et tamen, ut alia omittam, hic dicis Si mea Libertatis definitio agnoscatur certum est Libertatem nullo modo competere
― 504 ―
voluntati, Voluntati enim nullomodo competere potest Libertas nisi pro Agente agnoscatur. Quippe Agentium solummodo est Libertas. Scio te Episcopii exemplo posse teipsum excusare, qui in principio dissertationis suæ strenuè rejiciens Facultatum operationes subinde tamen relabitur in argumentationes quibus supponuntur Agentes. permitte tamen ut amice moneam nisi hoc maxime caveas multum in hâc materia tibi facesses negotium, et tenebras sæpissime tibi offundes
(English) Ad reliqua de quibus dubitare videris ne in longitudinem molemque nimiam extendatur responsio rectius me et compendiosius satisfacturum credo si aliquas hic illic capiti xxi inseram explicationes quibus animi mei sensum negligentius forsan vel obscurius traditum clariorem reddam, adeo ut festinanti etiam, uti fit, lectori in posterum pateat, modo quæ tradita sunt memoriâ tenere non dedignetur.†1 Hæc cum Tu attente perlegeris et cum reliquis quæ in isto capite exposui contuleris plene tibi satisfactum iri spero. Quod si quæ postea tibi remanserint dubia et aliqua restant quæ vel obscura nimis, quorum te fugit sensus, vel parum veritati congrua quibus assensum præbere non potes, moneas rogo, ut aut te
― 505 ―
auctore corrigam, aut ulterius explicando, veritatem suâ propriâ luce nitentem tibi ante oculos ponam
(English) Si qua sunt in Epistolâ tuâ ad quæ non satis distinctè responsum a me credas, ignoscas rogo valetudini parum firmæ, quæ languidiorem me et ad scribendum minus aptum reddit. Quanquam spero ex annexis explicationibus†1 ex quibus mentem meam percipies perspicuum tibi fore quid ad singulas dubitationes tuas respondi possit. Vale vir Optime et ut facis me ama
Tui Studiosissimum
J LOCK
(Latin)
Oates 19 Nov. 1701
Excellent Sir,
I have read and reread your most welcome letter of 14 October, and at your suggestion have also read through Episcopius's treatise on Free Will. I do not think so magnificently of myself as to presume to find fault with anything in such great men's writings; I confess, however, that there occur some things both in his dissertation and in your letter that, were I present with you, I should earnestly wish you to explain, so that I could better discern how they can consist with one another and with the truth of the thing. But if I should wish to pursue the several doubts which can arise in other men's writings on this subject, and to reweigh them more exactly, the letter would turn into a volume; nor is it my way to confute other men's suppositions (unacquainted with them, I have in writing neither avoided other men's opinions nor followed [p. 501] their authority), but only to conform my thoughts, so far as I can discern from the things themselves, to the things themselves. This, my not consulting authors and my having made my reflections for myself, may be the reason why I have not used terms and expressions that are in common use on this subject. I ask to be forgiven for this.†1 Nor should I have mentioned here the very acute Episcopius, whose memory I hold in the highest respect, if I had not, on your recommendation, read through his treatise on free will, a treatise which you have made your own and which, you have informed me, throughout contains your opinion.
(Latin) These things were to be premised by me lest perhaps I should seem too arrogantly to disregard the writings of other men who have preceded me on this subject, or not to concede enough to their authority; which is, and ought to be, very far from my mind and from my mediocrity. I confess that I do not pursue names, but everywhere paying service to truth follow it alone wherever it leads; I therefore thank you greatly for endeavouring to bring me back to the path when you think I have gone astray.
(Latin) What you seem first and foremost to find fault with in this latest letter of yours is my definition of 'Liberty', which you say is 'too narrow'. When you produce yours we shall see whether it is wider than that which I have given in bk. II, ch. xxi, §§ 8 and 12. For when you say that 'Liberty is the dominion [p. 502] that a man has over any of his actions' this does not seem to me to be a definition of Liberty, since it says nothing other than that a man has the dominion over his actions which he has, which only comes back to this, that Liberty is the liberty which a man has over any action of his; from which it can follow that a man has no liberty whatsoever, for as you know there are some men who deny that a man has any dominion over his actions, but [hold] that all things are governed by predetermined and ineluctable fate. But if you say that you suppose that a man has dominion over his actions and that Liberty consists therein, then I ask what the Dominion of a man over his actions may be. For Dominion, whether it be a figurative word or for some other reason, seems to me just as obscure as the word Liberty, if not more so, and therefore not less to need definition. And thus I shall keep on questioning until the simple ideas, from which the Idea of Liberty is composed, are reached.
(Latin) I see from this letter of yours how great is the force of custom and how constantly it steals in upon the unthinking, even against their wills. You acknowledge, and you acknowledge candidly, that the Will is a faculty of the soul and that faculties are not Agents: and yet, to omit other things, you say here, 'If my [sc. Locke's] definition of Liberty is approved it is certain that Liberty in no way [p. 503] appertains to the will', for Liberty can in no way appertain to the Will unless the Will is recognized as an Agent. Inasmuch as Liberty belongs only to Agents. I know that you can excuse yourself by the example of Episcopius who, at the beginning of his dissertation strenuously rejecting operations by Faculties, nevertheless now and then falls back into reasonings in which they are supposed to be Agents. Allow me, however, to give you a friendly warning that, unless you are very careful, you will cause yourself much trouble in this matter, and very often obscure it for yourself.
(Latin) As regards the remaining things about which you seem to be in doubt, lest the reply should extend to too great length and bulk I think that I shall give satisfaction better and more compendiously by inserting here and there in chapter xxi some explications by which I may make my meaning clearer where it is set down perhaps rather negligently or obscurely, so that it may in future be plain to the reader, even if, as happens, he is in a hurry, provided that he does not disdain keeping in mind what has been set down.†1 I hope that you will be fully satisfied when you have read them through heedfully and have compared them with the rest of what I have set forth in that chapter. But if any doubts remain for you after that, and if any things are left to which you cannot give assent as being either too obscure, so that the meaning escapes you, or too little agreeable to truth, please inform me, [p. 504] so that either I may correct them on your suggestion or by explaining them further set before your eyes Truth shining in its proper light.
(Latin) If there are in your letter any things that you think I have not answered clearly enough, please make allowance for uncertain health, which renders me more languid and less fit for writing. Though I hope that from the annexed explications,†1 from which you will understand my meaning, it will be clear to you what answers can be made to your several dubitations. Good-bye, best of men, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCK

3045. Dr. Robert Pitt to Locke, 22 November 1701 (3024, 3057)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 169-70. For comment see Clark, Royal College of Physicians, ii. 463-4.
Nov. 22. 1701.
Sir
I apprehend, that you will be fully acquainted with the circumstance of our Affairs, when I assure you, that all the Squabbles among the members of the College (against their new statutes, officers, punishments, as of one in 7 or 8 Years) have no other foundation, <then>†d that that Anti College Party recommended themselves to the Apothecarys favour and Interest and consequently to the Publick, by obliging them in betraying the Profession to their incroachments for the present profitt. I confess, the
― 508 ―
greater part of the Nob. and Gentry etc. has been prevail'd on by so many Ap. and one half almost of the College to the prejudice of the Society.†1 About 20 Phys. of the Town have lately defy'd the College, when invited into its Fellowship. The pretence was the support of the University licence per totam Angliam; the true design to declare on the Apothecary's side. This Cause came to tryal before my Lord Cheif Justice Holt this week: who declar'd in the College Favour, that every Practicer of the Town is oblig'd to the College Examination and Licence.†2 The City begins to be sensible of the true state of the Case; and very many of the best Families, as well as many thousands of the meaner, have experienc'd, that many diseases are cur'd with few medicines, that ours are beyond exception, and that no profitt will ever be made on that Part. They observ, that even from the Poor, the Apothecary has greater profitt, then the Faculty from the Rich: That 90 in 100£ (of which bills we have had in the City very many lately) were the fees to the Ap. when the Phys. probably had 8 or 10 in his Fees. Those Expressions in the Papers can only be excus'd from the great provocations some time since given, by Lampoons, and the basest Characters industriously spread on every Member of the Dispensary: when nothing had been publish't but the first book of the transaction before the Committee of Aldermen. Besides, you are sensible of the humour of the Age, that a Contest of this Nature cannot be manag'd without coming in a little time to these Extremities. We are publishing an Account of the value and price of all the Medicines; leav it to the Publick to determine the profitt to be allow'd, and do only demand, that the Ap. be separately consider'd for his trouble of Attendance. Upon these Terms, we are satisfy'd, the People will apply for advice to the Physician, who has no end to interfere with the Cure of his Patient. I desire the favour of your Opinion, if you can recollect any thing, which may assist the most generous Design of this Age. We shall, as in Consultation, readily close with a Proposal supported with your Reasons. You will, as the General, judge better, being out of the
― 509 ―
Fray and your Orders will be as readily observ'd. Sir, At your leisure I hope you will oblige
Your most humble servant
ROB. PITT
Address: For Mr John Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: NO 22
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Pitt 22. Nov. 01 Answered. Dec 10
3046. John Lock (later Sir John) to Locke, 23 November 1701 (2716, 3136)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 176-7. Forwarded by Samuel Locke on 30 September 1702: p. 682; received by Locke on 6 October: Journal. I have failed to trace the voyage to Amoy or to identify Lock's ship. On this voyage he appears to have been a supercargo, i.e. the Company's representative on board for its trading venture, making all negotiations for the sale of the cargo and purchases of country goods, and dealing with customs officers, etc.; he would also be allowed to make a private venture. For the supercargoes in the China trade see Morse, East India Company trading to China, i. 66-77; above, no. 2224.
Honourable Sir
Since you were pleased to Honour mee with the Favour of a Letter to Surat, I esteem it a Priviledge given mee to write you from the remotest Parts my fortune Leads mee to, and should make use of it much oftener if my education and Imployments, which has bin from the School, with Merchants and Merchandizing, were able to furnish mee with such discoveries as has escaped the notice of those who have made it their peculiar business to search into the Pollicy, Religion, Goverment, and the products of these Forreigne countryes, which is difficult for mee to doe that goe noe deaper than a Sea Port, and am conversant constantly with people of my owne profession and the greatest part of my Time imploy'd in the disposeal of what I bring, and procureing effects proper for another market, but since I write to a person of soe great worth and soe well acquainted, how mankind coms to gather all their knowledge of these things, I shall not seek for further matter to troble you with then what I find in my dayly imployment
I come from Surat in the Service of his Excellency Sir William Norris his Majesties Embassador to the Great Mogull and Sir
― 510 ―
Nicholas Wait his Consull at Surat, with a ship of the Natives burthen 400 Tons, sailed by an English Comander and Officers, and Laschars or blackfellows, their wages and hyre of the Ship for 12 months with the Bottomry of what mony was advanced for her outsett will amount to 25731 Rupees which is 64 Rupees per Ton, A Europe Ship of that Burthen for 12 months, at the usual Demorage†1 the Companies pay is £9 Stg. per Ton at 27 Pence per Rupee, is Rupees 80 per Ton, soe that there is Lost by imploying a Europe Ship 16 Rupees or 36 Shillings in every Ton.
The Goods I brought from Surat were Putchuck,†2 Olibanum, Mirh, Cominseed, Cotton, and Pearle, all which renders good Proffit, especially Cotton sold for above 100 per Cent. but being very bulky noe great value can bee brought of it, and Pearle gives 30 per Cent if bought well, for the most part 2/3 of the Ships Stock is in Dollars†3 or other Silver.
Comodities proper for Surat, are Copper as much as can bee procured, formerly Quicksilver and Vermillion, but now not demanded, Sugar, Sugar Candy, Tutenegue,†4 Camphire, China Ware, and Gold, which last when it is at touch for touch,†5 and 100 waters,†6 that is full fine, 1 Tale of Gold is worth just 10 Tale†7 of Dollar Silver, but usually there is allow'd 3 or 4 waters, according to the demand for it.
At our first arrival wee agree with the Hoppo†8 or Custom Master for the Ships Messurage,†9 which with Presents, houserent, and Linguister†10 hyre, for the Ship I come in will come to 1500 Tale†11 or £500 Stg. and to purchase the foregoing Comodities, are obliged to trust the Merchants with most of our Mony and Goods and
― 511 ―
often are very dillatory in our dispatch, tho am now in hopes to Leave this Port in 3 or 4 days
The Trade from Surat to China is at Present the most proffitable, and by a modest Computation beleive may cleer 55 per Cent. for my Imployers which will bee neer £7000 Stg. when am engaged in any other Voyage I shall take the freedom I doe now to give you a short Account of it, presuming what is Proffitable to private Merchants here, is an encrease of Riches to the Nation, which being so, you that are one of the Protectors of our Comerce, and Love to nourish the Least branches of it, will not bee displeased with what may bee offerd, from
Honourable Sir
your Most Obedient Servant
JOHN LOCK
Amoy in China 23th November 1701.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Locke 23 Nov. 01 Answered 11 May. 03

3054. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 21 December 1701/1 January 1702 (2959, 3155)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, f. 103.
d'amst. ce 1 janv. 1702
Monsieur,
Je recu hier vótre agreable du 13 dec. qui nous a beaucoup resjoui, je venois de donner un mot de lettre a Monsieur Limburgh pour vous dire que j'attendois votre reponce, et que nous nous informions de toutes parts de vótre santé. je vous diray que je traitte presentement un fameu marchand de cette ville agé de 63 ans, qui depuis quelques annees, presque a toutes les entrées de l'hyver, est atteint d'un herpes pustuleux au cuisses et au jambes. auparavant il estoit fort subject a la gravelle, il a méme eté taillé, il y a seize ans par Monsieur Cyprianus. apres m'étre servi pendant un mois de plusieurs remedes internes et externes, avec peu de succes, j'y ay enfin fait appliquer l'Empl. ranarum cum Mercurio, qui en peu de jours a dissipé tout. je n'ay pas le moindre soubson d'aucune cause venerienne; mais jay du penchant de croire que ces maux sont accompagnez de Vermine que le Mercure tue. il boit une decoction de chine et prend deux fois la sepmaine d'un melange de Cassia, rheum et mercur. dulc. jay souvant gueri des personnes foibles de la verole par ces seules emplastrations couchez sur les bras, le long de l'épine, les cuisses et les jambes sans y joindre aucun autre remede qu'une decoction de salseparille ou semblables. cela fait venir le flu de bouche lentement, et sans peril. il faut confesser que le Mercure a une grande vertu, soit pour tuer toute sorte de vermine, soit pour adoucir nos humeurs. ma pratique, qui augmente tous les jours, est un grand obstacle a ce que j'ay commencé d'escrire touchant l'œconomie animale,†1 outre que ce que nous en scavons est fort imparfait. jay besoin de plusieurs recherches pour lesquelles jay peu de loisir. toute la famille vous presente ses tres humbles respects, et vous souhaitte un prompt retablissement d'une parfaitte santé, pour cette nouvelle année, et les autres, quil plaise a Dieu de vous accorder. monsieur Veen est souvent pris de son crachement de sang, et devient foible. ma femme continue a se bien porter. et nos enfans font assez bien (grace a Dieu). tout le monde commence a avoir meilleure opinion des affaires publique, et si ce nouveau parlement entre vigoureusement
― 518 ―
dans l'interest commun, on croit pouvoir abaisser la france. Je suis avec le dernier respect,
Votre tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON

3055. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 23 December 1701/3 January 1702 (3043, 3128)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, f. 149. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, f. 219. Printed from the copy in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 525-8. Answers no. 3043; answered by no. 3192.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Quod lectionem tractatus Episcopii de libero arbitrio tibi commendaverim, id eo fine non feci, ut viri illius autoritate contra te utar: Nihil minus: Scio enim in sincerâ veritatis inquisitione nullam valere autoritatem humanam, sed tantum momenta rationum quibus veritas adstruitur. Nec ego, licet Episcopii sententiam approbem, vellem illius autoritate constringi, ut omnia, etiam quæ salvâ principali veritate in dubium vocari possunt, admittam, nedum phrasibus ac loquendi formulis ab ipso usurpatis alligari me patiar. Sed illius legendi tibi autor fui, ut ex illo cognosceres, nos jam à multo tempore renuntiasse illi sententiæ, quæ statuit animam intermediis facultatibus agere; sed asseruisse tecum, animam immediatè per seipsam intelligere ac velle. Unde cognoscere posses, quando communem loquendi usum secuti utimur vocibus
― 519 ―
Intellectus et Voluntatis, nos iis non intelligere facultates realiter ab animâ distinctas, sed ipsas intelligendi ac volendi actiones, quas anima immediatè ex seipsâ elicit. Hoc ego etiam brevioribus verbis significatum dedi in Theologiâ meâ Christianâ, lib. II. cap. XXIII. § 1, 2. Itaque si per incogitantiam ex inveteratâ consuetudine mihi forte exciderit, voluntatem esse liberam, rogo ut id meo sensu accipias, ac si dixissem, actio volendi est libera, seu, homo in eliciendâ actione volendi est liber: Ac proinde pro verbis meis, Si tua libertatis definitio admittatur,†a certum est libertatem nullo modo competere voluntati, hæc substituas, certum est actionem volendi neutiquam esse liberam; seu, hominem non liberè velle. Gratias interim tibi ago, quod inconsideratam hanc meam locutionem mihi indicaveris: ego annitar, ut in posterum omnem ambiguam locutionem vitem, et ab inolitâ loquendi consuetudine non abripiar, ne ulla in verbis meis sit obscuritas.
(English) Libertatem ego definivi per dominium in actiones. Quia vox Dominii tibi explicatione indigere videtur, simplicius dico, libertatem esse facultatem hominis actionen suam vel eliciendi, vel non eliciendi. Qui alterutrum tantum potest, non est liber. Per actionem autem ego intelligo actionem quamcunque, etiam actiones internas intelligendi ac volendi. Circa quascunque actiones non habet homo hanc facultatem
― 520 ―
eas vel eliciendi, vel non eliciendi, sed alterutrum tantum potest, eæ non sunt liberæ. Et quia illi hanc facultatem tribuo circa actiones volendi, ideo eas liberas voco: quando hac facultate homo destitutus est, libere nec vult, nec velle potest.
(English) Utinam facultas esset coram tecum de omnibus his disserendi, et ex ore tuo pleniorem omnium circa quæ hæsito explanationem audiendi, meamque sententiam ac loquendi phrases distinctè explicandi, non dubito, quin fœlicius totam hanc quæstionem terminare possemus. Nunc etiam circa ea, quæ explicationis gratiâ addidisti, hæsito, an statuas, judicium illud, quo formato non amplius in homine libertas est non volendi, sit actio mera intelligendi, eaque intelligendi actio sit libera, vel necessaria. Si in eâ eliciendâ hominem liberum agnoscas, non video quis inter nos, quod†a ad†a summam rei, maneat dissensus. Sed coram possemus hæc distinctius et exactius expendere: idque maximè percuperem, ut uterque in hac materiâ quantâ fieri potest perspicuitate nos expliceamus, et difficultatibus hinc inde oborientibus occurramus. Nunc quoniam id utriusque ætas neutiquam permittit, quæ misisti, semper quando de hac materiâ ago consulam, ne aut ipse errem, aut aliis inconsideratâ loquendi ratione errandi occasionem præbeam. Vale, Vir
― 521 ―
Amplissime. Salutat te uxor ac filia, D. Clericus, omnesque prosperam tibi precamur valetudinem. Generoso Domino Masham gratulamur continuatam dignitatem: Illi, ut et Dominæ Masham, totique familiæ ut annus hic ex voto fluat precamur.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS À LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 3 Januarii
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I did not recommend to you the reading of Episcopius's treatise on Free Will in order to use his authority against you: by no means: for I know that in the sincere search for truth no human authority is valid, but only the weight of the reasons on which truth is established. Nor, though I approve Episcopius's opinion, should I be willing to be so fettered by his authority as to admit all things, even those that can be called in question without prejudice to the most important truth; much less would I suffer myself to be bound by the phrases and expressions used by him. But I suggested your reading it so that you might learn from it that we [sc. the Remonstrants] have now long since renounced that opinion that held that the soul acts through intermediate faculties; but have affirmed with you that the soul understands and wills immediately of itself. Whence you could learn that when, following the common way of speaking, we use the words Understanding and Will we [p. 518] do not understand by them faculties distinct in fact from the soul, but the actions themselves of understanding and willing, which the soul elicits immediately from itself. I have also given this signification more briefly in my Theologia Christiana, bk. II, ch. xxiii, §§ 1, 2. If then, from inveterate custom 'that the will is free' has through inadvertence perhaps escaped me, please take it in my sense, as if I had said that the action of willing is free, or rather that a man is free in eliciting the action of willing: and accordingly for my words 'If your [sc. Locke's] definition of liberty is admitted "it is certain that liberty in no way appertains to the will"' please substitute 'it is certain that the action of willing is in no wise free', or rather 'that a man does not will freely'. Meanwhile I thank you for having pointed out to me this unadvised form of expression of mine; I shall strive in future to avoid all ambiguous forms of expression, and not to be carried away by an inbred custom of speaking lest there should be any obscurity in my words.
(Latin) I have defined liberty as dominion over actions. Since the word Dominion seems to you to need explication I say more simply that liberty is a man's faculty of eliciting, or not [p. 519] eliciting, his action. He who can do only the one or the other is not free. Moreover by action I understand any action whatsoever, even the internal actions of understanding and willing. If in respect of any actions whatsoever a man does not have this faculty of eliciting, or not eliciting, them, but can do only the one or the other, they are not free. And because I attribute to him this faculty in respect of actions of willing, therefore I call them free: when a man is destitute of this faculty he neither wills nor can will freely.
(Latin) Would that there were an opportunity of discussing all these things with you face to face, and of hearing from your lips a fuller explanation of everything abouth wich I am uncertain, and of clearly setting forth my opinion and manner of speaking; I do not doubt that we could terminate this whole inquiry more fruitfully. Now, even regarding those things that you have added by way of explication, I am uncertain whether you hold that that judgement, after whose formation there is no longer in a man liberty of not willing, is purely an action of understanding, and whether you hold that that action of understanding is free or necessary. If you recognize that a man is free in eliciting it I do not see what disagreement remains between us as to the chief point of the matter. But we could have pondered these things more precisely and carefully when face to face; and that I should most of all have desired in order that we might each of us explain himself about this matter with as much perspicuity as possible, and meet the difficulties arising here and there. Now, since the age of neither of us permits that, I shall always consult what you have sent when I am dealing with this matter, lest I should either go astray myself or give others occasion to do so through an unadvised way of speaking. Good-bye, excellent Sir. My wife and daughter and Mr. [p. 520] Le Clerc send greetings; and we all pray for your good health. We congratulate Sir Francis Masham on his continuance in office. We pray that for him, as also for Lady Masham and the whole family, this year may pass as they could wish.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 3 January
1702

3057. Dr. Robert Pitt to Locke, 27 December 1701 (3045, 3064)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 171-2.
Dec. 27. 1701.
Sir,
I defer'd Answering your Last: that I might give you a more distinct Account of the present state of the Faculty. The College had lately Judgment against Dr Levitt, who asserted the University licence over England against the College Act of Parliament, which obliges all Practicers in London to the Examination and allowance of our Society.†1 The University Gentlemen will not acquiesce, but intend to petition for an Act, to what purposes we cannot yet learn. This will make the whole affair publick, and make the design of the Dispensary better understood. But, not to trouble you with the repetition of many particulars in the Papers, the stress of the Affair lies, I presume, in this. That the Ap. being a Thousand,†2 and having 1500 Prentices, will invade all Practice to be able to live, will price the Medicines, forct†a in all Cases every hour, excessively. The People will stick close to the Apothecary, to avoid the expence of a Physician. The Ap. increasing now upon that exorbitant number will ruine the practice here, and afterward in all parts of England. The Fr. reduc't them by publishing the Medecin Charitable printed 100 times in 30 years,†3 by informing the Families with the usual forms of Medicine, and a Catalogue of all the Simples pric'd, to make them judges of the very low rates of the most usefull. They saw the expence of the Cure was very little more then the fees. Dr Patin†4 and Dr Guibert added 2 or 3 discourses of the fourbery and tromperie of Bezoar,†5 Perle, and
― 523 ―
the Pretious Stones and Gold etc. We are now preparing a discourse of that Kind accommodated to the present Practice.†1 The Town begins to be sensible, that all the Reputation has been lately given the Eminent Phys. by the Ap. as he in return complements the Ap. with a licence ad practicandum in Every Chamber. The Favour of your Judgment, which I hope will agree with that of my Lord Ch. J. Holt will lay the greatest obligation (tho to be own'd only to your self) on
Your most humble servant
R PITT
Address: For Mr John Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: DE 27 (?)
Endorsed by Locke: R: Pitt 27 Dec. 01 Answered Jan.
3058. Locke to Edward Clarke, 28 December 1701 (3025, 3078)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 155. Printed in Rand, p. 583.
Oates 28 Dec 01
Dear Sir
Yours of the 13th I received not till this day seventh night and the other which you mention to have writ me about the begining of November I received not at all. Had it come to my hands I should not have failed to have said something about the smal pox which that letter would have told me was got into your house. But god be thanked all has gon well, and I congratulate to you that the danger and trouble of that disease is well over. I made noe more hast to return my thanks to you for your last Since if I had writ the very next day my letter might have gon farther but would have come to your hands noe sooner For Sir Francis and my Cosin King make account to finde you in town to morrow and I should be very sorry if you should fail them.†2 I am sorry to finde you complain of want of strength. Bestir you self and you will find you have it.
― 524 ―
Crede quod habes et habes†1 and all is but little enough in the present state of Europe and England Though if the latter will exert it self as it ought I think much may be donne. I hope you left <Mrs.>†a Clarke and my wife well pray give them my service when you write. I am and have been for some time under the disorder of a very great cold which very much indisposes me for every thing, even writeing it self. only you may be assured that I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate and most humble servant
J LOCKE
Endorsed by Clarke: Mr Locke's Letter Received the 29th. December 1701/2.
3059. Peter King, later first Baron King, to Locke, 30 December 1701 (3051, 3060)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 160-1. Answered by no. 3060.
London Decemb. 30. 1701.
Sir
I got safe hither Yesterday about six a clock in the Evening, and†b- then delivered to Mr Churchill the bond that I brought from oates,-†b I heartily thank you for the favours done me at Oates — The King came to the house this day, and only Ordered the Commons to choose their Speaker, and to attend him again too morrow, when he would signify the causes of his calling this present parliament. There was a very full house, Sir Thomas Littleton was first proposed, and on the division of the house,
There were for him—212
against him—216
So that he lost it by four voices, and then Mr Harley carried it without a division; What the Consequences of this will be God only knows—Severals of our friends were in the Country, when they should have been here. My Humble service to My Lady with my Renewed thanks for her repeated favours—I am—
Sir Your most Humble and most affectionate Cosin and Servant.
P. KING.

3060. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 2 January 1702 (3059, 3061)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 189-90. Answers no. 3059.
Oates 2 Jan 01/2
Dear Cosin
I was in pain what journey you might have till the receit of your letter. I was very glad to be assured that you were landed safe. The loiterers will have more to answer for than they think if I mistake not mightily. Ladys desires you know are raised by Novelty and delay. My Lady is therefor very impatient to see the Kings speech. My indisposition of health spoils my curiosity. Have a care of your health. enjoy your self, doe all the good you can, beyond this I have not foresight enough to advise adieu
Yours
J L
All here greet you. pray when your man has a minutes leisure let him cary the inclosed to Mr Churchils

3062. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 8 January 1702 (3061, 3066)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 193-4. Answered by no. 3066.
Oates 8 Jan 01/2
Dear Cosin
Your two of the 3d and 6th I received not till last night. I should be sorry this delay should make us loose a good security. I think I formerly acquainted you at least I doe now that in business of hast you should direct your letters to be left for me with Mr Harrison at the Crown in Harlow: and then I shall have them next morning.
As to the business you propose if you like the man and his security my money is ready and you have but to send me word how much you shall want to make up what you have of mine in your hands £3000 and I will send you a bill payable at sight and this you shall be sure of, whether the Dorsetshire Mortgage be paid in Monday next or noe. this I tell you that that may not disturb this business if it should fail to be paid as you expect
― 527 ―
I have for some days past been miserably tormented with a violent pain in one of my ears. I am at present I thank god at some ease, but whether it will return again I know not. I am Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin
J LOCKE
My Lady and all here greet you well

3063. Awnsham Churchill to Locke, [8 January 1702] (3052, 3082) and Dr. Alexander Geekie to Locke, 8 January 1702 (3073)
B.L., MSS. Locke c. 5, f. 164, and c. 9, f. 213. The two letters appear to have been written on a single sheet of paper, and torn apart by Locke. The date of Churchill's letter from that of Geekie's and from Locke's note. Alexander Geekie, d. 1727, surgeon, is said to have been descended from 'a Neice of Inigo Jones in Somerset' (presumably Anne, wife of John Webb the architect; D.N.B.) and owned Vandyck's portrait of Inigo (probably the painting later acquired by Sir Robert Walpole and now in the Hermitage). He was master of the Barber-Surgeons' Company in 1719-20. He married by about 1690 a sister of Awnsham Churchill and had a son William. He was elected F.R.S. in 1710. He was a subscriber to Kneller's academy in 1711 and owned seven portraits by him, including one of Locke (pp. 754-5; later belonging to Sir Robert Walpole and now in the Hermitage), two of himself, and one of his brother (perhaps Awnsham Churchill). His son William, c. 1690-1767, graduated D.D. at Cambridge in 1729 and was a prebendary of Canterbury from 1731: Vertue, Note Books, i. 33, 134: v. 62; vi. 168; S. Young, Barber-Surgeons, pp. 11, 418; Historical Register, vol. xii for 1727, 'Diary', p. 27; etc.
[Churchill:]
Sir
I gott well home and I returne you and my Lady Masham many thankes for the many favours I received at oates, and I begg youl present her with my humble service, and to madam Masham, both Mr Mashams,†1 and mr Coste. My Brother Geekye has on the other side sent you his opinion about the payn in your eare, which I told him off. I saw the Bishop of Norwich†2 this
― 528 ―
day. who enquired for your Wellfare and I told him of the payn of your eare, he recomends to you a Blister behind your eare, he says he has known it aplyed to children with great success; I asked my Brother Geekie his thoughts of a Blister, but he thinkes it not safe for you to venture on.
Sir I am
Your assurd Servant at Comand
A. CHURCHIL
I expect and hope to hear of your amendment and perfect health†a
Address: For John Locke Esquire at Sir Fra. Mashams at Oates. To be left at the Crowne Inn In Harloe Essex These
Endorsed by Locke: A Churchil 8 Jan 01/2
[Geekie:]
Sir
I am sorry to hear of that great pain in your Ear. Pray give me leave to offer a remedy that I have had some experience of and that is To take a large Onion and wrap it in a Colewort†1 leaf and roast it in the hott Embers. pick it clean and beat it in a Stone morter with Tuo drams of Methridat halfe an ounce of Unguentum Nervinum and as much pouder off Fenugreek seeds as is sufficient to make it into the consistence of a Poultis spread it pretty thick upon a lining rag broad enough to cover the whole Ear and as far as the pain reaches, First stop the hole of the Ear with black wool then warm the poultis and apply it. Le it ly on 48 houres then renew it if need be. Please to take 4 spoonfulls of Hungary water and ten of Spring water mix them in a viol and Gargle with it often 3 or 4 times a day. Sir your great candor will excuse the obtrudeing my advice and beleive it is only my hearty concern for your ease and welfair that has makes me more obleidging than discreet. I am
Sir
Your obleidged and most humble servant
A GEEKIE.
Jan: 8: 1701/2

3064. Dr. Robert Pitt to Locke, 8 January 1702 (3057, 3077)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 173-4.
Jan. 8. 1701.
Sir
I hope you may receiv advantage from the use of this Mixture apply'd on Wool to your Ears. Deafness is usually occasion'd by the want of the purging of the Sordes†1 of that part; is very frequently remov'd by the warmth of wool only. This Medicine has very lately had its effect on several complaining of the dullness of their hearing. ℞ Ol. Rutæ ℥i Ol. Nuc. Moschat. per Express. ʒs fl. Benzoin. ʒi. Ol. Juniper Chym. gutt. xxx. You may, while you read, apply a Funnell of strong Paper, or such like, to your Ear, and receiv from a narrow-mouth'd vessel the Fume of a Decoction of the warmr†a Plants in Water and Wine, which will at the same time soften the grosser humours and open the Passages of the Secretory Vessels.
Since I last writt to you, the young Physicians have laid aside their design of petitioning in Parliament, and are willing to come in to the College. They tell me, they are now sensible, that the Apothecaries growing more numerous must destroy the Profession, if they carry their point in Parliament. They are treating with Sir Th. Millington†2 about some advantages they pursue for themselves and the Universities: What success this Treaty will have I Know not. They are secure of the greatest services our Society can give 'em. I apprehend, the strongest Argument we can use in Parliament, or with the People must be taken from the cheapness of all the usefull Medicines, and the unhappy practice of directing too many, or too much divided in all Case. Sir I wish you a happy and healthfull New Year.
Your most humble servant
ROB. PITT

3065. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 8/19 January 1702 (3030, 3146)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 179-80. Answered by no. 3198.
Rotterdam 8/19 January 1701/2
Dear Sir
I received yours with relation to my son Arent, and find you agreed with me in my sentiments with respect to what he had in his ey, and your further good advice as to him, for which I return you, as bound, my hearty and humble thanks.
But his mind is so bent upon England, the Cuntry, the Aire, the Temper of the people, that he should delight to accompany with,†1 are so abundantly more agreable to him, that he cannot resolve to settle here, but by necessity,
And what most of all inclines him to become a member of that, rather than this Commonwealth, is the most valuable or rather unvaluable Rights and Priviledges of England and Englishmen, above all the earth besides; and their likelyhood, being an Island, to continue them, the longest—
And to say the right of it, who can blame him?
The late great change in England,†2 and hopes that it may go farther, and continue, makes me my self, now almost reconcileable to it.
I onely wayt to see what farther changes maybe made, my Lord Sh—,†3 mr. Clark, and mr. Popple have great hopes and do intend to consult their and my friends concerning it; if they should find ground to incourage me to send him over or to consult yourself about it,
I humbly crave your assistance in the Case, if nothing can be obtaind, that may look like a future settlement for him, he must be content, how much soever against his mind, to settle here.
I keep him to his writing and cyphering, and the cultivating the English Tongue mostly, and have begun to read your Essay with him.
His Greek, Latin and french we do consterve, and he reads Italian books with a tolerable understanding, and with Dr. Kolhans, who salutes you, he reads high Dutch.
― 531 ―
We are in great longing here to see the next post what way your Parlement goes, especially considering their having chosen the old speaker,†1 of whom so much was said last sessions: And that against the Kings recommendation, who, they say, has obligd Sir Ch: H. that trusty Trojan, to resign, because he would not vote for Sir T. L.†2
What discourages them here is further this. That the factions are so potent that it was carryed but by a majority of 4. Which had it falne on the right, that is the Kings, side, could have given but small incouragement.
I tell them, they are not to think that it will go so as to the grand affair of Europe. Or that mr. H. had not the vote of a great number of Antifrenchmen, who have all along bin satisfyed in his integrity, however it came about that he was so traduced, or suspected last sessions.
This goes by a grand nephew of mine Jonathan, the son of Jonathan Furly of Colchester—who is going to marrow a Grand daughter of old Colonel Riches the father of Sir Robert Rich, whose brothers daughter he now goes to marry, she lives neare Chelmsford;†3 perhaps he will deliver it with his own hand. Time prevents me, the tide calling him away, and so with dearest respects to your self and that whole honourable family I rest in hast
Sir
your most humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
P.S. Just now comes a friend in with good news from Italy, viz. That Mantua capitulates with Prince Eugenius, but he will not without first communicating the Articles to the Emperour to whom the Duke of Mantua has sent an Ambassadour—
My thinks I see france sinking as fast, if not faster than ever Spain
― 532 ―
did. If we be not chous'd into a Treaty with the perfidious Wretch at last.
Arent tenders his humble service to you, and the rest of that honourable family
Address (written by an amanuensis): For John Locke Esquire At Sir Francis Masham's Member of Parliament At Oates Near Bishopstarford In Essex
Postmark: IA 20
Endorsed by Locke: B Furly 19 Jan. 01/2 Answered Oct. 12
3066. Peter King, later first Baron King, to Locke, 10 January 1702 (3062, 3070)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 162-3. Answers no. 3062; according to the endorsement Locke answered this letter on the 17th; nothing in his extant letter of that date (no. 3072) refers to it specifically.
London January 10. 1701.
Sir
I Received Yours by Yesterdays post but have not since talk'd with my friend about the Morgage I writ you, by the next you shall hear farther from me about that matter—Yesterday in a Committee of the whole house about 400 present, The several alliances made by the King were read, and the Quota's of the allies as to Land force being left to a Subsequent treaty—The Secretary†1 acquainted us, that the King and his allies were likewise come to a Conclusion about that, and that the King only wanted the approbation of the house to confirm it, That the
Quota for the Emperour was 90000
for Holland 102000
For England 40000 whereof 33000 was to be foot and 7000 horse and Dragoons,
after which the Committee resolved Nemine Contradicente
That the Proportion of the Land forces to act in Conjunction with the forces of the allys for making good the alliances should be 40000 men consisting of 33000 foot and 7000 horse.
― 533 ―
And then as to The Fleet they afterwards resolved with the same Unanimity
That 40000 men be Imployed in the sea service for the year 1702.
That for the maintaining the said 40000 men for 13 months four pounds per mensem shall be allowed for each seaman including the Ordnance for the sea service
These Resolutions were agreed unto this day by the house, and I hope we Shall now proceed on Vigorously and Unanimously to save our selves and Country from the growing power of France— I am—
Sir
Your most affectionate Cosin and Servant.
P. KING

Honoured Cousin
Sir your of the 3d per Instant I Received, It has been my Ceare To Know when Orenges came To Towne, but non good before this week, which I did purpose To send you This day If you had not sent, I give you my hearty thanks for your Kind Expretions to me and mine, The God of Heaven multiply his marcÿes upon you, A Thousand fould, I have sent by Lenham This day half a Hundred of Orenges They are The best as Could be bought, I hope you will find Them soe, Deare Cousin, It is A Hearty and A freewill, but A small Token, be pleased to Axept of it, God Grant They may doe you much Good, Allsoe I remember you desired to Know the name of the man that gott your books out of the weare house, His name Is George Hand, he Live In Checker yard In High-Street, neare Aldgate, Consirning our Account, If you pleas to send, me

Cousin your Faithfull Kinsman and Humble Servant,

3068. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 10 January [1702] (2712, 3231)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, f. 167. Year from Locke's endorsement. The letter perhaps accompanied no. 3069.
Jan the 10 1710
I thank you deare brother for thinking it long enough that we have suffer'd our old Amicable way of treating each other to be disturb'd, how I treated you in my last I have forgot but I never yet lost the memory of Your first friendship which made you allways substantially kind and very truely concern'd for me, and my son, whose wellfair you so tenderly regarded even in his childhood that you purchaz'd his heart so erly, that I honestly assure you that no man living has a greater share in it than yourself, nor has any want of a real sense of your concern for him, occassion'd his keeping at a distance from you; but to speak truely he is modest to a fault, and till he can conquer this excess (which few are guilty of) he will never be so kind to himself as you and I would have him: I am sure if the greatest honour for you or his having a most gratfull heart could bring him as often to you as you please you would have noe time to blame his being as a stranger to you, I am the more
― 535 ―
sory that he is so, because I find that he grows dayly more of his excellent fathers temper, and much belovd by all that converse with him, As for his Pupils they seeme intirely his, and for your comfort Sir (who recomended them) I assure you no Young Gentlemen in this place are more respected upon all accounts, and this prospurous care of my son will I hope make him very chearfull; and continue to him the kindness of those familys he endevours so faithfully to make happy. This deare brother were saying too much were I not writting to you who have so much right to know all that may give you joy of one I know you love. I will not tell you how well my being very near Jesus Coll:†1 agrees with me, nor how Easyly I live where I can dayly see what is so very deare to me, and so like to answer Your kind wishes. Pardon me this freedom not only because tis seldom that I am thus employ'd but because I am just as you deserve I should be
Your most affectionate sister and most humble servant
A: GRIGG
I wish you also many very happy and Peacefull yeares
honest W G has not seen this which would not be so full of faults if my Wits were not clouded by a Cold
Address: For Mr Locke
Endorsed by Locke: A. Grigg 10 Jan 01/2
3069. William Grigg to Locke, 10 January 1702 (1883, 3145)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 182-3.
Cambridge Jan: 10th 1701/2
Sir,
Your's of the first instant I reciev'd by yesterday's Post and take this first Opportunity of acknowledging the favor. I am asham'd I have not waited on you and should be more so if I had not something to offer which I hope you will allow of as an Excuse. The Proctor is this year of our College and they have made me his deputy, so that I have been oblig'd to constant attendance on the Exercise in the schools. I readily embrace the proffer you make
― 536 ―

3071. James Tyrrell to Locke, 15 January [1702] (2975, 3076)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 146-7. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London Jan: 15
Dear Sir
Tho' I have hitherto contented my self since I came to Towne with onely making Inquiry after your health from Mr: Pawling and Sir Fran: Masham, and was much concernd to hear it was not in so good a Condition, as in the Autumne, yet if I omitted to express my concerne for that misfortune by writing, it was out of no other Consideration, then that I feard letters without any other business might prove rather a trouble then satisfaction to you in the state you were in; but since I heard farther†a by Sir Francis, that you were much indisposed with a great Pain in your Ear that disturbed your Rest. I am so sensible of that affliction having bin much troubled with it my self in my youth, that I think it my duty to tell you some Remedies that I found did me good in that distemper: the first I tried was the Juice of Rew, some drops of which being squeez'ed into about a spoonfull of woemans milk warmed,
― 538 ―
was powred into my ear and some of the small sprigs of the same herb lightly put in after it when I went to bed, and it gave me ease before morning. at another time I tried with like success a large Onyon rosted in the Embers, till it was soft, and then it was put in a peice of old linnen, and clapt as hot to my ear as I could well indure it, I lying on that side when I went to sleep. a third Remedy was a peice of new bread, made very hot at the Fire, and some warm Brandy or Aquævita being powred upon it was applyed to the Ear after the same manner as the o'nyon; which allso gave me ease; but if the bread have Rye in it, 'twill be the better. If this find you (as I had rather it might not) still troubled with the same Pain, you may if you think good begin with which of these Receipts you like best; since they are all three good in their Kind, and being warm and discussive†1 are very proper for this Greif, which proceeds from a cold humour that falls downe on the Drum, and other parts within the Ear.
I have no more to trouble you with at present, but that I writ to you the last long Vacation after I returned from London to give you an account of my self and small Family, my daughter and son in Law being then with me at Okeley, since which wee are removed to Shotover upon the late decease of my Father, who dyed the 24th: of october, the Humour in his Legs ceasing to run, as they were wont, so that being turned†a back into the body, it seised his head and other Vital Parts and carryed him off in three days time, he was buryed at Okeley privately as he himself desired in his will; my son in Law and daughter are now come to live with me at Shotover; where (if you shall ever please to take so long a Journey) you shall be as wellcome as ever to
Your real Freind and humble servant
J TYRRELL
If your illness continue, and that my Presence could be any ways acceptable to you I should not grudg a winter Journey to give <you>†b a visite.
James is returnd safe from the Court of Hannover, whither he went last summer with my Lord of Mac.†2 and is much your
― 539 ―
servant. I hear our good Lord Pem:†1 will be made Lord Admiral pray God it prove true for the Publick Good.
Address: For John Lock Esqr at Sir Francis Masham's House at Otes.

3073. Dr. Alexander Geekie to Locke, 22 January 1702 (3063, 3079)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 214-15.
London. Jan: 22. 1701/2
Sir
I receaved yours yesterday and give yow hearty thanks for excuseing my officious advice and by the account of your illness which yow are pleased to give me yow seem to be willing to hear my opinion about it But to Judge righty of the cause of it is not
― 541 ―
easy without inspecking the Ear however give me leave to observe tho there are many causes of deafnes yet one or both these seem to have an influence upon yours. First Ear wax harned†1 and filling up the Meatus Auditorius and somtimes it happens to be prest down upon the drum which does it more effectualy the cavity there being narrow it stops it like a Cork The Other is pain which inflames and swells up the Glandulose coat of the Meatus therby bringing its side walls close together and if any ear Wax happned to be there it is much more harned by the heat and pain and the Ear less sensible of articulat sounds consequently Yauning masticatione or Swallowing is uneasie As to the last mentioned cause of which yow complain I have proposed a Pultis to be made into a consistency with Farina Fænugræci let it be made pretty moist that the liquor of it may soak into the Ear in order to soften the hard wax if their be any But if your pain be gone and yow have no reason to Suspect that to be wholly the cause but rather to proceed from some hard wax then please to take Vipers Fatt tuo drams Juice of Housleek one dram Mix them in a viol. Take a third part of it warm it in a spoon then take some black wool and roul it about the blunt end of a Silver Bodkin (as Surgeons use to arm their probes with Lint) dip this wool in the Warm'd medicin and Whilest yow ly on the hearing Ear pour it into the deaf one and leave the wool in the cavity putting a little dry wool over it to keep it from daubing your lining. Let this be done att night And if yow could with easy ly on the Well Ear all night so much the better. Please to lett it remain 5 dayes then renew it again; When yow wash in a morning, likewise after eating be sure to Gargle and blow your nose as vehemently as yow can if it gives yow no pain likwise rub your forehead and temples with Aq.Reg.Hungariæ. Pray apply your Watch to that temple of the side of your deaf of and let me know if yow can hear it. Sir Youl pardon my tedious scrible and beleive your recovery is earnestly wisht and not dispair'd of by
Sir Your most obleidged and humble servant
A. GEEKIE
Address: For John Lock Esquire [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: IA 2-

3074. John Shute, later Barrington, later first Viscount Barrington, to Locke, 22 January 1702 (2945, 3374)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 97-8.
Sir
On Monday I went to wait on my Lord Pembrooke, who was declared High Admirall of England in Councill the night before.†1 My Lord told me, after he had read your Letter, that it was his unhappiness, that he had it not in his power, to oblige a Man, who by the character, that was given him, deserv'd so extreamly well. But that he had but a very few places in his disposall, that were worth my acceptance (not more than that of a Secretary or two) and that he had a great many Friends to oblige: That they requir'd a head turn'd to that sort of Business; and were calculated for Persons, that had run thro' the lower forms of that office. I told his Lordship that his Majesty had given great satisfaction to all, that wish't well to their Country, in giving his Lordship greater power to oblige his Friends, than to any Man in England besides: That for my own part, tho' I cou'd pretend to no other merritt, than the Recommendation, I had brought; nor to any other fittness for the place, his Lordship was pleas'd to mention, than what Integrity and Diligence cou'd give; Yett that I thought if they cou'd give me any, I might venture to say, I was as fitt to serve his Lordship, as I was desirous to do it. But that however his Lordship might dispose of that; that I was very proud of his Lordship's good opinion; and shou'd take it as a great instance of it, if he wou'd allow me to wait on him sometimes: But his replying, that it was not in his power to serve me, seem'd to me too positive a deniall, to ask the trouble of my Lord Manchester†2 to introduce me (which I found I cou'd have easily procur'd) or allmost to think of any other way of solliciting his favour.
Thus Sir you have an account of the issue of this affair. But I hope you will not imagine that my gratitude is no greater than my success. My Expressions may be as unhappy, as my Endeavours have been: But my Resentments†3 of your Civilitys are much greater than my expectations ever were, of their answering your
― 543 ―
design. That was indeed as great as the generous Inclinations which form'd it; and was onely to be equall'd by the condescending conduct, that put it in execution. Both together make you an exact patern to great Benefactors; and show you at the same time, to be the epistle and copy of the Supreme; who gives liberally and upbraids us not. For you Study how to do good offices in that manner which may serve us most, and shock us least: knowing how to bestow a favour as if you receiv'd one; and to pursue the Interest of others, with more diligence and application, than most Men do their own. Whereby wee are kept from blushing whilest wee beg and from repenting of it, afterwards: and receive as much pleasure in your dextrous way of doing acts of Kindness, as in the benefitt wee receive. So that <in>†a a word, Sir, if I was to choose the Men in the World, I must sollicitt, and choose my success too, I wou'd be refus'd a favour by my Lord Pembrooke, and I wou'd receive one from Mr Locke. For his Lordship seems to me, to be possest of the polite way of doing the one; as much as Mr Locke is of doing the other. I onely wish I had deserv'd Mr Locke's favour, as well as I did my Lord's refusall.
Or if that be too much to desire, att least, that I had been as happy in making my addresses, as my Lord, and you Sir are in your different way of receiving 'em. Mr Locke was the first Man that tempted me to begg and therefore he must neither be angry nor surpriz'd at my mismanagements. Wee are commonly the least provok'd by a Beggar that has not learn't his Cant. But 'tis fitt for a Man that is rude and awkward to confess his fault, and to ask pardon: and that no body can do with more sincerity and less regrett. And 'tis worthy of Mr Locke to forgive. 'Twill be but correspondent to the kind Inclinations and the good opinion he has demonstrated he entertains for me in the whole course of this affair. Which has encourag'd me too much, in that faulty way, that Mr Locke has done, more than any Man living to destroy, for my Lord Pembrooke's deniall wholly to cure. I have satisfaction enough that this Occasion has given me an oportunity of discovering greater degrees of the most valluable Friendship, this world can bragg of, than I cou'd ever have had vanity enough to have beleiv'd, or than I shall have ever power to requite. But I still act in
― 544 ―
character, when I own my self incapable of making any other return, than the most hearty prayers and the most sincere and humble thanks of
Sir
Your most obedient Servant
J. SHUTE.
London Jan: 22. 1701/2
I must begg your pardon, Sir, for not giving this account last post: But I was call'd away from writing to you, by business <that>†a was unavoidable, tho' unforeseen; and which detain'd me, till 'twas too late.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Shute 22 Jan 01/2
3075. Dr. Philippe Guide to Locke, 22 January 1702 (2377)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 126-7.
A Londre ce 22 Janv. 1701/2
Monsieur
Apres vous avoir asseuré de mes tres humbles respects, et vous avoir souhaité une heureuse anneé a ce renouveau, je vous supplieray de me continuer l'honneur de vostre amitié et de me fairre la faveur, si vostre santé et vos grandes occupations le peuvent permettre, de me dire ce que vous pansés sur les meilleures manieres de gouverner ceux qui ont le malheur d'estre attaqués de la Consumption. Milord Eversham†1 m'ayant fait l'honneur de me mettre du nombre des medecins qui ont donné leurs avis a Milord Anglesey il y a douze a quinze mois, Je fus d'avis qu'il usast de tres peu de remedes et qu'il fit plus de fond sur une diete exacte que sur touts les Ingredients qu'on pourroit luy proposer. Je luy trouvay considerablement de la fievre, une inesgalité dans le poux ce qui avec le crachement de sang et une respiration peu libre, ne laissoit aucun doute, que l'impression de pourriture sur la substance du poulmon ne fust desja tres Considerable, apres luy avoir conseillé de se fairre saigner incessamment et d'user de quelque purgatif doux de temps en temps comme la Casse et la manne avec le sel prunelle j'estois d'avis qu'il devoit sortir de Londres au plutost
― 545 ―
et aller a la Campagne prendre le laict d'anesse soir et matin et le rest du jour se nourrir de laict de vache et de pain et si on trouvoit le temps de la diete fatiguant changer quelque fois manger du poisson des herbes des racines de scorzonere et sarsifiy etc†a mais comme on luy promit ici beaucoup plus qu'on ne luy a tenu apres quelque mois de mauvaises experiences entre les mains de quelque medecin il se retira enfin a la Campagne, ou je crois qu'il a suivi de gros en gros l'avis des medecins, beuvant du vin en quantité jusques a deux bouteilles apres le repas; Milord Eversham m'a dit qu'il vous avoit Consulté sur l'Estat de Milord Anglesy et que vous vous declariez pour une diete exacte preferablement a la drogue, je ne doute pas que vous n'ayez fait des observations propres a nous donner de grandes lumieres ladessu, ayez la bonté Monsieur de nous en fairre part, c'est un service que vous rendres au public, on sauvera peut estre plus que d'une fois par la la vie de quelque grand subject.
depuis le retour de Milord Anglesey nous avons esté pendant trois sepmaines fort occupés a rendre nos offices a ce seigneur nous avons esté du moins dix ou douze medecins a le voir, la fievre avoit de petits redoublements sur le soir. pour y remedier on proposa le Kina Kina, j'y trouvay de grands inconvenients, entre autre que par son astriction, il ne fit ce que nous avons veu les remedes astringents ont fait dans la suite qui est de precipiter les selles, et ma raison est que la cause du flux de ventre dans les consumptifs vient d'une serosité purulente qui de la poitrine penetre et dans la Cavité des reins et dans les intestins ce que nous avons veu en plusieurs Cadavres, les voyes par ou ses écoulements se font sont imperceptibles elles ont pourtant leurs ouvertures dans les intestins et ces ouvertures estant rendues plus serrées par les remedes astringents plus la matiere s'y accumule et y fait un plus long sejour et plus l'irritation devient considerable et le flux de ventre plus grand, Ainsi je laisse ces vains tiltres de Cordiaux et d'astringents qui n'ont rien de reel que le nom en†b- ce rencontre-†b et cours la risque d'estre tout seul d'un parti, je ne digere pas mieux cette maxime generale que la boisson et la nourriture liquide est contraire dans les flux de ventre puisque
(English) experientiâ mihi constat quod leniter eluendo acre et purulentum
― 546 ―
serum acredo et irritatio minuitur et si alvi fluxus ex toto non cesserit saltem eius impetus moderatur, hac methodo plurimos alvi fluxu hepatico vulgo dicto laborantes ad pristinam sanitatem restitui, frequentiorem opii usum in his casibus gravissime etiam fero, palam quippe est opium copiam succi nutritii e stomachi et aliarum partium <cavitis>†a emungere a quibus stomachus turgens vomitaritionem creat proxima die quod si forsan exuberans succus cavitatem intestinorum petat alvum movet prout expertus sum aliquando, præterea largo et constanti opii usu Expectoratio minuitur, sensim per quam procul dubio vita aegrotantium longius prorogari potuisset
Je prens beaucoup de part a la mauvaise nouvelle que Sir Francis Massan me vient dapprendre que pour surcroit d'affliction vous aves souffert une douleur d'oreille qui vous cause de la surdité permettez moy Monsieur de vous dire mon avis la dessus dans la passion que j'auray toute ma vie de rendre quelque petit service aux Illustres il faut excuser quelque chose je ne doute pas que vous ne jugies fort bien que la douleur que vous aves sentie et qui peut estre continue encor ne soit un amas d'humeurs dans la partie si l'amas est capable de resolution un pain chaud au sortie du four arrosé d'eau de vie ou autres tels remedes et appliqué contre l'oreille est tres propre et si la resolution des humeurs est trop difficile et que l'on ait quelque veue d'aider la suppuration,†b l'huile de vers dans quoy on aura fait bouillir des liamcons et des cloportes. en distiller quelques gouttes dans le trou de l'oreille et y mettre quelque morceau†b d'oignon, ou d'aill. ceci†c peut vous
― 547 ―
estre de quelque secours, mais il faut beaucoup de patience dans ces sortes de maladies je suis
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUIDE.
(Latin) I am certain from experience that acidity and irritation are diminished by the gentle washing away of the acid and purulent serum, and that if diarrhoea [p. 545] does not cease altogether it at least becomes less violent; by this method I have restored to their former state of health a number of people who were suffering from what is commonly called liverish diarrhoea. I also strongly disapprove of a too frequent use of opium in these cases; for it is clear that opium drains away the supply of nutritious juice from the cavities of the stomach and other parts, as a result of which the stomach becomes inflated and creates a tendency to vomiting on the following day; and if perhaps an excess of juice passes into the cavity of the intestines it moves the bowels, as I have sometimes found by experience. Besides this, a free and constant use of opium diminishes expectoration, a thing which might undoubtedly have prolonged the life of some patients.
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Guide 22 Jan 01/2 Answered 25
3076. James Tyrrell to Locke, 23 January [1702] (3071, 3167)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, f. 148. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Jan 23
Dear Sir
I am very well pleasd to receive the good news of your being free from pain under your own hand; and as for the consequences of it the deafness I hope that will wear off as the spring approches; in the mean while if <yo>u'l†a please to trie what I found did me good for the like distemper which allways accompanied the paine with a constant noise in my head, I here give it you, I took wool that was lately cut from the sheep somwhere about the head, and rubbed it in the freshest Civet I could get, till it the wool was pretty moist, this I made into two small parcels, puting one in each ear, if both were affected. and this did me a great deal of Good, and took away the noise, and brought my ear to purge, and then it would be quite well and the deafness go off. my Mother had allso a very good Receipt, which tho I never tried my self, yet I heard from others that it had done good to: it is no m<ore>†b then this, let the Cook maid take about a pound of leane fresh beef (the buttock is best) slice it thin, and throw about half a handfull of salt upon it, let it lye in this pickle about 24 hours, in a clean earthern pan or plate, then gently squeeze out the Gravy or brine, into a clean viol Glasse;†1 haveing first taken off the fat scum; you may take a spoonfull of this liquor warmed pretty hot and put into the Ear, let it lye there a while and then it may run out. you may use it at night going to bed, and in the morning after you are up; this is an excellent Remedy. but you may use the wool and civet
― 548 ―
all the time, especially when you goe abroad. so hoping one or both of these may doe you good, and that you may recover your health again not onely for the satisfaction of your Freinds, but the publick Good of Mankind, with my hearty thanks for your kind wishes but more for your kind Intentions, which I desire to see put into action I remain
Your most humble servant
J T
Address: For John Locke Esqr. this.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Tyrrell 23 Jan 01/2

3080. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 30 January/10 February 1702 (2924, 3124)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 141-2. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 122-3.
A Amsterdam le 10 de Fevrier 1702.
Il y a long-temps, Monsieur, que je devrois vous avoir remercié de l'Horace de Mr. Baxter, que vous avez eu la bonté de m'envoyer.†2 L'interprete de ce Poëte a entrepris une chose fort au dessus de ses forces, et ni la matiére, ni la forme de son edition ne sont supportables. Je croi que j'ai vû un Anacreon de lui,†3 qui n'étoit pas de meilleur goût. Cependant il méprise des Critiques, à qui
― 551 ―
il n'est pas digne de délier les souliers. J'ai donné il y a longtemps au Sieur Varenne, Libraire François, de Londres qui demeure dans le Strang,†1 un exemplaire <de>†a l'Histoire de la Médecine†2 cousu et couvert de carton, pour vous l'envoyer. Mais comme je connois la négligence des Libraires, je vous prie de le lui faire demander de ma part. Mon frere m'a recommendé expressément de vous l'envoyer, et de vous en demander vôtre sentiment. Mr. Teute,†3 que vous connoissez, m'a prié de m'informer de vous de la meilleure maniere de préparer l'Opium, dont on se serve en Angleterre. Comme il souhaite passionnément de le savoir, je vous serai obligé de me dire le plûtôt que vôtre commodité pourra le permettre, ce que vous en pensez et de m'envoyer la description. Mon Nouveau Testament s'avance peu à peu, et les Evangiles seront faits en peu de jours. C'est à mon avis la partie la plus difficule, à tout prendre. Mais je suis engagé à faire quelques notes sur St. Augustin,†4 qui ne sont pas achevées. Je ne lui fais pas plus de quartier qu'à un autre Auteur, quoi que je ménage un peu les expressions. Ces notes seront dans un douziéme Tome, jointes avec celles de quelques autres. Les libraires l'ont voulu ainsi, pour pouvoir vendre les autres tomes en païs Catholiques. Cela et quelques autres choses étant achevées, dans peu de mois, je me renfermerai dans une enceinte plus petite, et je regulerai mieux mes occupations, car enfin
— fugit interea, fugit irrevocabile tempus,
Omnia dum capti circumvectamur amore.†5
Tout le monde est ici très-satisfait du Parlement, et l'on espere de réduire bien tôt la France à faire des offres raisonnables. Dieu veuille bénir le tout, et nous conserver la Verité et la Liberté, qui sont ce qu'il y a de plus précieux dans le monde. J'ai appris avec
― 552 ―
plaisir que vous vous portiez mieux, qu'au commencement de l'hiver, et je prie Dieu de tout mon coeur qu'il vous conserve encore long-temps en santé. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
LE CLERC.
Madame Masham trouvera ici mes très-humbles respects. Je vous prie aussi de faire mes amitiez à Mr. Coste.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings in litle Lincolns inne fields ...†a the plough London
Postmark: FE 7
Endorsed by Locke: J: Le Clerc 10 Feb. 01/2 Answered Mar. 11

Sir
were you not a most generus friend I should not thus persecute you by giving you a freesh troble that nothing less can Excuse. —had you ben in town I had wayted one you, to have beged your advise in Relation to my youngest Son,†1 breed a Merchant and whose Time unhappily Expiered when nothing was to be dun in the way he was designed for.—some Commissioners of the Customes, were pleased to say he was so fite for Employment with them, or in the Treashury, Navye Offece or Admiralty, that were he but known he could not want it,—and a Great Merchant the other day Reproved mee, for not geting him Recommended to my Lord high Admiral,†2 asuring mee I need not fiend out a pertickular thing to aske, he having a general knowledge that would Capacittate him for most; he has bin Eight years in Holand and Mr Chitty with whom he served his Aprentisship served the Navye Office with Considerable Storess,—and has by a letter given him an advantagus Charector; I am no good beger; but was

3083. J.-B. Du Bos to Locke, 4/15 February 1702 (2982, 3133)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 244-5. Printed by G. Bonno in Revue de littérature comparée, xxiv (1950), 511-14.
A Paris le 15 de febvrier 1702.
Par ce que vous me dites de Gemelli monsieur je ne crois pas que vous aié beaucoup dempressement pour voir la relation dun premier voyage quil fit en France et en Hongrie la quelle il vient de publier. Si jay fait cas de son Giro del mondo cest plus par raport a la disette de relations ou nous sommes de linterieur de lAmerique Espagnole que pour lexcellence de celle quil nous a donnee.†1 depuis Thomas Gage†2 je ne pense point que persone en eut rien escrit qui soit imprimé. le libraire qui faisoit traduire les memoires de Pegnalossa qui a decrit ce meme payis a renoncé a son dessein.†3 cela ma procuré locasion davoir loriginal espagnol escrit de la main même de lautheur.
Labbé Mongau a traduit le troisieme livre des lettres de Ciceron a Atticus. je le trouvé bien hardi de continuer louvrage du deffunt abbé de Saint Real lequel avoit traduit les deux premiers.†4
Je crois monsieur que vous auré vu quelquns de nos Journaux des Scavants de cette annee. lon a donné plusieurs adjoints a monsieur Cousin qui les faisoit seul auparavant. le public est asse content de la suffisance de ces nouveaux autheurs mais il lest tres peu de leur honeteté. au reste ils ne se bornent point aux livres imprimez a Paris come le faisoit a peu de livres prez lancien Journal. ils ont deja donné lextrait de deux ou trois de vos livres et entrautres du dernier volume de monsieur Davenant.†5
Je vous serois bien obligé monsieur si vous voulié menvoyer ce livre avec celui du même autheur qui a pour titre essays on ways and
― 555 ―
means.†1 je vous prie encore di Joindre le troisieme volume de Ludlow†2 et un nouveau receuil de voyage imprimé il i a environ deux ans.†3 si vous en voulé charger le docteur le febvre il les donnera a monsieur de Villiers qui me les raportera. ce monsieur de Villiers est un perruquier francois qui a demeuré lontemps a Londres ou il est presentement pour ses affaires. il loge chez son fils qui est de sa profession le quel demeure dans St James street.
lon mecrit dItalie que le P. Pedruci Jesuite avoit publié son second volume des medailles du Duc de Parme.†4
lon imprimoit actuellement a Cremone le premier tome de letterati di Cremona.†5
les Jesuites ont fait imprimer a Boulogne quelques feuilles volontas contre lhistoire de la congregation de Auxiliis du pere Serri; il a pris le non de pere Le Blanc a la teste de son livre. il promettent dans peu une response dans les formes a ce livre a la quelle ils disent qun de leurs peres de Flandres travaille.†6
la nouvelle congregation que le pape a formee pour examiner sil faut toucher au Calendrier Gregorien est composee des Cardinaux Noris Ferrari et Pamfile et de messieurs Bianchini Zacagni, del Miro et Monti. ce dernier est un neveu de monsieur Cassini le quel a travaille lontemps a Paris avec son oncle.†7
Larcheveque de Sebaste evesque missionaire de Hollande acusé a Rome davoir favorisé le Jansenisme i a publié depuis peu un escrit pour sa defense le quel contient plusieurs particularitez tres curieuses sur la vie de monsieur Arnaud.†8
― 556 ―
lArcheveque de Rheims vient de publier un mandement pour faire recevoir dans son diocese la condamnation des propositions de morale faite par la derniere assemblee du clergé de France.†1
la guerre que nous avons presentement en Italie a esté cause que nos Geographes ont publié de meilleures cartes de ces payis que celles que nous avions, la plus part sur des memoires que nos ingenieurs ont envoyé de ce payis.†2 Je suis monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
DUBOS
Joubliois de vous parler de lhistoire du Roy par ses medailles. la premiere edition que le roy a fait faire a ses depens est tres rare et ne se vendra point. le roy la distribue lui meme. Anisson en fait une autre edition qui ne sera point si belle mais que lon poura avoir.†3

― 559 ―
