Sir
I remember a lady of France receiving from her gallant a note for a considerable sum said it was the best pen'd billet doue that ever she had received ... When necessarys are provided for, friendship is the best, most usefull, and most delightfull treasure that I know, therefor doe not think that the money is the most valuable thing in your letter ...
My lady and all our fires side (amongst which count me one) give our services to you and yours.
3089. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 10 February [1702] (3056, 3096)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 107-10. Letter and enclosure. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Febr. 10th.
without the common method of prefacing by apollogie Excuse or complement in few words I tell you my very ill health has occasion'd my silence not only to You but to the familly where you are, since
― 561 ―
ever since my returne from cornwall I have had an allmost constant uneasiness in my health and it has been a very reall one to my mind to hear by others the complaint of yours. I shan't flatter you to say I wish as well to it as my own. I am told you of latte have had an ear ach which has left you a deafness which is a very ill companion. I beleive if You would venture the Experiment it would doe you no hurt to try what I have seen very successfull. viz half juice of Rue half hungary water mix't and made warme in a spoon dip cotton in it and put in Your Ear when you goe to bed. and if Your pain returnes sow up in little bags Elder and Camomiel flowers: let them be boild in milk wrung out as dry as they can and lay them as warm as You can bare them to Your Ear. I think I se you laugh at my quacking but I have often observ'd this used with success.
I have this winter been resolv'd to take the best measures I could in order to the settling my affairs and have had great incouragement to beleive I shall not find it hard by making a right aplication to the King to receive the portion of 3000 ll promis'd me by the Queen when I first came into her service instead of my pention which was her desire to the King (in writing) that all her Women servants might injoy during their lives and What makes me more beleive it will be Easy is that all my fellow servant's both maids and Bedchamber Women that have aply'd to the King, have actually receiv'd it and that of twelve their remains only my self and one more that has not had, as well as ask'd it. I have been advis'd by my frends to ask a favour of you that may be highly usefull in this matter to me. It is that youle give me leav to ask Your recomendatory letter which would introduce me to make my aplication to my lord pembroke who I am told is Very Easy in giving his assistance by speaking to the King in things of this nature where he thinks the matter just and the party not undeserving his patronage. and that tho I have some reason not to doubt of my Lord Pauletts intrest with him†1 to the same Effect which would make the favour I ask of You more Easy Yet I am assure'd that your countenancing of me who have known me so long would give a great and reall advantage to me. and that I may make myself plainly understood by You in what it is I have to beg of my Lord Pembroke it amounts only to this that he would doe me the honour to once name my petition to the King
― 562 ―
as not unreasonable (may one say so Vain a thing of one's self once in ones life to so charitable a frend as You and for the hopes of a happy settlement for the future part of ones life to add) and my self not undeserving the Kings favour or at least not more then my fellow servants. I must tell you, in this matter I have my Lord Arlebemarles favour secure to me†1 and that if by ill luck he had not unexpectedly gon into holland and his returne more uncertain then I dare venture to delay having set this matter on foot it may be it had not been so necessary to have press'd You that if it be not highly inconvenient You Would doe me this favour on which depends so much of my future in the World with reguard to my outward circumstances
I hear send You inclos'd a short abstract of my Case which may be of some use to You in the case you shall think fit to doe me this kindness.
I beleive you had seen Mr Johnston and my Lord Paulett before now had not his Treaty of mariage intervene'd which is now finish'd: 'tis to the daughter of old Perigrine Bertue and the sister of Anthony Henly's wife.†2 tis a match of high terms in respect to mony but I wish there were other circumstances which I beleive by standers will think had been more to be wish'd for my lord. Ime heartily sorry to hear by a report in the town 'tother day of a new affliction come to Sir Francis's familly†3 it touches me sensibly because I forese the ill consequences it's likely to have Especially to the poor daughter. I don't pretend so much as to name public news to You it will be none to tell You the World is still the World and so like to Continue till Prince Eugene overcomes the King of France and the King of Sweed the Zar of Muscow, but who will pull down our formidable tyrants viz libertinism and dishonesty that distract's poor England God only kno's. I wish for my self and frends safe passage thro the Storms coming on us and to You in perticuliar all things that are good. who am
Your ever oblige'd and faithfull servant.
M L.
― 563 ―
This Case which I have inclos'd being only the matter of fact I desire you to allter as you think necessary. I forget not my humble service to my lady and Cosen Masham with my hearty Condolance if the ill news Ive heard prove true. if You can think of any other way may be usefull to me in this or to any other person I flatter my self Youle not be unwilling to assist me. the lords of the Treasury are allready inclin'd to favour this in which I se no great danger of oposition but would therfore willingly take them in a good mind. and not lose time.
[Enclosure:]
That the King having at the Queens death been pleas'd by my Lords Winchester†1 and Jersey†2 to assure her women servants that 'twas her desire they should be provided for during their lives and that his majesty took them into his protection and continued their pentions ever since.
That all of them both maids of honour and bedchamber women Except Mrs Lockhart and Mrs Cason†3 are upon their aplication to his Majesty provided for by having the portion of 3000 ll granted to them instead of their pention of 300 ll a Year. which was the only way of having this promis made Effectual to them.
That Mrs Lockhart at the Queens arrivall in England had her Majestys promis to be a maid of honour and in stead of that coming into her bedchamber had the Queens promis of the same portion as a maid of honour and this on severall occasions repeated to her self and others.
She therfore humbly begs his Majestys favour to her as he has been pleas'd to grant to the rest of her fellow servants.
Address: For Mr Lock at my Lady Masham's [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmark: FE 10
Endorsed by Locke: M: Lockhart 10 Feb 01/2 Answered 13

3090. Edmond Rumney to Locke, 10 February 1702 (2875, 3196)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 41-2.

Sir
I have now an occasion to make use of such a friend as you are; and in a case wherein you may do me a high kindness, without any great trouble, I hope, to your self; I have married my daughter Sarah to a Clergy-man, who now supplys Dr Pooleys†1 Cure here, and who can better give a character of him, than I; I know your acquaintance is great among persons of quality, and by it you may, I doubt not, obtain the grant of some small preferment; If you would, as you have leisure and opportunity, try your interest, I should be bound to acknowledge it: My other children, I thank god, are setled in the world indifferent well, and if I could see this setled too, it would be a comfort to my old age, and cause me to go with the greater satisfaction to the grave: If I have been to bold in asking this favour, let my love to my child excuse it, that obliges me to do what I can to promote her interest and well-being in an honest way, and 'tis that which has made me thus rude: If it please god to give you health and strength, I should be very glad to see you at your native place where you shall meet with a hearty wellcome from your very
Humble Servant EDMOND RUMNEY:

3095. Peter King, later first Baron King, to Locke, [17] February [1702] (3094, 3099)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 170-1. Printed in Campbell, Lives of the Lord Chancellors, iv. 575. Day and year from contents and Locke's endorsement. Answered by no. 3101.
London february <17. 1701>†b
Sir
This day was expected to be the greatest day of this parliament, the busyness thereof being to consider the rights and libertys of
― 568 ―
the house of Commons, mr Finch†1 moved for it, and he proposed the first question, which was assented to without any division, as were likewise two others, which were
1. That to assert the house of Commons was not the representative of all the people of England was subversive of the Constitution of the house of Commons†2
2. The same as to asserting that the house of Commons had not power to imprison others besides their members.
3. The same as to libels against the house of Commons
A fourth Question propos'd was th<at ...>†a Ref<lec>ting†a on the house of Commons and praying a dissolution of the parliament were tending to sedition etc that was oppos'd with Courage and heat, so that the Gentlemen who were for it moved to leave out the latter words about praying the dissolution of the parliament, upon which a motion was made to leave the chair, and thereupon the Speaker†3 took the chair and adjourn'd, by which means all the busyness of the Committee is fallen to the ground, and is as if it never were; which is a very great mortification to some people, tho, not to
Your most affectionate Cosin and Servant.
P. KING.

3096. Martha Lockhart to Locke, [c. 17 February 1702] (3089, 3189)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 111-12. Locke answered no. 3089 on 13 February. His letter is lost. The present letter almost certainly answers it, and was probably written within a day or two of its receipt.
My debt of obligation to you grows so fast that I'me without any hopes of repaying it except a sensible gratitude will pass with You for Your answer to mine and the favour You have don me in
― 569 ―
it accept 10000 thanks and beleive tis without complement I tell You I think Yours to L: P:†1 both in the matter and the manner so strangly well writ that if I am not highly brib'd by the intrest which the designe of it has to my advantage I would tell You that it apears to me without a fault to admiration: and let the success be what it will it will be allways a pleassure to me to think of the good nature You have shewn to me in this.
the inquiry's you make after my proscription to you in my last gives me indeed but no pleasure must be without some pain so this for I'me in great fear it should not be fit in your case and so want the success I in my observation have seen it have the Ear achs that I have been aquainted with have been cheifly amongst my Brothers and sister's and came on colds after giving great pains in the Ear broke and run sometimes more sometimes less and did allways leave a deafness for some time after. but because I would have a better authority then my own Ive sent 'twice to Sir Theodore Collodon†2 and am not with out hopes to've his direction (for talking with him on Your case tis what I find he makes use of in his practis) my receipt is this to take an equall quantity of juice of Rue and hungray Watter warme it in a spoon. take a lock of Cotton dip it in it till the cotton is all wett so put it in the hollow of your Ear (so as it may drop into the Ear) when You goe to bed pulling Your cap warm over it and ly on that side some time if You think fit to use it you'le oblige me to let me kno what Effect it has. were it in the power of Your quack to Cure as Easily as proscribe You should soon be Well. tho you did not name to me anything of what I told you about the familly where you are methought I saw it today in Sir Francis his face who did me the favour to Call here but I had not the heart to name it. I have time to say no more because the bell man Calls me having been busiy all day but my very humble service to my Lady etc. I am very much
Your obliged and Ever faithfull servant

3107. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 1 March 1702 (3105, 3108)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, f. 208. Printed in King, p. 252, with omissions and wrong year. Answered by no. 3108.
Oates 1 Mar 01/2
Dear Cosin
In compliance with yours of yesterday I write this evening with intention to send my letter to Harlow to morrow morning that Mr Harison may if possible find some way of conveyance of it to you before tomorrow night. The family and other circumstances I think are considerd right and have noe exception and the person I have heard commended for very well conditiond: But yet the objection made is soe considerable if the defect be to any considerable degree, that I think the yonge Gent concerned ought to manage it soe as to be well satisfied whether that be what he can well bear and will consist with the comfort and satisfaction he proposes to him self in that state before he seem to hearken to any such proposal, soe that he may avoid, what he can not consent to, without any appearance of a refusal. For to make a visit upon any such proposal, though it be desird without any consequence and offerd to be contrived as of chance, is yet a sort of address: and then a goeing noe farther, what ever is said, will be ill taken of her friends and consequently the whole family be disobleiged, which will have ill consequences and therefor should be avoided. For whatever reason a man may have to refuse a woman that is offerd him, It must never be known that it was any thing in her person. Such a discovery makes a mortall quarrell. If he that proposd it be the confident of the yonge Gent, and can be relyd on by him, and
― 581 ―
has said noe thing of it to her friends, he possibly may contrive an unsuspected interview and is the fitest person to doe it. If not the yonge man must find some other way to satisfie himself that he may not be discoverd. A†a friend†a of mine in German street who missed you narrowly when you came last from Exeter knows her very well and could give a perfect account of the inconvenience mentioned. But an enquiry there must be managed with great dexterity to avoid suspition of the matter and consequently talkeing of it.
But at worst if the yonge Gent cannot presently satisfie his doubt I think he need not be over hasty for the matter if I mistake not will keep cold.†1 I writ to you by the post last night. I have not time now to look over your account before I send away this letter but you shall be sure to hear from me in that matter before you goe out of town If you persist in the mind of goeing. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
JOHN LOCKE

3110. John Paschal to Locke, 5 March 1702
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 190-1. For the writer see nos. 1715, 1754. In December 1698 the house of commons required the Commissioners of Prizes to make up their accounts. The Commission was dissolved in June 1699, Paschal and another member, John Parkhurst, being appointed agents to recover arrears. They were in the Tower in April 1701; proceedings against Paschal continued at least until 1705: notices in Luttrell. He published a vindication of Parkhurst and himself in 1701, Mr. Paschall's Letter to a Friend in the Country (L.L., no. 2226), and a further vindication in 1702.
London 5 March 1701/2
Sir
I beg your pardon for giveing you this disturbance in your retirement, but I am encourag'd by the favor you show'd me formerly in re-commending me to your friends and particularly I remember, to my Lord Pembroke. And afterwards my Lord Sommers was generously pleas'd to provide for me. How I have bin treated, and how fatigu'd since the superceding that Office, you I suppose can give some guess, I am still in the remains of that Office, but without any salary, and yet at great trouble care and charge.
And now depending upon your generosity and compassion, I beg you to recommend me once more to my Lord High Admirall,†1 that I may be one of the Commissioners of the Navy. The king of his own accord without my asking, has told me himself he wou'd take care of me, it is about 3 years ago.
― 584 ―
Sir You'l pardon me if I say that I have behav'd my self in my late Office with diligence and integrity. And I have the vanity to think, that for all clamor that was last year upon us Commissioners, not an Enemy in the world thinks I have bin a knave in it.
I did not come into the Office with an Estate, nor have cheated the Publick in that Office to support my self now I am out of it, And if you believe me in this, your assistance wil in the highest degree be obliging to
Sir
Your most faithful humble servant
JOHN <PASCHAL>†a
Address: To John Lock Esqr

3111. Peter King, later first Baron King, to Locke, 7 March 1702 (3109, 3116)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 177-8. Answers no. 3109.
London March. 7. 1701.
Sir
As†b- to the Disposition of your mony, four hundred pounds are lent in my name at five pound per cent. per annum to commence from the 16th of february last to one Mrs Joanna Hunter, The security is good and sufficient, I having a Salt Talley of 400 l. as well as two houses worth near 50 l. per annum.-†b
—I have lent One Thousand pounds to one Silvester Harlackenden on a morgage of certain lands in Kent, I have for some reasons taken that Morgage in the name of one Mr Ford a very good friend of mine, the Gent. who had part of my chambers with me,†1 he hath given me a declaration of trust, five hundred pounds of that Thousand is yours, I believe that mony will not be long out, Now it is at five pound per cent. per annum, but with some other advantage of which you shall have a moiety—If it continue longer than midsummer next then I am to have after the rate of six pounds
― 585 ―
per cent. per annum—I have herewith sent you a declaration of trust—†1
—My†a- Cosin Freke hath in his hand for your account a Low wine Talley for five hundred pounds,†2 and he hath besides fourteen hundred pounds of yours in his hand, I would not lay out that fourteen hundred pound till I writ you again-†a—Salt talleys are now in great Credit, They are at par tho, at four years distance— Now My Cosin and so Mr Lowndes tell me, that the Low wine Tallys are as sure and good, tho, at present under some discredit, because the East India Companys have not paid in about 90000 l. which they ow for dutys upon Muslins which is part of the funds. It will not be long before this will be paid in, and then these tallys must come into good repute again—My Cosin adviseth me to buy tallys of this sort about the Course of One hundred and sixty or One hundred and eighty Thousand—These tallys carry the same Interest as Salt Tallys, and there is two per cent. discount on them, which is not on Salt tallys—My Cosin Freke will entirely follow your direction herein, and buy any sort of Talleys, or East India bonds, which a great many people buy, as you shall direct, and will either keep the Talleys till I Return, or deliver them to your order as you shall direct—If You write to him, Direct your Letter
To Mr John Freke to be left at Mr Benjamin Tudmans at the Crown in Lombard street London
I design for the West next Munday,†3 and hope to be back the latter end of Easter week,†4 if so, will wait upon you at Oates. I did see the person last Thursday night, but yet cannot make that entire judgment as I hoped to have done, The Grandmother said a great deale and the Grandaughter Not much, she has a defect in her hearing, but I think not exceeding deaf, however I am not determined, but hope to see you before any thing more is done—I have received your account and am satisfied with it—As for your mony out in my name I Shall be back again timely enough to do therein what shall be fitting—If any Service occurs for me in the West a letter directed to me at Exeter will find me—My time pressing
― 586 ―
I could not go to Mr Churchills to have him be a witness to the declaration of trust but Sir Francis is, if you do not approve of this, You shall have another when I return—Mr Lewens mony being received, I desire you to Cancel the declaration of Trust I gave you for that†a

Sir
I hope from the use of the Decoctum Guaic<i>†a and the Pedilavium that yow will find very greate advantage as to your hearing (for it is the same humor that affects your Ear and leggs too) These tuo Methods being intended to Attenuat and perspire Which I take to be the most proper in your case and I wold pray yow to prosecute them with the utmost dilligence. Please to drink the decoction For tuo Months together. I wold have yow be chearfull about it For I have good hopes of your recovery. Pray Let me hear from yow by Dear Brother Awnsham. I am
Sir

B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 206-7. The writer was the son of Mark Hildesly of Lincoln's Inn and Joan, sister of Sir Francis Masham. He was born about 1660; matriculated at Cambridge in 1674; and was admitted to Lincoln's Inn in 1676: Noble, Protectoral-house of Cromwell, ii. 53-4; Venn.

― 592 ―
question: Sir The occation of this trouble is, to represent†a a Proposall to you, which a Freind of mine has engag'd me in, the which I (not understanding it myself) have advised about with one who is in a Post of experience in the Admiralty, who does give me his opinion of it, as a matter that is not a Project, but a thing of use to the Nation: It is Sir In short thus, A Comander at Sea of my acquaintance, Capt John Breholt,†1 does Solicit me to get him a Comission to go upon an expedition to the E: Indies to reduce the Pirates there (the same Commission which Capt Warren†2 had about 3. years ago but cou'd not execute it being prevented by Death, my Freind proposes to doe it at his own costs and charges with a ship of 40. Guns and 200 Men, and to return in 15. months, and 3. Comissioners to be apointed to goe with him;

3124. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 6/17 April 1702 (3080, 3279)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, f. 143. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 123-4.
A Amsterdam le 17 d'Avril 1702.
J'ai appris, Monsieur, avec plaisir de Mr. Daranda, que vous vous portiez passablement bien, et je prie Dieu, de tout mon coeur, qu'il fortifie davantage vôtre santé. Je vous suis bien obligé de vôtre description de la préparation de l'Opium, et Mr. Teute m'a chargé aussi de vous en remercier de sa part, et de vous assurer de ses respects. J'avois donné ordre à un libraire d'ici, qui a imprimé les Secreta Monita Jesuïtarum,†1 d'écrire à Londres pour vous en envoyer un exemplaire, mais comme j'apprends un peu tard qu'il ne l'a pas fait, j'en ai chargé Mr. Daranda, qui m'a promis de vous le faire rendre. Il ne s'imprime ici rien de considerable, ou qui vaille la peine et la guerre, qui va commencer n'est guere favorable aux Libraires.†2 Il n'y a que la Chronologie de Denys Petau, avec des augmentations de sa main,†3 que je sâche être de quelque consideration. Le Dr. Whitby, qui avoit parlé si impertinemment de moi, et qui m'avoit promis par une lettre de corriger ce qu'il
― 598 ―
avoit mis, en use, comme je croi, de même que l'Evèque de Bath, c'est à dire, qu'ils offensent en public et qu'ils font des complimens en particulier.†1 Au moins je n'ai pû savoir s'il avoit rimprimé son Commentaire sur S. Paul, et le Chappellian de Mr. Vernon, Envoyé en Danemarc m'a même dit qu'il ne croyoit pas qu'on l'imprimât si tôt.†2 Quoi qu'il en soit, je n'en irai pas moins mon chemin, et pourvû que les honêtes gens approuvent mon travail, je me moquerai de ceux, dont la Religion n'est qu'un esprit de faction, qui ne se met en peine que de ce qui semble avantageux et non de ce qui est vrai. Je vois bien que, tant que je vivrai, j'aurai ces gens à dos, mais il faut s'en consoler. Je voudrois qu'il me fût aussi facile d'oublier la mort de mon pauvre petit garçon, que Dieu a retiré il y a trois semaines. Il faut néanmoins se soumettre à sa sainte Providence, qui fait tout pour le bien. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant
J LE CLERC.
Je vous remercie de l'honneur que vous avez fait à mon Frere de lui envoyer vôtre Ouvrage.†3 Il ne manquera pas de le faire lui même, dès qu'il l'aura reçu.
Mes civilitez, s'il vous plait, à Mr. Coste.
Endorsed by Locke: J: le Clerc 17 Apr. 02 Answered Jun 5

3128. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 14/25 April 1702 (3055, 3130)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 150-1. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, ff. 220-1. Answered by no. 3130.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Quod tantis à te affectus beneficiis nova à te petere audeam, in eo verum experiris antiquum illud, cui multum debemus illi plurimum nos debere velle.†1 Quæ filio meo affectu verè paterno præstitisti, et etiamnum præstas officia ac beneficia majora sunt, quam ut pro meritis ea agnoscere possim. Nihilominus etiam consilium tuum pro me petere valetudinis meæ ratio suadet. Retulit mihi D. Clericus, fratrem suum antehac aliquoties in arteriæ pulsu intermissionem passum, eumque medicamento à te indicato ab ipso malo fuisse liberatum. Simile quid mihi quandoque contingit, ideoque in simili fermè casu opem tuam ac consilium petere haud reformido.
― 601 ―
Verum ut certius de statu meo judicium feras, distinctius ac plenius quæ sit valetudinis meæ ratio tibi aperiam. Memineris credo me valde esse plethoricum, mihique jam à quadraginta annis et ultra tres ad minimum venæ sectiones quotannis adhiberi, et uncias decem aut plures quavis venæ sectione detrahere solere. Plurima observavi symptomata, quæ venæ sectionem mihi necessariam indicant; postremum omnium ac gravissimum est quædam alteratio circa cor, quam ego palpitationem cordis vocare solitus fui: verum eodem malo per intervalla recurrente tandem deprehendi, illam, quam cordis palpitationem appellavi, semper cum intermissione pulsus esse conjunctam: ideoque nunc, quotiescunque eam percipio, semper digitum arteriæ applico, et pulsus intermissionem deprehendo, sed exiguam tantum moram: nempe unius pulsus est intermissio; tum sequuntur quandoque decem, quandoque plures, nonnunquam pauciores pulsus; mox rursus unius pulsus intermissio: et singulas illas intermissiones mihi indicat illa cordis alteratio eodem momento cum singulis pulsus intermissionibus recurrens: tandem post aliquot ejusmodi intermissiones pulsus ad legitimum ac consuetum statum redit. Solitus sum venæ sectione isti pulsus intermissioni occurrere, neque eam pati, nisi post trium aut quatuor mensium spatium, quando plethora novam venæ sectionem requirit. Verum nuper post elapsos tantum tres
― 602 ―
à venæ sectione menses, alterationem circa cor vehementiorem percepi, illaque pulsus intermissio crebrior fuit, et diutius continuata: adhibitâ venæ sectione XXVI. dië mensis Martii rursus ad consuetum statum pulsus rediit. Sed quod me maximè sollicitum habuit, nondum elapsis à venæ sectione tribus hebdomadibus, videlicet XIII dië Aprilis, paulo ante prandium eandem alterationem circa cor et pulsus intermissionem, sed alio paulum modo interstinctam, percepi: Duos sensi arteriæ pulsus velociores, quorum prior erat vehementior, posterior languidior; hos excepit unius pulsus intermissio, eaque inordinata pulsus agitatio et intermissio vicenis circiter vicibus continuata est; exin pulsus ad ordinarium statum rediit: toto autem illo spatio eam cordis alterationem sine ullâ intermissione sensi. Idem symptoma sensi in prandio, post prandium, idque plus quam decies repetitum fuit ante vesperam. Exinde omnia melius se habuerunt. Quia inordinatus ille pulsus mox à recenti venæ sectione rediit, aliam etiam illius causam præter sanguinis copiam esse quærendam mihi persuadeo. Incepi itaque disquirere, an non ex alimento noxii quidam vapores possint excitari, qui hujus in pulsu inæqualitatis, ad quam plethora jam quandam in corpore meo dispositionem produxit, causa sint: deprehendi autem me illis diebus comedisse pisces marinos: et licet illos etiam diebus intermediis, cum nihil mali sentirem, imo per totam vitam
― 603 ―
meam sine ullo incommodo comederim; statui tamen ab illorum usu, ad tempus saltem, abstinere, et interim de remediis, quibus malo isti occurratur, dispicere: quia metuo, ne si talia symptomata sint crebriora tandem in apoplexiam desinant. Amicus quidam mihi commendavit usum radicis Gin-sem: herba est Sinensis; illius mentionem facit Jesuita Louis le Comte dans ses Nouveaux Memoires sur l'estat present de Chine, pag.316/342†1 Et hos tribuit illi effectus. Il purifie le sang, il fortifie l'estomac, il donne aux pouls foibles du mouvement, il reveille le chaleur naturelle, et augmente en mesme temps l'humiditè radical. Sed quando meam temperiem considero, nihil in me deprehendo simile: Sanguis qui mihi detrahitur est purissimus, nihilque in eo desideratur: stomachus mihi est validus, et quemcunque cibum digerit, arteriæ meæ pulsus vehemens valde est: itaque nullum deprehendo defectum cui tollendo radix ille adhiberi solet. Vigor corporis mei, per Dei gratiam, talis est, ut dicere possim mihi viridem esse senectam. Illud unum quod jam tibi aperui incommodum me sollicitum habet. Quare cum medicamentum, quod D. Clerici fratri præscripsisti fœlicem habuerit successum, etiam tibi quod me affligit malum aperui, ut, si eodem me remedio vel alio indigere judices, id mihi communicare digneris. Ignosces prolixitati meæ; malui prolixus esse quam obscurus, ut
― 604 ―
certius de meo malo illiusque remedio judicare possis. Uxoris meæ valetudo pro senectutis ratione nec admodum prospera, nec prorsus deploranda est: Dolore sciatico quotidie magis magisque infestatur: dextro oculo innascitur cataracta, ita ut illius oculi usum jam amiserit: Dum interim alter illi salvus est res domesticas prout potest administrat. Ita et anni et valetudo nos tabernaculum brevi dissolvendum inhabitare, et domicilium non manufactum ac æternum desiderare docent.†1 Ego ut quicquid annorum vitæ tuæ divina benignitas adjicere dignabitur placidà in senectute transigas ex animo opto voveoque. Te, Dominam Masham matrem et filiam, nec non juniorem Franciscum Masham, uxor ac filia mecum plurimum salvere jubent.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 25 Aprilis

(English) D. la Motte†2 quantum a me tuo nomine pecuniæ petierit numerabo.
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
In my venturing to ask you for fresh kindnesses after having received so many from you you will experience the truth of that old saying, 'To whom we owe much we wish to owe the utmost'.†1 The services and kindnesses that with truly fatherly affection you have done and are still doing my son are greater than I can acknowledge as they deserve. Nevertheless the circumstances of my health urge me to seek your advice on my own behalf also. Mr. Le Clerc has told me that his brother had formerly suffered several times from an intermission in the pulse of an artery, and that he had been freed from that same ailment by a medicament pointed out by you. Something similar sometimes happens to me, and so I do not greatly dread seeking your help and advice in a very similar case. But in order that you may form(?) a [p. 600] more certain judgement of my condition I shall disclose to you more precisely and more fully what are the circumstances of my health. I think that you will remember that I am exceedingly plethoric and that for the last forty years and more I have been bled at least three times a year and that ten or more ounces are usually drawn at any one bleeding. I have observed several symptoms that indicate that a bleeding is necessary for me; the last of all and the most oppressive is a certain alteration [alteratio] around the heart, which I had been wont to call palpitation of the heart, but, the same ailment recurring at intervals, I at length discerned that what I called palpitation of the heart is always associated with intermission of the pulse; and so now, as often as I perceive it, I always apply my finger to the artery and discern an intermission of the pulse, but only a short stop: that is, there is an intermission of one beat; then follow sometimes ten beats, sometimes more, now and then fewer; presently there is again an intermission of one beat; and that alteration of the heart, recurring at the same moment as the single intermissions of the pulse, indicates those single intermissions to me; at length, after several intermissions of the same kind, the pulse returns to its regular and usual state. I have been accustomed to correcting that intermission of the pulse by a bleeding, and not to undergo that except after an interval of three or four months, when the plethora calls for a fresh bleeding. But recently, after only three months had elapsed since a bleeding, [p. 601] I perceived a more violent alteration around the heart, and that intermission of the pulse was more frequent and longer continued. After I was bled on 26 March the pulse again returned to its usual state. But what made me especially anxious was that when three weeks had not yet elapsed since the bleeding, namely on 13 April, shortly before dinner I perceived the same alteration around the heart and intermission of the pulse, but the latter divided in a somewhat different way: I felt two quicker beats of the pulse, the first more violent, the second more languid; the intermission of a single beat followed these; and this irregular agitation and intermission of the pulse was continued about twenty times; after that the pulse returned to its ordinary state; moreover during the whole of that time I felt that alteration of the heart without any intermission. I felt the same symptom at and after dinner, and it was repeated more than ten times before the evening. Since then everything has been better. Because that irregular pulse returned soon after a recent bleeding I am convinced that some other cause besides my fulness of blood is to be sought for it. Accordingly I began to investigate whether my food could not be stirring up some noxious vapours that may be the cause of this unevenness in the pulse, to which the plethora has already produced some disposition in my body. Well, I found that I had eaten sea-fish on those days; and although I ate them on intermediate days also, when I felt no ill effects, indeed have eaten them all my life without any [p. 602] trouble; nevertheless I decided to abstain from the use of them, at least for a time, and meanwhile to look about for remedies by which to correct that trouble; because I fear that, if such symptoms become more frequent, they may end in an apoplexy. One of my friends has recommended to me the use of the root Gin-sem: it is a Chinese herb; the Jesuit Louis le Comte mentions it in his Nouveaux Memoires sur l'estat present de la Chine, p. 316/342,†1 and attributes these effects to it: 'Il purifie le sang, il fortifie l'estomac, il donne aux pouls foibles du mouvement, il reveille le chaleur naturelle, et augmente en mesme temps l'humiditè radical.' But when I consider my constitution(?) I find nothing similar in myself: the blood that is drawn from me is very pure and nothing is wanting in it; my stomach is strong and digests any kind of food; the pulse of my artery is exceedingly violent; and so I find no defect for the removal of which that root is usually employed. By the grace of God the vigour of my body is such that I can say that I enjoy a green old age. That trouble alone that I have now disclosed to you makes me anxious. Wherefore, since the medicament that you prescribed for Mr. Le Clerc's brother had a happy issue, I have also disclosed to you the ailment that afflicts me so that, if you judge that I need the same or another remedy, you may be so good as to communicate it to me. Please forgive my prolixity; I preferred to be prolix rather than obscure so that you can judge more certainly about my [p. 603] ailment and its remedy. My wife's health, by reason of old age, is neither altogether favourable nor entirely to be despaired of: she is daily more and more attacked by sciatic pain; a cataract is growing in her right eye, so that she has now lost its use; meanwhile, while her other eye is sound, she manages the household affairs as best she can. Thus do years and infirmity teach us that we dwell in a tabernacle shortly to be dissolved, and that we should wish for an abode not made with hands and that is eternal.†1 With all my heart I wish and desire that you may pass in calm old age whatever tale of years the goodness of God will deign to add to your life. My wife and daughter join with me in sending our best respects to you, to Lady Masham and her daughter, and also to the younger Francis Masham.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 25 April
1702

Oates 20 Apr. 1702
Esteemed Sir,
Your letter of the 25th was delivered to me today while I was at table. Dinner being finished, I reply with what speed I can, for nothing is dearer [p. 605] to me than your health. Intermission of the pulse without any more grievous trouble very often attacks persons who are well otherwise, and passes away again without the help of remedies, as I have more than once experienced in myself. Nevertheless I think that this symptom ought on no account to be neglected in you, especially at this season of the year, which is so abounding in apoplexies. Whatever threatens your health I attribute entirely to the plethora to which you are very much disposed by nature and which must therefore be removed and guarded against in every way. If the intermission of the pulse still remains, or a movement irregular in any other way, I should recommend bleeding again, notwithstanding the recent blood-letting. But whether you are bled or not, I think that you will do very wisely if you abstain from wine and all other kinds of vinous or fermented drink, and instead of them use barley-water or at most very small beer, also that you should use nutritive food, especially meat or fish, very sparingly, or spiced dishes(?), and instead of them be content with vegetables and broths made with barley or oatmeal: this your constitution advises, this the early spring season advises.
(Latin) As regards the remedy that I prescribed for Mr. Le Clerc's brother: I have completely forgotten it; nor indeed had I remembered having given him any advice until by chance Mr. Coste recently reminded me of it. I should [p. 606] greatly wish that Mr. Le Clerc or his brother would copy out that remedy for me, whatever it was, so that if I judge it to be serviceable you can employ it. This in much haste as the letter-carrier is about to leave. This whole family, and I with it, send our best wishes to you and your whole family. Good-bye, and continue to love me your most affectionate
J LOCKE

Dear Cosin
I leave it to your discretion to dispose of a Thousand pounds of my money on such funds or securitys as you shall think fit. Only if you will take my opinion as if I were adviseing you in a matter of your own concerne I should reason thus. You think the bill for supplying deficiencys will pass: But if it should not what then will your malt tickets be worth? I suppose noe thing at all. For if that bill should not pass now in your good humor in the begining of a new reigne I suppose it scarce will hereafter when the publick debts increase and the continuance of a chargeable warr demands large supplys. For then if any difficiencys shall be considerd
― 612 ―
certainly those will first be provided for which happen under the present ministry, and the odium of the more ancient be left upon the former ministry who should have provided or managd better. Now I aske whether it be not too great a venture to hazard upon the uncertainty of such a bills passeing, the principal, in expectation of 18 or 19 per Cent gain which is all one as to lay above £80 to 20 that the bill will pass. This I take to be the case at this distance, possibly you upon the place know better. I who aime not at growing mightily rich could be content with less profit upon surer funds and therefore am inclind to have it laid out either in Bank or East India stock or some such other funds where it might pay interest and yet be ready at any time to be had, when I could get a good land security for it. For there it is my desire to place it. Here I tell you my inclination. But nevertheless as I said in the begining, I leave the absolute disposal of a thousand pounds to you to be put out by you as freely as if it were your own. It is impossible for one at this distance to have all the light and views that you have upon the place, and the time spent in writeing forwards and backwards often looses the occasion. Therefore doe with the thousand pound mentioned as you would with your owne, and think not that in soe doeing you shall be accountable for the success.
Pray tell me whether the parliament have charged all transfers in the Bank and East India Company with one per Cent.†1
You say not a word in yours of 25th in answer to my inquiry whether it would be time enough to take the Abjuration Oath in Trinity terme, or whether it must necessarily be donne before the end of this terme. I am concerned to know and am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant

3136. John Lock (later Sir John) to Locke, 28 April 1702 (3046, 3240)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 178-9. Forwarded by Samuel Locke on 5 May 1703: p. 783.
Surat the 28th. Aprill 1702
Honourable Sir
I wish my education and the way of business I have bin imploy'd in, had taught mee suteable expressions to return thanks for the favour I received by yours of 21th. March 1701.†1 The Trifles you were pleasd to accept of were soe far below the praises you give them that, they merrited not your notice; being Lately arrived from China†2 and the Ships for Europe on their dispatch, I have not the Time to enquire who the Founder of the Jesuits Colledge was, or the time it was built but suppose not Long after the Portuguezes settled at Goa,†3 those that first made these Stones which goe by the name of the place†4 were Jasper and Antony, and the receipt Left to the Colledge they Lived in, in the Rainy Season, I will endeavour to Learne of the French Jesuits and Capucin Padres what their composition is.
Aureng Zeeb the Present Emperor as I am inform'd by his Excellency Sir William Norris Baronet, now on his return for Europe.†5 is neer Ninety Six years of Age, and a Man of Great Temporance, worn out rather by Age then any Violent diseases, drinks noe Wine, nor makes use of Women to doe his constitution harm, neither eats or wears any apparrill, but what is the produce of a smale maintenance which he had when <he>†a Lead the Lyfe of a Priest or Facquir before he usurpt the Throne, which he gott by the Pollicy and assistance of his Sister, put four of his Brothers to death or made away with them, and confin'd his Father about 6 years in Prison where he died,†6 he has reign'd neer 46 years and Govern'd his Kingdom with great wisdom, appoints Eunuchs to
― 614 ―
bee in the most private appartments of his Umbrahs†1 that nothing is don but what is knowne to him even in their secret retirements with their Women, has Harcarrars†2 or newswriters in all his Provinces, and neer his Ministers to write him all manner of informations, nor will suffer them to Visit one another to prevent Cabals. which his good intelligence has often Prevented. My Lord Embassador has the 10 first years written in Persian, but the Emperour will not permit the History of his Reign to be carry'd on any further, his Excellency has also his Picture†3 which his Lordship promist mee if he had an Opertunity to shew it you before he deliver'd it the King, he would do me that favour, and also gratifye your Curious inquiries into the Actions and manners of these People.
There are four Sons which will all make their Pretentions to the Crowne after his decease, and those that have the greatest force have the neerest title to the throne, but some are of one Opinion, and others of the contrary, but as yett not knowne who will bee the Successor to soe wise a Prince, and tis thought he will dye peaceably and fall Like a Leaf from a Tree, when the Force of Nature has quite forsaken him.†4
We have Braminees of Several Casts here, but never had any acquaintance with any they not understanding our Language nor wee theres, but since you are pleas'd to point out to mee what may bee both usefull and pleasant, I shall this Season when the Ships are gon make some Search after those that are most Likely to furnish mee with some knowledge of their Religion, and Morals and the Laws of their Country. desiring your Pardon for what have here venturd upon to acquaint you, untill can have time and more Leisure to give you a fuller Account of this nature. desiring the Almighty to have a Perticular Care over your Person crave Leave to remain
Honourable Sir
your most Obedient Cosin and humble servant
JOHN LOCK
Address: To The Honble. John Lock In London per the Scipio Q.D.G.

3138. Locke to Edward Clarke, 23 May 1702 (3113, 3152)
Oates, 23rd May, 1702.
Rand, p. 586.
Dear Sir,
By a letter I received this day from Mr. Churchill I find he has received from you the hundred pounds for which I spoke to you when I was in town,†8 for which I return you my thanks. I wish my health would have permitted me to stay there a little longer, both that I might have had the opportunity to have prevailed with
― 617 ―
you to take some care of yours, and to have settled the account between us to this time. By my reckoning the balance remaining due to me the 22nd instant (which was the day whereon Mr. Churchill mentions his having received the last £100 from you) is £35 16s. 4d. If you find it to be so, pray send me the account drawn out and signed, that I may return you the counterpart of it signed before you leave the town. If you discover any error in it, then pray send me a draft of it as it stands in the book, that I may rectify mine by it, and then sign and send it you.
And now give me leave once more to press for my sake, for the family's sake, for your country's sake, not to neglect your health. Get on horseback as fast as you can; it is a thing worth the riding for, and I am confident riding will do. I hope I shall have that promise of you before you remove further from me. My service to Mrs. Clarke, and your son, and the rest of your family, to all whom I wish prosperity and happiness. I am,
Dear Sir,
your most humble and most faithful servant,
J. LOCKE.
Pray let the enclosed with my kindest service be conveyed to my wife.
Address: For Edward Clarke, Esq., Member of Parliament. To be left at Richard's Coffee House, within Temple Bar, London. Frank.
Endorsed: Mr Locke, to send him a copy of the account balanced, signed, etc. Received the 25th May, 1702. Answered accordingly the 6th June.
3139. Anthony Ashley Cooper, third earl of Shaftesbury, formerly styled Lord Ashley, to Locke, 23 May 1702 (2610, 3623)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 39, f. 15.
St: Giles's May 23. 1702†a
Mr Lock
It is some years ago that I settled my affaires so that I thought I could have depended (as I then told you) on being exact and punctuall in the Payment of your Annuity.†1 if some late Engagements
― 618 ―
in the Publick affaires have been the Occasion of such a Neglect and Disorder in my Private ones, that I have been dissappointed in this Expectation and you in the Promise I made to you so long since; I do not plead this as my Justification, but as some Excuse for a Fault I shall never committ again in my Life: since what I have sufferd in this respect of my private Circumstances as well as in my Health and otherwise is a sufficient Dispensation for me in the making my Life as private as my Inclination would have it to be, especially after having been so long banishd the Commonwealth of Letters where you are pleasd still kindly to assist and encourage me.
You may depend on my return of your year's due, the moment I can be master of the sum: which I hope will be in a very short time.
When I have the honour of seeing my Lady Masham; I doubt not but to satisfye her that it was nothing but my Ill fortune that prevented my wayting on her before I left the Town. I begg you to present my Humble service to my Lady, and am your faithfull humble servant
SHAFTESBURY.
3140. Mrs. Frances St. John to Locke, 29 May [1702] (2675)

I having taken the freedom when you were in town to ask your opinion as to the consern of my health makes me venture to continue troubling you a seccond time by letter, and shall take it as a great favore if you will give your self the trouble of giving me your judgment
I haveing had a very seveer fitt since I se you the extremity of which lasted for 4 or 5 hours, and my sences much gon, till I vomitted which I did of my self and that did releive my head, tho' so long as the paine continued my head was affected and dosed, from which I mostly apprehend my dainger, I have since taken Sir Theo Colleden†1 advice which is to take that vomitt which he says will streinghten my stomach and not weaken it,

3141. Jean Barbeyrac to Locke, [May/June 1702] (3232)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 140-1. Date from Locke's endorsement and date of answer. Jean Barbeyrac, 1674-1744, jurisconsult, known principally as the translator and annotator of Pufendorf's De Jure Naturæ et Gentium: D.B.F. He resided in Berlin from 1697 to 1710.
Monsieur
Quoy que je n'aye pas l'honneur d'être connu de vous, je prens la liberté de vous écrire, sans appréhender de passer pour trop hardi dans votre esprit. Quand ce que la renommée publie de votre
― 620 ―
affabilité pour tout le monde, ne me rassûreroit pas; je trouve un sujet plus que suffisant de confiance dans les bontés que vous venez de me témoigner par l'entremise de Monsieur Coste.
Agreés donc, Monsieur, que je vous en témoigne moy même ma reconnoissance, et que je m'acquitte d'un devoir aussi indispensable, du moins autant que la foiblesse de mon génie me le permet; car j'avouë, á mon grand regret, que je ne sçaurois trouver des expressions assez fortes, pour vous faire connoitre combien je suis sensible á un honneur si grand et si peu attendu. Qui m'eût dit, en effet, lors que je me mis á jetter sur le papier, sans dessein, et pour mon usage simplement, quelques Remarques, concernant le Style de la Traduction Francoise de l'Incomparable Essay, ou plutôt de l'ouvrage accompli, sur l'Entendement Humain;†1 que ces minuties me procureroyent l'avantage glorieux de voir mon nom parvenu jusques aux oreilles de l'Excellent Autheur de ce Livre, et qu'elles m'attireroyent même des témoignages authentiques de sa bienveüillance? Aussi, Monsieur, quoy que Monsieur Coste veuille me flatter de votre approbation, je ne sçaurois m'imaginer qu'une production aussi peu considerable ait pû vous inspirer les sentimens favorables où l'on m'assûre que vous êtes á mon égard: Elle n'en a êté, tout au plus, que l'occasion; et aprés vôtre generosité, je me tiens redevable de vos faveurs á la mémoire de mon Oncle,†2 qui vous a êté cher, ainsi que Monsieur Coste me l'apprend. Je sçavois bien, Monsieur, que Mon Oncle avoit bien des amis en Angleterre; mais je ne croyois pas que vous l'eussiez connu particuliérement; et si j'avois seulement soupconné, de son vivant, qu'il eût quelque rélation avec vous, je luy aurois demandé une lettre de recommandation pour vous, comme une des plus grandes graces que je pouvois attendre de luy. Ce qu'il n'a pas fait luy même, pendant sa vie,
― 621 ―
sa mémoire le fait aujourdhuy, presques avec autant de succés; et, comme s'il vous demandoit de vive voix quelque part dans votre bienveuillance, pour un Neveu, qui luy a de grandes obligations; á la premiere occasion, que le hazard vous présente, vous me faites faire mille offres de services, et vous me communiqués des corrections et des additions, qui répandent un grand jour sur un des plus beaux endroits de votre Livre.†1
Mais ce qui me rend confus au dernier point, c'est que vous poussiez l'honnêteté jusques á me faire demander mon sentiment sur cet Ouvrage admirable, et á témoigner souhaitter que je prenne, á l'égard de la matiére, la même liberté que j'ay prise á l'égard du style de la Traduction. Je vous assûre, Monsieur, que si le sentiment de mon incapacité ne me tenoit continuellement en garde contre les surprises de l'amour propre, il y auroit là dequoy flatter extrémement ma vanité. Et je ne sçay si on ne seroit pas un peu pardonnable, de s'abandonner aux douces illusions que peut éxciter la pensée d'un compliment comme celuy lá, venu de la part du plus grand Philosophe de ce Siécle. Mais heureusement pour moy, la foiblesse de mon génie se fait voir par trop d'endroits, pour ne pas m'empêcher de conclurre de lá autre chose, si ce n'est qu'on trouve en vous autant de modestie, que de pénétration et de sçavoir, et que vous réünissez dans vôtre personne ces deux qualités, d'ordinaire assez incompatibles. Pour moy, qui ne me regarde, et avec beaucoup de raison, que comme un Ecolier, il faudroit que je fûsse bien temeraire pour ozer porter mon Jugement sur un Ouvrage aussi profond et aussi bien médité que votre Essay. Je ne puis, Monsieur, m'attribuer que le droit d'y gouter et d'y admirer, avec tout ce qu'il y a de gens, qui sçavent penser, toutes les beautés qui éclattent, á chaque page, et dans les raisonnemens, et dans l'économie, et dans le tour des pensées. Ce n'est pas que je n'aye trouvé, par cy, par lá, quelque petite difficulté. Mais comme vôtre Livre est un de ceux qu'il faut lire et relire plusieurs fois, je dois présumer qu'á une nouvelle lecture, tout cela s'évanoüira. Et quand même, aprés avoir pris toutes les précautions necessaires, et apporté toute l'attention dont je suis capable, il resteroit quelque endroit, doù je ne pourrois pas me tirer; tout ce que je devrois en conclurre, c'est que j'e n'ay pas assez de penetration pour entrer dans vôtre pensée, ou pour comprendre les raisons que vous avez eües de vous exprimer d'une
― 622 ―
certaine maniére. Ainsi je suis persuadé, que si je vous proposois mes doutes, vous les dissiperiez aisément d'un seul mot. C'est pour profiter de vos instructions et de vos Eclaircissemens, que j'ay prié Monsieur Coste, de vous demander votre sentiment sur une difficulté qui m'est venuë dans l'esprit, au sujet des Idées Simples.†1 Comme j'accepte avec plaisir l'offre que ce digne Interprete de vos penseés m'a faite d'un commerce réglé de lettres, j'espere que vous daignerez bien avoir la bonté de me faire sçavoir par son moyen en quoy je me suis trompé. Je souhaitterois fort, Monsieur, être á portée de vous le demander moy même de vive voix.
J'ay toujours eu beaucoup d'inclination pour l'Angleterre, que je regarde comme le Centre des Sciences. Mais depuis que je sçay que mon nom est un peu connu de vous, et que la considération de Feu mon Oncle vous fait prendre quelque interêt en ce qui me regarde; je sens redoubler extrémement mon desir, de sorte que si j'avois de quoy vivre par tout où je voudrois choisir mon domicile, vous me verriez, Monsieur, bien tôt voler dans vôtre heureux Climat, pour profiter de l'honneur et de l'utilité que je retirerois d'avoir accez auprés d'une personne comme vous. Mais comme je ne sçay pas si la Providence me fournira jamais les occasions de satisfaire en cela á mes voeux les plus ardens, et que j'y prévois de grands obstacles; je vous supplie, Monsieur, tout éloigné que je suis de vous, de vouloir bien me continuer votre bienveuillance, comme vous avez daigné me l'offrir avantque je vous fûsse connu en aucune maniére. Je suis, avec des sentimens trés sinceres d'une reconnoissance extréme et d'une profonde veneration
Monsieur
Votre tres humble et trés obéïssant serviteur
BARBEYRAC
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke A Londres
Endorsed by Locke: Barbeyrac 1702 Answered Jun 15

3142. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 1 June 1702 (3135, 3147)

Oates 1 Jun 02
Dear Cosin
I thank you for your care and caution in the business of the morgage which was proposed. Twas too much to be ventured upon uncertainty.†a A better I hope will come.
I thank you also for the news you sent me in your last. I doe not much like it, but tis not your fault it is not better
I must desire you in your next to send me the date of Sir Francis's bond which is in your hands and the names of the witnesses to it, for tis likely I shall have an occasion to have them before I see you next
I shall be very glad to see you here at any time, and would give something you were here now. But I shall never consent you should doe soe wild a thing as you talked of to me and, as I perceive, since to Sir Francis viz that you should come down hither and return again the same day. Pray therefore never think of any such dangerous journy.†1 Come when you can but come to stay at least one night if it cannot be longer. I am
Yours
J LOCKE

Sir
I herewith returne you the petition you sent me with my name added to those 3 gents who have already signed it pray with my service give them my thanks for their civility to me in the case to which it would have been an additional favour if they had pleased to have let me know the grounds which cheifly moved them to petition which possibly touchd at in the petition would have added some grace and force to the petition it self. Sir
Your very humble servant

3146. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 2/13 June 1702 (3065, 3171)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 181-4. Answered by no. 3198.
Rotterdam 13 June 1702.
Dear Sir
I could not omit by the oportunity of the bearer my son,†1 to salute you and that honourable family where you reside, knowing that you are longing there, to hear how it goes with us, and our Allyes, here. But we are so barren of news, that its a wonder upon the opening of such a scene of affairs; We fancy had the King (of never to be forgotten memory as the old-newly-restored magistrates of Tergoes stile him)†2 lived, we should have seen other guess things acted against the disturber of Europe. And that we should have had the Troops we had contracted for sooner.
We had some months agoe a printed list of 135000 men, And now we want them, we cannot find the one half of them. Our allyes come so leisurely to our assistance, that we know not what to think of it.
We have been kept long in suspence whether any body had declared or no, but the States, but now at last we find to our satisfaction that the Queen, and the Emperour have also declared, on the same day.†3
But we want to this day about 15000 of the English, and yesterday we received but the news of 9000 Germans arrived.
Of the English Troops till the arrivall of the Generall 10 days agoe,†4 there were very few officers higher than Lieutenants, And now they are come, they keep out of harms way, and were yesterday by Clusters yet, upon the Exchange here, and in the Hague; when the news (but God be thanked false) came that our Army under the Command of the Earl of Athlone, was beaten by the french Army under the Command of the Duke of Burgundy and Boufflers:†5 which made people to grumble at them and them to withdraw, for very shame I suppose. But they write from the Leger that they expect the Generall, and their officers the 15th in the Camp.
― 627 ―
You will doubtless have understood that the french drew the most of their forces out of flanders, (leaving us to do what we would, or could rather, with so few men, there).
And thought to have caught Count Tilly at Santen,†1 wherefore the Earl of Athlone was ordred to repaire to before Nimmegen to secure that Garrison. And being there posted, Tilly understanding that the french were 2 to one, wisely retreated to Athlone, and there they have continued till the 10th Instant, attempting nothing against each other, which is no wonder on our side, the french by supplies being grown, as they write, double our number. So that the 10th Instant they decamped, to come behind our Army; and getting to Mook to surround our army. But the Earl having timely notice sent a detachment of 4000 horse, to posses that place, and there to amuse the french. While himself discreetly retired under the Canon of Nimmegen, putting part of his men into the Graw,†a †2 which they might have taken had they marcht on; A boat coming from Nimmegen sunday morning†3 at 9 a clock, and having seen many wounded men brought into the Town, and heard much shooting after his departure, supposed the Armies engaged, and others that we were routed—which seemd a good handle to some, which they were well pleasd to make use of, to Argue that thus it would go, till we got a head again: For some fooles and knaves long for it. But all honest and wise men, that are in possession of their liberties, are resolved to keep them.
A parson in the Hague beginning to talk at that rate from his prattling box, the States gave him a reprimand, forbad him medling with such matters, or they knew what to do with him.
Yesterday we had the news of the storming of the Counterscarps of Keyserswaart, and that its thought they wilbe masters of that place before 2 days to an end. I wish it prove so.†4
Generall Coehoorn†5 in flanders, with a handfull of men has taken the fort St. Donaes, and Bombed Isabella, but understanding the
― 628 ―
french were coming towards him, too strong, has been forced to quit Isabella, and retire to his trenches before St. Donaes.
Had he had men, as he desired and orders he doubts not but he could have had Antwerp, or ostend, (so bare had the french left flanders) before this. But what we had not we could not send him. There are now 3 ships arrived from England with men etc—and we live in hopes that the rest will follow.
But what will, or can be done with our fleet, if designd for the Straits, is not easy to apprehend. In the extremity of the hot season, there wilbe nothing to be done there, and when that's over, 't wilbe high time to be returning home, except you had some harbours there to ly secure in.
In Zealand The Burgers of Tergoes, that famous place, which in the year 1692 was taken in stead of Dunkerk, have restored their magistrates, who were most illegally turnd out, for defending their charter of Rights, and most villanously condemned, some to death, some to other punishments, by sentences conceived in the Hague, by the Commissioners whom the K. sent to turn them out, and constitute their enemies their judges, who had liberty given them, to pass such sentences against them, but not to execute any of them till further order from his Maj. by which they had time given them (on the earnest sollicitations of their wives and children) to acknowledg a fault, where none was committed and crave pardon, (which their Relations were told would be graunted).†1
These men the Citizens have restored to their dwellinghouses, and offices, driving out the other. And this goverment being so restored, wrote to the States that they would soone send their Deputies to the Assembly to deliberate about the security of the Province, and the other weighty affaires that at this time do occur—
The first day, difficulty was made, by the other Deputies from that Town, But they addressing themselvs to the gecommitteerde Raad—or Council-Committee (with whom the Authority of convening the Assembly of States is lodgd) they ordred them session, And accordingly they were admitted by all; and the Novices slunk away, as dogs that have lost their Tayls. The first thing these Patriots voted for, was the debarring any receivers of the Revenues or Taxes, from sitting in the Assembly.
― 629 ―
As they came from the Assembly they were saluted with acclamations by 4 a 500 of the chief citizens of middleburgh,†1 and it was half an houre before they could pass the throng through the Abby (or Pallace) yard.
Theres a noble spirit up in Zealand for liberty, and doing Justice upon those that have not a little playd the Devils with the Treasure, and priviledges of the cities and province, in which Middelburgh leads the van.
They strive to imitate the people of England, in claiming their liberties, and whereas Ignoramuses do looke upon us as the most variable nation in the world, and the most restless they say that we are the most peaceable, and constant nation in the world. Always constant to our Laws, Rights and Priviledges, always obedient to our Princes, so long as they governd by our Laws; yea bearing many infractions, till they grew so many that they were no longer to be born.
They have in middelburgh agreed upon 24 Articles, to be propounded to the Senate of that city, tending to an inquisition into the late maleadministration; and provision for their future security; which they intend to lay before the senate, or vroedschap, by 6 at a time.
1. To provide for the security of the Island, and cities therein.
2. To find ways and means for paying their fleet, and armies, that their soldiers may not desert, and they lose their Credit with their Allyes.
3. To seek such ways and means as may not be heavy to the common people.
4. To appoint Committees to inspect the public accounts.
5. To enquire who lately causd £9000†a sterling to be paid†b to Monsieur Odyck†2 on the account of his Ambassage, when the Province owed him but £1000. sterling?
6. To inquire into the coin, who ordred the coining of so many doyts, which now to the great dammage of the poore, are put down. Who ordred the Coining of so many twopences, (pretendedly (for the East India Company) at 34 per Cent losse. As also whether
― 630 ―
the Zealand Rix Dollers are good. And how to prevent the loss of the poor commonalty.
7. To inquire what pattents, or dispensations have been given for great parcells of Land, to free them from the public Taxes, by which other lands not so good, have been charged the more. And if such dispensations are valid.
8 where all the mony for the Sale of Surinam is?†1
9 what's become of all the mony come of the Agreement betwixt this and the Province of Holland, about the Turf? And where that contract is?
10. By what means some of our magistrates, or their folk, have imported such great quantities of french wine lately, and sent it into Holland?
11. whether the public Revenues (of the old soveraign) being a burthen to the Contrey, ought not to be forthwith sold? And by whose direction they have been farmd so low?
12 How the States may take in their owne Ordonnances,†2 which have been sold so low, and yet brought to account for the full summe; This would bring in great summs of mony, and is both Just, and necessary.
13 how the deficiencies of certain Towns in paying their quota to the public Taxes may be best recovered, that the burthen may not be too heavy on middelburgh, and others be favoured.
14. Whether it be not fit that proclamation be made, under rewards and penalties ordering all men to bring in an account of what they have given for offices for this 15 years last past at lest etc—
15. Who have been admitted to offices without taking the purgatory oath?
16 Who have taken Oaths to particular persons, whether to the Stadholder, to the Premier Noble, or to any other persons: seing such oaths cannot subsist with the oath of fidelity to the Land.
(As we had here in Rotterdam knaves that first swore to our Balju, that (if they being nominated came to be elected by the Prince,) they would never Vote otherwise than he and another of the Vroedschap should direct, nor in church nor in state.)†3
― 631 ―
17. To inquire what causes are yet depending, and where the mony of the product is, which ought not to be left in the private hands of a Vendumaster,†1 but immediately to be deliverd into the Common cash of the Province—
18. The like for the Great Ransoms paid at sale of prizes, and for the mony come of the Prizes and goods taken: And to keep to the Resolutions of the State in these cases. This will raise much mony—
19 To lay aside all Titular offices that are of no service at all, of which there are not a few; to the great burthen of the Province, and directly contrary to the Resolutions of the States.
20 The like as to those titular Companies, that are constantly paid, and not a man of them in being
21. To erect a Committee to introspect all the retroacts for 15 years past: what has been determined in the name of the States, prejudicial to the soverainty of this Province: Illegally not being resolved in any of the Senates (or Vroedschaps) of the Cities; under pretence of incident matters. What has been don despotically to the oppression of particular persons; unequall Taxations etc— And especially to the violating of the priviledges of the Cities. And among other things that all magistrates be of good reputation, and not guilty of such enormous crimes, as render citizens unfit to be free burgesses, much more than, to be partakers of the Soverain Authority, and in the Exchequer.
22. That All Treasurers and Sherifs etc do give an account of the monies of the Province, And of all fines where the state is to <have>†a their share, and the poore theirs, that they, who highly want it, may not be deprived of it.
23. That the Accounts of the Receiver Hodenpijl may be brought into the accounting chamber, and their advice concerning them may be heard.
24. That all offices that shall come to be vacant, may be publickly expos'd to sale, and the mony bestowed to the profit of the Contry.
Here is work enough to begin with, some of these Articles may be extended further, and, as occasion requires, others added to them, that are of great weight, in which all the Inhabitants are concernd for their lives, libertys and estates, wives, and children—
― 632 ―
church and state, every one, in his station; and therefore every one ought to mind them. Legal satisfaction ought to be given to every one.
He that speaks against these things is obstinate, and ignorant of the Right that the chief citizens have in the goverment of their free state—
The magistrates are but our fellow burgesses, and must give an <account>†a of their Actions, Salus populi suprema lex est.†1
We are no mans slaves, nor to be driven as Cattle. Every one in a ship, seing the ship running upon a Rock, may stave it off. much more than may a Ruler, if he sees the President neglect his duty, on pretext of order, will not doe what he ought, but will act imperiously, as if the city and state were to be governd by him, and will cal the Assembly together, dissolve it, put the question, or refuse to do it, according to his capricious good liking, he that sits next him may doe his office, and rebuke his insolence—
For 'tis impossible that such a one should discharge his Duty, that at this time a day will neglect what is necessary to be done— makes himself guilty of a most ruinous disorder. while he seeks to hinder a due inspection into things, being conscious of his owne guilt: being so far from contributing towards such an examination, which accuses none, but onely tends to bring things to light, to lay things open, that due order maybe taken about them; that he brow beats those that would have things made manifest, trampling upon particular persons.
But such make themselvs guilty of all the mischief that may ensue, and unfit for the Goverment, For we want not now Tyrants, and ungodly weathercocks, but men of truth, honour and Justice, that will mind the good of their fellow citizens and deare native Cuntry—
They that will now sleep, put of assemblyes, delay affaires, and play with the public concern, as if we were in a time of full peace, are enemies to their Cuntry; We are entred into a terrible war, and our contry especially is as it were surrounded by a dreadful and cruel enraged enemy. The lest slip or disorder at first, may beget a terror in our people, give courage to our enemy, and bring all into confusion.
― 633 ―
Especially considering we come out of a stadholders overpowering government, where all things have been carryed with a high†a after the humours of a few favourites under the specious name of the States, doing what they have listed, for about 30 years together, and so managing our affaires, that they are almost past redress—
But however we must be the more diligent, and instead of the senates meeting once a week, and that day spent slovenly enough, it ought to meet dayly, till we are brought into such a state that we can sit still with safety—
Sir This is the spirit that begins to Rise, and Rule in Zealand, God prosper it, and make it flourish, till all oppression and oppressors be purged out—
The States have lately publisht a placcaat†1 by which they give a premium to all that shal bring up a privateer, or ship of war, for every person they shall bring in 75f and for every piece of ordinance according to the bullets they carry—for every pound of bullets f75—v.g. suppose it be ship of 50 guns each carrying a 12 ld bullet the premie is
f45 000:—
And if 200 men a f75
f15 000:—
A good incouragement to scowre the seas of privateers—we hear that in the winter your Parliament were upon some such project, but that it goes back†2 —We understand you not in plain terms, as little as we do those now in the management of things. I am as ever Sir yours—
in great hast
Address (written by an amanuensis): To John Lock Esquire at Sir Francis Masham's At Oates
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 13 Jun. 02 Answered Oct. 12

3147. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 4 June 1702 (3142, 3149)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 220-1.
Oates 4 Jun 02
Dear Cosin
Mr Spranger†1 proposed to me yesterday a Mortgage for £600. It is of one Mr Thompson of Burntwood or there about.†2 He commends the security and the honesty of the man, whose Character also he says may be known by the present Morgagee for it is now at present in Morgage to a citizen, who cals in his money for an occasion he has, He talks of £500 more and of ingageing an other farme. If you like the Character of the man (which pray by Mr Churchil or somebody else informe your self of, for as I take it the Morgagee lives about Holburn bridg, Mr Spranger will informe you) and the security Pray take it. Mr Spranger will come to you about it either the later end of this or the begining of the next week
I intend to bee in town the 15th day of this month if my health permit: I tell you this that you may take some leisure moment between this and that to draw out my account for I shall not stay in town if I can help it above one night. The harm which my lungs sufferd when I was there last I have not yet got off
Pray take noe notice of my comeing to town to any body else. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
My Lady and all here greet you

3148. Henry Layton to Locke, 8 June 1702
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 21-2.
Henry Layton, 1622-1705, author, besides other books, of a series of pamphlets on the immortality of the soul, a doctrine which he rejected: D.N.B. He believed in 'the Soul's Materiality' and was concerned with the
― 635 ―
question whether matter can think (Locke, Essay, IV. iii. 6); for this see Yolton, pp. 159-60. Locke possessed seven of the immortality pamphlets, including both parts of A Search after Souls, 1693-4?: L.L., nos. 1698-1704.
Jun: 8. 1702.
Sir
It is somewhat above a fortnight since I receiv'd your very civil Letter. of which I have thought fit hereby to give you the Notice, that you may be the better assur'd that the direction of your letters are likly to bring them safe to mee, and to give you thanks for the Easie reception of my book, which was offer'd to you as a very good Judge upon this argument and as one who hath suffer'd some measure of persecution, for but saying that thing was possible, which I endeavoure to maintaine as very probible.†1
If you take purpose to send mee an opinion thereupon I pray you to send mee such a direction as may bring my reply to you. and I have no more at present to communicate save that I am.
your very much Oblig'd friend and humble servant
HENRY LAYTON
Address (not in Layton's hand): For John Lock Esquire.

3151. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 19 June 1702 (3149, 3156)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 222-3.
Oates 19 Jun 02
Dear Cosin
Yours of the 18th I received with what it inclosed By which I understand that a morgage of the land proposed by Captain Tomson not being to be had time enough to serve Captain Thompsons occasions, he proposes the giveing me a Statute or a Judgment†1 per interim.
Pray give my service to Mr Spranger and tell him I am sorry that this falls not out according to his and my expectation. That I doe
― 637 ―
not know but the way of security he proposes might prove safe enough. But there is accident it may be liable to, and will be more trouble than the ordinary way of a plain direct morgage. I am old and infirme and cannot bear the thoughts of any bustle and therefore cannot bring my self to quit an old way I am acquainted with, for a new one I am a stranger to and may have trouble in it. Pray tell Mr Spranger I intended to have seen and talked with him when I was in London, but my ill health permitted me to stay in town but one night. Pray excuse me to him that I have not writ to him. yours came soe late that I have not time to write two letters about this business before the departure of the messenger that carrys our letters. And since it was necessary I should write to you about it. I hope this to you will be satisfactory and sufficient that I am unwilling to meddle with any thing but a plain safe morgage in the case. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
JOHN LOCKE

3153. Mrs. Elizabeth Burnet, formerly Berkeley, to Locke, 20 June 1702 (2980, 3164)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, f. 235.
Salis: June: 20: 1702
Honoured Sir
Haveing lately read a book writ in answer to some objections made some time ago to your most excelent Essay, and according to that litle judgment I have thinking it tho not worthy of its subject yet comendably performed, I thought you might not be ill pleased to know a litle more of its Author then you might as yet be informed of; her Father for I suppose you know 'tis a Female writter, was a Capatin of a ship in K Jeames time and dyed about the time of the revolution; I think he was a scoch man, as her Mother is a scoch women, who aplying her self to the Bishop in hopes to gett some old arear, I came to that litle acquantance I have which is seeing her Daughter three or four times. they were left in mean curcumstances, and I know not by what misfortune of ill compeny both the writter of the late book and her sister turned papist and are so I think at this time, your Champion is unmaried, and having as you see a more then comon genius write three plays, partly to gratefy her humer that was studious, but more I beleeve to help her too live, that sort of writing where it takes being the most profetable; but as you will allow by her late litle book, 'tis great pety her studys are not better directed, and I can't but admier that one of such clear thoughts can be of a relegion that puts such schacles on the exercies of thought and reason, if by any accident you see her, or think it fit to take farther notice by writing to her I wish you could be an instrument to free her from those erors, she would perhaps pay more difference to you then to any other, which would be not only a kindness in its self, but make her more capable of the asistence and incouragment of her Frinds; she knows not at all that I have informed you of her, but since by accident I knew this, I thought it might not be amis to let you know;†1 the Bishop comands me to give you his most humble service wee were
― 639 ―
sorry to have no more of your compeny while in Town†1 nor yet to hear you are coming this way, where you will be most truely wellcome to the Bishop and
Your much Obiged and most Obedent Humble servent
E BURNET
It would be a great favour if you would make the Bishop and my humble service acceptable to Sir Francis and my Lady Masham
