3154. J. Maer to Locke, 22 June [1702] (3150)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 194-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London June the 22nd
Sir
When I resolvd to wait on you with my proposal, twas in hopes to have return'd with a great deal less pain then I did. Had I not tried it enough to be past all doubt of its truth, I would never have offer'd it to the severe examination of a man I esteem'd thoroughly learn'd, and of no common wit, to value a thing the more for being dear, and difficult, or the less, for being cheap, simple, and easy. As I judge this art so, tho the noblest, and usefull'st in nature, it gave me too much trouble and confusion, to be forc't to talk of it publickly, and have it, and my self expos'd a jest to boyes, and women; but perhaps twas due to a stranger in rags, with a club in's hand, suspected a rogue, and despis'd as a beggar. If the infirmities of age disgust you with life, and make you thinck nothing more in't worth your care, or consideration; I can onely complain of Nature for decaying you too soon, and not giving me the power to unload you of your years, or recruit you with half my remaining vigour, which believe me I would willingly part with for a few years friendship with you, in full confidence of having it doubly restor'd by the accomplishment of the work with your concurrence. If we both live a year longer, and fortune enables me to go thro' with it my self (for I have had so ill success with my first application for help I shall never try another) you may possibly
― 640 ―
be converted from your Heresy. Should you die before, and I be deceivd in my hopes, I dont care how soon I follow. The pleasures of life an't worth the pains ont, and Ide willingly quit one, to be rid of tother. I had some reasons to ask my letter again, and have both my name and hand unseen. Where I am, I pass for a dutch man, and no body thincks what I am doing. Pray Sir let it be so still, if you should thinck fitt to make enquiry after me. As you have no inclination to do me good, I cant imagine you'll have any to injure me, which making my writing, and purpose known to some of your acquaintance will greatly do; so in burning one, and forgetting t'other, you'll extreamly oblige
Your most humble servant
J. MAER.
Address: For Dr Lock at Sir Francis Masshams at Oates near Harlow in Essex
Endorsed by Locke: J. Maer 22 Jun 02
3155. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 23 June/4 July 1702 (3054, 3204)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 104-5.
Monsieur,
Je vous remercie bien humblement de la bonté que vous avez eu, de me faire envoyer par Monsieur Limbourgh la relation de ce qu'on a trouvé dans le Cadavre du feu Roy d'heureuse memoire.†1 elle contient des particularités singuliers et qui marquent l'etat triste ou étoit son corps desja caduque, avant l'accident qui luy est survenu par la chute, et auquel il n'auroit apparemment pas pu survivre longtemps. cepandant nous ne scaurions nous consoler encore de la perte que cette mort facheuse a produite a toute l'Europe, qui se voit menacée d'un terrible ennemi, que vous nommiez fort bien dans une de vos lettres, the Westeran Turk, qui porte la desolation par tout. Jespere pourtant que si les cours interessées a la conservation de leur liberté, concourent ensemble de bonne foy, le tems poura retablir les choses, et je vous assure q'autant que je connois de protestans icy, ils sont tous de bonne
― 641 ―
volonté de consacrer une bonne partie de leur biens, pour conserver le reste et le repos de leur conscience.
depuis que jay relu une seconde fois vótre livre de l'entendement avec attention, et que je commence a me rendre vos pensees familieres, je decouvre de plus en plus nótre profonde ignorance, et que la plus part des hommes croyant entrer dans la connoissance de la realité des choses se payent de mots, qui dans le fond ne signifient rien, et parmis un si grand chaos de remedes, que nos auteurs de la Medicine nous ont debité avec tant de confidence, si on examinoit les choses de pres, combien de fausses experiences ne trouveroit on pas? et reduits a un tres petit nombre, auquels il y auroit quelque certitude? il est certain que ne pouvant connoitre le veritable arrangement des particules de chaque substance, il nous reste que d'étre fort attentifs au phœnomenes des maladies et aux effects des remedes, pour en tirer quelque utilité. cecy me donne lieu de vous demander l'etat de vos jambes. on ma dit quelles sont mieux. je vous diray que le malade dont je vous ay fait Mention, et qui se trouva subitement gueri avec l'emplastr. ranar. cum Mercurio, a eu une rechute quelque tems apres. son herpes a ensuitte gaigné presque tout le corps. cela n'a plus obei a l'application du mercure, ny a plusieurs autres remedes, l'usage des succs d'herbes dont je vous ay fait mention parassoit faire le mieux. je me suis enfin servi de l'onguent suivant qui a entierement fermé ses ulceres et dissipé ses pustules. ℞ picis liquid. butyr. recentis et ab omni salsedine depurat. ana ℥i flor. sulphur. ʒii m.f. unguentum. on en a frotté le mal une fois le jour, et tout c'est dissipé en huict jours de temps. il a pris les eaux de Spa il y a sis septmaines, et se porte encore fort bien. je ne scay ce quil en sera dans la suitte. Comme nous souhaittions d'avoir vótre portrait jay fait un effort de vous faire tirer sur les tailles douces dont vous nous avez honoré. jy ay joint ce que je croyois y manquer, et ce qui est assez bizare, tous ceux qui vous connoissent, disent que nótre peintre a le mieux reussi. noté que le portrait est de grandeur naturelle.†1 Monsieur Daranda qui la vu a ce dernier voyage ne put pas assez admirer la chose, et Messieurs Limburgh et le Clerc disent quils vous y reconnoistroient, quand méme ils auroient vu le tableau dans un endroit etranger. vous ne scauriez croire Monsieur combien cela nous
― 642 ―
contente. nous avons pris la liberté de vous placer au cercle de la famille qui orne notre sale, ou vous disnáte un jour avec messieurs Clarc, Furly etc.†1 nous sommes fort charméz du petit livre de la religion des Dames.†2 ma femme ne scauroit se lasser de le lire. on la traduit icy, mais fort mal. cela m'a donné l'occasion d'en faire une traduction pour l'usage de mes domestiques. je croi y avoir conservé la pensée de l'auteur, et suivi le genie de notre langue. il ny a que le titre qui me fait un peu de peine. je n'ay scu avoir l'original anglois, ou il y a apparemment, the Religion of a Gentlewomen, ce qui a mon sens n'est pas tout a fait bien traduit en francois en disant la religion des Dames; parceque le mot de Dames est capable de donner d'abord l'idee de quelque livre de galanterie, et en effet cela a abusé plusieurs personnes. cela ne fait pas le meme effet en anglois ny en notre langue. quoy que je trouve le mot de Gentlewomen ou de Vrouw trop incomplet je croy quil auroit esté egalement mieux pour l'importance de la chose de dire lettre de .n.n. a Madame Howard,†3 sur la Simplicité de la religion chrestienne. jay mis a ma traduction. D'eenvoudigheyd van de Christelyke Godsdienst verbeelt in een brief van de heer n.n. etc aen Mevrouw Howard etc.
je finis par les tres humbles respects de toute la famille. Ma femme se porte bien a miracle: Monsieur veen raisonnablement pour son age et sa caducité. nos enfans font assez bien jusqua present. graces a Dieu. je suis avec le dernier respect,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur.
P. GUENELLON
d'amst. ce 4 Juillet 1702
Address: For Mr. John Locke at Mr. Powlings over against the plough. in little lincolns inne feilds. London.

3158. Charles Masham to Locke [Summer? 1702]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 1-2. Year from Locke's endorsement.
The writer was Sir Francis's seventh son. He was admitted to Queens' College, Cambridge, on 17 December 1696; B.A. 1701; M.A. 1704; fellow of Queens' 1704; ordained deacon 20 December 1702; priest 19 September 1703: Venn. In 1705 he went as chaplain to the East India Company's station on St. Helena; he died there about August 1706, apparently as a result of drinking too heavily: Esther Masham's letter-book, pp. 245-59, 270-9. See also Carpenter, Thomas Tenison, pp. 355-6 (as Marsham).
Sir
I fear you'll be no less surpriz'd at, and angry with my boldness in troubling you, then the cause that induces me to it; But not being able to think of any body else whose advise I might rely upon better then yours, I hope you'll pardon this presumption. My imprudent management of my affairs since I have been at the University has run me into debt, which I dare not let my Father or Mother know, for if I should it would but procure me their uttmost displeasure, and perhaps no releif, tho' even some debts have been contracted for Necessarys. However the thoughts of being in debt, and the fear of its being discover'd, together with my present inability of clearing myself, doe very much disorder me and hinder my settling my self rightly to my studys, and being every day more and more perplex't, and less able to apply myself to my business, I thought it more advisable, e're t'was too late to own my fault and past indiscretion, (How much soever I may expect to be reprov'd for it, as I own I deserve) then let it run on
― 645 ―
to my ruine and suffer my self to be driven to such <streights>,†a and to the use of such means, as may be both desperate in the design, and fatal in the prosecution. The Debt which I have Contracted, besides what I have paid with my money out of France,†1 amounts to 70 ll. Tis not all to one, nor was it contracted on a sudden, but by Degrees ever since I have been at the University. I most humbly beg, Good Sir, if it lyes in your power to advise me what to doe in this Case, or any other ways to assist me, that you would be pleas'd to doe it, for thereby you would be the sole Author of all the Happyness I shall ever enjoy hereafter; for if it should be known to my Father it might ruine me for ever; therfore I humbly desire this may be conceal'd from all, even from my sister too; for I fear the discovery of it to my Relations would procure nothing but their sharp reproofs for my ill husbandry, adding yet more weight to my trouble and afflictions, but unable to make me more sensible of my folly then I already am, or more resolv'd for the future to avoid whatever may tend to the bringing me into the like Misfortune. Sir be pleas'd to pardon this boldness as well as all other past faults and to accept of all Due respects from him who is
Sir
your most Humble and obedient Servant
CHA: MASHAM
Address: To John Lock Esqr [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Endorsed by Locke: C: Masham 02

3159. Peter King, later first Baron King, to Locke, 4 July 1702 (3157, 3161)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 185-6. Answers no. 3157; answered by no. 3161.
London July. 4. 1702.
Sir
I†b- have at length finished Capt. Thompsons morgage for 600 pounds, The morgage is dated yesterday and is made of lands in Southweald to me and you in trust for you, so that you must keep an account of this morgage with Capt. Thomson—I shall only make
― 646 ―
you debtor to me for so much mony paid on your account to Capt. Thompson, and as I shall receive any interest from him will give you credit for the same—I had the 600 l. from Mr Churchill, for which I must give you Credit,†-b As to your other Concerns I hope to see you this day sevennight and believe that I shall be able to perswade My Cosin Freke, who manages my concerns for me, to come with me, If so, we will come in his Charret†1 —My Humble service to Sir Francis and my Lady, The Parliament is dissolved,†2 The Writs for a new one to issue about the midle of the next week—I am Sir
Your Most affectionate Cosin and Servant
P. KING.
Mr Spranger will be with you next Tuesday, and will expect that you should consider him for procurement.

3161. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 7 July 1702 (3159, 3163)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 228-9. Answers no. 3159.
Oates 7 July 02
Dear Cosin
I am glad Captain Thompsons security proved to your likeing. I thought I had had enough money in your hands that lay dead to answer that morgage, if it be imploid soe much the better. But of this I have noe enquiry now to make, when you come your account will give me a view of the whole. I shall be very glad to see your Cosin Freke here with you, and he will be very wellcome to Sir Francis and my Lady.
I have an account from Mr Tilson that our Commission is passed, soe that I think it convenient, (Pray tell me if be not
― 648 ―
necessar) to take the Oathes at Chelmsford at the Sessions there next week.†1 I aske you also whither the certificate which is to be signed by the parson and Churchwardens where I take the Sacrament ought not to be on stampd paper.†2 If soe pray send me one in your Thursday nights packet and direct your letter to Mr Harrisons at the Crown in Harlow that soe I may be sure of it Friday morning, and write by that post whether it be not necessary to take the Oathes now, this being the next quarter-sessions after the passeing the Commission. And if the forme of the Certificat of the parson and churchwardens be prescribed by the Act of parliament pray send me also that forme, for we have not the Act here and if I faile in any circumstance I shall be disappointed and loose my labour if that be the worst <of it>.†a
I am glad to find by the paper you sent me, which I take to be Dr Musgraves,†3 that your father is in soe good a way of recovery. I very much like the Doctors proceeding with him, and have onely one thing to suggest to be added to the method he has put him upon, and that is Ens veneris which I think would be very good in your fathers case. All this family salute you. I wish you could come a day sooner. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
Pray give my humble service to your Cosin Freke and his brother.
You will see by what I have said that I had writ this letter before I found your note of July 2d Wherein you tell me the state of your fathers condition came from Dr Musgrave.
Address: For Peter King Esqr member of Parliament. To be left at Mr Potmans in the Middle Temple London Frank.
Postmark: IY 8
Endorsed by King: Mr Lock July. 7. 1702.

3163. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 9 July 1702 (3161, 3180)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 230-1.
Oates 9o Jul 02
Dear Cosin
Since mine to you by the last post I am informed that the forme of the Certificate which the minister and churchwardens are to give to any one who takes the Sacrament in order to take the test and Oaths required, is printed in stampd parchment ready to be filled up as any one has occasion, one of these (which are to be had amongst the stationers in town or at the stamp office) I must desire you to bring down with you, for I shall be at a loss without it. Pray take care not to neglect nor forget it, but send your man to get it as soon as you receive this. Wonder not that I press soe small a business with soe much earnestness. It is a matter of great concernement to me and if I should fail of it I know not of what ill consequence it may prove.
I Conclude my desireing you to be here to morrow (I was going to adde) would prove to noe purpose. But just here Sir Francis
― 650 ―
comes into my study to let me know he shall goe to London to morrow and perhaps return again in the evening. If he does soe I would desire you to come with him by that means I shall have you a day the longer and you will loose not time by it in town for whither he comes out of town to morrow night or Saturday morning, the latest of these ways I am sure he will be here early Saturday morning, and soe my time with you will be inlarged. and even soe be too scanty for our business togeather. I am
Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE

3164. Mrs. Elizabeth Burnet, formerly Berkeley, to Locke, 15 July 1702 (3153, 3207)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, f. 236.
Sir
I read your letter of the 2d of July as I do all you write with pleasure and profect, and as I was ever of the same openion as to the maner of managing disputes so I resolve to be in my practice more perticulerly carefull for the time to come; I do not remember my letter enough to recal how I spook of Mrs Troters book, but I am sure I did not think meanly of it, tho I might of my own incapacity to be a judg; but not only the arguments but modest and unafected stile pleased me extremly, I know I liked the whole, but don't know if I was in the right in doing it, but now it is aproved by so many better Judges I will think I am not mistaken; and I should gladly follow all your other directions in making a Frindship at least doing her what good Offices I could had I not a stronger bar then difference of religion, and which I thought I had hinted enough for you to understand in my last, which made me leve it as a doute if you should take more perticuler acquantance; the fassion of her religion which allows great libertys, her stract curcumstances, and being forced as it were to write plays, and
― 651 ―
consequently to contract Idle acquantance, has left great blemishes on her reputation, and tho I am very willing to think her in great measure injuried, yet my charity will be laughed at if not sencured should I show that regard that is due to her good understanding, and tho she in her book and in conversation shows a great respect to your Judgment yet she has as I have ben told spook with great contempt of some who have talked very gently with her one the heads of religion, so that cevelity without a regard for their understandings will I fear make slit impressions, however this would not discourage me, did not the other reason create a shiness which 'till by observing her so as to be more perswaded it was or at least is ill grounded can't be quit laide aside, tho what good offices I can do her to resque her from any sort of defects I think charity allows and I will endevour as far as is consistent with prudence; I beleeve her curcumstances can't make what you mention improper, but while I am out of Town I know not what to say more, or how to direect to perticulers, did you know what books she wanted or desiered that might be to her a usefull present, but I am quit ignorent in all things of this patane; her name is Catherine Troter she now lodges in the second House in Beaufort street†1 on the left hand, her sister is a maryed woman and lives in this Town, and I know not if she will not be with her ere long; I am full of hopes in reading your kind intention of seeing Salisbury but addition of I doute quit dampt it, however I may and will hope to see you here if not, at least at London or —sea,†a †2 a place I have had long <an>†b ambetion to be in; I desire you will not trouble your self to answer me with your own pen, if you are at any time at leasure to dictate to a servent it will be very acceptable for 'tis uneasy to me to give you trouble tho I gain by it; the Bishop is as unwilling to lay aside the thoughts of seeing you as I am, wee are both very truely
Your Much obliged and Most Humble servents
EB
July: 15: 1702
― 652 ―
if it is seasonable the Bishop with my self send our good wishes to Sir Francis for his success, and our humble service to his excelent Lady

3165. Dr. Alexander Geekie to Locke, 16 July 1702 (3125, 3168)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 228-9.
London July 16. 1702.
Sir
I receaved yours this morning and well pleasd I was to hear of the eruption of Matter. but whether from the outward or inward cavity of the Ear yow doe not mention. However cleansing of the remaining Ulcer is very proper and to that purpose Please to take an ownce of Mell Rosarum and one dram of the Tincture of Myrh and Aloes made with Brandy. Mix them together warm it a litle and arm your probe as before with Wool dip it in the Mixture and put it into the Ear leaveing by the sides of it room enough to give a discharge to the matter this is to be repeated every 24 hours or once in 12 if the discharge be great and the stench offensive. Now I could heartily wish my self with yow for it requires some inspection. Pray Sir lett me hear from yow how this succeeds For I am in great hopes it will doe yow a great deal of service. I pray God give yow health and recovery. I am
Sir
Your most humble servant A. GEEKIE
Pray give all with yow my most humble service.
Sir Till the Mixture be gott please to apply nothing to your Ear but some of the Cotton which is used to take the oyl off your florence wine†1 and if yow please to keep some of it alwayes in the outside even When yow dress it with your medicin it will be the better for the parts now are tender and naked and the ambient air should undergoe a litle cribration†2 before it comes att a Weak part.
Address: For John Lock Esquire att Oates in Essex
To be left with Mr Harrison att the Crown in Harlow
Postmark: IY 16

3167. James Tyrrell to Locke, 18 July [1702] (3076, 3195)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 149-50. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Dear Sir
I was very well pleasd to hear the other day by Sir Fran: Masham, that you were rather better then worse since you last Journey hither,†2 where you stayd so little a while that you were gone before I knew you had bin here, or els I should have done my endeavour to have seen you: as I really intended to have done this week at Otes, for I think it long since I enjoyd that satisfaction, but I have had so much business to do before I went out of Towne that I have scarce had a day to spare, and to morrow God willing I leave it for 3 or 4 months; but when I come up again shall beg leave to wait on you, since I cannot be so happy as to see you here; I suppose you have heard of the decease of two of our old Acquaintance not long since, honest Dr: Fairfax,†3 and, Mr: Stringer,†4 so
― 654 ―
that those of our Time are now reduced to a very few and therefore there is the more reason for us that remaine to love one another during that short span of life that is left us; which I pray God to continue to you as long as to my self, or rather longer,†a as one that can contribute more to that great End, the Publick good of Mankind.
Since I came to this Towne I have bin cheifly imployd in fiting another volume for the Presse, which will continue our History to the end of King Rich: second:†1 and I wish what I have allready written may not prove too tedious to nice Readers: I have however had spare time to dip into some new books, as one writ against your self, or by one Mr. Lee,†2 I wish the Gentleman would have spared finding fault with others for obscurity when oftentimes one cannot†b- tell whether-†b he writes for or against your opinion, but a book of Controversy in a Folio, larger then that he writes against is never like to gain many Converts in an Age when books of that kind are so little studied: but there is a worse book in the consequence of it lately come out, calld Second thoughts concerning the nature of humane souls,†3 wherein he labours to prove that the immortality of the soul as such in its owne nature, is a pure heathenish Invention, utterly different from the Intent of Christianity, which asserts it to be so onely from the pure will of God declared in Scripture, and to begin onely from the Resurrection. but that which has bin received with most Applause is your Cos: Kings critical History of the Creed,†4 wherein he has shewne a great deal of Learning and Judgment: and is well approv'd of by my Lord P.†5 with whom I have lately discoursed of it; I saw his Lordship this afternoon, he is well, and is glad to hear you are so, and desired me to remember him to you: I have not read my Lord Clar: Hist†c of the Rebellion etc.†6 as yet, but reserve that satisfaction till I come to Oxford, where I hope to get it cheaper then here; it is very finely printed, and much for the credite of the university;
― 655 ―
this is all I have to trouble you with, and if I may receive a few lines in answere to let me know how you doe; directed to Shotover to be left at Oxford, you will fur<ther>†a oblige Your most humble servant
J T
I pray give my humble service to Sir Francis and his Lady with many thanks for his late kind Invitation to Otes which I could have bin so happy as to have accepted of. I hope next Terme†1 to be out of your debt, haveing hitherto had a great deal of money to pay for debts, and Legacies since my Fathe died.
Address: For John Lock Esqr [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmarks: IY 18; LA (?)
Endorsed by Locke: J Tyrrel 18 Jul. 02 Answered Aug. 13

3170. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 27 July/7 August 1702 (3130, 3192)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, f. 152. Locke's immediate answer (4 August) is lost.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Ex filii literis afflictam ejus percipio Valetudinem, quæ me valde
― 657 ―
sollicitum habet. Scribit se jam a quinque hebdomadibus febri laborasse, de qua Medicus Londinensis consultus pronuntiaverit hecticam esse. Addit se multum, et meo judicio nimium, indulgere tristibus de priore suo infortunio cogitationibus, quibus ego malum hoc magis exasperari credo. Vereor ne et parentum absentia ipsum affligat: Vellem ego, si res meæ permitterent, ipsi adesse, ut præsens præsenti tristes illas cogitationes excuterem. Literis idem jam præstare conatus sum. Res illius eo in statu non sunt, ut ita se affligere deceat. Negotia illius quotidie augmentum capiunt, ut non levis spes affulgeat fortunam priorem superari posse. Interim valde a febri illâ hecticâ metuo. Vereor ne illius jam initium contraxerit præteritâ hyeme. Scio febres hecticas inveteratas incurabiles fieri. Rogo per amicitiam nostram, ut paucis lineis mihi statum filii perscribere digneris, et utrum spes sit recuperandæ valetudinis. Jussi ut rotunde ac candide omnia quæ animum ipsius affligunt, tibi tanquam parenti aperiret. Aërem Londinensem fortasse ejus pulmones non ferunt. Quicquid sit, rogo ut aperte ac plene judicium tuum de ipsius statu mihi scribere velis, ut mature quid ex usu ipsius sit deliberem. Ignosce quod hanc tibi molestiam imponam, eamque paterno affectui imputa. Multa sunt quæ me circa filium
― 658 ―
sollicitum habent; sed si supremo omnium arbitro aliter sit visum, illius ut me voluntati subjiciam officium meum esse novi: spero tamen filium mihi fore superstitem, neque mihi nec uxori unquam miseriam illam obventuram eum ut lugeamus. Ego jam valetudine fruor prosperâ: intermissionem illam pulsus à quatuor mensibus non sensi. D. Clericus Genevâ à fratre suo responsum accepit, se hortatu tuo aquam bibisse. Alterius remedii nullam mentionem facit. Dicit tamen D. Clericus te illi etiam usum pilularum quarundam præscripsisse. Verum earum nullam in literis mentionem fecit frater. Ego interim tibi, ac Generoso Domino ac Dominæ Masham summas pro benevolentiâ erga filium gratias ago, vobisque me totum devinctum profiteor: Utinam illud officio aliquo testari possem! Vale, Vir Amplissime. Salutem à nobis officiosissimam dicito Domino ac Dominæ Masham, totique familiæ honoratissimæ.
Tui Amantissimus
P. A LIMBORCH.
Schoenhoviæ†1 7 Augusti
inline image
veloci calamo.
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
From my son's letter I perceive that his health is injured, which makes [p. 656] me exceedingly anxious. He writes that for the last five weeks he has been suffering from a fever; a London doctor who was consulted about it declared that it is a hectic fever. My son adds that he indulges much, and in my opinion too much, in melancholy cogitations about his former misfortune, by which I think that this trouble is the more exasperated. I fear that the absence of his parents may also be distressing him: if my affairs permitted I should wish to be with him, so that, being present together, I might shake out those melancholy cogitations. I have already tried to do the same thing by letter. His affairs are not in such a state as to make it fitting for him to distress himself thus. His business dealings are increasing daily, so that there is a steady ray of hope that his former fortune may be surpassed. Meanwhile I am exceedingly afraid of that hectic fever. I fear that he contracted the beginning of it already last winter. I know that inveterate hectic fevers become incurable. I ask you in the name of our friendship to be so good as in a few lines to write me a full account of my son's condition and [to tell me] whether there is hope of his recovering his health. I have bidden him to disclose to you roundly and candidly, as to a father, everything that distresses his spirit. Perhaps his lungs do not tolerate the London air. Whatever it may be, I ask you to write me openly and fully your opinion about his condition, so that I may betimes consider what may be serviceable to him. Forgive me for giving you this trouble and charge it to fatherly affection. There are many things that make me anxious about my son; but if the Supreme Arbiter of all things wills otherwise I know that it is my [p. 657] duty to subject myself to His will; nevertheless I hope that my son will outlive me and that the misery of mourning him will never befall either myself or my wife. I am now enjoying good health; for four months I have not felt that intermission of the pulse. Mr. Le Clerc has received a reply from his brother at Geneva, that on your advice he drank water. He makes no mention of another remedy. Mr. Le Clerc says, however, that you also prescribed for him the use of some kind of pills. But his brother makes no mention of them in his letter. Meanwhile I give you, and Sir Francis and Lady Masham, my heartfelt thanks for your goodwill towards my son, and acknowledge myself wholly obliged to you. Would that I could bear witness to this by some service! Good-bye, excellent Sir. Please give our best respects to Sir Francis and Lady Masham and the whole most honourable family.
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH.
Schoonhoven†1 7 August
1702 in haste.
Address: Amplissimo ac Præstantissimo Viro D. Joanni Locke
Endorsed by Locke: P: Limborch 7 Aug. 02 Answered 4

3171. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 27 July/7 August 1702 (3146, 3198)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 185-6. Answered by no. 3198.
Rotterdam 7 August 1702
Dear Sir
The bearer hereof is my son Benjohan, instead of myself, who am still chained, and I may truly say, as that knave in the Gospel, pretended, I have marryed a wife and cannot come†1 — yet I live in hope, that once her affaire wilbe ended, now he is removed out of the way who hitherto has letted. But when that is done, I can not yet come, I have married a wife with a sister who believs that she cannot live, if her sister should go so far from her, and my wife beleevs if she should go to take leave of her, that she would immediatly fall down dead at her feet. And it would sound very harshly to separate them upon any occasion that is not the most pressing imaginable—But you may say can you not come, and leave the sisters at home? Can you not Crosse the seas without your wife, as well now as 13 year agoe? I must needs say no, and yet yes, Could my wife be persuaded to let me go. But she, who has reason to know me after 8 years and a half practising me, knows me to be so careless a fellow of my own health, and so imbecil, and soon toucht, upon the least neglect, of my self, where she is not present, to repaire the dammage I have sustain'd, that she can as little bear the thought, of letting me go alone, as she can of letting her sister stay here alone; There being no person, Doctor nor other, that so well knows her nature and infirmity as she, which is very true. Upon the whole I see not but I am bound to Holland, for one life at lest. Thus much for this melancholy theam—
You may now well expect news from me; which I know would be acceptable to that Worthy family where you are; Had I any thing acceptable to write. But we are so barren of good news, that I have little to say—
You have doubtless been throughly informd, how we have been miraculously preservd from the Destroying of our Army before Nimmegen, the taking Nimmegen, the cutting off 3 Provinces at a clap, and occupying the same posts as in the year 1672 when they came before Naerden and Woerden. Of which they were so sure, that Boufflers was heard to say, as a Switzer deserter here related,
― 660 ―
qu'il dineroit ce meme jour a deux heures a Nimmegue. And yet, wondrous to tell, no man punisht for this Treachery or at lest Neglect—There being when the Enemy appeard before the Gates, nor Cannon upon the Wall, nor Gunner, when the free Burgesses brought them thither, to shoot them of; but were forced to fetch mariners from on board a yacht of the States that lay in the River—†1
The freemen of Nimmegen finding that their Magistrates, for many years past had depriv'd them of the Priviledges, by charter due to them, and opprest them by many intolerable ways— thought fit to oblige those that had been instruments in those cases, to quit their places to such, as would swear to govern them by their known Laws, and charter; Bommel, and Tiel, two other Towns in that Quarter followed their example—But that so displeas'd the Kn—s who made out the majority of the Assembly of the States of Gelderland, fearing it might be their turn next to turn out, that they, contrary to all order, and Rule, instead of meeting this time, at Nimmegen, assembled at Arnhem, and refused to admitt the New Deputies from Nimmegen, but received the old ones, declared all they had done to be seditious, and sent Commissioners to inquire into it, and to punish the Ringleaders.
These Commissioners, were by order, fetcht in by the Garrison,†a conveyd with drawn swords to the Stadhouse, where they cashierd the New, and restored the old Magistrates.
The Burghers protesting, and resolving to appeal to the States General, who, as they say, are constituted umpires betwixt the States of the Province, and any of the Voting towns who are integral members of the Assembly and so have no Jurisdiction over each other, according to that so celebrated maxime in this Goverment, Quod par in parem non habet Imperium;†2
Which yet in your house of Commons is of no force at all, they very frequently, satis pro Imperio,†3 exercising a Jurisdiction over their fellow-members, to the censuring of them, and even expelling them the house—
They sent also Commissioners to Bommel and Tiel, but having no garrison in either place, they were, instead of being ownd and obeyd, arrested—†4
― 661 ―
This day we had a whisper on the Exchange that last Wednesday was shamefully neglected a great advantage our army had against the french,†1 and with it suggested that it might be by some, who, from such miscarriages as above mentioned, might drive the People to cry out again for a Stadholder—if so, God have mercy upon us, for then our Latter end will be worse than our beginning—
In Zealand the Reformation goes better on, they are more unanimous, having the majority in the Assembly, who, for the detecting and discarding of villains, and bringing in men of Integrity, Interest, merit and Zeale against the Common Enemy, have ordred that all the members of the State, and all magistrates and officers, that within the term of 15 years last past, have had any vote in giving offices, or have received any offices, shall purge themselves by Oath, that they have nor received any mony for their vote, nor given any for the offices they possess—By which many have accused themselvs and are eo ipso discarded, and declared uncapable.
And now I have no more to say, and so having sufficiently wearyed myself, and you, it being midnight and I to be up by 5 to morrow morning, after most hearty tender of my, my Wives, and sons most humble service to your good self, Sir Francis my Lady, and the rest of that honourable family, I crave leave to conclude myself
Sir
Your most humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
My son takes with him a packet of books that came from the Professor Limborch for you
Address: For the Honourable John Locke Esquire These Per A. QDG.
Endorsed by Locke: Ben Furly 7 Aug 02 Answered Oct. 12
3172. Francis Limborch to Locke, 29 July 1702 (3122, 3181)

Honoured Sir
Haveing received last saturnight a letter from my Father (who
― 662 ―
with my mother I thank god continues pretty well) where in he desires me to give his most sincere respects to your worthy self Sir Francis and My Lady Masham, and to tell you that Monsieur Le Clerq had written to his brother to geneve, concerning the receipt you had given him, he had received an answhere from him, that he had lost itt, and remembred onely you had advised him to drink water; and given him some pills; butt whatt they were he could nott tell, and so desires iff you might remember Sir, whether you have somuch goodnesse as to Consider whether any wayes they could be servisable to my father, that in future, incase such a fitt meight seise him againe he meight thereby be able to prevent itt; he desired me also to make his excuse for nott writeing himself, which by some extraordinary accidents he hath been prevented and was now oblidged againe to goe outt the towne upon account off some affaires off our Church, butt Intends itt immediately after his returne. by this opportunity I take also the fredome to begg your pardon for the misfortune I had in the losse off your paper which really vexed me so and made me ashamed to write to you my self concerning itt, and I hope you'll the sooner forgive itt, since itt was occasioned by such an unhappy accident, which, so j did not hurt myself worthy mentioning yett frighted me; as to my owne disposition I have nott Caughed these four or five dayes, butt finde thatt when j walke up and downe in the citty and cheefly comeing where a greatt smell off Coales is or near a packers house very faint and shorth breasted, butt in the Country I walked and rode with Mr Wright for 7 or 8 hours together and knew nothing off itt, which makes me keep outt the Citty as much possible, I continue still in the morning and evening to my milk butt aboutt dinner time am very hungry and eatt my vittles with a very good appetite which gives me hopes j shall be soone well againe; I humbly begg once more pardon for my unfortunate accident, and for the trouble j putt you to in reading this, and humbly crave leave to subscribe my self in all sincerity
Honoured Sir
Your most oblidged humble and obedient servant
FRANCIS LIMBORCH

3179. William Popple to Locke, 15 August 1702 (3173)

Sir,
Being now returned out of the Country, and both my wife and self in a good way of recovery (though neither of us yet well) we return you our acknowledgments for your kind concern about our health. Pursuant to your Order of the 3d I send you here inclosed Mr Churchill's Receipt for the 214 £ 4sh 9d which I paid him upon your account. As to the Taxes, your Observation is right. Your Board was taxed in the Verge of the Court,†1 and each Commissioner's share did amount to but 75 £: But it seems there happend a great Deficiency that year, occasioned partly by the Admiralty's paying in Westminster, and some other reasons that I remember not: However, the fact is, that upon this Deficiency the whole Court, from the highest to the lowest, were re-assessed and obliged to pay another Quarter, which made each Commissioner's share amount to £:93:15:-: according whereunto yours was computed. I am
Sir,
Your most obedient and most humble Servant

― 675 ―

3188. Locke to Dr. Daniel Whitby, 17 September 1702 (2536, 3203)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 285. Copy written by William Shaw. In his answer (no. 3203) Whitby gives the date of this letter as 2 September; as he did not receive it until 28 September Shaw's date is preferable.
Oates 17 Sept 02
Reverend Sir
Mr Churchil told me lately that he was reprinting your comment upon the Epistles.†2 By what you published in your preface to the Corinthians in your first edition I find that <you took what>†c my indisposition of health and aversion to controversy made me say in answer to yours of the 11th of Jan 9 8/9 as an yeilding of the cause.†3 If I trouble you again on this occasion it is to undeceive you in this point but still with my former designe of avoiding controversy in print if you will permit me. As to your opinion of the same bodys being raised I have noe thing to say, you may if you please establish it with what arguments you have without
― 677 ―
concerning me in it. But if you will continue to quote me and to set my words in your book to be confuted.†1 I cannot but think you desire to have a contest with me And then I hope you will not take it amiss if I defend what I have said from those attacks which have not been made in a way wholy suitable to that profession you make of freindship and esteem for me. I know not what interpretation you may put upon my desireing to be left out in that preface of yours to the Corinthians, whatever use you shall make of it I doubt not but to convince you it was out of respect to you. I am
Sir Your most humble servant
JOHN LOCKE
Endorsed by Locke: J L to Dr Whitby 17 Sept 02

20th.
It will not be more wellcome to you to hear that Cadis is surrender'd to the Duke of Ormond of which we have news this night†2 then it will be to me to hear of your health And that you have not forgot your old frend in Jerman Street tho I am the first perhaps that tell you this news I suppose you will have heard that the town of Venlo has surrender'd the Effect of my Lord Cutts's happy success in storming the fort.†3 don't accuse me for giving you a Shatterd account of Cadis since the news is come in since the bell man Went by and all I yet kno of it is that it certainly is so. but Without any perticuliars. 3190. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 24 September [1702] (3189, 3550)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 115-16. Year from Locke's endorsement.
I was resolv'd to intermit one post†1 in hopes the news I sent you might prove true. I am very sorry it did not. and have only to Excuse my self for the writing it to tell you twas brought me by a servant from the post house. and having never had wrong from thence before I beleivd it; was overjoyd at it and being sure twould have the same Effect on you was at the pains to write, and send my letter after the bell man had been some time gon. And to make amends for this imposition as twas the first news letter I have writ this summer so I think it shall be the last. however I shall have this advantage by it that it brings you two letters in my debt and my certain knolledge of your justice and civillity wont suffer me to doubt but I shall have the pleasure of a letter from you in returne which I have been so long a stranger to and should court you much oftner for did I not think both my letter's and your answering em would be too troublesome to you. If I would indulge my self in complaining I could tell you I have been in great danger of relapsing into my old indisposition of Vapours or what elce you pleas to call it. I am a strickt practitioner of your rules but can't brag that they have had the success You would wish. I have receivd a letter from my lady which I shall very speedily answer if you pleas my humble service to her Mrs Hester etc and beleive me very much
Your faithfall and humble servant

(English)
Oates 28 Sept 02
Vir Amplissime
. . . . .
De valetudine satis constanti quod scribis maxime lætor, et quod palpitatio illa cordis molesta amplius non fuerit gaudeo. Quæ ad
― 680 ―
sanitatem tuendam faciunt tam recte et prudenter moderaris ut sperem te diu ab illo aliisque morbis tutum et sospitem futurum, præcipue si dietæ mediocritati venæ sectionem si plethoram vel sentias vel metuas quotiescunque inde malum ingruit addere velis
(English) Nunc demum si placet ad diu intermissa studia redeamus. habeo jam præ manibus literas tuas 3o Januarii datas In quibus videris mihi dubitare an ego statuam hominem esse in Volendo vel in Intelligendo liberum, Ita enim quæstionem tuam interpretor etiam tu rogas an actio volendi vel intelligendi sit libera. Ad quam quæstionem sic respondeo
1° Generaliter nempe quod meâ sententiâ homo in omni actione tam volendi quam intelligendi liber est si ab actione illa volendi aut intelligendi potuit abstinuisse. si non non.
2° Specialius, quoad voluntatem, aliqui sunt casus in quibus homo non potest non velle, et in omnibus istis volendi actibus homo non est liber quia non potest non agere. In cæteris ubi potuit velle vel non velle liber est
3° Quoad actus intelligendi in ista voce intelligendi suspicor latere amphiboliam nam significare potest actionem cogitandi de aliquo subjecto et in isto sensu homo plerumque liber est in istiusmodi actionibus intellectus: v: g: possum cogitare de peccato
― 681 ―
Adami vel inde amovere cogitationem meam ad urbem Romam, vel ad artem bellicam præsentis sæculi. In quibus omnibus et hujusmodi aliis infinitis liber sum quia pro libitu meo possum de hoc vel illo cogitare vel non cogitare. Vel actus intelligendi potest sumi pro ea actione <qua>†a percipio aliquid esse verum et in hac actione intelligendi v.g. quod tres anguli trianguli sunt æquales duobus rectis, homo non est liber quia excussa demonstratione non potest non hoc intelligere. Homo potest plerumque non aperire oculos, vel non advertere aciem oculorum ad hoc vel illum objectum, verum apertis et conversis ad solem vel lunam oculis necessario videt et splendorem et figuram quæ se offert intuitui videndam. Quod de oculis dixi ad intellectum transferre licet: Par utrinque est ratio. Sed de his hactenus. Si satisfactum tibi sit gaudeo. Sin dubia restent utere libertate tuâ ego paratus sum et in his et in omnibus quantum in me est tibi obtemperare. Tui studiosissimus
J LOCKE

(Latin)
Oates 28 Sept 02
Excellent Sir,
... I am very pleased by what you write about your sufficiently steady health, and am glad that that palpitation of the heart has not been further [p. 679] troublesome. You are managing the things that make for the preservation of health so rightly and prudently that I hope that you will long be safe and sound, unharmed by that and other illnesses, especially if to moderation in diet you will add bleeding if you feel or fear a plethora, as often as trouble from it assails you.
(Latin) Now at length, if you please, let us return to long discontinued studies. I have now before me your letter of 3 January, in which you appear to doubt whether I hold that a man is free in Willing or in Understanding, for so I interpret your question; you also ask whether the action of willing or understanding is free. To this question I answer thus:
1. Generally, indeed, that in my opinion a man is free in every action, as well of willing as of understanding, if he was able to have abstained from that action of willing or understanding; if not, not.
2. More particularly, as regards the will: there are some cases in which a man is unable not to will, and in all those acts of willing a man is not free because he is unable not to act. In the rest, where he was able to will or not to will, he is free.
3. As regards the act of understanding: I surmise that there lurks an ambiguity in that word 'understanding', for it can signify an action of thinking about some subject, and in that sense a man is for the most part free in actions of the understanding of that sort: for example: I can think about Adam's sin, [p. 680] or remove my cogitation thence to the city of Rome or to the art of war in the present age. In all these actions and in countless others of the kind I am free because I am able at my pleasure to think or not to think about this or that. Or an act of understanding can be taken for that action by which I perceive that something is true, and in this action of understanding, for example, that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles, a man is not free because when the demonstration has been examined he is unable not to understand this. For the most part a man is able not to open his eyes or not to turn his gaze to this or that object, but when his eyes are opened and turned to the sun or moon he necessarily sees the brightness and the shape that present themselves to his observation. What I have said of the eyes may be transferred to the understanding: the principle is the same for both. But enough of this. If you are satisfied I am glad. But if any doubts remain please use your freedom: I am ready to comply with you as much as I can in these and in all things. Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) Please give my best wishes to your wife and daughter and to our common friends.
Sir Francis and Lady Masham send their greetings to you and your family.
Address: Mijn Heer Mÿn Heer Philip van Limborch t'Amsterdam

3195. James Tyrrell to Locke, 6 October [1702] (3167, 3253)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 151-2. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Shot: Oct: 6
Dear Sir
At my Returne from a Journey of about a Fortnight which I made into Sussex with my Daughter and son in Law about 6 weeks since I found yours, which was very wellcome to me, since it brought me the good news of your being rid of that (to my own woful experience) tormenting and acute paine in your Ear, and tho it has left its usual Consequence Deafness behind, yet it is a great Comfort to be free from pain, and I hope your hearing
― 684 ―
will be again restord to you, either by proper Remedies, or of it self; among the Remedies, I wish you would be pleas'd to trie that I told you (which was a Receipt of my Mothers) of the Juice or Brine of raw, lean Beef; since I have known it doe good to divers, and particularly to Dr: Beeston,†1 Warden of New Colledg, when he was about your years: if you will trie it, and that you have lost your former Receipt I will send you another how to prepare it, in short, if you could by some warme and mollifieing Things now and then put into your Ears bring them to purge and send forth Ear Wax, you would then recover your hearing in some measure, for till that could be obtaind, I could never hear, when in my youth, I was much in your Condition; and was very sensible what a melancholy uncomfortable thing the want of all Conversation was.
But to give you some Account of my self, I have not bin without Mementos of the frail Condition of the best establisht health, for assoon as I came from my Journey, I was seisd with an intermitting Feavour, that held me 5, or 6 days and lay very much in my Head, but at last I got it away by means of the Bark; and I have since kept it off by drinking the bitter Decoction, with some Tincture of Steel in it, which has done me a great deal of Good; so that I have gone abroad, as far as Oxford these ten days, but am not as yet restord to my former state of health, but hope I may be by degrees: As for Mr: Lees book,†2 those few in Oxford that have read it, complain of the Tediousness of it, since he is not onely contented to find fault, but will take a great deal of paines, to comment upon what you have writ, and to explaine it his owne way when indeed it was much clearer before; so you may rest satisfyed that Performance may advance, but will never confute your Ingenious Essay: If you have not read my Lord Clarendons first volume of the History of the civil wars I would recommend it to your perusal, it being full of lively, (and I beleive for the most part) true Characters of the cheif Persons concernd in the publick Affairs of that Time, besides many curious particulars of secret History not before publisht; the second volume is going to the Press my Lord Roch:†3 having promised to bring it, or send it down
― 685 ―
in a short time. in the mean while they go on with a new Edition of the first volume.†1 My paper will afford no more room then to pray for the Return of your hearing, which with my humble ser<vi>ce†a to Sir Francis, and his Lady is all at present from your af<fec>tionate†a humble servant
J TYRRELL
Wee are all well here, and very much satisfyed, since my sister Russel being returnd from Nevis, with one of her Daughters,†2 the other my Lady Stapleton†3 a yong Widdow having bin here above this twelve month, they are now all with us together with my sister Birch†4 and Judith,†5 so that wee have a full House.
My son James is gone into Ireland to his Command, but I hope will returne by the middle of the next month.

3198. Locke to Benjamin Furly, 12 October 1702 (3171, 3224)
B.L., MS. Eng. letters c. 200, f. 16. Printed by T.I.M. Forster in Epistolarium, 1845, pp. 14-16; Original Letters of Locke, etc., 2nd ed., 1847, pp. 133-6. Sent to Benjohan Furly to be taken to Furly: p. 690. Answers nos. 3065, 3146, and 3171; acknowledged in no. 3224.
Oates 12 Oct 02
Dear Friend
Did I not think you are soe well satisfied of my esteem and friendship, that you will not doubt of it whither I talk to you, or whither I hold my peace, I should not have been soe long silent after the receit of three very obleigeing letters. You see I have ingenuity enough to acknowledg my debts, though I have not wherewith all to make you returns in the like kind. All the action is on your side the water, and dayly furnishes matter: We here make noe noise, and I am too far out of the way (which I am not sorry for) to hear any thing that does not. And whither it be saciety†1 or dull old age, or any thing else, I have noe curiosity to be prying, or to acquaint my self with the bias or bent of affairs, only I shall always be glad to hear of publick events that tend to the prosperity and preservation of my country, and the security of Europe. I promised my self much satisfaction in your company here this sommer, and 'tas been a great disappointment to me to miss it. Besides the joy it would have been to me to see You again I flatter my self we could have passed some days togeather not unpleasantly, though news and politiques had been excluded out of our conversation. I think my self upon the brink of an other world, and being ready to leave those shuflings which have generaly too broad a mixture of folly and corruption, should not dispair with you to find matters more suited to the thoughts of a
― 688 ―
rational creature to entertein us. Doe not think now that I am grown either a Stoick or a Mystick. I can laugh as heartily as ever, and be in pain for the publick as much as you. I am not grown into a sulleness that puts off humanity, noe nor mirth neither. come and trye. But I have laid by the simplicity of troubleing my head about things that I cannot give the least turn to one way or t'other. I rather choose to imploy my thoughts about some thing that may better my self, and perhaps some few other such simple fellows as I am. You may easily conclude this written in a chimny corner in some obscure hole out of the way of the busy men of this world. And I think not the worse of it for being so: And I pray heartily it may continue soe as long as I live. I live in fear of the Bustlers, and would not have them come near me. Such quiet fellows as you are, that come without drum and trumpet, with whom one can talke upon equall termes, and receive some benifet by their company I should be glad to have in my neighbourhood, or to see some times though they came from totherside the water. Though I have noe thing to say to you nor send to you but my hearty good wishes, which are far from news to you, yet I am you see got into a veyn of talking, and know not how long I should run on in it, did not my arm stop my hand. I have of late soe great a pain in my arm when I write, that I am often fain to give off. But tis not strange that my frail tenement has decays in it, tis rather to be wonderd that it hath lasted soe long. If my continuance in it might be of any service to you or any of my friends or to any good man I shall be glad For I am with great affection and sincerity
Dear Friend
Your Faithfull friend and humble servant

Sir

3200. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 16/27 October 1702 (3192, 3352)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 153-4. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, ff. 221v-222. Printed from the copy, with an omission, in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 530-4. Answers no. 3192.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Multis me obruis beneficiis, quorum memoriam nulla unquam eluet ætas. Nunquam ego de immutatâ tuâ erga filium meum benevolentiâ dubitavi: Verum officii mei esse credidi, et ipsum monere, ut in omnibus tuo, non secus ac paterno consilio obsequatur, te enim illi in Angliâ vere esse patrem, et πολλῶν ἀντάξιον ἂλλων;†3 et
― 691 ―
apud te intercedere, ut solitâ illum benevolentiâ prosequi digneris: Non quod vel minimum de animo tuo dubitaverim; sed quia me id officii pro plurimis filio meo præstitis beneficiis tibi debere credidi. Gaudeo quod cum valetudine etiam pristinus animi vigor, et cum eo pristina familiaritas filio redierit. Otium ipsi grave est: crescentibus negotiis etiam animi alacritas incrementum capiet. Ego hactenus Dei Gratià bene valeo: ante septem circiter hebdomadas plethoram mihi molestam sensi, sine tamen gravi cordis palpitatione: quare venæ sectionem adhibui; atque ita omnis illa molestia evanuit.
(English) 1. Quæ de libertate hominis in actione intelligendi ac volendi scribis, tecum verissima agnosco; nimirum in omnibus actionibus, à quibus homo potuit abstinuisse, esse liberum: minimè verò, si abstinuisse non potuit.
(English) 2. Similiter quosdam esse casus, in quibus homo non potest non velle, et non agere; quia facultate non agendi destitutus est. Sed vero in omnibus actibus obedientiæ ab ipso præstandis, et ob quos non præstitos pœnæ reus fit, liberum credo; neque quemquam posse pœnæ reum fieri, ob non præstitum actum sibi minimè possibilem, aut ob præstitum sibi inevitabilem. Nihil enim homini magis liberum esse debet, quam id ob quod pœnæ reus fit.
― 692 ―
(English) 3. Hominem esse liberum, ut contemplationem vel cogitationem suam ab uno objecto avertat, et in aliud dirigat, atque hoc respectu in actionibus intellectus liberum posse dici, tecum agnosco. Verum hæc actio, si accuratè loqui velimus, propriè est actio volendi, non intelligendi: avertit enim homo cogitationes suas ab uno objecto, et in aliud dirigit, quia non vult priores cogitationes continuare, et quia vult novas inchoare. Quod vero intelligendi actionem attinet, quâ homo aliquid percipit esse verum, eam rectè dicis non esse liberam: idque locum habet, tam in percipiendis iis quæ Philosophi per solam intelligentiam cognosci dicunt; ut, bis duo sunt quatuor; idem non potest simul esse et non esse, etc. quam illis quæ excussâ demonstratione cognosci optimè dicis, videl. tres angulos trianguli æquales esse duobus rectis. Idem etiam locum habere censeo in aliis intelligendi actibus, quando res est obscura aut dubia, et nullæ sunt rationes evidenter eam probantes, aut pro utrâque sententiâ rationes sunt æqualis ponderis: tum enim homo aut necessariò suspensus est, aut dubitat, aut leviter tantum assentitur, ita tamen ut falli posse se credat. Adeo ut intelligendi actio accommodata sit rationibus ac argumentis, quorum pondere in hanc aut illam partem inclinatur. Qualia plurima sunt in vitâ humanâ. Et actio illa intelligendi
― 693 ―
non mutatur, quamdiu non accedunt novæ rationes, aut rationum quibus rei veritas innititur clarior et evidentior perceptio. Non nego tamen in ejusmodi cognitione inevidenti fieri posse, quin et sæpius contingere, ut nullâ accedente novâ luce, aut magis distinctâ perceptione, homo aut eliciat plenum assensum, aut opinionem suam mutet: Verum illa judicii mutatio aut assensus, non procedit ab actione aliquâ intelligendi, sed volendi; quia nimirum homo, licet novâ ratione minimè illustratus, judicium suum in alteram partem inclinare vult. Scimus affectus nostros valde inclinare judicium nostrum; itaque indulgendo affectui cuiquam qui me in alteram partem impellit, eò etiam judicium et assensum meum inclinare possum. Atque ita judicium hoc meum erit actio mixta, partim intelligendi, partim volendi: quatenus intelligendi est actio, seu rem percipit, est necessaria: Verum quicquid in judicio liberum est procedit ab actione volendi, quatenus scilicet ego rationibus allatis acquiescere volo, ut judicium feram. Qualem actionem mixtam ego etiam credo fidem nostram esse, prout explicui in Theologiâ meâ Christianâ lib. V. cap.IX. §§ 21, 22, 23. ibique plenius ostendo, quomodo actio intelligendi et volendi in Fide Christianâ concurrunt: solummodò ex inveteratâ loquendi consuetudine usus sum vocibus intellectus et voluntatis, quibus
― 694 ―
actiones intelligendi et volendi designo, juxta ea quæ jam declaraveram lib.II. cap.XXIII. §§ 1, 2. Hæc sic distinctè consideranda existimo. Verum nolim ego multum contendere, utrum illa libertas etiam sit dicenda inesse actioni intelligendi; dummodò constet hominem in actione illâ liberum esse; et hominem liberè ab unâ cogitatione se convertere in alteram. Distinctione tamen hac adhibitâ puto rem dilucidius explicari. Et sic etiam similitudo tua ab oculis desumta plenius applicatur. Quod enim homo non aperiat oculos, aut oculorum aciem non advertat, hoc facit quia ita vult: oculi autem quando aperiuntur et in objectum diriguntur, illud quale se oculis repræsentat necessariò conspiciunt: si in debitâ distantiâ oculis objiciatur, etiam necessariò distinctè videtur: si nimis remotum sit, distinctè videri non potest; neque homo libertatem habet procurandi, ut objectum in tali distantiâ ipsi distinctè appareat; sed si distinctè contemplari velit, libertatem habet propius accedendi. In his puto nos consentire; atque ita in summâ rei nullum esse dissensum, licet forsitan in modo explicandi aliqua discrepantia sit. Vale Vir Amplissime et salve ab uxore, filiâ, ac me
Tui Amantissimo
PHILIPPO À LIMBORCH.
― 695 ―
Salveant quam officiosissimè à nobis Dominus ac Domina Masham, totaque honorata illa familia.
Amstelodami 27 Octobris
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
You overwhelm me with many kindnesses, the memory of which age will never wash away. I have never doubted your unchangeable goodwill towards my son, but I thought it to be my duty both to admonish him to follow your advice in all things as if it were his father's, for you are truly a father to him in England and 'are worth many other men';†3 and to intercede with you to be [p. 690] so good as to pursue him with your wonted goodwill: not because I have in the very least doubted your spirit, but because I thought that I owed you that duty on account of the many kindnesses done to my son. I am glad that with his health his former vigour of spirit has also returned to my son, and with it his former sociability(?). Idleness is burdensome for him: as his business increases his cheerfulness of spirit will also increase. By the grace of God I am so far in good health; about seven weeks ago I felt some trouble from my plethora, but without oppressive palpitation of the heart: wherefore I was bled; and so all that trouble disappeared.
(Latin) 1. I acknowledge with you as most true what you write about the liberty of a man in the actions of understanding and willing: that is, a man is free in all the actions from which he was able to have abstained; but by no means free if he was unable to have abstained.
(Latin) 2. Likewise there are some cases in which a man is unable not to will and not to act; because he is destitute of the faculty of not acting. But in all acts of obedience that are to be performed by him, and for the non-performance of which he becomes liable(?) to punishment [pœnæ reus], I believe that he is free; nor can anyone become liable(?) to punishment for not performing an act that was entirely impossible for him, or for performing one that he could not avoid. For nothing ought to be more free for a man than that on account of which he becomes liable(?) to punishment. [p. 691]
(Latin) 3. I acknowledge with you that a man is free to turn away his contemplation or cogitation from one object and to direct it to another, and that in this respect he can be said to be free in actions of the understanding. But this action, if we want to speak carefully, is properly an action of willing, not of understanding; for a man turns away his cogitations from one object and directs them to another because he does not wish to continue his former cogitations, and because he wishes to start new ones. But as to the action of understanding by which a man perceives that something is true: you say rightly that it is not free; and this applies in perceiving both those things which Philosophers say are learnt through the intelligence [intelligentia] alone, as, twice two are four, the same thing cannot at the same time be and not be, etc.; and those which, as you very well say, are learnt when a demonstration has been examined, viz. the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles. I think that the same applies also in other acts of understanding when a thing is obscure or doubtful and there are no reasons clearly proving it, or the reasons for either opinion are of equal weight: for a man then is necessarily in suspense, or doubts, or assents only slightly, yet as if he thinks that he can be mistaken. Thus the action of understanding is accommodated to the reasons and arguments by whose weight it is inclined to this or that side. There are many such [occasions] in human life. Moreover that action of understanding is not changed as long as no new reasons accede, [p. 692] or a clearer and more evident perception of the reasons on which the truth of the matter rests. Nevertheless I do not deny that in inevident knowledge of this kind it can happen, indeed it very often happens, that without the accession of any new light or a more distinct perception a man either elicits a full assent or changes his opinion: but that change of opinion, or assent, proceeds not from any action of understanding but from one of willing; doubtless because the man, although not enlightened by a new reason, wills to incline his judgement to the other side. We know that our passions strongly affect our judgement; therefore by yielding to any passion that drives me to the other side I can also incline my judgement and assent to it. And so this judgement of mine will be a mixed action, partly of understanding, partly of willing: in so far as it is an action of understanding, or as it perceives a thing, it is necessary; but whatever in a judgement is free proceeds from an action of willing, in so far, that is to say, as I will to be satisfied with the adduced reasons in order to form a judgement. I believe also that our faith is a mixed action of this kind, as I have explained in my Theologia Christiana, bk. V, ch. ix, §§ 21, 22, 23, where I show more fully how the actions of understanding and willing are combined in Christian Faith; only that through an inveterate habit of speech I have used the words understanding [intellectus] and will, by which I denote the actions of understanding and willing, in accordance with what I had already declared in bk. II, ch. xxiii, [p. 693] §§ 1, 2. I think that these things should be considered separately in this way. But I should not very much wish to contend whether that liberty should also be said to belong to the action of understanding, so long as it is agreed that a man is free in that action, and that he turns himself freely from one cogitation to another. Yet I think that when this distinction is used the matter is set forth more clearly. And in this way your comparison with the eyes is also more fully applicable. For if a man does not open his eyes or does not turn his gaze [to an object], he does this because he so wills; again, when his eyes are opened and directed to an object they necessarily see it as it presents itself to them; if it is put before them at the appropriate distance it is also necessarily seen clearly; if it is too distant it cannot be seen clearly; nor has a man liberty to bring it about that an object at such a distance should appear clearly to himself; but if he wills to view it clearly he has liberty to draw nearer. I think that we agree about these things, and so there will be no disagreement in the chief point of the matter, although there is perhaps some variance in the manner of setting it forth. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and greetings from my wife, my daughter and myself,
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH. [p. 694]
Our best respects to Sir Francis and Lady Masham, and that whole honourable family.
Amsterdam 27 October
1702
Address: Amplissimo Consultissimo Viro D. Joanni Locke
Endorsed by Locke: P: Limborch 27 Oct 02

3204. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 30 October/10 November 1702 (3155, 3274)

Monsieur,
Jay honte de repondre si tard a vótre derniere. depuis trois mois une dysenterie epidemique nous a point laissé de repos, et il est vray que cet embaras est cause que jay differé de jour a autre a vous ecrire. et comme je m'informois de votre etat chez Messieurs Limburgh et le Clerc, et quils ignorassent vótre indisposition, cela me faisoit croire que vous vous portiez mieux; il est vray aussi qu'on ne scauroit a mon sens rien adjouter de mieux au remedes qu'on vous applique. je crois tousjours qu'une decoction de salse-parille et de chine vous seroit utile, et de vous purgotter legerement quelquefois avec la Casse, la rhabarbre,†a et le mercure doux†2 bien preparé. je confesse qu'a votre age il faut étre fort retenu pour droguer le corps, principalement quand il est si emacié, outre que je scay que vous vivez tousjours d'un grand regime. il seroit a souhaitter que vos fluxions (tant que cette cause subsiste dans vos humeurs) reprissent cours aux jambes. quelque leger vesicatoire entretenu ouvert avec les feuilles de choux rouges, ne conviendroit
― 699 ―
ce me semble pas mal. enfin Monsieur je voudrois de tout mon cœur pouvoir contribuer quelque chose pour vótre soulagement, cela nous fait une peine extréme de vous voir patir si long temps, et nous esperons tousjours d'apprendre que vous aurez recu quelque amandement.
Ma femme a eté fort enrhumée depuis son retour de la Campagne, il y a deux mois. une toux seche la beaucoup incommodée, et elle a eu meme quelques acces de fievre double tierce, je craignois méme une glaires quon jette par bas dans la dysenterie, qui par leur acrimonie erodent les veines et causent le flux de sang.

3205. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 4 and 5 November 1702 (3201, 3209)

Oates 4o Nov 02
Dear Cosin
Had not my health with strong hand held me back from such a journey at this time of the year espetialy to London I had certainly upon reading my Lord Peterbroughs message to me in your letter obeyd my inclination and come to kiss his hands before he went; Nor could the considerations of my health have hinderd me nor the remonstrances of my friends here against it, If I could have seen any thing wherein I could by waiting upon him have done any service to his Lordship. As it is there is noe thing I have borne soe uneasily from the decays of age, my troublesome ear, my breathless lungs, and my being unable to stir, as the being stopd in paying my respects in person upon his goeing upon such an expedition. And yet I know not what I could doe were I in London but intrude upon his Lordship unseasonably amidst a croud of business, and rob him uselessesly of some of his time at a season when he cannot I know have a minute to spare. But when I have said and revolvd all this, I find my self dissatisfied in not seeing of him, and tis a displeasure will rest upon my mind and adde weight to that of those infirmities that caused it. If I could hope that in this my state of confinement and impotency there was any thing remaind that might be usefull to his Lordship, that would be some comfort and releif to me. And if he could find out and would let me know wherein I might be in any way serviceable to him in his absence, it would make me put some value upon the litle remainder of my life.

3212. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 15 November 1702 (3209, 3213)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 243-4.
Oates 15 Nov 02
Dear Cosin
I desire you to return my most humble thanks to my Lord Peterborough for the extraordinary honour he designes me And I am utterly ashamd it should cost him soe much trouble, But the joy I am in with the hopes I have of kissing his hands before he leaves England makes me overlook every thing else and think of noe thing but the happynesse of seeing him on Friday next.†2 I shall not faile god willing to be at the Crown at Epping by eleven of the clock at farthest And I wish his Lordships affairs would permit him to set out soe early as to be there by that time, the days being now short and the ways durty and I would not have him benighted. Pray therefore if you can prevaile with him to be there by eleven. I will be sure to be there before that time. Sir
Yours of the 7th October I received by yesterdays Post and am sorry I am forc'd to be thus backward in my acknowledgement of the favour by not knowing of it sooner. I promisd my self the satisfaction of waiting on you at Oates the last summer, but this journey was delay'd upon the account of the 2 little books I sent you, for I was unwilling to appear without 'em. They came forth at last and I sent 'em by the Coachman according to directions I had formerly received from you designing my self to have followed 'em the next week, but then a young Gentleman a pupill of mine fell ill of the smallpox: 'Twas my duty to take all the Care I could of him during his illness in the Absence of his Relations and I think my Concern for him has been Equal to it. This Accident put by my intended journey for that time and has furnished me with an Excuse to some few friends who have been so kind as to blame me for my not writing to 'em. He is now very well recover'd, and gone for some time to take the Country Air, so that I do not despair of being able to see you before Christmas. My mother I thank God is

Sir

3214A. Dr. Richard Burthogge to Locke, 20 November 1702 (2617A, 3278A)
Oxford, Museum of the History of Science, MS. Buxton 7. Transcript made by Charles Babbage: see no. 1737A, n. The round and square brackets are those of Babbage's transcript. I have silently corrected the accents, etc., of the Greek words. I have not checked the citations of Ainsworth, etc.
Nov. 20. <1702>†a
Sir
You have very much Honour'd as well as encourag'd me by your obliging Letter of the 9th Instant which came to hand this morning. I presum'd indeed to present you one of my discourses on three verses in the 8'th ch. of the Epistle to the Romans†1 as a mark of my great respect. But being conscious that it contained several things not generally received I durst not take the confidence to own that treatise in a particular manner to you till I had let it try its fortune. But now Sir that you have shewed it so much kindness and me so much respect as to command my further thoughts about some notions therein I assure myself to say that without admitting these Ideas I embrace concerning the Αἰῶνες and Χρόνοι Αἰώνιοι I could not read many places in the new Testament†b- with any-†b understanding and Profit. I confess I never met any Author who set out the notions or any thing like them with distinction and clearness But on some occasion (near twenty years ago) comparing Exod 21.6 with Lev. 25.40.41 I observed that olam in the Hebrew and Αἰών in Greek did sometimes
― 710 ―
signify a determinate Age that is a space of time from one jubilee to another.
In Exod 21.6 where we have the law of the servant who had his ear bored it is said He shall serve his Master for ever le olam in the Hebrew and in the LXX εἰς τὸν Αἰῶνα which says Mr Ainsworth†1 ad Loc. is (as Maimony†2 there explaineth it) till a Jubilee. St Hierom (If I do not misrember) goes the same way. Buxtorf in his Opus XXX Annorum†3 ad Voc. olam gives the text the same version. Manasseh ben Israel in his Conciliation†4 on Leviticus Quæst 7. Acquaints us that R. Joseph Albus†5 in Icarim understood the text in the same sense, Et serviet ei in perpetuum ubi perpetuum denotat tempus ad Jubileum usque. And Manasseh himself yields the interpretation in that place is good. And good it must be yielded by all who with judgment consider what is said Levit 25.39.40.41. If thy Brother by thee be waxen poor etc thou shalt not compel him to serve as a Bond Servant; as an Hired Servant, as a sojourner He shall be with thee unto the year of Jubilee and then he shall depart from thee etc. Here that service which Exod 21.6 is said to be le-olame and εἰς τὸν Αἰῶνα for an Age. <Thus>†a our translators make it a service for ever and R. Kimchi†6 a service for Life is limited to be a service but untill a Jubilee. For this service in both places must of necessity be the same, seeing the servant spoken of in Leviticus is the servant with the bored ear who is spoken of in Exodus and was to serve Le-Olam for no other servant†b- but He,-†b if he was an Hebrew, a brother, was to serve above six years Exod 21.2. Now if the time of the Legal Dispensation (commonly called the Mosaical Seculum) was measured and distinguished by Jubilees and the time from Jubilee to Jubilee was called Olam in Hebrew and in Greek ὁ Αἰων an Age; Is it not very consequent that then the time of that dispensation was a system
― 711 ―

of several Ages. And consequently Is it not also very congruous that it should be called οἱ Αἰωνες the Ages or Χρόνοι Αἰώνιοι (Times rather than time) His secular times. This is further confirmed from the use of the expressions in the Scriptures where they carry this sense and can be understood in no other. I have shewed it of Χρόνοι Αἰῶνιοι in my late treatise and it is as manifest for οἱ Αἰῶνες in 1 Cor. c 10 v 11 and Hebrews 9.20.†1 It is said I Cor. c 10 v 11 that τὰ τέλη τῶν Αἰώνων not the end of the world as our Translators render it but the Consumations (or ends) of the Ages [viz. the ends of the times of the Law] are come unto [as it were to meet] us Christians. The meaning is that as in the times of the Law men then had but the Figures so we Christians now have the good things themselves in Christ Jesus; For he As he Died He Cried out τετέλεσται, Consumatum est, It [the Law] is Fulfilled or Ended: and accordingly the veil of the Temple was then rent. In Heb 9.26 it is said that Christ appeared to make a sacrifice of himself once ἐπί συντελείᾳ τῶν Αἰώνων in the Consumation of the Ages (in the plural) that is in the end of the Legal dispensation or Seculum. But (what must be observed for a distinction between the Expressions) it is not said ἐπι συντελεία τοῦ Αἰῶνος (in the singular) as it is in Matt 28.ult. where our Saviour hath his eye upon the συντελεία Αἰώνος which his disciples Enquired after Matt 24.3 and which he himself calleth v 14 the End [τὸ τέλος] the end of the Jewish Polity and civil (as well as sacred) Government at the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple which they thought would last as long as the world or to the end of time it self.

I have other things to say upon this subject but these are the principal, of which if you shall please to vouchsafe me your impartial censure it will either rectify or confirm me and each way oblige extremely
Sir
Your most humble and devoted Servant
RICH BURTHOGGE
Address: This for John Locke Esquire at Oats 
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Burthogge 20 Nov 1702 <Answered>†a Feb. 27.
― 712 ―
