3222. Lady (Mary) Calverley to Locke, 28 November [1702] (1749)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, f. 7. Written by an amanuensis, apart from the signature. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Dear Sir
I am obliged to make use of a Secretary, my breast at present being so painfull that my writeing hand is disabled. they have pronounc'd it a Cancer,†1 so that I am afraid I shall never again have the pleasure to salute you with my own pen.
I have a boon to beg of you, before I leave this life, I dont question a kind return from you, haveing had all my life time such proofs of your freindship; It is this that you would please to write a billet to my Lord Peterborough, and direct it to me in Soho square, in favour of Mr Banbary, an honest parsons son, though but five and twenty has been some years set up Bookbinder.†2 but the world has so frown'd upon him, that he has been forc'd to leave of his trade and is now destitute of all helps. What this unfortunate man petitions, is that my Lord would have the Goodness to take him along with him to the Westindies. he writes readily and well, and hopes by that qualification to be serviceable to my Lord. and if No Ensigns or other place be to be dispos'd of, he would throw himself under my Lords protection hopeing by his diligence to recommend himself to his Lordship, and in the mean time desires onely necessaries for life; such acts as these must recommend us in the next
― 718 ― 
world, for which reason without saying any more, I depend upon ye, As always shall whilst is in Being,

Your most Obliged Humble servant
M CALVERLEY
28 November
Pray let me know how your own health is.

3223. Locke to Edward Clarke, 30 November 1702 (3152, 3257)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, f. 107. Printed in part in Forster, p. 65; in full in Rand, pp. 587-8.
Oates 30 Nov 02
Dear Sir
I was glad to see your hand some time since upon a cover which brought me a letter from my wife. And I have since that been mightily rejoyced to hear from several hands that you are returnd to town in very good health. I doe not expect that the place you are in, or the affairs you there meet with should much increase it. But yet I hope you will take care that it shall not sink it again. There will be I doubt not holydays of some kind or other for you at Christmas. And then what should hinder you to take a little air. A few days spent here then I think would doe you noe harm and I am sure would obleige more than one here. Doe not blame me if I desire to be happy once more in your company. I have been little better than out of the world these last twelve months by a deafness that in great measure shut me out of conversation. I thank god my hearing is now restored again and it is in your power to make me yet more sensible of that blesseing. It would be folly in me to count upon an other Christmas: come then and let me injoy you this. My Lady who gives you her service joyns with me in this request and says that in this uncertain world she knows noe thing soe desirable as the conversation of friends. And therefore she nor I are not to be blamed if we take care to secure yours early, that noe thing may fall in between to rob us of our hopes
I was gon thus far when I received my Lady Caverlys under your cover. I am very sorry to find her under those circumstances of health she mentions. Pray give her my most humble service and assure
― 719 ― 
her that I will not fail to obey her commands the next post, if I have not time, as I fear I shall not, before the messenger goes now. I am

Dear Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
Pray with the inclosed let my service goe to Mrs Clarke and all the family at Chipley. Pray give my service to the Batchelor

3224. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 2/13 December 1702 (3198, 3226)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 187. Probably carried by Arent Furly: p. 721. Acknowledges no. 3198.
Deare Sir
yours by my son Benjohan I heard with pleasure read in my sick bed, and yesterday yours to Arent, and now I am hurryed up, the wind being easterly to write this, tho little able to do it—you write well, that this design of Arents should have been managed better, but there wanted time—no opportunity has presented since my Lords first kind invitation in Generall terms for any friend of mine†1 —for assistance or preferment in affaires or the militia, of sending him over—, I know not whether to hope or fear that he may come too late, consideratis considerandis, he began well here,†2 and his brother will want him rather then a stranger—I stand betwixt both willing to please both—However I am willing Arent does this journey to England—But if my Lord be gone—he cannot follow him to any port with trunks and luggage, but must come back—I commit the thing intirely to providence, and your good counsell—I thank you for your good advice about my cough; my dyet is water gruell, and drink water with a tost—and sometimes with a rosted apple—I thank god my cough abates, and I begin to eat of a fowle— But the first flesh I tasted was of a powderd†3 goose my son brought out of England of which I eat heartily, and it revived me, and then of a second, and then of a third goose, in which we remembred the Goose—Thus you see one Goose agrees well with another—my
― 720 ― 
service to Sir F. my Lady and all that noble family. I am not able to run further with my hand, but my affections know no limit and so I rest

Dear friend
your most affectionate friend and humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
Rotterdam 13 December 1702

3226. Benjamin Furly to Locke, [c. 8/19 December 1702] (3224, 3286)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 188-9. Probably the letter enclosed by Benjohan Furly in his letter of 8/19 December to Francis Limborch, and forwarded by Limborch with his letter of 12 December, no. 3227.
Dear Sir
I hope my son Arent has ere this sent, or delivered you mine by him.†1 By which you will have understood how much I ballanced in my mind about his intended Voyage. And yielded rather to his importunity, than any great ground I had to expect that it could be of any great advantage to him, tho I never doubted of my Lords good will both to him and me, or to him for my sake.†2
But what now startles me is that I am by these letters now come on, told by a friend, that all honourable and profitable places, have for some years past been so reassumed by the crown, vested in it, and given by pattents under the great seale, that there is little or nothing left in the Governours power to do for any man, that may countervaile the hazards, of so long and sickly a voyage.†3 And this is wrote me by a friend for Arents sake.
Wherefore I this evening charge him to do nothing without my Lord Sh—†4 yours, and mr. micklethwaits advice:†5 who I doubt not may easily understand the Truth of it.
I am apt to beleev it, because my son Benj. telling me mr. Simon Clement†6 was to go as Secretary, I wrote to him, being glad to hear it, desiring him to take care of my son, and not doubting but my Lord would place him in a post under his care, Answers me that he should willingly do it, if should go. But that that is uncertain, for that notwithstanding all my Lords indeavours for him, he could not obtain a graunt of it for him;
― 722 ― 

which to me does not a little confirm what the other writes. So that there seems to be little or nothing in my Lords power, tho his will be as great as can be desired, to do for him, but in the martiall part, by sea or by land.
I begg therefore your advice to my son as a father to us both, He is under no necessity, God be thanked, to be exposed to such hazards, unless we could see a morall certainty as it were that he might with an advancement that might counterballance those hazards.
On the contrary we want him at home, and if he should go, which I do not now expect, we shall be put to the Inconvenience to seek a stranger to supply his place.
I have not else to add save endeared respects from my wife and children, as well as my self to yourself and that honourable family where you are, remayning.
Dear Sir
Your most humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
Now my cough has left me, I am afflicted with a Tenasmus.†1 pressing and looseness, I have purged thrice with Rubarb dryed black, which has done me good, but the pressing, with gripings continue.
Address: (written by an amanuensis): For John Locke Esquire At Sir Francis Masham's 
Endorsed by Locke: B: Furly 170 2/3

3230. Charles Mordaunt, third earl of Peterborough, to Locke, 26 December 1702 (2306, 3244)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 125-6. Printed in King, p. 239.
Sir
The lady that made you a visitt with mee†1 would not lett me writt, till I could tell you all was gone afore, and that the first Easterly wind we follow, I wish we were as sure of successe, as we are of your good wishes, and I assure you Sir I have some pretence to them, From the very sincere respect and inclination I have ever had for you, Our Vigo successe†2 hath a little abated our vigour, a fault too often committed by the English, and we seem not so willing as the Dutch to raise new recruitts for the next Campaigne, I confesse (after the school boy fashion) I am for giving the Ennemy the rising blow when they are down, and I hope to convince you in the west Indies, that if Providence gives us successes we will not sleep upon them, Sir if I make a prosperous voyage and Live to come back again, I shall not have a greater pleasure, then to meet you where we parted last.
Sir
your most affectionate Friend and servant

3231. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 26 December [1702] (3068)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 168-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Sir
Tho I am almost as weak as Water I cannot but thank you for your kind leter to my son, and the obliging part you gave me in it. rememberences from old friends are ever wellcome, and to find you so heartyly concern'd for my son is a comfort to me, and will I am sure be entertain'd with great respect, and gratitude by my grave Young man, who pleas'd himself with the hopes of waiting on you Next Munday, but the sudaness of my illness much like what mov'd your compassion for me in St Bartholomew Close;†1 will not pirmit him to leave me. My fainting took me when perfectly at Ease in body and Mind, first with drowsyness and next with that decay of spirits which lasted so long that my friends concluded me irrecoverable. this frighted my son, who methinks should be more willing to part with me than I find him. These gentle advertizments, I desire thankfully to improve. I thank God I am in no paine nor under any discontent, nor doe I question Gods blessing on him whome I hope to leave behind me. If my Cousen King†2 be with you give me leave to present my service to him, I hope he and his Cousen Grigg will be deare, and fast friends, tis what I wish, as also that you may excuse the feble hand that now wishes you a happy new Yeare, My heart is as it uses to be very sincere, else I would not at this time assure you that I am
Your much obliged friend and humble servant
St Stephens day

3232. Jean Barbeyrac to Locke, 27 December 1702/6 January 1703 (3141, 3590)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 142-3.
A Berlin ce 6 Janvier 1703.
Monsieur
Je n'ay jamais ressenti un si grand honneur, ni un si grand plaisir, qu'en recevant vôtre Réponse.†1 C'eût êté beaucoup pour moi que vous daignassiez seulement agréer la liberté que j'avois pris de vous écrire; Mais les Personnes généreuses, comme vous, n'obligent pas à demi, elles ne sont point contentes, qu'elles n'ayent répandu leurs faveurs á pleines mains. J'en fais une heureuse expérience par les honnêtetés dont vous me comblés á un tel point, que j'en suis confus. Pour les éloges qu'il vous a plû me donner, je n'ay garde de me flatter qu'ils me conviennent. Je les regarde comme un tour obligeant et ingénieux, dont vous vous servés, pour encourager une personne en qui vous croïés aperçevoir quelque disposition à chercher sincerement la Verité, et à suivre ses lumiéres. Je connoi trop bien mon peu de génie, et quàm mihi sit curta supellex,†2 pour tirer de vos honnêtetés aucune conséquence en ma faveur, si ce n'est que j'ay eu le bonheur de me trouver du nombre de ceux à qui vous avés eu occasion de faire éprouver les éffets de votre générosité. Je mettrai, Monsieur, á profit toutes vos bontés, en tachant de me rendre digne de votre bienveuillance, et d'une partie des louanges que vous me donnés, mais dont je ne trouve en moi aucun fondement.
Apres cela, Monsieur, je vous suis infiniment obligé des Eclaircissemens que vous avez bien voulu me communiquer sur quelques endroits de votre Livre. J'en suis entiérement satisfait. Je prendrai la liberté de vous proposer mes doutes, to<utes les>†a fois qu'il m'en naitra quelcun qui sera capable de m'embarrasser, puis que vous m'y invités si obligeamment. Mais, selon toutes les apparences, je ne vous donnerai pas souvent cette peine, parce que, plus on médite votre Ouvrage, et plus la lumière, qui y brille de toutes parts,
― 728 ― 
dissipe les nuages que causoit la nouveauté, la profondeur, et l'abstraction de vos idées.

Votre Critique de ma correction d'Aristophane,†1 me paroit, Monsieur, si juste, qu'elle suffiroit toute seule pour me faire abandonner cette Conjecture, quand même j'en aurois êté auparavant bien persuadé. Mais je l'ay proposée, plutôt pour engager quelcun á m'expliquer ce passage, que pour rendre service á ceux qui, comme moi, pourroyent y avoir êté embarrassez. J'ay depuis fait inserer dans la Republique des Lettres quelques autres petites Observations de même nature, sur lesquelles je serois bien aise de savoir votre sentiment, si tant est que vous ayiez pris la peine de les lire.†2 Mais je travaille présentement à une Traduction, dont je fonde la plus grande partie du succés sur l'approbation avantageuse que vous avés donné a l'original, dans votre Traité de l'Education. C'est le Livre de Jure Naturæ et Gentium, du Baron de Pufendorf. Je ne manquerai pas de faire bien valoir, dans une Préface, le jugement que vous avés porté de ce Livre, en le mettant au dessus de celui de Grotius, De Jure Belli et Pacis.†3 Je prie Monsieur Coste de vous communiquer le plan sur lequel je travaille, et j'espere que vous voudrés bien m'honorer de vos bons avis, comme vous l'avés fait au sujet de la maniére d'apprendre votre Langue Angloise. Au reste, Monsieur, je croirois mal répondre a votre générosité, si je refusois l'offre obligeante que vous me faites de m'envoyer une Bible Angloise et un Dictionnaire; sur tout êtant dans un païs où l'on ne trouve pas de ces sortes de Livres. J'ay marqué á Monsieur Coste par quelle voye il pourroit me les faire tenir. Avec ce secours, et la méthode que vous me prescrivés, j'espere de pouvoir un jour connoitre parfaitement toute la beauté de vos ouvrages, quand je serai capable de les lire dans leur Langue originale.
Si jamais ma Traduction est imprimée, vous agréerés, Monsieur que je vous en envoye un exemplaire, comme une foible marque de
― 729 ― 
ce que je voudrois être capable de faire pour vous témoigner combien je suis sensible á toutes vos bontés, et avec quels sentimens de reconnoissance et de veneration je suis

Monsieur
Votre tres humble et trés obéïssant serviteur
BARBEYRAC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke A Oates 
Endorsed by Locke: Barbeyrac 16 Jan 0 2/3

3234. Locke to Catharine Trotter, later Mrs. Cockburn, 30 December 1702
Mrs. Catharine Cockburn, Works, ed. T. Birch, 1751, vol. i, pp. xix-xx.
Mrs. Trotter's Defence of the Essay (p. 638) was published by William Turner and John Nutt. She tried to conceal her authorship; she wrote about it to Thomas Burnet of Kemney on 9 December 1701, and he kept the secret: her Works, ii. 155-6, 164. Birch believed that Mrs. Gilbert Burnet learnt it through questioning Mrs. Trotter: ibid., vol. i, p. xvi.
Oates, 30 Dec. 1702.
Madam,
There was nothing more public, than the obligation I received from you, nor any thing more concealed, than the person I was obliged to. This is a generosity above the strain of this groveling age, and like that of superior spirits, who assist without shewing themselves. I used my best endeavours to draw from you, by your Bookseller, the confession of your name, the want whereof made me, that I could, whilst you kept yourself under that reserve, no more address myself directly to you with good manners, than I could without rudeness have pulled off your mask by force, in a place where you were resolved to conceal yourself. Had not this been so, the bearer hereof had not the first time have come to you, without a letter from me, to acknowledge the favour you had done me. You not affording me an opportunity for that, I designed to make you some small acknowledgement, in a way, that chance had opened to me, without your consent. But this gentleman transgressed my order in two main points of it. The one was, in delaying it so long: The other was, in naming me to you, and talking of matters, which he had no commission from me to mention. What he deserves from you for it, must be left to your mercy. For I cannot in earnest be angry with him for procuring me, without any guilt of mine, an opportunity to own you for my protectress, which is the greatest
― 731 ― 
honour my Essay could have procured me. Give me leave therefore to assure you, that as the rest of the world take notice of the strength and clearness of your reasoning, so I cannot but be extremely sensible, that it was employed in my defence. You have herein not only vanquished my adversary, but reduced me also absolutely under your power, and left no desires more strong in me, than those of meeting with some opportunity, to assure you, with what respect and submission I am,

Madam,
Your most humble, and most obedient servant,
J. LOCKE

3240. John Lock (later Sir John) to Locke, 11 January 1703 (3136)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 180-1. Forwarded by Samuel Lock on 10 December 1703: no. 3403.
Honourable Sir
By the Scipio that sailed from hence in the beginning of May last, I acknowledged the receipt of your Favour of 21 Mar 1700/1 from Oats, I have Learnt since that the Colledge at Goa where those Stones are made that bare that name and alsoe Jasper Antonio, has bin founded by a Missionary Jesuit 140 years since or thereabouts and supported since by the Gifts of the Roman Catholicks, the composition of the Stone was contrived and first made by Jasper Antonio a Jesuit and Member of that Colledge, and the receipt remains in the hands of his Successors, who as much as in them
― 736 ― 
Lyes keeps the Secret to themselves, tho many in Goa pretend to counterfeit them,†1 as I am inform'd the chiefest of their composition is Bezoar, seed Pearl, musk and some other perfume. the Bezoar the Portugues buye here And carry to Goa for that use is commonly the broken peeces of the Goat Bezoar, which is sold for Less price then when are entire stones which are worth 1 1/4 rup. per Tola <which>†a is about 6s 3d. per Ounce, there is of this Bezoar to bee found in the Entraile of most Beasts, such as Elliphants, Camills, Cows, Goats and Munkeys the 3 first are very Large, but the Munkey Bezoar is the dearest and most esteem'd in Phisical Preparations commonly Long and smale, as one's Little finger and others as big as a Straw, in most Bezoar stones there is commonly enclosed a piece†b of Stick, Stone, dirt, or kernell, I entend to send you a muster of each Species, if can meet with them.†2

Bramines, there's enough of in Town, the greatest part mighty Ignorant in the history of their Religion, especially those of the Gentu's and Banians,†3 the Moors follow†c- the Precepts-†c of the Alcoran which is well enough known in Europe, most of their knowledg is in a few Prayers and Ceremony used over the dead, when the Banians, and the Women come dayly morning and evening to wash in the Town†d River, and some other extraordinary occasions, and this knowledge they hand down from father to son meerly by Practice, and conversation, and not by studdying Books and reading as is more usual in Europe, which makes them know little of former ages who was their first Prophet and Instructer and how Long their Religion has continued from him, There is amongst these Bramines Several Casts, amongst the rest One that distinguishes themselves by the Name of Vertiats,†4 they say their first Prophet came from the Northward and a place called Vercapoor, neer the Kingdom Casmire, one that dyed for the welfare of his Brothers, he profest Chastity, poverty and Obedience, acknowledg'd One God Eternal, Omnipotent, Spiritual, Present in all places, and other attributes as wee doe, his followers Burn their Dead, and
― 737 ― 
beleive the transmigration of the Soul according as hee deserves and behaves himself in this Life, his Soul goes either into a Lyon, or a Mouse, Apes Wolfs etc. if you enquire of any of the common Banians why they wash or mark themselves in the forehead with a Little yellow or red paint and put a few Grains of Rice or wheat upon it, the Answer they presently make is the Padres and their Book says soe, but very few amongst the Padres can read it themselves, and what knowledge any European can gain must bee by short questions and one or 2 at a Time for they find it difficult to understand us and wee them. I converse sometimes with Padre Diuse a French Jesuit†1 a Man of a Sober Life, and Good Learning and very inquisitive into these matters but professes he finds it very difficult to inform himself in their Customs, and it was of him I had what I write you of the Vertiats, he did not remember their Prophets name nor how Long it was since his Time. if these smale informatione are diverting to you, every Ship shall bring you some of them, wishing the Greatest felicities may attend you, I am

Honourable Sir
your Most Obedient Servant
JOHN LOCK
Surat 11th. January 1702
Address: To the Honourable John Lock In London per Arabia†a Merchant†2 q.D.G. 
Endorsed by Locke: J. Locke 11 Jan 0 2/3 Answered Dec. 14
3241. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 19 January 1703 (3239, 3242)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 260-1.
Oates 19 Jan 0 2/3
Dear Cosin
I am very much pleased with the begining of yours of 16th And now I take the liberty to enquire of you what became of my letter
― 738 ― 
to Mrs Trotter. Tis easy to beleive that Misunderstandings will arise But is good or harm like to be the Consequences of them? And now give me leave to propose a case in law to you. Suppose an English merchant here should receive a letter from a Spaniard in Spain concerning some ordinary private matter concerning which the English merchant had writ to him before the declaration of the warr, haveing never writ to him since, nor heard from him but this once. Is there any danger in the bare receiveing such a letter (which conteins noe thing relateing to matters of any publick concernment in the least) without answering or haveing any farther correspondence with the writer? If there be I doe not see how a man can avoid it. But being of opinion that noe body can be in danger but by his own act, I desire you by the next post to let me know what the danger is (if there be any in such a case), and what is to be done to prevent the danger if such a case should happen.†1 I am

Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE

Honored Sir
I now return you My heartiest thanks for your great generosity to me, and all the obligations laid on me at Oates.†2 When I parted from you I intended to transcribe and send the papers I gave you some account of, but meeting with two other books, after†a I came from you, which medled with the same subject, I have writ more than I designed. I heartily beg you to pardon my sending such a tedious deal of stuff, where as I should have sent but one sheet and half. I am so burthensome to you both when present and when absent, I am perfectly ashamed, and indeed I could scarce prevail with my self to send the enclosed when I found the sheets were so
― 740 ― 
many.†1 My most humble service to my much honoured Lady Masham, to the young Lady, to worthy Mr Francis, and to Mr Coste. An Appendix consisting of six chapters added in the second edition, of his Analysis Æquationum universalis.†2 What I said of Millefolium, as being of great virtue to give ease in Asthma's, when smoak'd as Tobacco, I had out of the Works of the Learned for May, 1702. Mr Marchand there spoken of, cals the plant, Achillea montana penæ. The original account is in a piece that hath this title. Lettre de M. Blondel a un de ses amis, par laquelle il l'informe de ce qui s'est passé dans la dernier Assemblée de l'Academie Royale des Sciences.†3 Sir I have given you too much trouble alread<y>,†a and therefore without saying any thing more I beg lea<ve>†a to subscribe myself with my whole heart

3244. Charles Mordaunt, third earl of Peterborough, to Locke, 27 January 1703 (3230)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 127-8. Printed in King, p. 240.
Had I not with Doctor†b Lock left of wondring att any thing long agoe, I might with surprise writte this letter, and you receive itt with amazement, when I lett you know our American Expedition
― 741 ― 
is Fallen as a mushroom rises in a night, I had my orders to be abord the 16th, all my equipage, and servants gone, and the 14th I was sent for to the place of wisdome to be ask'd this question, whether I could not effect with three thousand men what I was to have attempted with above double the number, I modestly confest my self no worker of miracles, and being tould that the States had desired the Dutch Squadron and land Forces might be employ'd upon other services, since the season was so farr spent, and the winds contrary, I likewise desired they would excuse my going if the season were past, when I was sure the force would not answer what the world expected from her majestys Arms and the preparations so long talk'd off, besides these three thousand men I was to depend upon were but 2800 when they left Cales,†1 and before my arrivall must†a- have been-†a employd for fower months against the French in their strongest Islands and probably reduced to half the number att least by disease and the accidents of warr, I am sure Sir this att least does not surprise you, that I refus'd to goe to the other world Loaded with empty titles and deprived of Force, these mysteries of state I will not pretend to unfold att presant, but before I return to my Farm, I will have an other meeting in Essex.

Sir
your most faithfull Friend
PETERBOROW

― 746 ―

3253. James Tyrrell to Locke, 15 February [1703] (3195, 3263)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 153-4. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Feb: 15
Dear Sir
I must in the first place beg your pardon for leting your first letter go so long unanswerd, which was indeed rather by chance then designe, for not long after I receivd it, I resolvd to have come downe to you with Sir Francis, and have there passed most of the Christmass Holydays in so agreeable a conversation, but I was disappointed of that satisfaction, being calld out of Town so much on the sudden, that I forgot to take your letter along with me; in order to answere it, but when I came home I found my errour too late, and therefore resolvd to retreive it when I came up again, which I should have done in a few days, had I not receivd yours, with a gentle Admonition for my silence:†1 I must now congratulate your unexpected recovery of your hearing, which I hope you will now enjoy, till it shall please God to bring you to that more happy and perfect state, where in Eyes, and Ears. will be no longer necessary.
I must now thank you for your reading so carefully, my Introduction to the first volu.†2 and am pleasd you are so well satisfyed with the performance: as for what you say of my omission in puting downe the value of the English Saxon money and of the Thrymsa in particular. I confesse it; for partly from the uncertain Account I could give of it, (notwithstanding the help from Sir H. Spelman's Glossary)†3 and partly that I did not then think it of any great consequence to be known, I omitted it; but hope to make some amends for it, in the Introduction, I designe to my last volume of Eng: History, wherein I shall (God willing) give an Account of the English Saxon Coigns, and the value of their money, compared with those of the Kings after the Conquest, till the ounce of Silver was alterd from 20d: to 36d: in the time of Edward the fourth and then to 5s: as it remains to this day: in the doing of which I shall persue your method. of considering the weight of Each Peice as far as it can be known, tho as for the Thrymsa, it will be (I doubt) a hard
― 749 ― 
matter to retreive it, because it was the name of a sum, and not of any particular coign;†1 But to come to the business of your last letter, as for Dr: Hudson the present Library Keeper at Oxon, he is a Person I have the happyness to know, he is a man the most fit for that Imployment, that has ever come into it since Dr. James.†2 he has put the Library in much better order then it was, and is puting out a large Additional Catalogue of those books that have bin brought in since the making of the former, and is so industrious to augment it by a dayly Addition of new Books, that he has desird the like favour from me, as he now does from you, and which I think I shall comply with, having given my first volume allready: I can onely tell you further that this learned man is now correcting the press for the new Edition of all the works of Euclide, which will come out e're it be long with new Schemes, and some Scholias by Dr: Gregory; the present Professor of Astronomy,†3 whose Institutio Astronomica,†4 lately put out, is worth your perusal, having there more†a- fully explained-†a several things; that were very obscure in Mr: Newtons Physical Treatise:†5 so I hope you will not let the university Library want so considerable an Addition as your works, which if you please to transmit thither, I will take care to carry them downe, and deliver them, to the Library Keeper,†6 to whom you may write in the mean while directed to Dr: H. at his Chamber in University College; which is all I have to say upon that subject; and to speake a little of matters of a more Indifferent nature, I thank you for the kind offer you made me of your Advice as to my health, which I thank God is so well confirmd since my last sickness, that I have had no need of any Physick, as for my son he is lately come out of Ireland, and hope he will returne thither again this summer in a better Post: my Daughter is at my house in the Countrey with her Husband; but has not bin yet with Child.

so wishing you all health and happyness, and that you may receive
― 750 ― 
more satisfaction in reading my second then first volume;†1 and hoping to see you for a few days before I go downe, I remain

your most humble and faithfull servant
J TYRRELL.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Tyrrell 15 Feb. 0 2/3

3255. [Dr. Knightly Chetwood] to Locke, [20 February 1703]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 93-4. The writer's name from Locke's endorsement; the date from the contents and the endorsement.
Knightly Chetwood, 1650-1720; D.D. 1691; dean of Gloucester 1707: D.N.B. He was related through his mother to John Shute (p. 352), and his wife was a first cousin of Shute. He appears to have been chaplain-general of the army at this time.
Saterday night.
Cambridge.
Sir Your judgment was verified in the distemper of the M. of Blanford: he di'd at six this evening, full of red spots, and swell'd.†1 The Duke took kindly, and all the Physitians comended, your prescription. but it was too late. To Morrow the sorrowful Duke, and Duchesse, go for St Albans, and I to Temsford,†2 whither I hope to reach by morning service.
I pray my Lady Massam to take care of your health, though shee will do it without mee. you will please to proceed in the design you are upon, so as not to entrench upon that repose which is most justly due to you. The blessed sun will come in to your rescue, and I trust to find you better next visit: which I hope will be speedily, for we must live as I travel, Post: and hastily enjoy blessings greater than sons, and heirs.
I desire you to keep me in kind remembrance: for my freinds are my Mistresses. The parting of soul, and body is but a faint resemblance of the final parting of freinds. you will pardon my odd, and abrupt writing, and commend me to my good Lady Massam.
Address: To Mr Lock at Oates This. 
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Chetwood 20 Feb. 0 2/3

3263. James Tyrrell to Locke, 3 April [1703] (3253, 3283)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 155-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
April 3d.
Dear Sir
In persueance of your kind Encouragement I make bold to send you these additional sheets concerning Power, that you may get Mounsieur Cost, or some other hand, to transcribe those Additions and Alterations you have made to them; but if there are any that do not belong to these sheets, but to the other Places in the first
― 757 ― 
Edition, which I have bin allready altred and are pasted into my book, I desire you would send me those fresh Additions and alterations in a loose paper; with†a- references to the Pages and lines.-†a but as for those that belong to these sheets, they may be transcribed either into the margins or blank pages, which you shall think best: there needs no great hast in this performance since if it be done when I returne again to Towne about a month or 6 weeks hence, it will be time enough.†1 as for news the most considerable is, that the Sevenneeses, have given the French Kings Forces another considerable defeat, wherein they have killd 1000, or 1200 men, they have taken a small Towne, and have thereby got more powder or materials to make it.†2 there has bin allso another Engagement between some loose Troops belonging to Count Stirum, and the Bavarians, in which the former being but 800 foot†b , and the latter 4000 foot†b : they were put to flight and some few men killd, but the greatest loss is that the Prince of Anspach, that commanded them is killd.†3 wee expect by the next maile to hear of an Engagement between the Duke of Bavaria, and Count Stirum, the last letters bringing news, that they were actually engaged when they came away:†4 the league with Portugal is not yet in the Prints, but is looked upon here, as concluded:†5 so with my thanks for your good Conversation at Otes, and other favours, and praying for the Continuance of your health I remain

Your humble servant.
J TYRRELL.
Mr: Collyns†6 is well, wee had a pleasant Journey up. onely when wee came to Town wee heard that his man had bin set on by Theives in the Forest, and his horse taken from him, and nothing els, but it was found the next day not†c- far off-†c the same Place

which gives me some reason to think, that it was not Theives, but too much of Sir Francis's strong beer, that stole away the Fellow's understanding, and made him fall off his horse; which was taken up the day wee came to Town: the Lady†1 was now pretty well but much disturbed at her mans not coming home till 2, or 3, on munday morning. I pray give my service to worthy Monsieur Cost:

I am
Dear Cosin

3271. Anonymous to Locke, 20 April 1703 (3323)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 192-3. I cannot identify the writer. His use of the form 'ane' and perhaps the word 'overly', as also his address for a reply, mark him as a Scotsman.
Sir
The earnest desire I have to be satisfy'd about what you write concerning a very important mater, makes me presume to give you this trouble. I neither have any Learning nor do I pretend to it, nor am I so vain as to imagine I can produce any thing worthy of your regard. and therefor if the thing I am now to consult you about were not of so great consequence, I belive I would not take the freedom to trouble you with it; especially since I am not at all known to you. I have consider'd it very often with all the attention I could, and have likewise told my difficulty to some others, but could never get that satisfaction I wished for. Therefor I resolv'd to propose it to your self, and I doubt not but your goodness will induce you to solve it to me; not only because it arises from your own Book, but because it will mightily help me forward in my enquiries about that great Point. The thing I aim at is your Demonstration of the Existence of a God, Essay concer. Hum. Und. L.4. c.10. You tell us, Sir, that this is the most obvious truth our Reason discovers, whose evidence is æquall to Mathematical
― 765 ― 
<certainty>;†a that we may know it more certainly than that there is any thing else without us, if we will but apply our Minds to it as we do to several other enquiries: and you propose the Argument you make use of, as sufficient to let us see how obvious and demonstratively certain a Truth it is. This mightily inclines me to belive, that it is great dullness and stupidity in me not to perceive the force of it. Yet since it is as much my interest to be well inform'd about this fundamental article, as it is theirs who have far better Heads; I perswade my self you will not alltogether despise my weakness, but charitably assist one who desires nothing more than full information about maters of this kind.

You take the rise of your Demonstration from the clear Perception a Man has of his own being. In the next place you show, that bare nothing can not produce any reall being: from which you justly infer, that from Eternity there has been something. You proceed in the fourth Section to tell us, that what had it's being and beginning from aneother, must allso have all that which is in and belongs to it's being from aneother too; and I make no doubt of the consequence. but here lies my difficulty. It appears to me that there is a link of the chain of your Demonstration wanting: for before you draw conclusions from a thing's having had a beginning, it should have been shown that it really had a beginning. 'tis true you hint at this in the end of the præceeding Section; but I humbly conceive that one of the fundamental Steps of the Demonstration should not be hudl'd up so, and only brought in overly†1 by the bye. but whatever be of that, since it is evident, as I think, that the Demonstration cannot proceed without it, it should not have barely been suppos'd and advanc'd without any shadow of proof, as it is here. If it be said, no body doubts that he himself had a beginning. I answer; that is very true, but yet those Gentlemen who pretend to be Infidells in this point and assert the Eternity of the World, maintain that we were form'd of præexistent Substance, and produc'd according to the naturall course of things, only by vertue of those Powers which exist in them, whereby their various changes and allterations which we dayly observe to happen are brought about. now whether they have reason or not for this their assertion, yet I may affirm, I think, that it is not self-evidently false: and
― 766 ― 
therefor I must know how to demonstrate it to be false, before I can pretend to have evidence æqual to mathematical certainty that it is really so. and this, I think, must necessarly be demonstrated to make your reasoning conclude: for it is in vain to tell me, that since bare non-entity certainly could not produce a reall being, and since I certainly had a beginning, therefor there must be a God who produc'd me; this I say will not conclude, except it be as certain that I could not be produc'd by aneother cause. If it should be said that the cause, whatever it be, to which we owe our beginning, is God: these Gentlemen would answer, that then the World is all we have for a God; and so your Demonstration makes us sure of nothing but this, viz: that there is such a thing as the World. You demonstrate infallibly that from Eternity there has been some reall being possess't of Power and Knowledge. but this holds true as well according to these Gentlemen's Hypothesis, as according to yours; it holds true though we suppose there existed no other powerfull knowing Beings than those which make up this World; and consequently does not prove the Existence of a Superiour Being, which yet is the thing should be demonstrated. I am not wholly unaccquainted with what is commonly advanc'd to prove, that the World could not have been from Eternity, and that Mankind could not have been produc'd by any other cause but such as we suppose God. but, whatever probability these arguments infer, I don't know if they reach to Demonstration: and any thing of this kind which to me appears to come nearest it, is so metaphysicall, that one must be something us'd to abstracted Speculations before he be duely capable of it; and therefor it can not be said to be so very obvious.

What follows in this Chapter does not, I think, at all touch my difficulty: for from the 7 to the 12 Section you only prove more at large than you had done before, that from Eternity there must have been some cogitative being; and the following Sections are wholly employ'd about enquiries which are to be made after the being of a God is established.
Thus Sir I have propos'd what I had to say with all the clearness I could: and tho it appears very evident to me, yet I think it so improbable that you should give us a weak unconcluding argument, for a clear obvious and invincible Demonstration, that I can not but suspect I have not fully comprehended what you write.
I beg leave to add two or three lines concerning the Quotation you make out of Cicero, in the end of the 6 Section. This, I belive,
― 767 ― 
when duely consider'd will startle a bold Atheist; but it would still be more convincing to me if what follows†1 was evidently answer'd.

They who do not see but Mater, motion, and thought may be eternal, will easyly grant that the frame they are presently in is admirable, and in most cases above our reach. yet they will say that it may rationally be suppos'd they have fallen into it without the direction of a superiour being, since they have had ane Eternity to arrive at it; and one might imagine that they could scarcely miss falling into some very wonderfull frame in ane Eternity. this looks the more probable when we consider, that all we understand of the constitution of this Universe is so agreeable to the naturall powers of mater, motion, and thought. and why should it be irrationall to think, that it is only the imperfection of our Knowledge which hinders us to see exact conformity between these causes and the Effects which are produc'd in the Universe; since still the more we discover of the nature of things, the more still we see the agreement is betwixt them. They who show us a great many instances which cannot be accounted for from these nor from no other principles, and which non-plus the ablest Philosophers; yet they say God does not bring about these things by his immediate power, but by second causes, as they call them. now this seems to overthrow the argument. for have we not ground to conclude, that our ignorance how naturall causes work in these instances, is no reason to deny their efficacy; since we nevertheless allow that they æqually work in these, as in other instances which we think we can explain. I expect you will rid me of these scruples: which did nothing prompt me to but curiosity and a desire after knowledge, I hope it might be excus'd in me; but since it concerns a mater of such moment, and about which it behooves me so necessarly to be well satisfy'd, I doubt not but your love to your fellow creatures, and your compassion on them who are Labouring to find out the Truth, will engadge you to give me ane answer. when you favour me with one (which I heartily wish may be quickly) please to direct it thus. To Mr James jermyn, to be left with Mr David Erskine†2 Advocat, at his chamber in the Writer's Court, Edinburgh. jermyn is not my name, but that other Gentleman will know by it to whom he should deliver your Letter. Since all I design by giving you this trouble is
― 768 ― 
to receive information from you, and to get my doubts remov'd, I think there is no need for me to set down my own name, especially seeing, in all liklyhood, you would no more know me by it than by this feign'd one. I am sensible of how litle value my good opinion is of such a man as you, yet I'm sure there is none who esteems you more, and I may say, who loves you more than

Sir
Your most humble tho unknown Servant.
April. 20. 1703
Endorsed by Locke: Anonymus 20 Apr 03
3272. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 23 April 1703 (3269, 3275)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 271-2. The opening passage is printed in King, pp. 260-1. Answers no. 3269; answered by no. 3276.
Oates 23 Apr 03
Dear Cosin
I told you that the Terme had got you: nor am I dissatisfied that you mind your business. But I doe not well bear it that you speake soe doubtfully of makeing your self and me a holy day at Whitsontide. I doe not count upon much time in this world and therefore you will not blame me, (if you think right of me) for desireing to see and enjoy you as much as I can, and haveing your company as much as your business will permitt, besides that I think some intervals of ease and air are necessary for you. I cannot but looke upon a visit from Mr Bond as a very great favour. I have since I saw you looked over the account you left with me and know noe thing to the contrary but that it is right. Since you speake so uncertainly of your comeing hither I think it would not be amiss if you would send me down declarations of trust for the three Morgages taken in your name viz Mrs Hunters Mr Gotwards and Mr Jollifes. would seale them up and deliver them to Mr Churchil to bring them to me, whom I expect here in a little time.

I expect you should bring some news out of the west that you and I should talke of. At least I have a great many things to talke to you about and you know you are always most welcome to
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant

3273. Samuel Bold to Locke, 26 April 1703 (3243, 3326)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, f. 42.
Steeple 26th Apr: 1703
Honoured Sir Towards the close of the last week I received yours of the 15th of March inclosed in one from Mr Churchil bearing date the 15th of this Instant, in which He acquaints me He would have sent yours much sooner, but that He heard I was gone into Staffordshire. But I have not bin (excepting once at Dorchester) four miles from Steeple, since I arrived here after my departure from Oates. I returne you my most hearty thanks for your most kinde letter, and your favourable acceptance of the papers inclosed in my last to you. I acknowledge my self very much obliged to my Lady Masham, and to every one of that most worthy Family, that they are pleased to vouchsafe to admit me to a share in their esteem. I pray you present my most humble service to my Lady, and to every one in the
― 770 ― 
family. I shal be very unwilling to give my Lady any occasion to think me not sincere in my professions of Respect for Oates, The place, where, as at present stated,†1 I could spend all my time with more abundant satisfaction and pleasure, than any where else. I did not, indeed, think of taking any Journey this summer; But seeing you are so express that I must come to Oates, I wil do the utmost I can to wait on you all. my Mare hath been under the management of Farriars almost ever since I came into Dorcetshire, she is at present under the care of one. But I am told she wil be in a condition to be rid in a few weeks. I question whether she wil be fit for a Journey before May is out. But if I may understand by a line from mr Churchil that the month of May is a more seasonable time, than some of the following months, I wil come up to London in the Coach before that Month goes out, if God continue health and ease, rather than you shal have occasion to think me wanting in so ready and chearful a compliance with every thing you can propose, as is due from

your most obliged humble servant
SA: BOLDE
I heartily bless God you pas'd over the last winter so wel, and I heartily pray that ease and a competent measure of health may be long continued to you. I observed your directions as to Tobacco, and do not exceed three pipes a day.
I began not to read Mr Lee,†2 til about a week before your letter came to me, having wasted a great deal of time in books about Convocational Rigths to as little purpose, as I shal some more in looking over Mr Lee, who seem's to me as far as I have yet read to be as Impertinent an Author as I have mett with. I hope to give my Lady Masham, and you, a more particular account of the Book, when I shall be so happy as to wait on you both at Oates.
Address (not in Bold's hand): To John Locke Esqr

3274. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 27 April/8 May 1703 (3204, 3288)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 108-9.
Monsieur,
Depuis ma reponce que ju l'honneur de vous ecrire sur la fin de l'année derniere, nous avons apris avec bien du plaisir par le canal de Monsieur Limburgh, que votre santé se retablissoit de plus en plus. vous avez tousjours vecu d'un grand regime, et c'est apparemment ce qui vous a tiré d'affaire. en ce pays on a trop peu d'attention a la diette, quoy quil comprenne le plus essentiel de la Medecine. nous avons lu avec beaucoup d'edification la seconde partie du traitté que la religion chrestienne est raisonnable,†1 qui nous met de plus en plus dans le bon chemin, et nous eloigne de cette malheureuse passion de parti. plust a Dieu que tout le monde voulut se rendre a la solidité de vos raisonnements, et que reduisant le fondement de la foy a si peu de principes, nous nous estimions tous freres en Jesus Christ et quil ny eut plus que paix et charité parmis tous les chrestiens. je croy vous avoir ecrit que ma fem<me>†a etoit revenue malade de la Campagne a l'automne passé, elle se portoit un peu mieu quand j'eu l'honneur de vous ecrire dernierement, mais depuis elle a tousjours reculé. sa poitrine a eté depuis constamment agitée d'une tou si facheuse, quil n'y a eu aucun remede que par les narcotiques. cette violent concussion luy causa il y a pres de trois mois une hæmoptose†2 assez considerable. ses forces ont tousjours diminué depuis. je la mis au lait de vache (moitié eau d'orge mondée)†b il y a quinze jours. cela parut d'abord calmer sa fievre, et nous commencions a esperer quelque bon retour; mais depuis quatre jours sa fievre a beaucoup augmentée, ce qui nous a fait quitter l'usage du laict. c'est une grande affliction pour moy et toute la famille de voir son pauvre etat. vous connoissez ses vertus, et la perte que ce sera pour moy de perdre une si bonne compagne. elle avoit tousjours esperé de vous revoir un jour, et dans trois ans quand notre fils pierre aura achevé le temps de son engagement,
― 772 ― 
elle esperoit vous aller voir avec luy. Mais l'homme propose et Dieu dispose. je prevois sa fin en bref, et je me prepare le mieu que je puis a supporter la douleur que sa mort me causera. je demande votre consolation et la continuation de votre amitié, dont jay plus besoin que jamais, dans la triste solitude ou je vais entrer. adieu l'affliction me saisit le cœur. la pauvre mourante vous dit un eternel adieu. esperant de vous revoir dans le paradis. je suis

Monsieur,
Votre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON.
d'Amsterd. ce 8 Mey 1703
Endorsed by Locke: Dr. Guenellon 8 May 03 Answered 7.
3275. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 30 April 1703 (3272, 3276)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 273-4. Printed in King, pp. 259-60, omitting the first and last paragraphs.
Oates 30 Apr 03
Dear Cosin
I here inclosed send you the receit for Mr Conyers. I think Mr Marton should pay one half years interest before an other becomes due. I have reason to think they receive it as soon as it is due.
I am puzzeld in a little affair, and must beg your assistance for the clearing of it. Mr Newton in Autumn last made me a visit here. I shewd him my Essay upon the Corinthians with which he seemd very well pleased, but had not time, staying but one night, to looke it all over. But promisd me if I would send it him he would carefully peruse it, and send me his observations and opinion. I sent it him before Christmas,†1 but hearing no thing from him I about a month or six weeks since writ to him, as the inclosed†2 tells you with the remaining part of this story. when you have read it and sealed it I desire you to deliver it at your convenience. He lives in German Street†3 four or five doors west of Mrs Lockharts. you must not goe on a Wednesday for that is his day of being at the tower.†4 The reason why I desire you to deliver it to him your self, is that I would fain discover what is the reason of his so long silence. I have several
― 773 ― 
reasons to think him truly my friend, but he is a nice man to deale with, and a little too apt to raise in himself suspitions where†a there is no ground. Therefore when you talke to him of my papers and of his opinion of them pray doe it with all the tenderness in the world, but talke soe to him of them, as to discover if you can, why he kept them soe long and was so silent. But this you must doe without askeing why he did soe, or discovering in the least that you are desirous to know. You will doe well to acquaint him that you intend to see me at Whitson tide, and shall be glad to bring a letter to me from him or any thing else he will please to send. This perhaps may quicken him and make him dispatch those papers if he has not done it already. It may a little let you into the freer discourse with him if you let him know that when you have been here with me you have seen me busy on them (and the Romans†1 too, if he mentions them too, for that I told him I was upon when he was here), and have had a sight of some part of what I was doeing. Mr Newton is really a very valuable man not onely for his wonderfull skill in Mathematicks but in divinity too and his great knowledg in the Scriptures where in I know few his equals. And therefore pray manage this whole matter so as not onely to preserve me in his good opinion but to increase me in it, and be sure to press him to noe thing but what he is forward of himself to doe

In your last you seemd desirous of my comeing to town, I have many reasons to desire to be there but I doubt whether ever I shall see it again. Take not this for a <splenetick>†b thought. I thank god I have noe melancholy on that account. But I cannot but feele what I feele. My shortness of breath is soe far from being releived, by this renewing season of the year, as it used to be, that it sensibly increases upon me. 'Twas not therefore in a fit of disperitedness or to prevaile with you to let me see you that in my former I mentiond the shortness of the time I thought I had in this world. I spoke it then and repeat it now upon sober and sedate consideration. I have several things to talke to you of, and some of present concernment to your self, and know not whether this may not be my last time of seeing you. I shall not die the sooner for haveing cast up my reconing and judging as impartialy of my state as I can. I hope I shall not live one jot the less cheerfully the time that I am here, nor neglect
― 774 ― 
any of the offices of life whilst I have it. For whether it be a month, or a year, or seven years longer, the longest any one out of kindeness or complement can propose to me is so near nothing when considerd, and in respect of eternity, that if the sight of death, can put an end to the comforts of life, it is always near enough espetialy to one of my age to leave no satisfaction in liveing.

The books I intended you are now packed up in a box send me word to whom you would have them directed. I am
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J L

3278. Locke to Anthony Collins, 4 May 1703 (3293)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, f. 17. Copy made by or for Desmaizeaux. Printed presumably from this text, or a copy of it, in A Collection of Several Pieces, 1720, pp. 252-3.
Anthony Collins, 1676-1729, the deist: D.N.B.; J. O'Higgins, S.J., Anthony Collins, 1970. There is nothing to show how he became acquainted with Locke.
Oates. 4 May. 03.
Sir
None of your concerns are of Indifference to me. You may from thence conclude I take part in your late great loss.†1 But I consider you as a Philosopher and a Christian: and so spare you the trouble of reading from me what your own thoughts will much better suggest to you. You have exceedingly oblig'd me in the books of yours that you have sent me,†2 and those of mine you have been at so much trouble about. I receiv'd but just now the packet wherein they and your obliging letter were: that may†a be my excuse for so tardy a return of my thanks. I am overjoy'd with an intimation I have received also that gives me hopes of seeing you here the next week. You are a charitable good freind, and are resolvd to make the decays and dregs of my life the pleasantest part of it. For I know nothing calls me so much back to a pleasant sense of enjoyment, and makes my days so gay and lively as your good company. Come then and multiply happy minutes upon, and rejoice here in the good You do me. For I am with a perfect esteem and respect
Sir
Your most Humble and most Obedient Servant
JOHN LOCKE

3278A. Dr. Richard Burthogge to Locke, 4 May 1703 (3214A)
Oxford, Museum of the History of Science, MS. Buxton 7. Transcript made by Charles Babbage: see no. 1737A, n. The round and square brackets are those of Babbage's transcript. I have corrected silently the accents, etc., of the Greek words.
Most honoured Sir
I have the honor of your kind letter of the 27'th Feb. 2/3. And take particular notice of your desire I would add what further I have to say concerning the acceptation of Olam and Αἰῶν in the holy scriptures. It would Sir be troublesome to yourself to read as well as to me to write All that can be said on this occasion and therefore having first <observed>†a that the words being often used and in senses very different the meaning of them must be determined by the subject matter and the circumstances. I will now proceed to instance in some few particulars. To begin then with Me-olam and with a word that answers to it the Greek viz ἀπ' αἰῶν (—) These words are not always to be taken definitely but in diverse places must be understood indefinitely and indeterminately. Thus Me-olam is used Josh. 24.2. Your Fathers dwelt beyond the Flood Me-olam Not from Eternity or from Everlasting nor precisely and strictly from the beginning of the Created world for neither of these senses will consist with the times in which the Fathers lived who are mentioned to wit Terah and Abraham. But the word must be taken (as our Translators well render it) with a latitude in a popular and indefinite sense, in Old Time or long ago which in Latin would be olim a word that seems to come from olam. It is true Me-olam in this place is rendered by the LXX, ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, from the beginning; But then, As ἀπ Ἀρχῆς is no more than ἀπ' αἰῶν (—) so it must be understood not definitely and precisely, from the beginning of all time but as ἀπ' αἰῶνος is used by the same Men Gen 6.4 where they render Me-olam by ἀπ' αἰῶνος—οἱ γίγαντες οἱ ἀπ' αἰῶνος which is well rendered by our translators (who) were of Old; and I see no reason why ἀπ' αἰῶνος which is used by the LXX Indefinitely in Gen 6 for of OLD or in ancient times should be rendered definitely by our Translators in Luke 1.30†1 [prophets] which have been since the <world>†b began. I rather think in regard the Scriptures tell us
― 778 ― 
nothing of any prophets who at the beginning of the World spake of raising a Horn of Salvation to Men in the house of David that it might have been rendered more conveniently which were of old or which were in antient time And this I would have thought even though it should have been ἀπ' ἀρχῆς in the Original Greek (which had it been would have better countenanced the ordinary translation) I say I should have thought so notwithstanding that because ἀπ' ἀρχῆς in effect and in true meaning signifies the same with ἀπ' ἀιῶνος [q.d ἀπ' ἀρχῆς Το Αἰῶνοσ] and that Αἰῶν doth not only signify the time of the whole world but the time of any seculum or Age so that ἀπ' αἰῶνος is from any known and famous Epocha any remarkable event any Revolution or Mutation that is made a Head of Account in Time and the ἀπ' Αἰῶνος in the text I last mentioned might as well have been rendered since the Flood or since the giving of the Law etc as since the beginning of the world and methinks this uncertainty should strongly Argue for an indefinite indeterminate version of the text which without the transposition that is in the original may be read thus <καθὼς ἐλάλησεν>†a διὰ στόματος τῶν ἁγίων προφητῶν αὐτοῦ τῶν ἀπ' Αἰῶνος and be thus translated; As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets which were of OLD.

Thus also the phrase εἰς τὸν Αἰῶνα which is sometimes rendered [For ever] by our translators (as) particularly in I Ep. Pet. C.1 V.F25 But the word of the Lord endureth for ever, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα for here it seems very well rendered it is not always to be understood so. For John 14.16 a text rendered by our Translators thus, that he [the paraclete] may abide with you for ever, εἰς τὀν Αἰῶνα and is commonly understood to mean untill the end of all time (This very text) is understood by the Learned and Judicious Mr. Chillingworth (who appropriates the whole into the Apostles) but in a sense restrained and Accommodated to the subject treated of and consequently εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα is interpreted by him to signify not Eternally without end but perpetually without interruption and for the time of the Apostles Lives†1 in the sense that a like phrase is used Philemon 15 That thou mayest receive for ever ἵνα αἰώνιον αὐτον ἀπέχῃς that thou mayest have him a perpetual servant to serve thee not for a certain term but as long as he lives.
For my own part I am apt to think that the phrase εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα
― 779 ― 
John 14.16 might well enough be Translated to the end of the world provided it be understood of the world that then was and so to mean unto the end of that seculum: And the rather for that it is not said εἰς Αἰῶνα, simply: but εἰς τὸν Αἰῶνα with a restrictive particle for in this restrictive sense the LXX do use this very expression Exod 21.6 where it is εἰς τὸν Αἰῶνα and rendered by our Translators, for ever, but as I have shewed in my former Letter by comparing that Text with Levit. 25.40 (it) must be understood but till a Jubilee.

In this interpretation of the phrase εἰς τὸν Αἰῶνα, what is said Matt 28 ult. seems a parallel to that John 14.16. For in Matthew our Saviour promises his disciples (as he doth in John) to be with them [namely not in person but by his spirit] πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας which is rendered, alway, but is to the letter all the Days [that remain] ἕως τῆς συντελέιας τοῦ Αἰῶνος. Our translators I confess do render the whole passage thus, And lo I am with you alway even to the end of the world. but to the Greek it may be translated, And lo I am with you all the days (that remain) till the consumation of the (present) Age or Seculum, according to that Matt 24.34 This generation shall not pass till all things are fulfilled. In truth our Saviour in Matt 28. ult doth not speak of years or of days of years For he says not, Lo I am with you all the years, or, all the days of the years, but barely, All the days till the consumation and consequently seems to have an eye upon the Hebrew way of expression used by Jacob Gen 47.9 and so to intimate the shortness of the Time (that it would not be long) before the consumation of that Age.
I do not think the ἡμέρα Αἰῶνος mentioned by St Peter Ep.2. ch 3 v. ult to be any of the days of the age meant in Matt 28.v.ult. I rather think that Day to be the day of which that whole Age or Seculum and perhaps all Time was but the night according as St Paul distinguishes Rom. 13.12 where he says the night is far spent the day is at hand to wit, the Seculum in which the seasons of refreshing were to come from the presence of the Lord Acts 3.19, 20, 21. And thus the ἡμέρα Αἰῶνος is to be understood of the times of the Restitution of all things which were to come after the consumation of the former Age which ended in the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple for then I take it began the great Apocatastasis†1 when there was to be New Heavens and a New Earth in
― 780 ― 
which everlasting Righteousness†a was to dwell but not without interuption for there are seasons of refreshing. Thus I understand St Peter who Ep 2 ch 3 speaks first of the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple with the Dissolution of the Jewish Œconomy in v 10, 11, 12. And then of the Apocatastasis or Restitution in the ἡμέρα αἰῶνος the eternal Jubilee of the New Heavens and New Earth v.13. Nevertheless [or notwithstanding the consumation of the former Seculum] we (who profess Christianity) according to his (Christ's) promise look for New Heavens and a New Earth So Rev. 21.1.

To conclude it must be observed that olam αἰὼν κόσμος οἰκουμένη are words used promiscuously in the Scriptures one for another as appears from Hebr. 11.3 by Faith we understand that the words τοσ Αἰῶνασ (the Heavens and the Earth) were framed etc. So Heb.2.5. Unto the Angels hath he not put in subjection τὴν οἰκουμένην τἠν μέλλουσαν the world that is to come which he further limits by περὶ ἧς λαλοῦμεν of which we speak. And in the same sense of the world as it stands for a particular age or Seculum I understand κὸσμος to be taken Matt. 13.35 which our translators render I will utter things that have been kept secret ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου from the foundation of the world As in like manner Eph. 1.4 which our translators render, According as he hath chosen us in him (Christ) before the foundation of the world πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου;F I understand in both places the giving of the law by the foundation of the world, and the rather because it is not κρίσις but μεταβολὴ κόσμου in both texts and consequently speaks not of the first Creation but of some revolution of the world that is of the Mosaic Seculum.
I have ended Sir with what I have to say in answer to your request and will enlarge this long trouble no longer than to assure you it is not your misfortune only to meet with a sort of creatures which swarm every where And that I am
Most Honoured Sir
Your most Humble Servant
RICH BURTHOGGE
Totnes May 4. 1703
Address: For John Lock Esquire These 
Endorsed by Locke(?): Dr Burthogge 4 May 03

3279. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 4/15 May 1703 (3124, 3319)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 144-5. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 124-5.
A Amsterdam le 15 de May 1703.
Il y a long-tems, Monsieur, que je devrois vous avoir remercié du livre sur le Symbole, que vous m'avez fait la grace de m'envoyer.†1 Cest un livre plein d'esprit, et qui marque beaucoup de lecture dans l'Auteur. Tout ce que je craindrois c'est qu'il seroit propre à diminuer le respect que l'on doit avoir pour ce Symbole, dans l'esprit de ceux qui l'entendent plus simplement. Mais ceux qui cherchent des décisions et des condamnations d'heresies, y trouveront, sans doute, leur compte. Il y a a deja quelque tems qu'un Libraire de Londres a reçu un petit paquet pour vous, Monsieur, où il y a deux exemplaires de deux petits Poëtes Latins,†2 et deux du I. Tome de la Bibliotheque Choisie.†3 Ce libraire se nomme Caïlloué;†4 c'est un François. Prenez la peine d'écrire à Londre, pour faire retirer ce paquet. Un exemplaire sera, s'il vous plait, pour vous et l'autre de la Bibliotheque et des Poëtes Latins pour le fils de Madame vôtre Hôtesse. Il pourra peutêtre y apprendre quelque chose, mais pour vous, Monsieur, je ne vous conseille pas d'y rien lire. Je me donnerai l'honneur de vous envoyer par le premier Convoi mon Nouveau Testament, qui est à présent entierement achevé.†5 Si la forme, que j'ai donnée à cette Version, n'est pas bonne, la matiere la fera excuser. L'Ouvrage du P. Petau De Doctrina Temporum, est achevé, à une Préface près.†6 J'en fais l'Extrait dans le 2. Tome de la Bibliotheque Choisie.†7 Je fais beaucoup d'usage dans ce livre des Ouvrages de Mr. Cudworth comme
― 782 ― 
vous le verrez, et je puis vous assurer que l'extrait du Ch.I.†1 a extrémement plû à tout le monde de deça la mer. Je ne doute pas que le reste ne soit aussi très-bien reçu, dès qu'on le verra. Je m'en vai reprendre tout de bon mon travail sur l'Ancien Testament, pour donner le Tome des Livres Historiques. Vous verrez dans le 2. Tome de la Bibliotheque Choisie quelques livres nouveaux de ce païs, qui sont de quelque usage. Je me suis informé de vôtre santé, de tems en tems, de Mr. de Limborch mon voisin, à qui Mr. son fils mande exactement vos nouvelles. Je me rejouïs de ce qu'elle est meilleure, et je prie Dieu qu'il vous la conserve telle jusqu'au bout de la carriere. Je suis, Monsieur,

Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.

3281. Samuel Locke to Locke, 5 May 1703 (3194, 3403)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 221-2.
London 5th May 1703
Sir
Th'Inclosed†1 came verry lately to my hand By the ship Scipio: from Suratt, where my son John was I thank God in good health this tyme 12 month: and hath much Improov'd in experience of the affaires in India, as also those of China, Mallacka and South Seas. to the gennerall satisfaction of the Court of Directors: who are now placeing him in a higher station: wherein hee will have one of the greatest shares off theyr buysinesse and Trust at Suratt and Bombay under his Conduct; with a Reserve of Liberty to himselfe to Returne next yeare if hee thinks fitt: or when hee pleases: according to his Request made to them.
We lament the losse of our Ambassador Sir William Norris who dyed on the voyage: beyond the Cape of good Hope. homeward bound:†2 I have lost a good friend in him and so hath my son John: being much in his favour. the Secretary Mr Harlewin†3 promiseth mee when his papers, Comes up. I shall have the oportunity to shew you old Aurenge Zeeb's picture;†4 The Present from him to the queen is a dagger sett with diamonds.†5 which, with a letter in sumptuouse manner writ in the Persian language is presented to her Majesty 2 days since. and sent to Oxford to be Translated.†6 in short our Embassy has Cost a vast som of mony to little purpose occation'd by the underhand and fowle practises of the old E.I. Company theyr Creatures, by which our Trade and nation will suffer Intollerable hindrances and Embarrasments at Surat especially: and other parts of India:
this week by th'arivall of the Loyall Cook from Fort St George wee recieve the Mallencholly news of the losse by fire neer Metslepatam of the ship the Norris outward bound, wherein wee had for the New Company theyr account the vallew of £110200 sterling of which there was about £90 000 in Silver:†7 this falls wholly on the
― 784 ― 
additionall stock of the said new Company: and no part on the new united Company stock.†1

Sir I have a letter from Batavia of the 15th June last where our President Mr Catchpoole was. and the Rest of the Chusan Factors. who were all Returning againe back for Chusan†2 and among them Doctor Pound,†3 who was verry well and sent mee a kind remembrance. I wish Sir that either my selfe or son Could Render you advyse of more Importance. or Could be anyway serviceable to you: nothing would be more acceptable to either of us: I am Sir with most hearty respects:
Your most humble servant and Cossin.
SAM: LOCKE  Sir Pray my Respects to Sir Francis Massam. wee have 2 ships bound hence for Suratt will depart about 14 days hence.

3282. Peter King, later first Baron King, to Locke, 6 May 1703 (3276, 3284)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 192-3. Answered by no. 3285.
Inner Temple. May. 6. 1703.
Sir
My Lord Shaftsbury†a- sent me Yesterday for your account a Bank note for One hundred pounds,†4 I gave him my receit for it, but he desires that you would your self send a receit for it, mentioning the time when the said Hundred pounds was due,-†a and on my
― 785 ― 
delivery of your Receit, he will deliver me up mine again—I told the messenger that I would write you of it, but that I hoped speedily to see you, and in all probability I should have the receit then but not before—This being ascension day was an holiday in Westminster hall,†1 so that I hoped to have seen Mr Newton this day, but The swelling in my Cheek whereof I writ you by the last hath kept me within all this day, I hope it is now over, It was increased very much yesterday, and to such a degree that I was advised to bleed, and accordingly sent for a Chyrurgeon, who told me that bleeding would not signify much in this case, but that there was a great deale of Collected matter which must be discharged by lancing, which method I Consented to, and assoon as the operation was over, I found immediately a great deale of ease, and the swelling is now almost gone—There is not yet any foreign Maile, but there are some ships come from Amsterdam, and the Convoy reports, that eight hours before he came away, News came That the French had been thrice repulsed at Kintziger Dale, and were marched off.†2 This News is Credited, and I hope it will prove true—I hope to wait upon you next week and to find you very well— —In the Mean time—I am—

Sir
Your Most affectionate Cosin and Servant.
P. KING.
Address: For John Locke Esquire [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford] Frank. P. King. 
Postmarks: MA 6; GC

3283. James Tyrrell to Locke, 6 May [1703] (3263, 3324)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 157-8. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London May 6.
Dear Sir
Being summond hither as a witnesse a fortnight sooner then I otherwise intended to come up, I desired Mr: Churchil to give you
― 786 ― 
notice of it and that your Books had bin safely deliverd at Oxford, and presented by me to the Library keeper, who returnes you his Thanks and humble service, and he sayd that it should not be long e're he writ to you himself, and I saw your†a book†a afterwards in the Library with a chain to it, ready to be put up,†1 but the small ones did not need it, this I told Mr: Churh<ill>†b but since he forgot (as he tells me) to write you word of it, I am obliged to give you notice of it.

I hope if the weather proves warme to see you in Towne the next week, for now is the best time (as I suppose) for your Constitution, when it is neither too hot nor too cold, but of this your self is the most proper Judg, onely should be glad to see you here before I go downe againe, which will be about a week hence; in the mean while I desire you would remember to order the Additions to those sheets I sent you, to be fairly transcribed into the margins of them, and that you would either send, or bring them up with you, as will best stand with your Conveniency. so hoping you continue in the same or rather a better state of health then when I left you, I remaine
your most obliged and humble servant
J TYRRELL
My son†2 and daughter are well and much your servants.
I pray give my humble service to worthy Sir Francis, and his good Lady with my thanks for all their favours. I know not whether you have yet heard, that honest Mr. Collyns buried his Lady, about a month since, and is gone out of Towne to his Fathers;†3 she never was out of her chamber after her lying in.
Address: For John Lock Esqr [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]

3284. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 7 May 1703 (3282, 3285)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 275-6. Answers no. 3276.
Oates 7 May 03
Dear Cosin
I am very glad to find your intention was better than you expressed it, and am not displeased with your caution. You will always get credit by being better than your word, and never loose any thing by husbanding your promises. I say not this that I need or pretend to instruct you, but to advise you to that which you already doe is commendation without a complement. There are I find upon searching some <declarations>†a expired, they shall be cancelled when you come. I am glad you have two such conveniencies in comeing hither as you mention, Mr Collins's Company and Chariot. I look on him in all respects as a very valuable acquaintance, a Generation of such yonge men to come upon the stage as the Old drop off would give new life to the age. Pray before you come let your man aske Mr Pawling whether he hath no thing to send. He told me he had, and I shall be glad to receive it by you. And if Mr Churchil hath any thing new worth the sending I doubt not but you will bring it. My service to all my friends as you see them particularly to Mr Collins. I hope you received mine with the inclosed receit to Mr Conyers, and a letter to Mr Newton. Pray forget not the business of that inclosed letter for it has put me for some time in pain, I am
Dear Cosin
your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
We all here long here for Saturday Come seventh night that we may welcome you and your fellow traveller. Pray set out early that we may have the more of your company
Since I writ this Tuesdays letters are come†1 and I thank you for your concerne for me. Of that and other matters I hope to discourse with you the next week
Pray bring with you a sheet of twelve peny stampd paper.

3285. Locke to Peter King, later first Baron King, 8 May 1703 (3284, 3289)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 40, ff. 277-9. Answers no. 3282.
Oates 8o May 03
Dear Cosin
After the letter I writ you yesterday was gon I received the good news that your pain and swelling were much allaid by lanceing. It was the proper operation in the case. by what you said of it in general I knew not what to advise and soe chose to let it alone till I saw you. I conclude the Surgeon opend it in the inside, but finding you say noe thing of it, I fear he neglected to prescribe you any thing to reinse your mouth with, to clense the inside of the impostume to prevent the collection of matter there again. If you have noe such thing, and the orifice be still open when you receive this inclosed note, get it made presently, and when you have it, take ever now and then a mouthfull of it, and soe stir it up and down in your mouth, to force as much of it as you can into the impostume, doe this till it is healed up. I hope your German news will prove true. My Lord Shaftesburys business we will doe when you come here, as you rightly answered. I am Dear Cosin
Your most affectionate Cosin and humble servant
J LOCKE
