3286. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 30 April/11 May-14/25 May 1703 (3226, 3424)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 190-1.
Rotterdam 11 May 1703
Dear Friend
I am extreamly obliged to you for the favour of yours of the 19 past, shewing your great concern for my son Benjohan, of whose recovery we had often but very smal hopes†1 And tho the losse of him would have been one of the greatest afflictions that could have befaln me in this world, yet we had given him up. He came from the Exchange, on a post day very ill, but hid it, till my dearest, (who in this his sickness has shewd herself a most tender mother indeed) discerning something from his not eating of something that he usd to love, askt him if he were not well, which he acknowledging, she indeavourd to persuade him to ly down, which we have oft found to be a means to bring him to rights, But he having business in his mind that must be writ that post, and trusting nobody could do it so well as he, he went out, in the cold. When he returnd he was forced to ly down, being unfit to write, my wife gave him a Cordiall with which he fell asleep: but waked in a feaver, which continued for 14 days increasing, which made us to the Doctor we had (who said that he was not able to bear many such fits) send for a Doctor from the Hague; but when he came the feaver was abated, and every day continued to abate; and at last turnd to an intermittent, or Tertian Ague, so that we judgd him past danger. He then recovered so much strength, that he said, Mother, tomorrow I will quit my chamber and go down into the Counting house; But that evening, apprehending himself stronger than he was, he over eat himself, and would eat salade.
The next morning instead of coming down, my dearest found him in a Cold fit which was very violent and a hot fit as violent followed upon it—which dured almost all that day. And increasd severall days, in so much as the bed on which he lay and my wife sat shaked so, that he wonder'd what power it was that could so shake all. This continued thus for 14 days or longer, but afterwards diminisht again, and shifted, but continued in so much that he grew so very weak with it, that my wife feared sometimes he would dye in her arms, fainting away often. In this condition our apprehensions for him increased.
― 790 ― 

At length came a letter from mr. D'Aranda, who hearing how it was with, was, we thank him, so far concernd for him, and us, that he wrote me a letter earnestly recommending to us the use of Chinachina,†1 upon about 30 years experience, with great success, and without any inconvenience, to any of the many he had given it to, to his great charge. He recommended the taking it the 1/8 part of an ounce (which is ʒjF I suppose) for a dose 2 or 3 houres after the hot fit, in Rhenish wine, or, almost any other, to him, more acceptable vehicle, and so every 3 or 4 houres a dose (onely avoiding to take it within 2 houres before and after the fit; and before and after eating, till the ague should leave him, and then continue to take it morning and evening for a fortnight after, and after that onely 3 or 4 doses evry fortnight, for about 2 or 3 months, being all this time very carefull, not to take cold, not to do any excess in eating, or drinking, to abstain from all kind of fish, roots, pulse, and salt meats, to which he is much inclined. This we communicated to the Doctors, but neither of them would hear of using China china, and my son was averse to hear of taking physic for 3 months together, and to be so tyed up in point of abstinence and dyet. Saying he should never be very wel til he set his teeth in a Westphaly ham roast, or a piece of salt beef, and smoakt beef. At same time we received a letter from my Lord Shaftsbury also recommending china china. But he seemd as little enclin'd to it, as his Doctors. But finding his Ague to continue, and his strength to decrease, he said to my dearest, Monsieur Boyd (whom I presume you know being a familiar french of Mr. Popples, who has livd some years in Carolina, and but a little before had rid me of my Cough, onely by prescribing me to take 4 times a day a thea Cupfull of fair, stone-strained†2 water in which was infused Cachiou)†3 may perhaps have a remedy for me as well as for my father, pray desire my father to ask him upon the Exchange. Which I did, and he understanding that he had a Tertian, or rather double Tertian Ague, for now it was changed to a double Tertian, replyed, Yes, I have an infallible Cure, and I can assure you that within 3 days after he has taking my remedy he shall have his ague no more, as having cured severall hundreds, without any failure in any one. Whereupon I told him what Mr. D'Aranda had wrote me, and recommended to me; he told me that his remedy was a preparation
― 791 ― 
of China china; but that first he must take a vomit to cleanse his stomack and the next day a purge, the third day rest, and the fourth day begin with the china china pills. And that he need not take the 1/4 part of what mr D'Aranda prescribed, nor continue it so long. I told him he was too weak, I feared, to undergo that fatigue, he replyed if he had but strength to write his name, it was enough. At same time came a good friend, and acquaintance of the Doctors in, to visit us, an Amsterdammer, who related that he having kept his chamber 17 weeks of an Ague, an Englishman coming to him told him he would cure him in 2 days, and accordingly did by china china. At same time came in a Jew of Amsterdam who in like manner recommended china china from experience in his family: but this could not prevaile with the Doctor to admit it, my son being so wondrous weak; who left other medecins for him to take.

But when the Doctor was gone, we set his medecines aside, and tooke the china pills, which had the promised, and wished for effect to our joy—a while after, when we saw the effect, my wife told the Doctor for good news that her son was rid of the Ague. The Doctor was glad, but when we told him that we had not used his medicines, but china China, he was surprized, and said 'tis well if it so continues, but I fear, I fear, I have seen so many ill after-claps. But if this goes well, I will use it. I told this to monsieur Boyd, who replyed, he would not advise him so to do, unlesse he had the right Correctorium.†1 However the Doctor dismist, my son has, now been severall days abroad on the Exchange, felicitated by all his friends. The dose he tooke was 3 pills or the quantity of a good large nutmeg of the conserve, made up into 3 pills: taken 2 ho: before the cold fit came. 2 houres before eating, and so every 2 houres, even in the time of the hot fit it self provided it was somewhat abated, And thus to continue every day after his ague was gone till the 2 gallypots he sent him, were out. But he presuming now again that all was well, and no further care nor fear of anything—would take no more of his medecine, and eat all things, fish, ham, sallet and what not: And last post day laboured till after midnight to dispatch some accounts that were longed for. At which time came to hand this your acceptable letter late at night. The next daying being fast-day†2 he had his Ague again, but it was conceald from me, under
― 792 ― 
the Colour of his resting after his night labour; but at last, they confest he had had his Ague, having vomited twice, and that that was the true reason of his lying so long. Then I would suffer him to eat nothing but water gruel, of which he was in his weakness grown weary, I made him take his conserve again, and take a glass of English Canary upon it, which my wife has had this 9 or 10 years. This morning he has also taken a dose, and this 2 days being blustering weather he has kept within doores.

In the understanding of your directions I am in some doubt one of the characters being altered and not clear, whether it be ʒj or ʒss. but the doctor thinks it must be half a dram. Then he must take the first week ʒj. The second ℈ij. The third week every morning ʒs. Then for 6/w every morning ʒj. And for 6 weeks after every other morning ℈j. Washing each dose down with a glass of stomack wine. I intreat you to note what wine is best, whether old Rhenish, Canary, Frontinjac,†1 Malmsey, Malaga, or Pontac, or vin de Cahors. As also what may be needfull to be observed with respect to his dyet: for your advice will have weight with him. Onely Water gruel he nauseats.
While I have been above staires writing this, now I come down to breakfast, I find my son gon to bed with his Ague; which makes me fear he will not so easily get rid of it, as last time. But I hope we shall keep him now easily to the constant use of his medicine, seing you assure us, that all inconvenience comes from the taking too little, and quitting it too soone.
Adi 15th
This not going forward last post, I have to ad that since my son has been free, and being fine weather has been every day on the Exchange. And mr. Boyd assuring him he needs not take any more of that medicine, now his pots are empty, he inclines to wave it, but I am resolved to get it, and give it him as you prescribe without any correctory, seing you say it may be securely taken, by any man in perfect health, so soon as I can learn to know the good from the bad,†2 of which the greatest quantity is as I am informd. But mr. Boyd has promisd me himself to go and pick it out for me.
Adi 22
We are come thus far, and I have not yet got any china china, and Yesterday at Table my son got his ague again. But could not be
― 793 ― 
perswaded to go to Ly down, till he had written 2 or 3 letters— when he had done he lay down, and rose not till 10 a clock today, having had his Ague very hard till 7 this morning. He had it also the day before from 8 in the morning, at which time my dearest causd him to go to bed, but conceald it from me, till 4 in the after noone—pretending nothing else but wearyness. He had again friday night wrote late, saturday morning at 7 he went in a boat to fish in the mase,†1 stayd in the sun till noone, and after he had eaten of the fruit of his labours, he went to the garden, and there laboured watering his plants till evening, that he was scarce able to stand, but would presently go to bed supperless. Just now mr. Boyd sends me china china.

I have now been at the Exchange and spoke with mr. Boyd, who tells me, that fatigue cannot have renewed his ague so strong, but that it must be that he has not been throughly cured. And attributes it to the defect of the china china, which he finds not so good here as in England, where he never used to give above one ounce, whereas he now gave 2 ounces, But he says 'tis needfull that he purges with Epsom salt,†2 before he begins to take the China china —(which he prepares with spirit of Juniper and saltartari)—He must take an ounce of Epsom salt—1/3 overnight and 1/3 in the morning in one draught and 2 houres after the rest, and then a while after some Broth to help it to work—
I know not what to say to it, but at present he seems to ail nothing. While I am writing comes a rumour of a post riding a full carreer through the Towne, and saying that he brings tydings that the French and Bavarians are totally routed, and the Elector taken prisoner.
Which makes me leave off till I can heare the certainty one way or other, of so incredible news—
ady 25—
Since the above I have been at the Hague, but find that news utterly false, I was unwilling to be the spreader of a false tale, and as unwilling to let this go without bringing such good news if true. That Bon is surrendred you will have understood last post.†3 As I came out of the Hague it was said that our army was broke up to seek the french and oblige 'em to fight if they can—when I went
― 794 ― 
from home the 23d. I left my son in his Ague, but next day and today that he tooke China china again, he has been, he and all our family salute you, and the whole family where you are, as also doth

Dear friend
your affectionate friend and humble servant,
BENJAMIN FURLY
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 25 May 03 Answered 27
2724A. Locke to Thomas Burnett of Kemney, 2 May 1700 (2709)
Kenneth W. Rendell, Inc., 154 Wells Avenue, Newton, Mass., catalogue no. 108, 1975, item no. 19. The catalogue entry, including the square brackets, reprinted here. Previously in Charavay sale, 15 and 16 May 1975, item no. 168. Answers no. 2709.
Oates, 2 May 1700
I herewith returne you Mr. Leibniz's papers which you did me the favour to send me and which by your letter ... I finde I shall have a more convenient opertunity to discourse with you about when I have the honour to see you in town.†1 If, in the meantime, you have an opertunity of writing to that very learned and civil gentleman, I desire you to give him my most humble service and let him know how much I value the honour he does me in bestowing any part of his time and thoughts upon what I have writ[ten and] think the pains I have mislaid on my scribblings not wholly lost if [they] might serve to excite him to write a just treatise on a subject which he has so maturely considered and which I have made so imperfect an essay upon. As to the business you mention to me ... I received not your letter (which I perceived should have come by your lady†2 ...) till about a week after her return to town. So that the answer you had by her, before yours came to hand, makes you, I suppose, expect nothing farther in answer to that commission from you then to me which was over before I received it. The gentleman from whom you will receive this brought me yours.†3 He will assure you how ready I shall be to serve you on all occasions ...

Index of Correspondents in this Volume
This index is by the numbers of the letters, italics being used as in the text to indicate letters not by Locke. A bracketed number is either for a letter between persons other than Locke, in which case it appears under the names of both writer (or writers) and person addressed, or for an item other than a letter. If there is correspondence in earlier or later volumes between Locke and a person in this index it is indicated by the citation of the next volume or volumes in which any of it occurs.
The citation immediately following a name is that of a biographical note on the person. For persons concerned with only one or two letters the citation is omitted sometimes if the biographical note occurs in the headnote and is insignificant.

Recurrent Designations other than Proper Names
This list is intended to enable readers to identify persons mentioned in the letters in this volume by dignities, nicknames, and similar designations. These designations are variable; a person may be indicated in several ways.
Bachelor, the: John Freke
Capitaine de Marine, le: Raymond Formentin
Chancellor, Lord: Sir John Somers, Baron Somers
Gloucester, bishop of: Dr. Edward Fowler
President, Lord, of the Council: Thomas Herbert, earl of Pembroke
Salisbury, bishop of: Dr. Gilbert Burnet
Worcester, bishop of: Dr. Edward Stillingfleet or Dr. William Lloyd according to context
The Masham family at Oates: Sir Francis Masham; Lady Masham (my Lady); Esther Masham (Mrs. or Madam Masham); Francis Cudworth Masham (Mr. Masham); other sons
The Clarke family of Chipley: Edward Clarke; his wife Mary (Mrs. Clarke); their second son John; their eldest daughter Elizabeth (Betty—Locke's 'wife'); and others
The College: Edward Clarke and John Freke the Bachelor

†1 The collection published by the Churchills as A Collection of Voyages and Travels, some now first printed from original manuscripts. Others translated out of foreign languages, and now first published in English. To which are added some that have formerly appeared in English.... With a general preface, giving an account of the progress of navigation, 4 vols., folio, 1704. L.L., no. 3118. The originator of the project is unknown; if it was not Awnsham Churchill, he evidently took the work to heart, supervising if not editing it. He probably consulted Sloane as well as Locke: p. 249. Locke's quest for a copy of Navarrete (nos. 2483, 2632) is probably connected with the project; so perhaps also the desire for information from Henry Greenhill (nos. 2573, 2781); if the Italian book mentioned on p. 135 is Gemelli Careri, that also belongs. The two Churchills were granted on 9 December of this year what was in effect copyright for fourteen years for the English narratives and the translations of foreign books that they had brought together: Cal. S.P., Dom., 1700-2, pp. 168-70. Not later than 1704 they envisaged two further volumes: Locke's will; these formed part of the second edition,
― 173 ―
1732; one item listed in the grant was kept back for vol. v. There are an account and criticism of the book in Richard Hakluyt and his Successors, ed. E. Lynam (Hakluyt Soc., 2nd ser., vol. xciii, 1946), pp. 80-6. The preface on the history of navigation is attributed to Locke in the third edition, 1744-6, and is included in the editions of Locke's Works published between 1794 and 1826. There is no adequate ground for the attribution.

†1 The lower house of the Convocation of Canterbury met on 10 February to elect its prolocutor: Luttrell.
The Convocations of Canterbury and York are the provincial assemblies of the Church of England. From Henry VIII's time they met at the same time as Parliament. In 1664 the clergy lost the right of taxing themselves, and thenceforward the Convocations did not meet for business until 1689. In that year the lower house of the Convocation of Canterbury rejected William III's scheme for a Comprehension for the Nonconformists and William did not allow it to meet again for some time. A pamphlet published in 1697 (A Letter to a Convocation Man) claimed for it a place in the constitution equal to that of Parliament and its rights became a subject of controversy. As a concession to the Tories William now allowed it to meet again for business: G. M. Trevelyan, England under Queen Anne, vol. i, Blenheim, 1930, pp. 284-7; G. V. Bennett, The Tory Crisis in Church and State, 1688-1730, 1975.
†2 Francis Atterbury (bishop of Rochester 1713-23; D.N.B.; Bennett, as above; no. 2632), The Rights, Powers, and Priviledges of an English Convocation, 1700 (L.L., no. 143c); White Kennett, D.D. (bishop of Peterborough 1718-28; D.N.B.), Ecclesiastical Synods and Parliamentary Convocations ... vindicated from the Misrepresentations of Mr. Atterbury, 1701 (L.L., no. 1625); it was published by A. and J. Churchill.

†4 These statements are in part incorrect. They relate to an attempt to drain the Pontine Marshes and have no connection with Minturno, which is about 35 miles SE. of their nearest point. This is established by Du Bos's letter to Toinard of 17 April 1701, N.S., in which he writes of the 'montagnes de Terracine et de Piperno, aux pieds desquels est LAufente palude': B.N., MS. N.Acq. fr., no. 560, f. 359v. In 1699 Don Livio Odescalchi, duke of Ceri (Encic. italiana), revived a project formed by Cornelio Meyer (Cornelis Meijer; Thieme, Lexikon), but was compelled by local opposition to abandon it: T. Berti, Paludi Pontine, 1884, pp. 114-19. I have found the name Laufente Palude elsewhere only in Baudrand; it is apparently derived from the Ufente (Aufente), a stream flowing into the sea near Terracina. The marshes at Minturnæ are mentioned by Plutarch and Juvenal: Pauly, Real-Encyc. Horace's Satire is his account of his journey from Rome to Brindisi (Satires I. v. 1); it was through the
― 299 ―
Pontine Marshes that he travelled by canal-boat. Hadrian's inscription on his coins, 'Tellus stabilita', refers not to land-drainage but to his good government which ensures that the earth gives freely of her increase: British Museum, Coins of the Roman Empire, vol. iii, by H. Mattingly, 1936, p. cxxxv. Meijer's treatise is L'arte di rendere i fiumi navigabili, Rome, 1696.

The work was published in octavo at Paris, 32 volumes (or parts of volumes), 1686-1723 (the title changes and the volume numbers cease after vol. v); with continuations, etc., there were probably 50 volumes altogether, the latest, 1736. Locke owned copies of vols. i-xii of the quarto series; he gives the dates of publication as 1690-1700: L.L., no. 2306. He received vols. vii-xii on 14 May 1700: Journal; he now apparently received a copy of vol. iv to make up his set.

†1 After its publication in 1700 Coste again read his translation of the Essay to Locke, and then and later found passages that needed improving for style or meaning. He made some alterations on Locke's recommendation ('par l'avis de Mr. Locke'); he owed many corrections to Barbeyrac; Locke communicated to him a number of additions before they were printed in the posthumous fifth edition of the Essay (1706). In 1707 Coste sent copies of the alterations and additions to Leibniz. They appear to belong to four classes: additions by Locke to the English text; improvements by Locke, mainly stylistic, of the English text; corrections of errors in the first edition of the French translation; and stylistic improvements of the translation. I am unable to specify any alterations as due to Barbeyrac's stylistic criticism; it may have affected the English text as well as the translation: Coste, 'Avis' prefixed to second edition of his translation, 1729; letters from him to Leibniz in Leibniz, Phil. Schriften, ed. Gerhardt, iii. 391, 392-9. Barbeyrac also criticized Leibniz's Nouveaux essais for style and orthography: Leibniz, S.S. VI. vi. 546-51 and p. xxv.

†1 Tin had been farmed from the twelfth century or earlier, the Tin Farmers being empowered by the king to buy all the tin mined in Cornwall and Devon. As the easier deposits of ore were exhausted new methods of mining were introduced, with greater capital requirements, and with the consequent strengthening of the farmers' position as against the London Company of Pewterers. In 1663 and 1687 the Company complained that the farmers sold tin at too high a price to its members, and so cheaply to foreigners that the Company would lose the export trade in pewter goods to the Dutch. There was a fresh petition to the Lord High Treasurer (Godolphin) on 18 November of this year. The Godolphin family and the Lord High Treasurer were much concerned with tin-mining: C. Welch, History of the Worshipful Company of Pewterers of London, 1902, pp. 131-2, 158-9, 173; J. Rowe, Cornwall in the Age of the Industrial Revolution, 1953, pp. 10-11, 13-16.
